# ARC42 — IDE Architecture

This is the single source of truth for the product's architecture, current behavior, limitations, and roadmap. The README is an entry point, not a second architecture description. Documentation is written in English for developers, maintainers, and users.

## Section 1: Introduction & Goals

### 1.1 Requirements Overview

The product is a desktop IDE built with Tauri, React, TypeScript, Rust, and Monaco, with a reusable browser frontend. Its goal is a reliable development environment with Java tooling, deterministic refactoring, and a workspace-scoped Pi agent. IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate is a capability benchmark, not a compatibility or feature-parity claim.

The desktop currently provides workspace registration and switching, a file explorer, editor tabs, document previews, Java language services, RefactorKit integrations, Git diff review, Pi terminal sessions, and first-party XCOM tooling. Native capabilities are not simulated in the browser.

The Java operational baseline comprises language-service integration, symbols and refactoring, compilation, application execution, delegated tests, a JDK debugger console, structured JDI runtime inspection and socket attachment to an external JVM. Effective Maven/Gradle project synchronization and the broader IntelliJ-class debugger workflows remain incomplete.

Executable requirements and their verification scope are indexed in [Appendix A: requirements](docs/arc42/appendix-requirements.adoc). Test fixtures and historical requirement baselines are development artifacts, not alternative documentation authorities.

### 1.2 Quality Goals

1. Protect the user's source code and unsaved changes.
2. Keep requests and results bound to the active workspace and document version.
3. Report unavailable tools and failures clearly; never invent successful results.
4. Preserve the separation between reusable UI, application logic, and platform adapters.
5. Keep editing responsive and verify behavior with real tools as well as isolated tests.

### 1.3 Stakeholders

- Developers need dependable editing, navigation, refactoring, execution, and debugging.
- Maintainers need clear boundaries, reproducible checks, and understandable documentation.
- Distributors need supported operating systems, licensing information, and installation/update policies.

### 1.4 Product Roadmap

The target is a production-ready alternative for IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate workflows: JVM and web development, semantic refactoring, enterprise frameworks, databases, tests/debugging, version control, and remote development. It is not a promise of binary plugin compatibility or of every feature in every JetBrains product. At qualification time, record the reference IDEA edition/version, supported tool versions, and remaining differences. Do not publish a parity percentage without a reproducible comparison.

The earlier Java expansion freeze is superseded. The current implementation is the starting point, not a completed production milestone. RefactorKit is the central analysis/refactoring engine, not merely a developer utility; the IDE owns interaction and safe change coordination. See [ADR 0017](ADR.md#adr-0017--refactorkit-first-refactoring-and-shared-change-coordination). Execution remains separate, as decided in ADR 0016.

A separate Maven fixture qualifies a managed JPA field and JPQL property rename with Hibernate/H2, as described in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope). The desktop has a bounded manual HTTP client with memory-only Basic/Bearer fields, explicit OAuth Client Credentials acquisition, configured browser Authorization Code/PKCE, and requests from active `.http`/`.rest` editor buffers, a bounded OpenAPI route picker for pasted documents and user-selected UTF-8 JSON/YAML 3.0/3.1 files, and a first JDBC slice for explicit connections, schema inspection, driver-quoted identifier insertion and SQL execution. The JDBC tool uses a user-selected workspace JAR and JDK, retains connection details only in memory, requires explicit trust and submission, and bounds metadata and query results. H2 has focused Linux native GUI acceptance for explicit queries, typed parameters and manual transactions; other drivers and servers remain unqualified. A source-built RefactorKit candidate returns typed locations for direct static Spring Data `@Query` JPQL property paths in an entity-field rename preview. The IDE preserves and displays the two tested locations in its Linux release/no-bundle native GUI, and incomplete project closure disables managed Apply. This qualifies only the bounded static-query review slice against the tested candidate and fixture; released-provider behavior and broader Spring/Jakarta/JPA, XML/YAML, migration, database and OpenAPI workflows remain open, so M5 is incomplete.

**Dependencies:** M0 → M1 → M2 establish the critical foundation. These are acceptance dependencies, not a blanket freeze on independent implementation while a native-host test is blocked. M3 and M4 build on it; M5 needs their JVM workflows. M6 can progress alongside enterprise work once snapshot/project contracts are usable. Advanced engine operations can be delivered individually rather than blocking every other track. M7 depends on the same source-change and lifecycle boundaries. CI, security, accessibility, OS qualification and performance work start in M0 and continue throughout; they are not postponed until M8. A limited Linux preview may precede Windows/macOS qualification, but must be labeled accordingly.

These are advertisements, not live-project qualification, and must be rechecked when the engine changes. The catalog is not a complete description of every CLI operation. In that inspected matrix C is absent, and Kotlin/TS mutations include proposal-only or refused capabilities. An overlay flag also does not prove that the IDE supports unsaved-buffer transformations.

The implemented Java batch cleanup and the planned migration recipes and IDE-mediated Pi refactoring reuse the change-coordination boundaries described in [section 8.4](#84-planned-shared-refactoring-workflow). They must not introduce an unreviewed Apply path. Build, tests, debugger control, database queries and deployment are not RefactorKit responsibilities. The detailed [language backlog](#145-missing-capabilities-by-language) separates upstream engine work from integration and qualification.

The IDE now exposes RefactorKit's Java `changeSignature.removeParameter` through the saved-method cursor preview and Apply workflow when the synchronized project context advertises stable, managed authority. RefactorKit validates the selected method and bound call sites; the IDE does not infer semantic safety. The operation remains unavailable without that provider capability, and provider refusals remain authoritative.

#### 1.4.3 Qualification Projects and Measures

Maintain versioned acceptance projects for:

- Maven and Gradle multi-module Java, dependency sources, generated roots and overloaded/inherited APIs;
- Java refactoring with unsaved buffers, external edits, Unicode/line-ending differences, incomplete classpaths and interrupted transactions;
- mixed Java/Kotlin with explicitly supported compiler/toolchain versions;
- Spring Boot/JPA plus database and HTTP integration;
- a TypeScript web application connected to a JVM service;
- Git conflicts, remote/container execution and plugin lifecycle;
- representative small and large workspaces on the advertised operating systems.

The shared [Java reference inputs](tests/story/fixtures/java-effective-project-reference.ts) produce separate Maven reactor and Gradle multi-project workspaces for the M2 project-system gate. Their build qualification is described in section 10.1; engine import, synchronization and editor acceptance require their own evidence.

For each supported scenario, check engine analysis and refused cases, real build/test behavior, editor-model reconciliation, native UI interaction and packaged-application behavior separately. Measure cold import/index time, warm updates, navigation/refactoring latency, memory, cancellation and recovery; agree thresholds before declaring acceptance. Exclude or label unsupported language/framework/version cases instead of counting them as successes.

#### 1.4.4 Immediate Development Order

1. Continue qualifying native workspace activation using persisted bootstrap and DOM observations. Distinguish JavaScript bootstrap, workspace activation, and test navigation failures before changing the product. Section 10.1 records the slow-provider correction, the packaged UI chunk failure and the two post-activation test failures. Preserve failed runs and investigate remaining cases without a diagnostic cause.
2. Continue native Java/refactoring qualification beyond the focused Linux opening, recovery, close-guard, plain-JDK and Maven/Gradle/JUnit results/rerun GUI checks. Focused Linux GUI evidence covers project-local wrapper dispatch from synchronized Maven/Gradle Run, separately selected Maven Failsafe source sets in app and library using context v4, production coverage from a custom Gradle integration-test source set, and coverage for a two-module Gradle Kotlin DSL dependency. For a daemon advertising the read-only guarantees, the IDE now requests `project.context.aggregate` after explicit Gradle evaluation to obtain full provider-qualified v3 identities for a composite; older daemons retain the selected module/source-set v3 fallback. The included app and library pass the Linux composite GUI scenario on JDK 21 with Gradle 9.8.0 and a source-built daemon, and with Gradle 9.8.1 and the RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 review candidate used for Java compiler diagnostics. Earlier packages returned incomplete project identities. The Linux GUI also distinguishes two included builds with the same project path, main class and JUnit method during Run, discovery, selected-method coverage and test debugging. The Linux AppImage covers those workflows and a breakpoint inside a project dependency JAR. Extend qualification to broader composite layouts, mixed-language graphs, other operating systems and the provider distribution intended for release (see [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope)). The separate Gradle 9.8.0/JDK 25 provider integration test for direct and nested included-build reporting remains service-level evidence, not GUI qualification. Java starters now include pinned Maven and JDK-compatible Gradle wrappers; first-use downloads and generated wrapper execution now have real-tool Linux qualification with JDK 21 and 25. The focused Linux release/no-bundle profile now passes a Maven Build Helper `CUSTOM`-to-`CUSTOM` move and a Gradle additional-`MAIN`-to-declared-`MAIN` move with preview, Apply, Rollback and exact input restoration; an applied-source copy of the Gradle project also passes offline `gradle test`. Broader project shapes and operating-system coverage remain open. Broaden module selection and additional-root support, larger or mixed-language project graphs, test workflows, composite debugging beyond the one fixture, real-provider refactoring and the OS matrix. Retain a blocked result only when the required host or provider is actually unavailable.
3. Finish external-change and recovery qualification beyond the focused Linux comparison/history/missing-file/storage-access, per-buffer capacity and truncated-journal checks. The comparison GUI now changes a source during an in-flight adoption checkpoint and verifies that a later Save refuses the newer revision. Continue qualifying in-buffer edits during modal confirmation, storage failures beyond the bounded source/recovery ENOSPC GUI cases, workspace-wide pending-draft and retained-content GUI limits, additional corruption families and the OS matrix; qualify wider watching beyond bounded open-file polling and verify hosted execution and branch-protection use of the M0 core workflow.
4. Broaden RefactorKit position/binding, snapshot and editor-reconciliation qualification. A real Maven/JUnit test-classpath overload-selection and rename-preview regression now passes on Linux. A separate cross-module move failure was reported against a daemon build whose identity was not retained. Section 10.1 records the controlled rerun against the source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon containing the staged-binding fix: cross-module Apply, dependent-module updates, offline reactor verification and Rollback pass, and the earlier staged-binding refusal is not reproduced with this daemon. Continue qualifying additional external dependency scopes, build layouts and native editor reconciliation.
5. Broaden RefactorKit whole-file format/import previews to more source layouts and project contexts. JDT LS document and selected-line range formatting now use Monaco's Format Document and Format Selection commands on the synchronized active buffer. Both have focused Linux GUI coverage that preserves the unsaved draft and saved source; broaden project/style cases and the OS matrix. Settings > Editor stores workspace-scoped indentation size and spaces/tabs and can apply an existing Eclipse formatter-profile XML by workspace-relative path and exact profile name. The native service validates the XML, copies it into private session storage and applies it through JDT LS; an XML profile editor and broader profile/style qualification remain future work. RefactorKit's managed Java formatter now accepts a selected workspace Eclipse formatter profile: the native workspace service reads and validates its XML, passes it to preview, and binds the provider-attested path, profile name and content hash to saved Apply and dirty-editor prepare/confirm. Focused Rust, adapter, controller and dialog tests, plus the dedicated `formatter-profile` Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario, qualify this consumer path for one Maven fixture and the installed daemon (section 10.1); broader project/style combinations and the OS matrix remain open. Broaden project/style cases without writing project preferences implicitly. Selected-SDK class/member renames have capability-gated Monaco context-menu actions and `Shift+F6`/`F2` shortcuts with focused Linux GUI coverage. Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios on source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 cover class moves from Java Project rows and the Commands palette, same- and cross-module moves, offline `mvn -o verify` on applied-source copies, exact rollback, Java-reference refusal and review-only Maven-reference safe delete. Safe-delete Apply now requires an explicit provider capability for complete project-wide reference analysis, including build and resource files; the Maven story checks a type referenced only by the POM and keeps an eligible preview read-only while the provider lacks that capability. Broaden reference coverage and the OS matrix. Keep proposal-only extraction/signature variants explicitly limited.
6. Broaden the effective Maven/Gradle synchronization described in section 6.8, qualify JDT LS against the selected SDK and effective project context, and expand extraction/signature/module operations as the engine becomes qualified.

These are planning priorities, not permission to deploy, publish, upgrade the external engine or silently promote feature validation tags. No delivery dates are committed until capacity, compatibility scope and upstream readiness are established.

#### 1.4.5 Missing Capabilities by Language

This is the maintained handoff backlog for future RefactorKit work within M1–M6, with the related IDE responsibilities made explicit. It covers the language workflows in this roadmap, not every optional language plugin in the JetBrains ecosystem. Entries remain open until their defined scope is qualified; the table is not an implementation claim or a second executable-requirement index.

**Evidence baseline:** the installed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 launcher was inspected through `--version`, `--help`, `capabilities`, and `commands --json --schema-version 1`. The matrix advertises Java, Kotlin, TypeScript and JavaScript. Individual operations can support fewer extensions than their language adapter. Other languages below are not advertised by this runtime; that does not establish their absence from every source branch, library API or future release. No engine upgrade is implied.

Use these distinctions when preparing upstream work:

- **Integration:** reuse an existing capability; add or complete IDE contracts, native/adapter/controller wiring and editor actions.
- **Qualification:** an existing path needs real-project, compatibility and safety evidence; do not describe it as an absent engine implementation.
- **Engine:** explicitly refused support or proposal-only transformations need upstream semantic support or qualified managed mutation before Apply can be offered.
- **Assessment:** the requested capability is not established by the inspected interfaces. Check RefactorKit's source/library API and suitable compiler/LSP backends first; then implement or extend upstream only if necessary.

These are work categories, not permission levels. `--apply` in CLI help does not override proposal-only/refused metadata. SDK discovery, project import and IDE presentation do not belong to a duplicate semantic engine. The shared foundation below applies to every language table.

Preserve checked/dynamic/mixed completeness instead of presenting untyped guesses as exact bindings.                           |
| Navigation and editing intelligence            | **Integration/Qualification:** reuse available completion, hover, signature help, symbols, diagnostics, definitions/references and the TS/JS session infrastructure; qualify synchronized buffers, prototypes/classes, dynamic access and incomplete-analysis refusals. |
| Semantic rename and module/file moves          | **Engine/Qualification/Assessment:** semantic and local rename remain proposal-only. Cover imports/exports, globals, lexical scopes, prototypes, CommonJS/ESM and public consumers; report computed-property/reflection limits instead of global replacement.           |
| Extract/inline, signature and class operations | **Assessment:** discover reusable backend refactorings; qualify closures, `this`/`super`, hoisting, async/generators, mutation, evaluation order and prototype behavior before upstream managed transformations.                                                        |
| Formatting, imports, fixes and migrations      | **Assessment/Integration:** establish actual formatter/import/code-action support and qualified JS-to-TS or API migration recipes; respect generated/minified files and dynamic semantics.                                                                              |
| React/Vue/Angular and configuration            | **Assessment/Qualification:** qualify JSX, supported component/template/style references and source/resource plans; reuse framework services shared with TypeScript where their JavaScript mode is supported.                                                           |

##### C — Qualified After TypeScript

C is absent from the inspected runtime matrix and help. Historical target-version references are not acceptance evidence. Assess the available RefactorKit source/API and compiler integration before creating a new backend; prefer qualified Clang tooling over an IDE text-rewrite engine.

| Missing product capability                       | Work category and upstream scope                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Compiler and translation-unit context            | **Assessment:** toolchain/version admission, compilation databases, include paths, target/platform flags, preprocessor definitions and supported language standards; expose incomplete or conflicting translation-unit context. |
| Semantic navigation and diagnostics              | **Assessment:** parser/index/compiler-backed symbols, definitions/declarations, references, types, hover/completion and diagnostics across headers and source files, including supported unsaved overlays.                      |
| Rename and source/header moves                   | **Assessment:** scope/linkage-aware local/global/function/type/member renames, include and file moves; report macro expansion, conditional compilation, ABI and external-consumer limits.                                       |
| Extraction, inlining and signature changes       | **Assessment:** preserve pointer/aliasing, lifetime, ownership conventions, side effects, control flow, variadic calls and declaration/definition consistency; refuse unsupported preprocessing cases.                          |
| Safe delete, formatting and include organization | **Assessment:** establish complete usage/dependency checks, supported formatter/include tooling and transactional plans with real compile/link/tests.                                                                           |

##### C++ — Optional Extension of the C Track

C++ is also not advertised by the inspected runtime and is not an implicit addition to the agreed C milestone. If selected, qualify it independently; C acceptance does not establish C++ safety.

- **Assessment:** reuse a qualified compiler context while adding namespaces, overloads, templates, concepts, modules, inheritance/virtual dispatch, operators and type/call hierarchy.
- **Assessment:** qualify rename/move, extract/inline, change signature, member/hierarchy transformations, safe delete and include organization against RAII, constructors/destructors, access control, special members, template instantiation and ABI constraints.
- **Qualification:** require header/module and multi-configuration compile/link/tests, unsupported macro/template refusals, exact review/apply and recovery before product admission.

##### HTML and CSS — M6 Web Resources

Neither language is advertised by this RefactorKit runtime. Editor highlighting is not semantic tooling.

- **HTML — Assessment:** parsing/diagnostics, tags/attributes, component/template expressions, IDs/classes, links/assets and accessibility references; coherent element/component/file/asset rename/move and supported template extraction with framework-aware binding.
- **CSS — Assessment:** selectors/classes/IDs, custom properties, imports/assets and supported CSS-module/preprocessor context; find usages and rename/extract/move while preserving cascade, specificity and scoped styles. Qualify SCSS/Sass/Less separately if included.
- **Integration/Qualification:** feed resource references into shared TS/JS/framework plans; rendering/browser tests remain separate IDE/tooling checks, not RefactorKit execution responsibilities.

##### XML, YAML, JSON, Properties and Build Descriptors — M2 and M5

These resource languages have no advertised semantic adapter in the inspected matrix. Specific Maven commands already exist and must not be confused with a general POM or Gradle editing engine.

- **XML — Assessment:** schema/namespace-aware symbol and reference models; qualified Spring/JPA/persistence/mapper, Maven and other explicitly supported descriptor identities, references and source-linked rename/move plans.
- **YAML — Assessment:** schema-aware keys, anchors/aliases and document boundaries; supported Spring configuration, OpenAPI and selected deployment-resource references without broad string rewrites.
- **JSON — Assessment:** schema-aware keys and references, supported package/TypeScript/configuration/OpenAPI identities and project-linked changes; retain JSON/JSONC syntax and comments where applicable.
- **Properties — Assessment:** escaped keys/values, bundles/localization references, Spring configuration and resource-linked rename/move plans with encoding preservation.
- **Groovy/Gradle and Kotlin DSL — Assessment/Engine:** establish supported build-model/DSL services and binding of tasks, plugins, dependencies, modules and source sets. Qualify dynamic expressions and implicit receivers. This is source/build-descriptor analysis, not permission to run arbitrary build scripts; Kotlin scripts are separately refused in the current engine.

##### SQL, JPQL and HQL — M5

No query-language adapter is advertised by the inspected runtime. Source refactoring must never execute a query, migration or schema change.

- **Assessment:** dialect/version and offline schema-snapshot context, parsing/diagnostics, table/column/view/routine references and supported embedded-language ranges.
- **Assessment:** JPA entity/property and query-parameter binding, JPQL/HQL and supported native-query references; preserve aliases, identifiers, quoting, overloads and dynamic-query limitations during coherent source/query rename plans.
- **Assessment/Qualification:** generate a reviewed migration proposal only when schema compatibility can be established; its execution requires a separate database/migration approval and adapter. Connections, credentials, consoles, schema browsing and live completion metadata belong to database tooling, not RefactorKit mutation authority.

##### Optional Languages Outside the Current Delivery Sequence

Python, Rust, Scala and general Groovy are not advertised by the inspected runtime. They are recorded for assessment, not promised as completed or automatically scheduled language tracks.

- **Python — Assessment:** interpreter/environment and import graph, compiler/type-checker/LSP admission, semantic symbols/navigation/diagnostics, rename/move/extract/inline/signature/import plans; report dynamic/reflection/decorator limits. Runtime/tests/debugging remain Python-tool adapters.
- **Rust — Assessment:** Cargo/target/features/workspace metadata and a qualified compiler/rust-analyzer bridge; macro-aware navigation, ownership/lifetime-aware transformations, module/import updates and formatting, with generated-code/refused-case boundaries. Cargo execution is separate.
- **Scala — Assessment:** compiler/version and sbt/Maven/Gradle context, implicit/given/extension and mixed JVM semantics, navigation and transactional transformations; qualify supported Scala versions independently.
- **Groovy — Assessment:** static/dynamic modes, JVM and DSL binding, mixed Java references, navigation and safe transformations; report metaprogramming limits. Gradle DSL admission does not establish general Groovy support.
- **Shell, Python/Rust build scripts, TOML, INI, Markdown and other highlighted files:** no standalone RefactorKit semantic feature is promised by highlighting. Assess only explicitly selected resource/reference needs; ordinary editing, document preview and language-server integration remain IDE capabilities.

##### Upstream Handoff and Completion Criteria

For each selected feature family, prepare a bounded upstream task specifying language/versions, reusable primitive or missing API, semantic inputs/project context, result schema, supported and refused cases, snapshot/authority requirements, source/resource effects, recovery and compile/test acceptance. Consult actual engine source/API before labelling assessment work an unimplemented transformation. Implement there, not in a second IDE AST/regex engine; integrate only the resulting qualified capability.

A feature is complete only when its engine behavior, managed mutation authority where needed, IDE path and relevant real-provider/native acceptance are separately evidenced. Preserve the Kotlin navigation → Kotlin refactoring → TypeScript expansion → C qualification order. Optional tracks do not displace M0–M5 or justify upgrading conservative requirement tags.

**Outside RefactorKit:** for all languages, project/build execution, launch/test discovery and result trees, coverage/profiling, debugger protocols/UI, general terminals, Git operations, database query execution, HTTP clients, deployment, remote/container transport, plugin runtime and distribution/updates remain IDE or specialized-tool work in M0/M4/M5/M7/M8. Record their gaps in those milestones rather than assigning nonexistent build/run/debug commands to RefactorKit.

## Section 2: Constraints

### 2.1 Technical Constraints

- UI and web core cannot import Tauri APIs. Platform access goes through ports and adapters.
- Monaco is the only code editor; its assets and workers are bundled locally.
- Workspace-bound language, RefactorKit, and Java execution paths are resolved against an authorized workspace. Version and workspace checks reject stale presentation.
- JDK, JDT LS, RefactorKit, Maven, Gradle, and Pi are external runtime tools with their own compatibility and licensing requirements.
- RefactorKit owns its semantic analysis, project-model results, refactoring plans, and transformations. The IDE does not create a competing semantic project-model library.
- The JDK and build tools own compilation, test execution, application execution, and debugging.

### 2.2 Product Constraints

A missing provider is an unavailable capability, not permission to simulate its results. Browser behavior, isolated native-command substitutes, real external tools, native GUI tests, and packaged-application tests are different verification scopes.

XCOM-specific redistribution requires separate licensing review. Existing first-party integrations do not authorize publication of third-party proprietary assets.

## Section 3: System Context & External Actors

### 3.1 System Context Diagram

See the [C4 system context diagram](docs/c4/system-context.md).

### 3.2 External Systems

| System                  | Responsibility                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Developer               | Selects workspaces, edits code, reviews transformations, and authorizes execution                                                                                                                                                          |
| Filesystem and Git      | Stores project content and repository history; supplies status and diffs                                                                                                                                                                   |
| JDT LS                  | Provides Java document diagnostics, completion, hover, signature help, references, workspace Java symbol search, same-document symbol highlights, document symbols, bounded code actions, and binding-aware rename across open Java drafts |
| RefactorKit             | Supplies capability-qualified analysis, symbol information, navigation, imports, and refactoring                                                                                                                                           |
| JDK, Maven, Gradle      | Compile, test, launch, and debug project code                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Pi                      | Owns its terminal interaction, models, tools, chat history, and agent behavior                                                                                                                                                             |
| System browser and authorization server | Own interactive OAuth login/consent and grant issuance; the IDE receives a bounded loopback response and exchanges the code |
| HTTP services and JDBC databases | Execute explicitly submitted service requests and database statements |
| Steam/XCOM installation | Supplies machine and SDK information for explicitly scoped first-party tooling                                                                                                                                                             |

## Section 4: Solution Strategy

The application follows ports-and-adapters architecture. Reusable components display state and invoke application callbacks. Application controllers coordinate use cases. Native adapters translate requests to Rust commands; browser adapters implement supported browser behavior or report that native behavior is unavailable.

Semantic intelligence and execution are deliberately distinct. JDT LS serves synchronized editor documents. RefactorKit supplies project-level deterministic analysis and transformations. A separate Java execution port delegates to the installed JDK and build tools. This avoids waiting for nonexistent RefactorKit execution commands and avoids duplicating its semantic project model.

Long-running Java tasks are asynchronous, cancellable native sessions. The general shell terminal has its own PTY lifecycle; Java Run retains its typed execution and debugging protocols. Debugging offers the JDK's documented `jdb` console and a selectable structured debugger using the public Java Debug Interface (JDI). The latter reads runtime state from the actual JVM through an owned helper process; see [ADR 0021](ADR.md#adr-0021--structured-java-debugging-through-an-owned-jdi-process).

The RefactorKit-first roadmap is reaffirmed in ADR 0017. The planned shared source-change workflow is described in [section 8.4](#84-planned-shared-refactoring-workflow); it is not an assertion that editor overlays, all advertised CLI operations or framework-wide transformations are already integrated.

## Section 5: Building Block View

### 5.1 Containers and Components

See the [C4 container diagram](docs/c4/containers.md) and [C4 component diagram](docs/c4/components.md). The editable diagram model is [the Structurizr workspace](docs/c4/workspace.dsl).

| Building block                          | Responsibility                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/contracts`                    | Shared request/result and state types                                                  |
| `packages/web-core`                     | Ports, state, application-neutral services and view models                             |
| `packages/ui`                           | Reusable layout, editor with local find/replace, terminal and presentation components  |
| `packages/browser-adapters`             | Browser implementations and explicit native unavailability                             |
| `packages/tauri-adapters`               | Typed IPC and event translation                                                        |
| `apps/desktop/src`                      | Desktop composition and feature controllers                                            |
| `apps/desktop/src/features/http-client` | Manually submitted HTTP request and response feature, with workspace-generation checks |
| `apps/desktop/src-tauri`                | Workspace authority, filesystem access, native processes, and tool transports          |
| `apps/web`                              | Browser composition without native platform access                                     |

The desktop command palette opens with **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P** or the **Commands** button. It lists settings, Java Intelligence, Java Project Model, Java Run and search actions, and only the Java editor actions admitted for the active document, cursor and advertised provider capabilities. For an active Java file that RefactorKit associates with exactly one package in the selected project, it also offers **Review move of package …** when the shared capability gate permits review. The saved RefactorKit model also contributes **Review move of Java type …** for each type identity it associates with the active file when the synchronized project-context gate permits the operation. Both commands open the existing reviewed preview flow; the palette does not apply edits directly. A focused Linux release/no-bundle Maven GUI scenario now qualifies the type-move palette entry through same-module and cross-module Apply, offline Maven verification on copied sources, Rollback and safe-delete refusals. Broader project layouts, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

**Ctrl/Cmd+P** opens **Go to File** for workspace-relative file-name and path search. The native search runs on a bounded blocking worker, ranks exact and prefix file-name matches ahead of path matches, and returns at most 200 results after inspecting at most 50,000 entries and 64 directory levels. It skips generated/cache directories and never follows symbolic links. Unreadable or unrepresentable entries and search limits are reported as partial or truncated results. Native root/activation checks and renderer workspace-generation checks reject stale searches and file opens. **Search Everywhere**, available from the header, the command palette, or **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+E**, combines the current command list, workspace file results, JDT LS workspace symbols when that capability is ready, and Java project-text results, including open dirty buffers. It presents at most 50 results per source, reports partial or truncated results, and shows a provider failure alongside results from other sources. Search requests and result navigation are bound to the active workspace generation; stale responses are discarded. Changing the query, closing the dialog or switching workspaces cancels an in-flight JDT LS workspace-symbol request; stale file and project-text responses are discarded. Component tests and the desktop TypeScript check cover this behavior. A focused Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario confirms one query returns file, Java symbol and project-text results and that keyboard selection of the JDT LS symbol opens its declaration without changing the saved file; it does not qualify packaged applications or other operating systems. The nested-Java Go to File path is validated through native GUI acceptance on Linux.

### 5.2 Java Tooling

RefactorKit compiler-error checks have a separate [runtime flow](#611-java-compiler-checks) from JDT LS document diagnostics.

If a Java buffer changes while JDT LS is starting, the first document-open notification uses the current editor text. The language controller verifies the workspace and session before sending that snapshot. A controller test delays the provider status response and checks that the first notification includes the intervening edit.

If JDT LS fails while initializing, the IDE closes the failed process and retains the error in the current workspace's language-service status. Refresh and WebView reload can still show the failure, and Start can retry with the selected configuration. A new initialization attempt or explicit stop clears the previous error.

When a reloaded WebView opens a Java document that is still synchronized, the native service accepts the request if the workspace, session, URI, language, version and content match. JDT LS retains the existing document without receiving a second `textDocument/didOpen`. A conflicting version or content remains an error, protecting the newer document snapshot from a stale open request.

All native JDT LS commands delegate process work, document synchronization, semantic requests and cancellation to blocking workers. Waiting for a language-server reply therefore does not occupy Tauri's main thread or an async executor thread. The inbound command names, serialized requests and responses remain unchanged; the existing service still checks workspace activation, session identity, document versions and cancellation. This follows Tauri's [command execution model](https://v2.tauri.app/develop/calling-rust/). The focused native qualification in section 10.1 verifies independent file opening while a real formatting response is delayed and rejection of its late edit after changing documents; it does not establish responsiveness of unrelated native providers.

The desktop and web builds use the same [Monaco 0.52.2 patch](patches/monaco-editor@0.52.2.patch). An explicit request for code actions cancels the automatic lookup already scheduled for the current cursor position. Otherwise the automatic lookup can cancel the user's pending request before a slower Java language server responds. Later cursor movements and marker changes still schedule new lookups. Recheck this behavior when upgrading Monaco.

The Java language controller owns JDT LS lifecycle, versioned full-text synchronization, diagnostics, cancellation, completion/hover/signature-help/references/definitions, document, range and on-type formatting, inlay hints, implementation, rename, full-document semantic-token, document-symbol, document-highlight, workspace-symbol, and code-action requests. Native startup copies the pinned configuration into a private, versioned runtime directory rather than writing to the managed JDT LS installation. The managed JDT LS installer uses pinned upstream release 1.63.0-202610191322 and prepares the separately labelled `idecompact1` distribution with the compact-class name correction described in [ADR 0035](ADR.md#adr-0035--pinned-jdt-source-correction-for-compact-compilation-units). JDT LS requires Java 25 to run; the installation manifest records that minimum. Startup also reads the mandatory JDT Core bundle’s `Bundle-RequiredExecutionEnvironment` header and uses the higher of the installer and bundle requirements, so an installation without an installer manifest can still refuse an older server JDK before creating runtime state. The bundle reader recognises `JavaSE-*` alternatives and folded headers in the main JAR manifest section, as specified by [OSGi](https://docs.osgi.org/specification/osgi.core/8.0.0/framework.module.html#framework.module.executionenvironment). Other execution-environment forms add no inferred minimum; this is a declared lower bound, not resolution of every OSGi dependency. Duplicate core bundles, malformed recognised requirements and unreadable or oversized archives refuse discovery. Inspection reads a regular JAR of at most 32 MiB, at most 16,384 entries and a manifest of at most 1 MiB without extracting files. Startup reports a clear compatibility error when the selected server JDK is below the resulting minimum. This server runtime requirement is separate from the JDK selected for a project. Monaco's Java semantic highlighting, inlay hints, outline and same-document symbol highlights use only the corresponding synchronized document version; stale results are suppressed. Semantic token indices are decoded against the server's negotiated legend and checked against the open document's UTF-16 boundaries before they reach Monaco. Java inlay hints are requested only when JDT LS advertises or dynamically registers the LSP provider; labels are plain text, and positions are checked against the open document and requested UTF-16 range. The current JDT LS preferences enable parameter names for literal arguments. Workspace search flushes open Java documents, cancels an older query when a new one starts, and rejects results after a workspace-generation or open-buffer change. Definition and implementation results are accepted only for canonical Java files in the active workspace; the definition query uses the current synchronized document and is enabled only when JDT LS advertises the provider. F12 queries RefactorKit first, then uses JDT LS for an unavailable, refused or empty result only while the exact active workspace, document path and URI, and source-buffer version still match; a retired RefactorKit project context is never bypassed. The JDT LS result must also match its active session and document before the guarded application navigation path opens it. The separate `Ctrl/Command+Alt+J` action directly queries JDT LS, and `Ctrl/Command+F12` remains Monaco implementation navigation. Target opening rechecks the source model version and workspace generation. Rename is capability-gated and accepts bounded, version-checked edits for synchronized, open Java documents. The desktop rechecks each captured document and commits all returned edits atomically to the editor drafts; saved files remain untouched. Closed-file references use the background-open and fresh-request workflow in section 6.2. Unsynchronized document edits, resource operations, stale versions, invalid ranges and overlapping edits are refused. Code actions request quick fixes, quick assists and the LSP `source` action family, then admit bounded, version-checked edits for the active document and other open, synchronized Java documents in the same workspace. The desktop rechecks target buffers and existing Monaco models before committing edits to unsaved drafts; saved files remain unchanged. A quick fix for a closed target remains a selection-only proposal until the person chooses it, following the source checks and background synchronization in section 6.2. Constructor, `hashCode()`/`equals()`, override/implement, and delegate-method actions use JDT LS generator extensions; their workspace edits pass the same validation before Monaco receives them. Each action presents a member-selection dialog. The backend validates selected fields and constructors against fresh JDT LS status, selected methods against a fresh JDT LS overridable-method list, and delegate field-method pairs against fresh delegate-method status before producing edits, and the dialog restores focus to Monaco. Stale versions, invalid or overlapping ranges, closed or unsynchronized document edits, resource operations, and generic server-command actions are excluded. Format Document and Format Selection are separately capability-gated by the initialized JDT LS session; the providers receive the active buffer's indentation settings, and their bounded, nonoverlapping edits are accepted only for the same synchronized document version. Range-formatting edits must also stay inside the selected lines. Workspace-scoped indentation and optional Eclipse formatter-profile settings are persisted by the desktop application. A profile must name exactly one entry in an XML file inside the current workspace; the native service validates it before replacing the session, copies its contents to a private per-session file, and passes that file and profile name to JDT LS. The workspace file is not modified. Applying a profile restarts JDT LS and resynchronizes open buffers, retaining their unsaved text. Settings accepts a workspace-relative path typed by the user or returned by the native XML file picker; the service still checks canonical workspace containment. The standard Linux native Java code-action profile verifies profile application, JDT LS restart, unsaved-buffer preservation, unchanged profile XML, and the selected next-line type-brace style in Monaco. Profile XML editing and cross-platform qualification remain future work. Applying a rename, code action or formatting result rechecks the editor model and version. Completion items may include LSP `additionalTextEdits`; the native adapter binds these to the requesting workspace, document URI, path and version, and Monaco applies them alongside the primary completion edit only when the identity is current and the ranges are valid and nonoverlapping. This admits same-document import insertion as an unsaved buffer edit; completion commands and cross-document workspace edits are not applied. The Monaco bootstrap loads the semantic-token, inlay-hint, completion, hover, parameter-hint, rename, code-action and formatting contributions so the registered providers are active. The installed JDT LS service smoke verifies full-document and range formatting, semantic tokens, literal-argument parameter hints, workspace-symbol lookup, same-document variable highlights and local rename, an import fix for an unresolved `List`, an edit-only quick assist for an `instanceof` cast, getter/setter generation, inherited abstract-method implementation, `toString()` generation, constructor generation, `hashCode()`/`equals()` generation, delegate-method generation and member sorting. The [native Java code-action GUI scenarios](features/workspace/native-java-code-actions.feature) verify that Monaco renders parameter-name inlays for literal arguments without changing saved source, and that unresolved-type import fixes, document and selected-line formatting, accessor generation, field rename, selected inherited-method generation, selected delegate-method generation, abstract-method implementation, `toString()`, constructors, `hashCode()`/`equals()`, and member sorting change only the active draft on Linux. A dedicated `source.organizeImports` profile verifies that used imports are sorted and an unused import is removed from the unsaved draft while saved source remains unchanged. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-code-actions-native-001:cross-file-rename` GUI profile verifies atomic draft updates for two open Java files and for an initially closed reference opened in background; section 10.1 records its toolchain scope. This native GUI evidence covers a release/no-bundle build; installers and other operating systems remain unverified. An explicit lifecycle action using the current project settings supersedes an automatic restart already scheduled for those settings. Controller tests exercise this ordering and ordinary settings-driven restarts. Concurrent activation of the same Java buffer joins its pending language-document open, including when the first session status arrives or a stopped session starts. Edits received during the open are sent afterward with an increasing version. When the main desktop WebView loads a new page, the next native Java operation retires the preceding JDT LS session before serving the editor. Reopened buffers acquire fresh document versions in the new session. Repeated reports of the same stopped generation leave a pending document startup in place. The retirement runs on the Java worker and leaves editor recovery and saved files under their existing authority.

Java document edits immediately retire their previous language-service diagnostics. Diagnostic events must match the exact tracked document version. After the newest full-text change is acknowledged, the controller requests JDT LS validation; coalesced intermediate versions do not trigger that request. A diagnostic-refresh failure does not resend an already acknowledged source version during close. Component tests cover these lifetimes. Linux native qualification with an isolated corrected JDT compiler verifies a real compact-draft error and a fresh warning after repair. The isolated RefactorKit SDK-compiler candidate also passes the explicit compact-source compiler check and draft repair in the native GUI. Section 10.1 records the provider and project scope; the IDE does not suppress compiler errors.

The desktop shortcut `Ctrl/Command+T` makes the activity sidebar visible, opens Java Intelligence and focuses its JDT LS workspace-symbol query. `Ctrl/Command+Shift+F` opens Java Project and focuses Find in Java Project, which searches supported project text files and open unsaved buffers. Both shortcuts work from Monaco and other non-text-entry focus, while ordinary text-entry controls keep the shortcuts for their own use. Workspace-symbol search still uses the managed Java language controller, preserving its workspace-generation, open-buffer and stale-result checks.

The [native Java language-intelligence scenario](features/workspace/java-language-service.feature), run with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-language-001:native:core` and installed JDT LS and JDK paths, passes on the Linux release/no-bundle application. Using JDT LS 1.62.0-202610131109 with server JDK 25, it verifies an unresolved-type diagnostic in Problems, field hover, method signature help and `String` member completion in Monaco. It also accepts JDT LS completion for `ArrayLi` as `ArrayList`, applies the `java.util.ArrayList` import to the same unsaved Java buffer, queries the `repeat` method's references through the Java Intelligence panel, and opens the call site while preserving the unsaved buffer. It also uses the separate `Ctrl+Alt+J` JDT LS editor action at the call site to open its workspace declaration without changing saved source; standard F12 remains RefactorKit navigation. Both that import draft and a separate Java draft survive a JDT LS restart. The same core profile also passes with repository-pinned JDT LS 1.63.0-202610191322 on JDK 25; see section 10.1 for its qualification scope. Saved Java sources and Eclipse project files remain unchanged; the temporary drafts are explicitly discarded before the application exits normally. The same AC-007 native scenario also passes with JDT LS 1.61.0-202607102111 on server JDK 21. This qualifies these editor interactions for one basic Java project. Production-adapter scenarios separately verify lifecycle, synchronization, cancellation, and browser boundaries through a deterministic Tauri harness. The overall requirement is `@partial`: full native lifecycle and cancellation, Maven/Gradle project contexts, installers, and another operating system remain unqualified.

The focused `test:story:req-ide-java-language-001:templates` profile passes the Java template scenario in [the Java language-service feature](features/workspace/java-language-service.feature) on a Linux release/no-bundle application with JDT LS 1.62.0 and JDK 25. The person types `sout`, selects the local template, enters `"hello"` at its snippet placeholder, and sees `System.out.println("hello");` in the unsaved editor buffer. For the `fori` template, the scenario changes the counter and bound through successive Tab stops after dismissing competing JDT LS completion proposals, then checks the generated body and unchanged saved source. It also expands the `main` template into a separate draft and verifies that its saved file remains unchanged. All template fixture files are restored before normal close. The same template scenario also passes with JDT LS 1.61.0-202607102111 running on JDK 21. This qualifies the complete set of seven local Java typing templates on that editor and host: standard output/error, main method, counted/enhanced loops, null checks, and try/catch blocks. The scenario preserves the saved source for every expansion and restores all fixture drafts before closing.

The focused `test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:test-templates` and `test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-templates` profiles each pass one Linux native GUI scenario in [the Java project-context feature](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) against a release/no-bundle application and a real RefactorKit daemon. The Maven scenario resolves JUnit 4.13.2, JUnit Jupiter 5.11.0, and TestNG 7.10.2 in the test compile classpath. The Gradle scenario prepares outputs with Gradle 9.8.0 or 9.6.1 `classes testClasses` against a populated offline cache, then explicitly evaluates project metadata in the IDE; its test compile classpath resolves JUnit 4.13.2, JUnit Jupiter 5.11.2, and TestNG 7.10.2. For each build tool, the scenario selects `test4`, `test5`, and `testng` in three test classes. It verifies the framework annotation and method body, a dirty test buffer, unchanged source bytes on disk, preservation of an unsaved main-source edit, explicit restoration and normal close. Gradle's aggregate project context remains partial because the unrelated Java conventional provider is partial; the Gradle effective provider and its test classpath are available, so the editor admits those templates using the owning provider statuses. Both scenarios also resolve Mockito 5.20.0 and Spring Boot Test 4.1.0, select the mock, stub, verify and test-class templates, and compile isolated temporary copies of the inserted code and equality assertions against the selected JDK and effective test classpath, supplying temporary declarations for assertion placeholders. They preserve unsaved editor state and saved bytes; they do not run generated tests or invoke a build tool on the inserted templates. The Gradle scenario's offline dependency resolution is qualified on the configured host repository. These scenarios do not qualify a packaged application, other frameworks or another operating system.

RefactorKit controllers present symbols, definitions/references, and reviewed refactoring plans. The name-based Java Definition/References panel reports a failed editor open as an error and contains provider navigation rejections; results from a stale workspace are discarded. For general CLI-backed Java refactoring, operation discovery permits a read-only preview, while Apply rechecks that exact Java language-kernel operation and requires stable, managed mutation authority; an aggregate `apply` flag cannot promote a proposal-only operation. Parameter rename remains a separate signature contract. Add Parameter uses a saved-source `mutationSelection` query and binds preview and Apply to the provider's selector hash; it refuses dirty or stale editor state. RefactorKit current source and the locally rebuilt 0.7.0 package advertise managed support for this operation; the previously cached package did not advertise its mutation-selection query and operation, so that distribution hides the action. Consumer, adapter and Rust tests cover request construction, selection attestation and hash checks. A Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario now verifies cursor selection, preview, Apply, offline Maven `verify` on a source copy, protected Rollback and clean exit for one package-private method with selected JDK 21 (section 10.1). The result does not qualify a released daemon, public or protected methods, or broader source layouts. For parameter reordering, the IDE sends the exact requested permutation only when the selected project-context provider advertises preview and managed Apply; focused contract and Rust tests cover operation and intent mapping. The Java editor context menu and command palette also offer cursor-based review when RefactorKit advertises saved-source mutation selection. That path binds the request to RefactorKit's provider-selected method and refuses dirty buffers or a stale cursor. Current RefactorKit supports bounded JDT-bound calls whose arguments are inert literals or exact local/parameter reads and refuses effectful or unproven expressions before mutation. The focused Linux GUI profile now passes for one package-private two-parameter Maven method with managed preview, Apply, copied-source `mvn -o verify` and exact Rollback (section 10.1). The previously cached 0.7.0 daemon did not advertise reorder; the locally rebuilt package now does. Public and protected targets remain refused pending external-consumer and hierarchy evidence. Change Parameter Type is capability-gated on saved-source selection and stable managed project-context authority. The locally rebuilt 0.7.0 package qualifies one bounded Maven case through Apply, offline verification and exact Rollback in the native GUI (section 10.1); the default provider, released packages and broader project contexts remain unqualified. Remove Parameter now follows saved-source method selection and stable managed project-context authority; one package-private Maven native GUI case is qualified (section 10.1), while RefactorKit remains authoritative for safety refusals. The Java Project view has separate provider-neutral paths for the RefactorKit scan/symbols outline and the versioned module, source-set and ordered dependency context; it does not derive an independent semantic model. Its bounded package/class/symbol presentation uses engine-reported file paths and lines to open a selected type or member through the shared Java navigation controller, which retains workspace-generation guards. Class rows also offer move and safe-delete review only when the synchronized provider advertises the corresponding preview operation. Safe-delete Apply additionally requires an explicit capability for complete project-wide reference analysis, including non-Java build and resource files; without it, an eligible provider plan remains review-only. Effective-context behavior and current integration limits are described in [section 6.8](#68-java-project-context). A Linux release/no-bundle Maven GUI scenario qualifies live scan/symbols output through the panel; broader project layouts, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. Monaco's Java definition and reference providers resolve the current UTF-16 cursor position against RefactorKit JDT bindings through a separate navigation port; implementation navigation uses the current synchronized JDT LS document and the standard language-server implementation request. The Java Intelligence panel uses RefactorKit for type and call hierarchy. RefactorKit definition and reference queries are independent of a JDT LS completion session; implementation requests use JDT LS. Authority, preview and verification limits are described in [section 6.6](#66-java-cursor-navigation). Saved-source refactorings use the editor protection and refresh flow described in [section 6.4](#64-refactoring-and-agent-flows). With an explicitly selected SDK and a capable provider, Monaco's editor context menu and `Shift+F6` shortcut offer reviewed type rename at the cursor; `F2` offers reviewed member rename. Captured Java drafts also support whole-file format/import previews. This remains a bounded subset, not general draft refactoring. Cursor-menu and shortcut actions and project-model move, rollback, referenced-delete refusal, the safe-delete preview-only gate, and moved-tab reconciliation have focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI coverage. Installers, other Java layouts and operations, and other operating systems remain separate.

Monaco Java file actions adapt the current editor document to that shared saved-source review. They depend on provider-neutral capability and editor contracts; native adapters own CLI invocation and transaction paths. [ADR 0017](ADR.md#adr-0017--refactorkit-first-refactoring-and-shared-change-coordination) records the admission and rollback rationale. The implemented controller relationships appear in the [component diagram](docs/c4/components.md).

The dependency-source controller consumes a dedicated provider-neutral lookup/read port. Its native service reuses the Java project-context session, while immutable library documents remain application state outside the writable workspace editor view model and recovery store. Runtime behavior is described in section 6.6.

The Java execution controller and panel own launch settings, workspace trust confirmation, save-before-execution, task status, console output, test results and debugger actions. Provider action errors appear in the structured debugger panel even before a new state snapshot arrives; duplicate state errors appear only once. The Tauri adapter implements the provider-neutral Java execution port and validates typed JDI views. Rust owns the actual processes, reads build-tool test reports and rejects mismatched workspace/session requests. For structured debugging, a private helper runs with the selected full JDK and either launches an owned debuggee or attaches to an external JVM through its JDWP socket. It returns threads, frames, values and events separately from application output; external application output and exit status remain with the target process. A sidecar build task lets the selected JDK or project build tool compile while a JDI session remains connected; Stop/Detach cancels both owned processes. A separate editor controller binds Monaco source annotations to the captured session and exact buffer lifetime/text. Workspace breakpoint preferences retain guarded source choices independently of the live process. Native source inspection retains file fingerprints and prepares checked startup settings; JDI supplies loaded types and executable locations. A separate native class-reload path captures selected compiled files, retains its private transfer file until the helper reports a correlated result, and retires local source binding. The connected JVM supplies redefinition support and validation; the IDE does not infer a source model from bytecode. This is runtime/source presentation, not an additional semantic project model.

The trust control remains available during preparation, execution and HotSwap. Revoking it prevents subsequent execution and class reload requests; Stop remains available for an existing execution. Workspace trust is checked from the current controller state before Java execution, after asynchronous preparation and immediately before handing the request to the native runtime. Withdrawing trust prevents a previously captured launch or discovered-test callback from starting work. HotSwap preparation checks trust again before compilation and before class reload, so withdrawing trust during an already authorised compilation prevents the subsequent reload. This does not terminate an execution already handed to the runtime. Focused production-controller tests cover callback capture, saving, monitoring suspension, project-context refresh, saved-buffer verification and the compilation-to-reload boundary; the asynchronous preparation and compilation races have not been qualified in the native GUI. A focused Linux release/no-bundle JDK 21 scenario verifies withdrawal at a real JDI entry suspension: Restart becomes disabled, Stop remains available, the debuggee stays suspended without application output, and explicit trust restoration enables Restart again. The same session then completes Run to Cursor with line-breakpoint muting and unmuting, preserves source inputs and closes normally without surviving processes. Other operating systems and packaged applications remain unqualified.

The [Java integration diagram](docs/c4/target-java-intelligence.md) distinguishes this implementation from planned advanced debugging and richer project integration.

### 5.3 Pi and First-party XCOM Features

Pi sessions use Rust-owned PTYs with docked or detached renderer attachments. Closing an attachment is not the same as stopping the workspace's Pi process. Read-only accessories do not assume authority over Pi's tools or conversation.

XCOM machine setup, project recognition, Foundry, and build-recipe review are first-party features. The [XCOM diagram](docs/c4/target-xcom2-setup.md) shows their separate boundaries. Project recognition does not authorize execution. SDK changes require review and reversible transactions. Foundry uses one native renderer and exact-plan approval. Build-recipe review is metadata-only: its approval is not a Build/Deploy/Cook/Launch executor.

## Section 6: Runtime View

### 6.1 Startup and Workspace Switching

Desktop startup authorizes the current workspace and promotes its registry entry before restoring workspace-dependent state. Initial file access waits for the file tree, editor restoration and semantic-session invalidation. Java status, Pi command discovery, RefactorKit availability/capabilities and XCOM checks run independently; their loading, unavailable and failed states remain visible in their own surfaces. RefactorKit status selects a recognized product-version line when launcher output includes a preceding runtime warning, so the warning does not hide the installed version. Optional checks do not grant execution trust or supply invented provider success. Each accepted switch advances a generation and invalidates stale editor/provider work; an obsolete optional check cannot settle the new workspace's activation or a controller that has been unmounted.

Native startup process probes and Java event polling run on Tauri blocking workers, keeping external processes and contended service locks off the window event thread. Workspace authorization/switch work also runs there and remains serialized, alongside managed RefactorKit capability-session establishment, so its root cannot change during that session's creation. The renderer retains its root-transition queue and stale-result guards. Explicit full refresh and workspace switching still wait for their coordinated service loads; this initial-startup change is not a universal responsiveness or worker-cancellation guarantee. See [ADR 0020](ADR.md#adr-0020--initial-workspace-readiness-independent-of-optional-providers) and [Tauri asynchronous commands](https://v2.tauri.app/develop/calling-rust/#async-commands).

Opening Settings reads the workspace registry without reauthorizing the active root. It preserves the native workspace generation used by file search and other operations. Startup and an explicit workspace switch establish authorization; a later registry read can refresh displayed metadata for the same workspace.

A same-origin classic [bootstrap observer](apps/desktop/public/startup-diagnostics.js) runs before the application module graph. It retains at most eight resource-load, runtime, unhandled-rejection or content-security-policy fault categories, known error classes and bounded JavaScript/CSS asset basenames, never error messages, stacks, request queries or rejection contents. The document, module entry, render request and main React commit publish diagnostic stages. These observations neither establish workspace authorization nor alter failure handling, source buffers or storage; an absent observer is unavailable evidence, not an empty fault history.

A switch with dirty editor tabs is refused with an instruction to save changes first. This check runs before buffer reset. Native Java execution is stopped before changing the active workspace; RefactorKit sessions are also shut down at that boundary.

### 6.2 Editing and Saving

Monaco retains one model per file. A reused editor must complete layout and acknowledge readiness for the newly active model before the inert opening placeholder is removed, including when returning to an existing tab. A failed layout remains an explicit failure with Retry rather than exposing an unqualified editor. Saving captures the requested content and serializes saves for the same file. Changes made while a save is pending remain dirty. Late saves do not restore tabs after workspace invalidation. A returned provider inventory updates only the saved file's metadata; it does not remove or resurrect unrelated UI buffers or change their selection.

The modified indicator compares ordinary typing and Undo/Redo with the last acknowledged saved text for that open buffer. Undo to exactly that text clears the indicator; Redo to different text marks the buffer modified again. A successful source read, explicit disk-snapshot adoption or completed Save establishes this comparison text. A Save records the text it actually captured, so later edits remain modified. Pending and queued saves keep the draft modified until their acknowledgments settle. New-file drafts remain modified until their first successful Save. Explicit recovery still marks its reviewed replacement dirty, as defined in [ADR 0018](ADR.md#adr-0018--workspace-scoped-editor-recovery-and-checkpoint-history).

The comparison text is held in memory for open buffer lifetimes. Close/removal and workspace invalidation retire it; validated editor renames carry it with the source buffer, and adopted external moves establish the newly read text. Unknown saved text keeps ordinary edits modified. User content and its modified flag publish atomically, so editor consumers cannot observe a new draft with the previous clean flag. Undo/Redo itself does not write source files or replace revision checks for later external filesystem changes.

After a successful editor Save of a non-Java workspace file, an initialized JDT LS session receives the standard [LSP watched-file change notification](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#workspace_didChangeWatchedFiles). This lets the provider refresh its own imported configuration, including Eclipse compiler preferences. The notification carries the saved file URI; workspace and language-session identity checks authorize a current regular file inside the workspace. It carries no editor text and does not save Java drafts. A notification failure is reported separately as a language-service synchronization problem after the successful file save. Java files retain their versioned document-save path. Session settings continue to govern project import and Gradle authorization. This integration covers editor saves; external filesystem changes, creation and deletion notifications need separate integration.

The Quick Open dialog searches workspace files without waiting for a fully expanded File Explorer tree. Search is available only after the desktop has an active authorized workspace; opening a result passes the workspace-relative path to the normal editor controller, and the renderer checks the workspace identity and generation both before and after opening. Its bounded results and skipped directories are described in section 5.1.

**Navigate Back** and **Navigate Forward** return to earlier editor locations through the header buttons, command palette or Ctrl/Command+Alt+Left/Right. The in-memory history holds at most 100 path-and-cursor locations for the current workspace activation, including same-file jumps and retained read-only Java source previews. A new jump after Back replaces the forward branch. Returning to a workspace file uses the ordinary guarded opener and retains open unsaved buffers; returning to a retained library preview uses its existing read-only document without a new provider query. Closed or retired previews are skipped. Failed file opens report failure without advancing the history. Accepted editor renames carry stored paths; workspace activation and disposal retire pending navigation. History stores line and column positions rather than semantic anchors, so arbitrary source edits can change what a stored position identifies. It neither saves document text nor persists across restarts. The keyboard shortcut leaves dialogs, terminal input and ordinary form fields to their own controls.

File Explorer shows conventional output and dependency directory names, including `build` and `target`, as folders whose contents load when opened. It does not recursively enumerate them during the initial directory listing. This allows a legitimate Java package named `build` to be reached without treating its name as proof that it contains generated output. Hidden metadata/cache directories retain their existing exclusions. Quick Open keeps its separate bounded search exclusions described in section 5.1. Expanded folders use the height of their visible contents, so scrolling File Explorer reaches the last file in a large Java package. Collapsed branches hide their children from interaction.

The File Explorer directory context menu offers **New File** and **New Folder** for an existing directory while other editor tabs remain open. Each accepts one child name without path separators; native commands create that child exclusively inside the registered workspace and refresh its parent. Generic file creation requires the selected parent directory to still exist and never recreates a missing path. The editor controller opens the exact returned file path. Duplicate targets and other creation failures remain visible in the dialog; existing files and folders are never overwritten. Every native file-tree mutation carries the workspace root and activation number from the last successful root listing. The command shares the lock used by workspace activation and refuses a mismatch before touching the filesystem. Results update the tree only while their originating workspace generation remains current. The dialog traps Tab and Shift+Tab within its controls and restores focus to the directory row after completion, cancellation, or Escape. **New File** remains content-agnostic. **New Java Type** creates an empty `.java` file for a class, interface, enum, record or annotation using an optional package name that is validated when supplied. At a uniquely identified ordinary source root with a current Java 9+ source set, **New Java Module Descriptor** validates a dot-separated module name, rejects the reserved `java.base` name, creates `module-info.java` with an empty `module <name> {}` body, and opens the descriptor as an unsaved draft. The wizard does not infer module directives; the developer adds the `requires`, `exports`, `opens`, `uses` or `provides` declarations required by the project. Component tests cover descriptor generation and source-root/source-level gating, and `javac --release 9` accepts the generated descriptor. A focused Linux release/no-bundle project-context GUI scenario verifies creation from a synchronized Maven library source root, preservation of an unrelated dirty Java draft, explicit save, and `javac --release 17` compilation alongside the library sources. This qualifies that Maven fixture only; packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. The name check accepts Java letters, letter numbers, currency symbols and connector punctuation at the start, with combining marks, decimal digits and format characters allowed later; control characters, reserved keywords and invalid segments are rejected, following [Java's identifier categories](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Character.html). It does not guess package names from conventional directory layouts; with a current RefactorKit context, it pre-fills a package only when one available source set and one ordinary provider-declared source root uniquely contain the selected folder and every relative segment is a valid Java package identifier. Generated roots, invalid package segments and ambiguous ownership leave the package blank. Record syntax requires Java 16 or later. When the current RefactorKit context identifies exactly one available source set for the selected folder, the wizard uses that source set's configured release, falling back to its source level when no release is declared, and refuses to generate a record below Java 16. If the context is missing, partial, or ambiguous, it reports that compatibility could not be checked and lets the user continue. The generated declaration opens as a dirty editor draft, so the new file remains empty on disk until Save. Component tests cover ASCII and Unicode identifier handling, package prefill and the low-release refusal; desktop unit tests cover unique project-relative source-set matching and unknown, generated, invalid or ambiguous context. Adapter tests cover request payloads, and Rust unit tests cover root/generation rejection and exclusive creation. The focused [native Java source-creation requirement](features/workspace/native-java-source-file-creation.feature) verifies class, interface, enum and annotation templates with `javac --release 8`, and the record template with `javac --release 16`, in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI. This evidence does not qualify packaged applications or other operating systems.

With one current ordinary source root supplied by RefactorKit, **New Java Type** places the file in the package directory beneath that root.
