Editing the package from `example` to `example.orders` therefore selects `example/orders/Created.java`, even when the dialog was opened in another package directory. The dialog displays the full workspace-relative destination and updates it when the name, package or source form changes. Without unique source ownership, it displays the selected-directory destination rather than implying automatic package placement. Submission uses current provider facts. Missing package directories are created under an existing source root in the same workspace-authorized native operation as exclusive file creation. A missing root, an existing target, a non-directory parent or a symbolic-link parent is refused. Failed creation removes only empty directories created by that request; existing directories and other writers' contents remain intact. The tree refreshes at the source root and the editor opens the resulting file as an unsaved draft. Without a unique ordinary source root, including generated or ambiguous ownership, the wizard explicitly keeps the selected-directory behavior and asks the developer to check the package layout. When current provider facts identify a generated source directory, the wizard explains that builds or code generation can replace its contents and recommends an ordinary source folder for hand-written types. This notice does not block explicit draft creation or infer generated ownership from directory names. Missing or ambiguous provider facts remain unknown. The IDE projects provider-owned root paths and does not infer a competing project model. Source creation qualification is described in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).

The same wizard offers **Compact source (Java 25+)**, producing an unnamed-package source with `void main() {}` and no explicit class declaration. It refuses a known source release below 25 and rechecks compatibility on submission. With unavailable or ambiguous context, it warns that compatibility could not be checked and permits explicit draft creation. The package field is hidden for this form. When a unique ordinary source root is available, a compact source is created directly at that root, even if the dialog was opened in a package directory. Contextual names such as `record`, `var`, `IO` and `java` are accepted; raw reserved names and invalid filename characters are refused. Implicit class filenames preserve Unicode format characters, unlike names in explicit type declarations. The new file remains empty on disk until Save, and unrelated editor drafts are preserved. This implements source creation, not broader entry-point discovery: the default discovery profile enumerates classic declared mains; the explicit Java 25 profiles described below require a compatible isolated provider. Developers can explicitly enter a compact class in Java Run using a compatible configured JDK. Verification scope is recorded in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).

File Explorer creation menus and dialogs belong to the current workspace identity and generation. A workspace transition remounts the tree and retires any unsubmitted file, folder or Java-type form, including its entered text; ordinary renders in the same workspace preserve the form. This prevents a directory chosen in the old workspace from being submitted in the new one. Existing native exclusive-creation and asynchronous workspace guards remain responsible for in-flight requests. Desktop integration tests exercise the real File Explorer component within the application composition. The focused Linux release/no-bundle native profile also verifies all three forms across real workspace transitions, preserving both workspaces and returning to the original one before creating and saving a source. Package and other operating-system qualification remain open.

When RefactorKit reports one complete named-module descriptor for the selected source set, the type wizard requires a package name for ordinary types and refuses compact sources, which belong to the unnamed package. It explains the selected module and preserves the form after refusal; no file or editor tab is created. Submission rechecks the current source level and module facts. Missing, partial or ambiguous module facts remain unknown rather than implying an unnamed module, and the wizard can still create a draft with that limit displayed. The IDE projects these facts from the provider context and does not parse module descriptors independently. Source ownership follows project-relative paths in v1/v2 and workspace-relative paths in v3–v7. The package/module relationship is specified in [JLS 7.4.2](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-7.html#jls-7.4.2).

The type wizard checks contextual restrictions on type names against the current provider-owned source level at submission: `var` from Java 10, `yield` from Java 14, `record` from Java 16, and `sealed`/`permits` from Java 17. These checks follow the standard, non-preview [Java identifier rules](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se17/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.8). Earlier source releases can retain those names. Without a qualified source level, these five names require project synchronization or a different name. They remain valid package and module-name segments. Ignorable format characters cannot bypass reserved or restricted-name checks. Type names containing them are refused because the compiler ignores them in the public type name, causing a mismatch with the file name. Other accepted source spelling is preserved. Component tests verify that a changed source level is checked before draft creation, without invoking file creation on refusal. A focused production-builder comparison with real JDK 21 and 25 compilers verifies release boundaries and all four ordinary type templates; this is service-level evidence for non-preview sources. The native source-creation profile separately verifies refusal of the five restricted names when source-level information is unavailable, an ignorable-character type name and a reserved word containing an ignorable character. It checks unchanged source inventories and editor tabs after every refusal. Release-specific name boundaries have not received native GUI qualification, and historical preview-language name restrictions remain unqualified.

When the initialized JDT LS session advertises document formatting, Monaco's **Format Document** action asks the provider to format the active Java document using the editor's tab size and indentation mode. When range formatting is advertised, **Format Selection** sends the selected lines through the same versioned synchronization path. Native code accepts only bounded, nonoverlapping edits within the open document; range-formatting edits must also stay within the requested lines. The controller and Monaco discard replies after a buffer or session change. Monaco applies accepted edits to the current editor model, leaving Save as a separate user action. JDT LS also reads project-local Eclipse formatter preferences from `.settings/org.eclipse.jdt.core.prefs`; request options control indentation, and project preferences can control style such as brace placement. A real JDT LS smoke verifies project next-line type braces together with the editor's four-space indentation. **Settings > Editor** stores workspace-scoped indentation size and spaces/tabs, applies them to Monaco and passes them to JDT LS formatting requests. It can also select an existing workspace-contained Eclipse formatter XML profile by relative path and exact profile name. **Read profile names** loads the uniquely named profiles from the saved XML in the active workspace. The reader validates the workspace-relative path, file size and XML. Select a name and use **Apply formatter profile** to change the preference. The native service validates the XML, uses a private session copy and restarts JDT LS while preserving open unsaved buffers. Settings can open the selected workspace-relative XML in the regular editor. The Linux native GUI formatter-profile scenario edits and saves its brace-position setting through that editor, restarts JDT LS, confirms the changed style on the unsaved Java buffer, then restores the fixture XML. This qualifies the workflow with JDK 25 and JDT LS 1.62 in a Linux release/no-bundle build; packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. The native file-picker path is also qualified as described in section 10.1. When JDT LS advertises its inlay-hint provider, Monaco requests hints for the visible Java range. The native service validates the synchronized document version and UTF-16 positions, drops provider tooltips and commands, and returns bounded plain-text labels for the unchanged range. The configured scope currently shows parameter names for literal arguments. This display does not edit or save source. Browser Java semantics, formatting and inlay hints remain unavailable. These provider-backed buffer actions are separate from RefactorKit's reviewed saved-source formatting plans. See the [Java formatting runtime interaction](docs/c4/runtime-java-formatting.md) and [Java inlay-hints runtime interaction](docs/c4/runtime-java-inlay-hints.md).

With the cursor on a Java declaration, open Quick Fix (`Ctrl+.`) and choose **Add Javadoc comment** when JDT LS offers it. The action inserts a documentation skeleton in the unsaved buffer. The developer supplies the descriptions. Undo restores the preceding draft. See the [Java documentation comment specification](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/javadoc/doc-comment-spec.html).

**Format Java while typing** in Settings > Editor is an optional workspace preference, disabled initially. When enabled, Monaco requests `textDocument/onTypeFormatting` only for characters advertised by the current JDT LS session. The native service enables the server request capability; this does not enable editor requests by itself. The typing provider survives temporary gaps in document synchronization, waits at most half a second for the exact typed buffer and uses its current language-service version. A further edit, cancellation, workspace/session change or withdrawn capability retires the result. Accepted edits are bounded, nonoverlapping and confined to the open document; they remain unsaved and participate in normal editor undo. Read-only dependency sources are excluded. The selected indentation options are forwarded to the provider. Verification scope and the focused native command are recorded in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).

Each open buffer has a process-local identity independent of its path, metadata object and opening timestamp. Editing, selection and ordinary Save preserve it; removal and same-path reopen replace it. Save/Close capture that identity before language synchronization or checkpoint waits, and recheck it before later actions. Save-all binds its original tab inventory rather than saving a newly reopened companion. An old completion cannot acknowledge, close or reactivate the new buffer; queued obsolete saves are dropped before provider I/O. Comparison and recovery reviews also bind the same identity. Removing an inventory entry clears its retired content/cursor state rather than reviving it when the path is re-added.

Native reads return a file revision. The desktop adapter sends that revision on later saves; a detected external change is refused instead of overwritten. Saves use a temporary file in the same directory, preserve existing permissions, flush the data, and publish it with a rename. This is not a guarantee against every possible concurrent external filesystem operation or a substitute for local history.

Native editor reads and writes run on blocking workers rather than the window event thread, so held source I/O does not prevent ordinary keyboard input. At most four source operations are admitted; excess work reports busy, and worker completion or failure releases capacity. Writers retain their serialization lock, expected-revision checks and atomic publication. Each command captures the canonical workspace root before dispatch, so a later workspace selection cannot redirect its worker to another root. Already-admitted operating-system I/O is not interrupted or rolled back; all four occupied workers can leave further source operations unavailable. This pool is separate from status inspection and recovery storage workers.

**Compare with disk** reads a separate immutable snapshot and presents the current buffer and inspected disk version without saving, discarding edits or advancing the save revision. **Keep editor buffer** cancels. **Discard buffer edits and use disk version** checkpoints the draft, then replaces only the still-current buffer and adopts the inspected revision. The dialog closes when the buffer is replaced. Language synchronization follows using the current editor text, so JDT LS startup and queued language work cannot hold the comparison open. Concurrent edits, pending saves, closed/reopened tabs, changed save baselines and workspace invalidation refuse replacement. Callbacks from a retired workspace, selected tab or editor owner are refused before inspecting disk, replacing a buffer or synchronizing its language document. Only the currently displayed comparison can authorize replacement, and repeated confirmation cannot start a second pending adoption. Other dirty buffers are retained; a subsequent external disk write is still protected by the normal revision-checked save. Deleted/inaccessible files produce an error rather than an invented disk version. Wider filesystem watching and three-way merge remain future work. Recovery and checkpoint history are described in section 6.5.

**External file change detection** is passive and covers open workspace files. Immediately, two seconds after each completed cycle, and on focus/visibility changes, the desktop checks the active file followed by one rotating background tab. Inspections are serialized, with at most two per cycle; detection latency for a background file grows with the number of open tabs and inspection duration. Hidden documents suspend inspection. Changed, missing or unavailable background files appear in an accessible list whose buttons select the corresponding tab for review. No buffer replacement, source write, recovery restore or save-baseline adoption occurs. **Compare with disk** remains the explicit resolution path. Results are guarded by workspace/generation, open-tab lifetime and save-baseline epochs, including equal-digest saves and same-path reopen. Providers without the optional operation remain unavailable rather than fabricating a disk result. This is open-file polling; recursive workspace watching and transient-change detection remain unavailable. See [ADR 0019](ADR.md#adr-0019--passive-active-file-disk-change-detection) for the decision and [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope) for verification scope.

The native status command authorizes the actual main window and current registered root before and after work, returns only correlated status, and limits streaming SHA-256 inspection to a regular file of at most 4 MiB. One worker is admitted at a time; a cooperative 250 ms processing budget and a ten-second adapter deadline bound ordinary work. A stalled filesystem call is not interrupted by those cooperative checks, but cannot spawn additional inspection workers. On Unix, descriptor-relative traversal refuses symlink ancestors, hard links and special files without opening FIFOs in blocking mode. Other operating systems need separate qualification. Inaccessible, oversized or unstable reads report unavailable, never unchanged. Polling is not an event history: it can miss changes reverted between probes, ignores inactive tabs and does not lock external writers.

**Tab close and lifecycle guards:** closing a dirty tab first drains language changes, attempts its checkpoint and saves, then rechecks for new edits before closing the language document and selected buffer. A refused final close retains the source buffer and attempts to reactivate its language document without reloading, replacing or saving text. The command controller rejects continuations from a retired workspace or effect lifetime, including unmount and React StrictMode replay; save-all stops rather than admitting Java execution from a retired lifecycle.

The shipped desktop and browser adapters close their local editor-session metadata synchronously. Metadata removal and the selected UI buffer close occur in one JavaScript turn, without an unnecessary await gap or source-content write. For an asynchronous provider, the view model additionally rechecks workspace generation, buffer lifetime, selected open-file identity, buffer version, exact content/dirty state and pending saves before removing any UI buffer. A stale result is refused and other tabs remain intact. This UI guard does not roll back an asynchronous provider's own session-side effects; future asynchronous providers need separate close/cancellation and revision-retention qualification.

Dirty buffers prevent document unload and native window close. Native listener registration/cleanup failures are sanitized, and late registration is disposed. A retired close listener prevents default instead of authorizing Tauri's automatic window destruction; it does not report into the retired UI. These guards do not establish general unload or every native close-race qualification; the focused held-Save Linux acceptance is described in section 10.

JDT LS semantic rename can include references in Java files that were closed when the command started. The first response identifies existing, canonical Java files within the active workspace; it supplies no applicable edits while any affected document is unsynchronized. The editor opens those sources as background tabs without changing the active file or saving drafts, sends their current contents to JDT LS, then requests the rename again. Only the fresh result can enter the existing atomic editor transaction. Every previously captured document must still match its text, URI, version, workspace and language-server session. Cancellation remains effective while files are loading or synchronizing; a repeated unresolved file or exceeded document limit refuses the operation. Existing drafts are never replaced by background reads, and a foreground open or workspace change retires a pending read. Resource creation, deletion and file renaming remain outside this editor operation. A `documentChanges` entry with a null version is used only to discover a closed file; after synchronization the server must identify its open version, consistent with the [LSP document identifier contract](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-languageserver-node/blob/main/types/src/main.ts). The legacy `changes` response is checked against the full captured open-document frame. Unit tests exercise loading, cancellation, stale frames and boundary refusal; native qualification is recorded separately in section 10.1.

Quick-fix discovery does not open additional tabs. When an edit-only JDT LS action references closed Java files, the native service captures their bounded saved text and returns a selectable proposal with no applicable edits. Only choosing that proposal opens its targets in background. The controller flushes current Java drafts, synchronizes the additional sources and requests the action again at the original selection. Both the proposed text changes and every affected source snapshot must match; the action title alone cannot select a replacement. Changed files, changed proposals, stale buffers, cancellation and workspace/session changes refuse the commit. The accepted edits use the same atomic editor transaction as semantic rename. Closed-source capture uses regular workspace files, at most 2 MiB each and 8 MiB across one query; repeated actions share that query's captured text metadata, while later queries capture it again. The existing draft-transaction limits also apply.

After a semantic workspace edit, the controller sends the modified draft texts to JDT LS and requests diagnostics for the current synchronized Java documents through its read-only `java/validateDocument` extension. The native boundary requires the exact open workspace, session, URI and document version; validation changes neither text nor document versions and does not save or run a build. This refresh lets an unchanged caller observe a method created in a background draft. A refresh failure preserves already applied drafts and reports the diagnostics failure separately. Native GUI qualification and its toolchain scope are recorded in section 10.1.

### 6.3 Java Execution

Synchronized execution resolves the selected existing module directory to its canonical filesystem path within the workspace before preparing build tasks. A trailing separator or dot spelling does not make a root module a different Gradle project. Provider-owned module and source-set selection and snapshot checks still apply.

Application Run and Debug can opt into **Application input (System.in)** in the saved launch configuration. The input panel sends UTF-8 text, appends one newline for **Send line**, permits an explicit empty line, and offers **Close input (EOF)**. Input belongs to the captured application session and remains separate from jdb commands and structured JDI actions. Rerun and Restart retain the captured setting; Build, tests, discovery, coverage and Attach ignore it. A missing runtime capability refuses an input-enabled application launch before execution.

The panel keeps at most 64 KiB of submitted bytes in memory and sends bounded chunks. Acknowledgements report bytes accepted by the transport, not bytes consumed by the application. Partial writes retain the original remaining bytes, including partial UTF-8 characters. Retries use the same sequence and content, so a lost acknowledgement cannot silently duplicate input. Workspace, generation, session or trust changes retire drafts and pending input; uncertain acknowledgements prevent further submissions. Input text is not saved in launch configurations or launch files. An application may itself echo or save what it reads.

Application input supports a full JDK 8 or later with `jar` and Java instrumentation. Java 8 provides its legacy instrumentation library. Later JDKs provide the `java.instrument` module. The IDE recognizes that module in the installed runtime image through the JDK's `release` metadata, including distributions that omit a separate `jmods` directory. The JDK compiles an IDE-owned startup agent in private temporary storage. The agent connects the application's `System.in` to an authenticated local socket before `main`; it does not transform application classes. Native writes are nonblocking, and Stop closes the channel and terminates the owned processes. An application that never connects has unavailable input. Applications that replace `System.in`, custom launch tasks that ignore JVM options, native descriptor reads, terminal control and `System.console()` are outside this text-input contract. The transport decision and alternatives are recorded in [ADR 0025](ADR.md#adr-0025--session-scoped-java-application-input).

Java runtime class names and concrete test-method selections admit Unicode identifiers, including supplementary letters, rather than requiring ASCII names. Shared contract checks and native checks enforce the same bounded lexical shape for Run/Debug, discovery, failed-test reruns, compiled declaration metadata and class reload. Names are kept exactly as supplied; composed and decomposed spellings are not normalized into one name. These checks follow the character categories in [JLS 3.8](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.8), retain the 512-byte UTF-8 identity limit, and reject control characters, command options and path syntax. They do not establish that a class or method exists: the selected compiler, test runner, JVM and semantic provider still decide that.

Compiled-class identity checks decode the JVM class-file format's [modified UTF-8](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se21/html/jvms-4.html#jvms-4.4.7), including surrogate-pair encoding for supplementary characters. Malformed names, mismatched binary names, changed class bytes and stale debugger selections remain refused. Loaded-class lists retain the JVM's UTF-16 string ordering across the native and web boundaries; Unicode names do not weaken duplicate, ordering or class-loader checks. Compiler/JVM Unicode tables vary by JDK, so lexical admission is not a promise that an older selected compiler supports every character known to a newer host. Verification scope is recorded in section 10.1.

Java Run can discover saved classic declared main methods for the selected synchronized module and source set. Discovery requests and displayed choices belong to the current workspace, launch configuration and provider instance. Changing these inputs, withdrawing trust or closing the controller retires callbacks and cancels an outstanding request through its original provider. Granting trust again requires a new discovery action. Focused production-hook tests verify this lifecycle, including provider replacement and changes during saved-buffer verification; this scope does not establish native GUI acceptance of those transitions. After the lifecycle change, the existing Linux release/no-bundle native profile passed ordinary main discovery and file/cursor Run and Debug for a declared JDK project and synchronized Maven and Gradle projects on JDK 21. Source/build inputs were preserved, windows closed normally and runner cleanup found no surviving processes. Trust-revocation and provider-replacement transitions themselves remain verified only by the focused controller tests. It requires a RefactorKit runtime advertising the qualified classic profile, bounded responses and cancellation. The IDE uses the provider's binary class names, including nested and secondary classes, and fills the main-class field when the person selects a result; selecting a result does not execute it. Manual entry remains available. Plain-JDK discovery through an explicit provider declaration has real-provider service qualification and focused Linux native GUI qualification for file-main Run and cursor-main Debug. The Java editor can also request the provider-owned enclosing type at the cursor as described below.

The Java Project panel implements **Declare plain Java project** for existing projects without Maven or Gradle descriptors. The person explicitly selects project-relative source roots, dependency paths, one compiler output directory, a Java release and the configured full JDK. The native command creates `.refactorkit/java-project.json` exclusively and opens it for review; it preserves an existing declaration and does not synchronize, compile or execute as part of creation. The form creates one main source set and optionally a named test source set, both with annotation processing disabled and the selected release. Test sources, additional test libraries and their distinct output directory are explicit. The form includes the main output and compilation dependencies in test compilation, while test libraries remain outside the main classpath. Optional separate runtime lists for main and test replace their shared dependency lists at execution time; tests inherit the main runtime classpath and extend it with their selected test runtime dependencies. Enabling a separate list first copies its existing dependencies, subsequent edits remain independent, and an empty runtime dependency list is allowed. Each source set output is included explicitly in the generated runtime list. Optional generated-source directory lists for main and test are also included in their compilation roots and retained separately as generated-root metadata. A source set may contain only generated roots. Their files must already be generated before synchronization; declaration creation does not create source files or schedule generators, and annotation processing remains disabled. Creation does not build either source set; the main output must exist before tests consume it. The form can add explicitly named modules with their own project-relative root, source sets, release, dependencies and outputs. Source and output directories must belong to their module root; dependency lists may refer to another module’s output. Compilation remains a selected-source-set operation: build dependencies first in the required order. Creation rejects duplicate module names, shared outputs and Maven or Gradle descriptors at a declared module root. RefactorKit owns validation and the resulting `java-declared-v1` project context.

File monitoring captures the declared provider source roots with the synchronized context, so Java changes beneath those roots also retire that context when a directory is named `build`. The execution consumer requires complete provider compiler facts, uses only the selected source roots and compile classpath, and passes `--release` and `-proc:none` to the JDK. A private empty source search path prevents javac from discovering undeclared sources through the working directory or dependency paths. For declared projects, execution preserves the provider's runtime classpath order and does not add compiled output directories implicitly. Additional runtime entries from Java Run are appended; they do not alter the declared compilation classpath. Tests and discovery consume the selected test source set, including nonstandard identifiers, and discovery scans only that source set's output directory while loading its declared runtime dependencies. A main selection is redirected only when the module has one test source set. Outputs required from another source set must be built first.

Real-service tests with JDK 21 and 25, release 17, JUnit Platform 1.13.4 and TestNG 7.10.2 qualify selected-method execution, fresh XML results, runtime-only dependencies, classpath precedence and discovery without test-body execution. A runtime dependency containing an unrelated test stays outside discovery. The isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate used for these checks projects Java providers into the Java context, so JavaScript assets generated by TestNG reports do not make that context partial; the global project summary and snapshot still retain other languages and their errors. This provider correction is required for the passing TestNG sequence and does not qualify the default installed daemon. The focused Linux release/no-bundle declared-tests GUI profile also passes both frameworks with JDK 21 and release 17: public form controls create an application with main and custom test source sets plus a library module. Build compiles the library for release 11 and the application for release 17 in the explicitly selected dependency order; class-file versions are checked independently, and the selected test calls the library. Selected-method Test produces independently parsed fresh XML, and discovery leaves test bodies unexecuted. A source-retained annotation requires a compilation-only JAR during test compilation, and the test verifies that its class is absent at runtime. Reflection separately loads one dependency inherited from the main runtime list and one added only to the test runtime list; both stay outside the compilation lists. The same GUI fixtures declare separate already-generated main and test roots through the form, compile both support classes into the selected outputs and call them from the selected test. These checks use normal and generated roots together; generated-only source sets have component and native declaration tests. No generator or annotation processor is executed. Source, declaration and dependency JAR bytes remain unchanged. Executing a captured discovery choice preserves its original method and framework after both current form values change. Both scenarios preserve source and declaration inputs and close without surviving owned processes. The [native declared-project scenarios](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) exercise this tested scope. Broader framework matrices, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

Modern JUnit engines receive an [output-directory provider](https://docs.junit.org/5.13.4/api/org.junit.platform.engine/org/junit/platform/engine/reporting/OutputDirectoryProvider.html) during discovery. Engine output is stored in private temporary directories and removed with the discovery operation; older engine APIs retain their existing discovery behavior.

Unit tests cover declaration creation, refusal, workspace retirement and compiler planning; a real JDK 21 compiler check verifies refusal of an undeclared workspace dependency and successful compilation after repair. The production native context, execution projection and main/cursor discovery services pass with the isolated qualified declared-project provider on JDK 21/release 17 and JDK 25/release 25. They verify explicit roots, empty compile classpath, missing pre-build outputs, primary/secondary/nested ownership, cancellation, stale-source refusal and unchanged inputs. These services do not compile or execute the fixture. A separate production execution-service test passes real Build, Run and JDI Debug on JDK 21/release 17 and JDK 25/release 25. Its custom roots and output paths contain spaces, the selected main source set has a nonstandard identifier, and the application uses an explicit dependency JAR. An invalid Java file outside the selected roots is excluded. Debug stops at the requested source line inside a package literally named `build`; the selected JVM, literal arguments and unchanged source/declaration contents are checked.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:declared-jdk` profile passes in the Linux release/no-bundle application on JDK 21/release 17 with the isolated qualified literal-root provider. It creates the declaration through the public form, opens the JSON, refuses to replace an existing declaration, synchronizes `app / main` and builds into the custom output. The physical source path is `source code/build/Main.java`; an invalid source outside the declared root is excluded, and the application uses the explicit dependency JAR. Run from the source-file action and Debug at the cursor select the provider-owned class despite a deliberately incorrect form value. Debug verifies a real JDI breakpoint and main frame before completion. Source/declaration preservation, normal window closure and no process survivors are checked. This qualifies the declared-project workflow for that fixture and local provider; other layouts, GUI SDKs, file-main Debug/cursor-main Run combinations, packages and other operating systems remain unqualified. An older provider can report unavailable context or a typed ownership refusal; the IDE never substitutes a guessed main class.

The Java editor's **Run main from this file…** and **Debug main from this file…** actions filter the provider query to the exact saved file in the configured synchronized module and source set. It does not infer module ownership or class names from the file path. One candidate starts through the ordinary execution controller with the requested Run or Debug operation only when enumeration of the selected profile is complete and non-truncated and its exact total is one. Multiple candidates, or an incomplete enumeration of that profile, require an explicit selection in Java Run, retaining the requested operation; an empty partial result never starts a guessed class. The list identifies the requested source file and keeps the provider’s coverage statement visible. Monaco model/version, workspace and saved-buffer checks reject a retired source frame. Launch-setting changes retire outstanding discovery, and the execution controller verifies that the selected class was actually accepted into the current configuration before starting it. Component tests cover unique, multiple, empty and retired-source results and preserve Debug intent through both unique and explicitly selected candidates. Debug uses the configuration’s selected debugger mode and the existing native debugging pipeline. Project execution retires the prior semantic context before the native request; further source discovery requires a fresh synchronization. Native acceptance remains separately scoped below.

The editor’s **Run main at cursor…** and **Debug main at cursor…** actions add an exact zero-based UTF-16 position to the saved-file query. They require RefactorKit’s enclosing-type capability; older runtimes return unavailable without a file-wide fallback. RefactorKit selects the innermost native type. The IDE verifies its source path, echoed position, binary identity and half-open declaration range, and accepts candidates only for that owner within that range. Moving the cursor or changing the model invalidates the captured action. A positively selected inner or sibling type without a declared classic main stays empty; the IDE never substitutes an outer or neighboring type’s main. The default classic result still reports partial launch-form coverage. Real-provider service checks on JDK 21 and 25 cover primary, secondary and nested classes, a dormant inner type, a split UTF-16 surrogate, outside-type refusal and wrong source-set ownership. The prior candidate without the enclosing-type capability reports unavailable. Native GUI qualification is recorded separately below.

Discovery is read-only and does not save, compile, load user classes or run main methods. Unsaved buffers are refused. The same captured buffer review is checked after the response and when selecting a candidate; workspace, configuration, module, SDK, context or trust changes retire the result and cancel an outstanding request. The native service checks snapshot, index generation, exact scope, context/schema, platform identities, selected launcher release and source ranges against saved text before publishing workspace-relative locations. The adapter rejects malformed or uncorrelated results. Old runtimes report discovery as unavailable. Cancellation is available through a public control and also follows context changes.

Coverage is explicitly partial: the first provider profile returns only classic public static declared mains, and an empty result does not prove that a project has no launchable class. The default profile does not enumerate inherited, Java 25 extended or compact/preview main forms. Incomplete source analysis is refused; source errors or missing generated sources/dependencies may require a Build and a fresh synchronization before discovery. RefactorKit owns launchability and binary names; the selected JDK and build tool continue to own compilation and execution. The IDE's real-provider service checks pass with the isolated classic candidate that corrects effective target-level reporting, on Linux and selected JDK 21 and 25. Maven fixtures cover JDK 21 with release 8 or source/target 8, and JDK 25 with release 8, release 25 or source/target 25. They verify nested/secondary classes, effective source/target levels, selected launcher release, file filtering, wrong-scope refusal, cancellation, stale sources and unchanged input files without compilation or execution. A separate real-service matrix with the isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 native-SDK API correction now qualifies `List.of` under Maven source/target 8 on JDK 21 and 25. With `--release 8`, the same source receives a compiler-error refusal and no launch candidates. Independent `javac` probes agree with both modes. The production TypeScript context adapter accepts all four actual provider responses: source-set syntax remains 8, while the SDK API profile is 21 or 25 for source/target and 8 for release. This qualifies the tested Maven entry-point and context consumer paths, not standalone diagnostics, SDK/dependency source navigation, Gradle API profiles, native GUI execution or the default installed daemon. The previous runtime reports unavailable without candidates. Plain-JDK probes using a root-level Java file and the conventional `src/main/java` layout both receive a partial `java-conventional-v1` context and `java.context.compilerOptionsUnavailable` from discovery. The explicit `java-declared-v1` declaration supplies these compiler facts through RefactorKit; the conventional fallback remains partial, and selecting a JDK alone does not supply missing compiler facts. Component and adapter tests separately check partial coverage and retirement of stale results. Native GUI qualification is recorded in section 10.1.

The implemented **Launcher discovery rules** control explicitly selects the classic declared-main protocol or the separate `java-entry-points-v2` inherited and Java 25 profiles. The editor file/cursor actions use the selected profile. Changing the profile retires outstanding requests and displayed candidates; a workspace or launch-configuration change restores the classic default. The v2 consumer requires provider capabilities and SDK/source/target 25 with preview disabled. It preserves the provider-owned launch and declaring types, invocation descriptor, construction eligibility, source or binary declaration origin, exact counts and bounded exclusions. The native boundary also checks the selected SDK executable/compiler digests and saved UTF-16 ranges; the global project snapshot and scoped analysis snapshot remain separate. Adapter, controller, component and native decoder tests cover these checks. Production-service Maven checks pass with the isolated corrected candidate on selected JDK 25/release 25: the same mixed scope returns compact and Unicode owners under the Java 25 profile and only matching classic owners under the inherited profile. They verify inherited cursor ownership, an inner type without a main, constructor refusal, input preservation and stale-source refusal. A separate classic-v1 production-service regression also passes on that candidate. The production TypeScript adapter accepts the actual global, inherited, cursor and empty-owner responses. Other SDK levels, Gradle, JPMS and package/platform checks remain pending. Compact and inherited-main GUI qualification is recorded in section 10.1. The IDE preserves the provider refusal and does not reconstruct launchability locally.

1. Open the **Java Run** activity and choose automatic detection or an explicit build tool.
2. Choose the workspace root or a workspace-relative project/module directory, then configure the main class and any additional workspace-contained classpath entries. Build-tool detection, compilation and tests follow the selected project directory; application Run/Debug can use a separate working directory. Classpath entries remain relative to the workspace.
3. Confirm trust: build plugins and project code can execute with the user's privileges and download dependencies.
4. On Build/Run/Run with JFR/Run tests/Run tests with coverage/Discover tests/Debug/Debug test/Debug integration test, save dirty buffers and reject execution if changes remain unsaved. Java saves and execution commands, including application and test debugging, persist Java files before launch and notify JDT LS asynchronously. Debug separately verifies its captured saved sources and breakpoint fingerprints. The language service can resume synchronization when its session is available.
5. Rust validates the actual main window, current registered workspace, and request/session identity, then starts an owned asynchronous task.
6. Tool output is displayed as returned, with an explicit truncation notice beyond the retained console limit.
7. Stop terminates the owned task. Workspace changes and application exit also terminate Java tasks.

**Reported compiler locations** makes recognized tool-output locations navigable from Java Run. It recognizes ordinary `javac`/Gradle Java error and warning lines and Maven compiler lines with bracketed line/column positions. The native reader resolves each reported file against the actual invocation directory and accepts only an existing Java file inside the session's canonical workspace. Paths outside that workspace, missing files and unsupported output formats remain unlinked in the console. This is a collection of reported locations, not a complete semantic diagnostic set; localized or differently formatted tool output may not be recognized.

Opening a location uses the normal guarded editor navigation, preserving open unsaved buffers. The callback checks the workspace identity/generation and membership in the displayed session report. Navigation is disabled while execution or launch preparation is in progress. It opens the reported line at column one: a Maven-reported column is shown as tool information without assuming its units or tab expansion. Positions describe the tool output and can differ from current editor changes.

The collection retains at most 100 distinct locations independently of the console's rolling output limit. Each pipe buffers complete byte lines separately, including UTF-8 characters split between reads; oversized lines are discarded rather than parsed from their suffix. Paths and messages have bounded sizes, ANSI color sequences are removed for recognition, and collection-limit notices do not imply a complete scan. A new execution session starts with an empty collection. Older native runtimes can omit this optional response field; the UI does not infer substitute locations. Separate HotSwap build-result output has not gained this structured presentation.

**Debug test** starts one concrete test class or method from Java Run or Commands; discovered test rows offer the same action while discovery is complete. It uses the structured JDI debugger independently of the saved application debugger mode. Trust, a full JDK with JDI, an explicit native test-debugging capability and a concrete selector are required. Current edits are saved first and changed breakpoint selections refuse launch. A discovered selection retains its original project, JDK, framework and test settings while using current saved source breakpoints. Application arguments and application JVM options remain separate from test JVM options. Rerun failed retains the captured test configuration and selects the failures from its fresh report. A test-debug rerun accepts multiple failed methods from that same concrete class and uses current saved source breakpoints after repairs. Breakpoint changes during preparation, withdrawn trust, unsaved edits and changed synchronized-project settings refuse the rerun.


**Debug failed tests** starts structured JDI from the results of a completed ordinary test or coverage session, including Maven integration tests. It retains that session's JDK, project and test settings and uses current saved source breakpoints, even after the current form changes. The native session offers the action only when its captured JDK supports JDI and its complete fresh report supplies usable failed selections from one concrete class. Missing capability information, incomplete reports and failures across several classes withhold the action. For a manually configured Maven reactor, native validation requires reports that identify one failed module, even when several failures share the same class and method name. When a report identifies a nested module, the IDE keeps the reactor for dependency resolution and restricts the test debugger and its saved source breakpoints to that module. Ordinary failed-test reruns can still target several modules. The selected test filter or TestNG suite and any qualified fork JVM settings remain in effect during synchronized test debugging. Saving, trust, workspace, breakpoint and synchronized-project setting checks apply before launch. Starting this debug session does not change the saved application debugger mode or repeat coverage collection. Descriptive or parameterized test names retain the report reader's documented whole-class fallback. The results panel lists the actual selections computed by the native report reader, bounded to ten visible entries with an additional-selection count. A selection of a whole class names that class and explicitly warns that its previously passing or skipped tests run again. Older runtimes without selection metadata retain the general fallback explanation; the IDE does not infer a method by removing parentheses or other formatting from a report display name.


For Gradle tests, the runtime correlates fresh XML cases with the public [MethodSource API](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/api/tasks/testing/source/MethodSource.html). It records the runner's public name and display name alongside its method identity, then matches the XML case by report directory, runtime class, reported name and outcome. Passing, failing and skipped cases with the same display name remain separate; conflicting identities within the same outcome have no method identity. The results panel shows and searches the runner's class and method. That class can be the executing subclass for an inherited test, so it is not presented as proof of the declaring type. Missing or ambiguous metadata leaves the method label absent.

An optional declaring-class value comes from inspection of the task's compiled classpath with the JDK [reflection APIs](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Class.html#getDeclaredMethods()). When the test's configured Java executable resolves to the Gradle JVM's executable and the task does not enable preview features, an isolated, bounded class loader inspects the classes in that JVM. With a different executable or preview features, an IDE-owned Java helper is compiled once with the Gradle JDK and invoked with the test task's actual Java executable after the tasks finish. Preview tests use this helper even when Gradle and the tests select the same JDK, because the Gradle JVM may not permit loading their preview bytecode. Each task's queries share one child process, with a ten-second child deadline and a thirty-second total enrichment deadline. The helper receives only the compiled classpath and method identities. The test's preview flag is retained, but application JVM arguments and agents are not copied; Java option injection environment variables are removed. Both paths load without class initialization and use static calls to JDK reflection APIs, avoiding project methods that happen to have the same names. A sole compiled declaration of the method name can supply its type regardless of visibility, including protected and package-private Jupiter methods and inherited interface default methods. When several public declarations share the name, JDK effective-method lookup must resolve one method. Conflicting non-public declarations, overloads, compiler bridges and synthetic methods withhold the value. Missing classes, linkage failures, conflicting declarations, unsupported identities or an unavailable helper omit this optional value while retaining the runner identity. The helper's files belong to private launch storage and are removed when the execution releases its metadata artifact. The results panel can show and search the separate declaring type. The lookup describes the configured compiled classpath; custom runtime class-loader substitutions and runtime-generated types are not qualified.

Source navigation prefers a matching saved-source failure frame. Otherwise, a compiled declaring type can reveal its method through the current synchronized JDT LS document outline. Without that value the action opens the runner class and explains why it cannot select a method; an executing subclass and method name alone cannot distinguish inherited declarations or overloads. The IDE matches the type and exact identifier at the provider's selection range, without interpreting decorated symbol labels or report display names. An inherited declaration can be opened when its source type resolves uniquely inside the reported module. A declaration in another module needs stronger ownership information and retains navigation to the executed type. Ambiguous overloads, truncated outlines, missing symbols or dirty source also retain class navigation. Opening a document allows up to five seconds for its language-service synchronization; a changed workspace, tab, buffer lifetime, content or document version retires the pending reveal. If a synchronized method lookup fails after opening the class, the results panel explains the fallback. Revealing a method in the current document does not reopen its tab or interrupt document synchronization.

This metadata also supports selecting the real failed method when its display name names another test. Rerun retains the executing subclass, independently of the optional declaring type. A private initialization script uses a [Gradle build service](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/build_services.html) to bound and close the metadata and inspection class loaders after the test tasks; project descriptors remain unchanged, and configuration caching is disabled for that invocation. Only complete data from that invocation is used. Missing APIs, unavailable output, conflicting identities or unmatched cases retain the report reader's fallback. Method selections still cover matching overloads and all their invocations; selecting one parameterized or dynamic invocation remains incomplete.

The JDI helper reserves a loopback listener before starting the test task; the test JVM connects to that endpoint in suspended mode. Maven Surefire and Failsafe retain their configured test runners and `argLine`, using the plugins' [debugging properties](https://maven.apache.org/surefire/maven-surefire-plugin/examples/debugging.html). Gradle uses temporary [test debug options](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/java_testing.html#sec:debugging_java_tests) on exactly one Test task in the selected task graph, with one worker, no periodic worker replacement and configuration caching disabled for that invocation. Project descriptors remain unchanged. Plain-JDK tests use their explicitly supplied runner classpath. Connection startup is bounded; an unavailable debugger or failed connection produces an execution failure. A connected suspended test has no arbitrary execution timeout.

The session owns both the debugger helper and build-tool process. Test output and final success come from the actual test runner and fresh JUnit XML, rather than from the helper's exit alone. Stop terminates both owned processes and the connected test JVM. Captured rerun keeps the original launch settings after the current form changes; new source breakpoints are captured and validated again. Test-session HotSwap is unavailable. Several Maven forks, arbitrary task graphs, other test engines and broader framework configurations still need qualification; section 10.1 records the verified scope.

**Synchronized module execution:** Java Run selects a provider-qualified module and source set published by an available Java Project context. The saved launch configuration retains the provider, module and source-set identities; snapshot and context authority are acquired again for each new execution. Legacy saved selections without a provider identity resolve only when the current context has one matching module; collisions require the developer to select a provider-qualified entry. A saved module or source-set selection absent from the current context remains visible for correction, but synchronized execution stays disabled until the developer chooses a current entry or synchronizes Java Project. Socket Attach requires manual configuration. The project JDK, Maven repository/profiles or explicitly evaluated Gradle settings govern the operation. Saving precedes metadata acquisition, and an editor change during acquisition refuses the launch, including an edit subsequently restored to the same text. Project settings or workspace changes also refuse the pending operation. A partial, missing or obsolete provider cannot fall back to a manually assembled project model.

Gradle capability checks and synchronized execution honor the executable selected in Java Project before consulting `PATH`. A workspace-contained wrapper retains priority; without a wrapper, a nonempty explicit selection must resolve to an existing absolute file and an invalid selection is refused. Only an absent selection falls back to `PATH`. Planning receives this executable before creating build steps, so a synchronized project does not require a second Gradle installation under the name `gradle`. Changing the selection refreshes the tool controls, and capability replies are correlated with that selection.

Starting a synchronized execution retires the Java Project context before build tools can change source-set outputs. The native runtime path obtains fresh metadata after compilation, but that does not republish a semantic context to the interface. Before a different new execution, synchronize Java Project again and select a current entry. Captured-session Rerun/Restart acquires current metadata with the original saved settings after reviewing saved buffers. The separate application working directory does not change these authority rules.

The native execution service verifies the choice against the owned RefactorKit session. Maven builds the selected module and its reactor dependencies from the project root; Gradle uses its selected project and source-set task dependencies. Run and Debug compile first, acquire fresh provider metadata after the build, and start the selected JDK with the ordered runtime classpath, including existing source-set outputs. Gradle prepares runtime artifacts through its own task dependency graph. Build for the standard Gradle test source set invokes the selected project’s `testClasses` task without running tests. When Run or Debug refreshes the context after compilation, a changed Gradle build root, logical project path or Gradle runtime JDK prevents launch. A declared resource output without resources may remain absent; an unavailable dependency JAR refuses runtime launch. Main and test source sets are supported, as are Gradle Build/Run/Debug for additional source sets. Custom Gradle Test, discovery and coverage operations first match compiled test directories. If multiple tasks share those directories, the mapping accepts only a task configured with the selected source set's runtime classpath, then validates its resolved paths before execution; remaining ambiguity is refused. Custom Maven source-set task mappings remain unavailable. The consumer accepts only RefactorKit's declared `main`, `test`, `integration-test` and `custom` source-set kinds; an unknown kind is refused instead of inferred from a directory name. Manual configuration retains the behavior in the following table. Native execution, discovery, coverage and captured-session verification is described in section 10.1. GUI qualification has its own narrower scope.

For synchronized Debug, the debugger captures the selected source set’s declared source and generated-source roots. It also captures roots from a dependency whose output directory occurs on the runtime classpath and belongs to a single source set. An evaluated Gradle context can also identify a project JAR on that classpath by its producing module and main source set. All entries for the archive path must agree on the provider, producer and fingerprint. Cross-module archives must also match the compile or runtime project dependencies published for the selected source set. If a declared runtime dependency has no corresponding classpath owner, the debugger withholds archive-derived source roots. Gradle test-result navigation checks the same facts before opening a declaration from a project archive. External artifacts attributed to the consumer and conflicting identities contribute no additional sources. A test worker may compile after debugger setup, so a provider-declared output can identify its sources before it exists. Application debugging obtains fresh runtime metadata after compilation.

The debugger fingerprints the captured sources and checks them again when binding breakpoints. Collection under a declared source root includes Java package names such as `build`, enforces traversal limits and refuses symbolic links. An ambiguous runtime source path leaves the source location unavailable. Maven dependency JARs, external library sources and custom runtime class loaders still need separate debugger qualification.

An included project can depend on an artifact substituted by another build in the surrounding composite. A context method that advertises `gradleBuildTreeProjectPath` supplies Gradle’s evaluated project path from the opened composite root when the IDE requests it. The IDE invokes the project’s qualified task from that root, preserving inclusion aliases and dependency substitution. Initialization scripts select their owning build and module before changing task behavior. Run and Debug compare the build-tree path again after compilation. Providers using the earlier context contract dispatch from the selected build directory. That earlier route supports a self-contained included build, while dependencies supplied only by the surrounding composite can fail resolution. A successful qualified launch can still be followed by a provider synchronization timeout. On Gradle 9.8.1 with the first build-tree path review candidate, a nested app using a library in its parent included build ran from the composite root, then repeated evaluation could time out after the JAR existed. A direct provider replay isolated the wait to Gradle’s configuration of the producer during dependency resolution in the export script. The corrected RefactorKit candidate exports the model after Gradle has prepared the task graph. The independent replay with an existing JAR and the packaged IDE workflow in section 10.1 both pass with that candidate.

Standard test execution, discovery and coverage use the selected module's test source set. An application-source choice resolves to the unique test source set published by RefactorKit; missing or ambiguous test choices are refused. Build of a selected test source set compiles its tests. Custom Gradle test execution, discovery and coverage use the explicitly selected source set and a uniquely matched Gradle `Test` task. Run with JFR is restricted to the selected main source set. Discovery uses the selected JDK and provider runtime classpath to inspect only the chosen test task's compiled outputs through Gradle's dry-run support; it does not run JUnit test bodies. Maven discovery first compiles the selected reactor and its test dependencies, then uses the selected JDK and provider runtime classpath to inspect only that test source set's compiled outputs. A manually configured Maven directory is compiled without recursing into child modules. Select a runnable module directory or synchronize the reactor in Java Project. Maven coverage report generation retains the captured repository and profile settings.

The dedicated Maven **Run integration tests** action invokes the full `verify` lifecycle so Failsafe can run integration tests and verify their outcome after project setup and teardown phases. Earlier lifecycle phases, including Surefire unit tests, also run. A class or method filter is passed through `it.test` for Failsafe; it does not filter the earlier unit-test phase. Failed-test reruns use the captured integration-test configuration. For synchronized Maven integration-test source sets, context v4 must attest exactly one complete Failsafe execution, its `integration-test` phase and `integration-test` plus `verify` goals, and one concrete `reportsDirectory`; the IDE uses that declared directory when collecting fresh XML reports. Missing, partial, ambiguous, unresolved, or unsafe report settings stop the operation before Maven starts. The IDE does not infer this kind from directory names or create or modify Failsafe configuration. Manual Maven integration tests retain the workspace-relative report-path setting.

The separate Maven **Run integration tests with coverage** action uses JaCoCo's integration agent and report goals during the same `verify` lifecycle. Because Surefire runs before Failsafe and both may use the configured test JVM argument, the resulting measurement covers all instrumented tests in that lifecycle, including unit tests and integration tests. The IDE reports this scope in Java Run and imports only fresh XML from `target/site/jacoco-it`; an older unit-test report cannot satisfy the integration coverage result.

Maven reactor support permits companion modules without tests. Tool completion and fresh test cases remain separate observations: the selected module's structured reports determine which tests executed. Missing or unchanged reports remain unavailable, and a requested selector without complete fresh results makes the IDE task fail even when Maven exits zero. Captured discovery selection and failed-test reruns preserve the original module, JDK, test JVM options and build settings and renew provider metadata before execution. A settings change or lost provider session refuses the repeated operation.

| Project type | Build                                       | Run                                                                                                        | Tests                                                                                                                                                                                                | Debug                                                             |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Plain JDK    | Compile Java sources with debug information | Compile and launch the selected main class                                                                 | Compile and run JUnit Platform/JUnit 4 tests with the ConsoleLauncher, or TestNG with its native runner, when the selected framework and libraries are supplied on the workspace-contained classpath | Compile and launch the selected jdb or JDI debugger               |
| Maven        | `compile`                                   | `compile exec:java`, or `exec:exec` with explicit application/JVM arguments, using the selected main class | `test`; integration tests use Failsafe `verify`                                                                                                                                                      | Compile, then debug with classes and configured runtime libraries |
| Gradle       | `classes`                                   | Application plugin's `run` task                                                                            | `test`                                                                                                                                                                                               | Compile, then debug with classes and configured runtime libraries |

Build and Run tests are separate commands. An optional test selector accepts a class name or `class#method`; Maven and Gradle also accept `*` wildcards, while plain-JDK JUnit and TestNG selections require an exact class or method. Maven delegates unit-test selectors through [Surefire's `test` property](https://maven.apache.org/surefire/maven-surefire-plugin/examples/single-test.html) and integration-test selectors through [Failsafe's `it.test` property](https://maven.apache.org/surefire/maven-failsafe-plugin/examples/single-test.html); Gradle delegates selectors through [test filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/java_testing.html#test_filtering), translating the method separator to a dot. Filtered Maven execution verifies that fresh reports contain selected tests. A nonzero compile or test outcome is presented as failure, not successful application execution. Ordinary Run tests preserves build-tool up-to-date/cache behavior.

After a test task completes, **Test results** presents suites, individual cases, durations and escaped failure details from fresh JUnit XML. Plain-JDK JUnit execution uses the [JUnit Platform ConsoleLauncher](https://docs.junit.org/5.14.1/running-tests/console-launcher.html); plain-JDK TestNG execution uses TestNG's native runner and JUnit XML reporter. Each runner writes to a unique directory for that run, which participates in the same freshness checks. The plain-JDK JUnit path supports JUnit Platform engines and JUnit 4 through a compatible Vintage engine. The TestNG path runs the supplied TestNG runtime. Both require the selected framework libraries on the workspace-contained classpath and neither provides coverage. Discovery inspects compiled classes using JUnit Platform, JUnit 4 and TestNG public APIs with the selected JDK 17 or later; it does not run test bodies, though a custom JUnit 4 runner may initialize. The user supplies the test libraries and, for JUnit, the ConsoleLauncher as workspace-contained classpath entries. Maven and Gradle continue to own their test execution and dependencies. See [TestNG's command-line and reporting documentation](https://testng.org/documentation.html). Results distinguish passed, failed, error, skipped and passed-after-retry outcomes. A reported case can open its test type through the initialized JDT LS workspace-symbol index when exactly one source declaration resolves inside the selected module. A provider-supplied package and type identity also resolves additional non-public classes declared in a differently named Java file. A conventional filename cannot override a contradictory package identity. Literal dollar signs in package and type identifiers remain intact. Nested binary class names, including Unicode Java identifiers, prefer the exact nested declaration and otherwise resolve to the unique containing top-level declaration in the same source file; truncated, stale or ambiguous results are refused. Gradle symbol lookup requires explicit, session-only authorization for JDT LS Gradle import; RefactorKit project synchronization does not grant it. For a failed or errored case, the IDE also reveals a stack-frame line only when the frame names the exact reported class, the matching Java source filename and a line inside the opened, saved buffer. The reader accepts both classic frames and the module/version and named-class-loader prefixes described by [Java’s `StackTraceElement` API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/StackTraceElement.html#toString()); those labels never supply source paths or establish module ownership. Dirty buffers, truncated, malformed, unmatched or out-of-range frames leave navigation at the resolved class declaration. For reactor-wide Maven results, a standard workspace-relative Surefire or Failsafe report directory selects the module in which JDT LS searches. When a parent and nested module both produced reports, the parent search excludes the nested module. The test's package and symbol identity still locate the source file. A configured Maven report also supplies module scope when its suite-level `basedir` agrees with the nearest Maven descriptor above the report and lies within the selected project. Other layouts and discovery retain the selected project scope. This line mapping identifies a source position in the saved buffer; it does not select a test method for execution. Focused unit tests cover runtime prefixes and refusal cases. Opt-in real-JDK tests verify `StackTraceElement` output and the throwing line of an actual named-module exception on JDK 21 and 25. Run them with `IDE_JAVA_TEST_NAVIGATION_JDK=/path/to/jdk pnpm exec vitest run apps/desktop/src/features/java-execution/javaTestSourceNavigation.jdk.test.ts`; they are skipped when no JDK is selected. The Linux release/no-bundle Maven and Gradle rerun scenarios on JDK 21 also execute the failing test body through a named class loader, preserve the JVM-generated `loader//` frame in the real JUnit report, and verify exact-line navigation, complete unchanged editor text, repair and save, rerun of only the repaired method with captured JVM/environment settings, restoration of the application draft and normal close with no owned process survivors. Full editor text is checked through native keyboard copy because Monaco virtualizes lines outside the viewport. The scenarios use JDT LS 1.63 on JDK 25 and the source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 r003 context provider; they qualify named-loader report navigation for the two tested fixtures. Native GUI navigation from named-module test reports, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. The process exit and reported cases remain separate facts: a successful tool task with absent, empty or unchanged reports does not become a green zero-test result. Reports are compared with a bounded inventory taken before execution; unchanged reports are omitted. Malformed fresh reports leave any readable cases explicitly partial, and interrupted tasks have unavailable results. This reports what the selected task produced, not discovery of all project tests or proof of full project coverage.

Gradle method-source navigation uses the compiled declaring class separately from the executing test class. When inspection with the test task’s JDK supplies code-source origins, the source action can locate an inherited declaration in a dependency module. These origins describe compiled inputs. The IDE refreshes provider-qualified project context without requesting Gradle evaluation, matches the executing output to one source set, and uses its runtime-classpath entries to identify the declaring source set. Directory origins must agree with that source set’s output directories. An archive must identify a separate producing module or source set; an external archive attributed to the consumer cannot authorize workspace-source navigation. JDT LS candidates are restricted to the producer’s own source and generated roots, excluding dependency analysis roots. The executing test must resolve to a class symbol. A different compiled declaring type can resolve to a class or interface symbol, with the same exact package, source-owner and uniqueness checks; a duplicate class/interface identity is refused. Workspace, context revision and reviewed saved buffers must remain current throughout navigation; unavailable ownership retains class navigation with an explanation. A dirty buffer prevents this saved-source review without discarding its edits. Rerun selection continues to use the executing subclass.

A read-only SDK query refuses its result when a saved source changes during the request. A complete provider `java.context.snapshotStale` refusal or a changed local saved-source check retires semantic context while retaining the live SDK session and evaluated Gradle model. A classified source-only notification can trigger the guarded read-only refresh described in [section 6.11](#611-java-compiler-checks); ordinary synchronization remains available when automatic refresh cannot run. Neither route evaluates build scripts, and the retired context cannot authorize another query. Unknown or malformed responses, changed SDK identities and refactoring failures still retire the session. Changed build inputs invalidate the evaluated model, and daemon loss also requires fresh synchronization; the person must use **Evaluate Gradle project** explicitly if only a partial Gradle context remains. The IDE does not evaluate build scripts as part of source navigation.

The discovered-test view supports case-insensitive search over display labels, class names and method names, plus a class/method filter. It keeps the full discovery counts visible and renders at most 100 selections per page in provider order. A visible method retains its class name when the class row is outside the current page or filter. Actions on discovered tests retain the test selection and launch settings from that discovery session. Java Run and saved coverage history use the discovery configuration name even if the person selects another configuration before launch. Maven and Gradle discoveries continue to offer coverage after the person selects a different launch configuration. A plain-JDK discovery has no coverage action. Filtering preserves the recorded results and the restrictions on partial or unavailable discovery. New discovery sessions reset the view controls. Component tests exercise the 10,000-selection limit, paging, partial-result admission, display context and exact run/coverage selection. The Linux release/no-bundle synchronized Maven and Gradle scenarios on JDK 21 verify filtering three discovered methods, an empty class view with unchanged totals, no test-body execution during filtering, and execution of only the selected method with the discovery session settings after the visible form is changed. Large-list native performance and broader framework/project layouts remain unqualified.

From a discovered class, **Open test class** uses the initialized JDT LS workspace-symbol index to open the unique declaration inside the module captured by discovery. The action is read-only and uses the same checks for stale, truncated or ambiguous results as test report navigation. Gradle lookup uses the explicit session-only JDT LS import authorization. Discovered method-name groups remain execution selectors and may represent more than one overload.

The test result view searches case names, class names, suite names, report paths and failure details using case-insensitive text matching. Outcome filters distinguish failures/errors, ordinary passes, skipped tests and passes after retry. The default order puts failures and errors first; report order and descending duration are also available, with unknown durations last. The view renders at most 100 case rows per page, preserving each case's suite and report path. Overall result counts, partial/unavailable status and the captured failed-test rerun selection remain unchanged by filtering or paging. A new execution starts with fresh view controls. Production component tests exercise the 10,000-case input limit, bounded rendering, page changes, metadata/detail search, duration ordering across suites and reset between sessions. A Linux release/no-bundle Maven and Gradle GUI scenario verifies search, outcome filtering and clearing the query against real reported cases while retaining complete counts and rerun admission. The large-case rendering bound is covered by component tests, not a native large-project benchmark.

Default report discovery searches the selected project and its subdirectories for Maven `target/surefire-reports`, Maven `target/failsafe-reports` during the integration-test action, or Gradle `build/test-results`, reading `TEST-*.xml`. Plain-JDK ConsoleLauncher and TestNG XML reports are read from the unique report directory created under `.ide/java/test-results` for that run. Maven reads the direct XML reports in each producer directory; nested TestNG `junitreports` copies are excluded to avoid counting the same execution twice or losing Surefire's JVM properties. Gradle also reads its task subdirectories.
