For a nested module selected through synchronized Java Project on Unix, the Maven 3.9 launcher keeps upstream modules in the reactor for compilation and dependency resolution. Test, integration test, coverage, debug and captured reruns then execute Surefire and Failsafe suites only in the selected module. The selected module retains its test filter or TestNG suite and qualified fork JVM settings. Configured workspace-relative report directories replace Maven/Gradle defaults; for plain JDK they are scanned alongside the session-specific test-runner directory. A custom Maven directory must identify the actual report producer directory, because its child directories are not scanned. Only regular workspace-contained reports without symlinks or hard links are read. Inspection is bounded to 512 files, 2 MiB per file, 8 MiB aggregate/presentation, 10,000 cases, 2,048 suites and 16 KiB of detail per case. Directory traversal also has depth, entry and cooperative time limits; a blocked operating-system filesystem call cannot be interrupted by that time check. XML document types and external entities are refused. Limit or freshness failures are visible and do not fabricate test success or prevent the underlying build task from running.

Test-source navigation belongs to the displayed report and its navigation action. Replacing the report, replacing the action or closing the results panel retires the navigation guard. Late completions cannot change the replacement report's pending state or error, and document opening and method reveal check that guard before changing the editor. JDT LS progress updates refresh the navigation implementation without retiring an action in the same workspace and language-service generation; replacing that session retires it. The panel does not cancel native execution or discard editor changes. Focused production-panel and method-navigation tests cover report replacement, late success/failure and retired editor navigation; those races have not been qualified in the native GUI. After this change, the Linux release/no-bundle framework-test profile passes ordinary source navigation and captured failed-test Debug with Jupiter/Gradle and TestNG/Maven, including a passing method inherited from an interface in another Gradle module. The tested fixtures use JDK 21 and preserve source/build inputs, close normally and leave no process survivors after cleanup. Report replacement during a held source query remains covered by the production-panel tests rather than this GUI profile.

An explicit Gradle **Run tests** action requests [`--rerun-tasks`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/command_line_interface.html#sec:rerun_tasks), including for an unchanged successful suite. The purpose is a new execution with fresh reports, rather than reuse of an earlier up-to-date or cached result. Gradle also re-executes the selected task's dependencies; this can take longer than an incremental build and does not delete generated outputs. Coverage and failed-test reruns retain the same execution policy. Project-disabled, skipped or empty test tasks still produce unavailable or incomplete results when no fresh cases exist; a successful build-tool exit alone is not a passing test suite.

**Rerun failed tests** requires complete fresh failure/error results, current workspace trust and the still-current completed native session. It saves dirty buffers again and uses that session's project, build tool and launch settings, rather than later form edits. Literal Java method names produce class/method selections; descriptive or parameterized names rerun their whole class, as explained beside the control. Missing usable class names, partial results and excessive selections refuse automatic rerun. Maven receives comma-separated selectors; Gradle receives repeated `--tests` and [`--rerun-tasks`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/command_line_interface.html#sec:rerun_tasks) so its failed selections execute again. For a reactor-wide Maven Run configuration with conventional Surefire or Failsafe reports, or configured reports with corroborated module ownership, the IDE retains the reporting module for each failure. On Unix with Maven 3.9, when the same filter would rerun cases in another module or failed modules require different filters, the IDE keeps the reactor and uses its private Maven test launcher to give each selected module its own filter. Dependencies can be built without installing their artifacts into the local repository. The launcher skips the test goals in unselected modules and retains earlier Surefire execution in the selected modules during Failsafe `verify`. Maven continues to own the build and test lifecycles. The IDE requires fresh reports from each selected module before confirming the rerun. **Rerun session** retains the module filters. On Windows a common filter can still select modules whose dependencies are already resolvable. When the module cannot be established for a configured report, rerun uses the captured project-wide selection. If that selection would also match a passing or skipped test in another report directory, the IDE requires a new run from the individual module. A new session replaces the old one, and stale polls or workspace continuations cannot replace its results. This path consumes build-tool reports and does not create a competing semantic project model in the IDE. Broader discovery and framework/report-format qualification remain planned; the measured coverage scope is described below.

The implemented coverage interaction is shown in the [C4 runtime diagram](docs/c4/runtime-java-coverage.md).

**Run tests with coverage** runs the selected Maven or Gradle test scope with JaCoCo 0.8.15 and displays measured instruction, branch and line counters, source-file identities and per-line instruction/branch counts in Java Run. A zero denominator has no percentage; partly executed lines count as covered while branch counters expose missed alternatives. Test failures can retain a complete measurement. Rerun failed tests retains coverage and the completed session's captured launch settings, and collects a new measurement for those selections. Coverage uses the same trust, explicit save, selected JDK, literal test JVM options, filtering, process ownership and stale-workspace guards as Run tests. Plain-JDK coverage is unavailable because that runner has no built-in test provider.

Maven invokes the pinned [JaCoCo prepare-agent goal](https://www.jacoco.org/jacoco/trunk/doc/prepare-agent-mojo.html) before `test` and the pinned report goal afterward, including after failed tests. Its standard generated `target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml` reports remain build outputs; discovery is limited to the selected project. A private execution-data file and a new JaCoCo session identifier distinguish each execution. Explicit test JVM options use Surefire late property evaluation to combine the owned agent with the private argument file. A fixed Surefire `argLine` that omits the agent property, in-process testing or conflicting project instrumentation can prevent measurement; the IDE reports unavailable coverage and a failed coverage action even if the tool exits zero. It does not rewrite the POM to repair such settings.

For Maven Failsafe, **Run integration tests with coverage** invokes [JaCoCo's integration agent](https://www.jacoco.org/jacoco/trunk/doc/prepare-agent-integration-mojo.html), `verify` and [integration report](https://www.jacoco.org/jacoco/trunk/doc/report-integration-mojo.html). The integration report reads Maven's standard `target/jacoco-it.exec`, so the IDE removes that project's prior execution file before starting and assigns the new run a unique session identifier. Surefire and Failsafe append their forked JVM data to that fresh file. The IDE labels this full lifecycle scope in the result view and only imports `target/site/jacoco-it/jacoco.xml` reports for this operation. Fixed argument lines, non-forked tests and conflicting project instrumentation can still make the measurement unavailable.

Gradle receives a private initialization script using the [JaCoCo plugin](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/jacoco_plugin.html). For manual project execution it configures Java projects below the selected directory and their ordinary `test` tasks. With synchronized project context it maps the selected module and test source set, resolves the source set runtime dependency graph when its test task starts, and produces a separate production `main` report for every Java project dependency represented in the selected build or a direct or nested included build. These reports share the selected test run's private execution data and JaCoCo classpath, so classes loaded from a project dependency are measured without running that dependency's tests. Synchronized Gradle reporting runs in a second Gradle invocation after the test process exits, including when tests fail, so included-build reports consume completed execution data. For a synchronized custom test source set, the IDE matches compiled test directories and, when outputs are shared, requires a candidate configured with the source set's runtime classpath; it validates the resolved paths before execution and reports production code rather than test code. An opt-in real Gradle 9.8.0/JDK 25 integration test covers a synchronized `integrationTest` source set and a three-build dependency chain containing the selected application, a direct included library and a nested included library; it verifies that each production report maps to its workspace-relative source root. This verifies build-tool execution and reporting, not native UI or RefactorKit project-context behavior. Separate Linux release/no-bundle GUI qualification with Gradle 9.8, JDK 21 and a daemon advertising `project.context` covers one included-build app and library, both production reports, and navigation to the measured library source with line decoration. Larger and mixed-language module graphs remain unqualified. Manual Gradle execution uses test-task finalizers; synchronized project coverage runs its aggregate report task after the test process, including after failures. `--rerun-tasks` prevents reuse of prior test execution data. Synchronized project reports share private execution data, while manual project reports use per-project destinations; every XML output has a unique path. The IDE sets the agent version, output destination and session identifier for this action; arbitrary project coverage configuration and other custom test-task layouts are not generally qualified. Build descriptors and source files are unchanged apart from the person's explicit source saves.

Only a complete bounded report carrying this execution's JaCoCo session identifier can supply measurements. Older, missing, malformed, linked or escaped reports cannot become a green zero-code measurement. Valid subsets are explicitly partial and the coverage action fails; interruption clears complete results. Import limits are 128 reports, 8 MiB per report, 32 MiB aggregate XML/presentation, 2,000 source files and 100,000 measured lines, with bounded directory depth and entries. The parser permits only JaCoCo's standard document-type declaration and never resolves external entities. Coverage describes compiled production code at execution time. With an available synchronized Java Project context, the IDE can open a measured line and show covered, uncovered or partial line decorations only when package/name maps to one declared main source path that was already open at the start of the run. For Maven's standard JaCoCo and Failsafe report paths, the report directory identifies the owning module. The IDE matches it to the synchronized module root before using the package and filename, so matching names in different modules can open their respective sources. The same rule applies when the workspace-root reactor's aggregator POM has no Java module entry. A report without a standard path or a known module can still supply counters. The controller retains that operation's source roots, captures the open editor buffers after saving, and suppresses source navigation if those buffers changed before the run completed. Context schemas v3–v7 supply workspace-relative roots through the native adapter, so coverage mapping does not add the selected project directory again or require Gradle identity fields for Maven sources. Legacy v1/v2 contexts retain their project-relative path interpretation. A project at the workspace root can open a measured source when the report and provider context identify that root and the usual source checks pass. The Linux x86-64 AppImage verifies this in a single-module Maven and Gradle project on X11 and KWin Wayland. Each fixture opens the source before running coverage, passes one real JUnit test and opens the measured file with covered-line decorations. The same coverage profile exercises both projects. A separate source-association check runs a real Maven reactor and reads the RefactorKit project context for its two modules, one of them nested. Both generate a standard JaCoCo report for `pkg/Shared.java` with different measured lines. The check passes both report entries and the provider context to the IDE's source resolver. It verifies each module's path when both paths are supplied as open and withholds the other link when only one is supplied. The packaged project-coverage profile passes on X11 and KWin Wayland with the same AppImage and RefactorKit runtime. The six scenarios cover synchronized Maven and Gradle modules, both build tools at the workspace root, Gradle dependencies and a custom Gradle test source set with an ambiguous candidate task. For both workspace-root projects, the GUI check adopts a changed disk revision and verifies that the link and decorations stay retired while the counters remain visible. It restores the original source and verifies that the old link stays retired. Generated-source association is unavailable. The IDE ties each source link and line decoration to the saved editor buffer captured for that run. Editing the buffer, adopting a disk revision or closing and reopening the file retires its link and decorations for that measurement. Undo or restoring the original text alone leaves them retired. Other unchanged buffers can retain their own links after a completed run, and the measured counters remain visible. Missing, ambiguous or unverified source mappings leave the counters available without source links or decorations. Partial project context continues to refuse source navigation for Gradle dependency reports. This does not prove external build inputs remained unchanged or bind arbitrary multi-module reports to source. A focused native Gradle 9.8/JDK 21 GUI scenario now maps coverage for one selected app and its included-build library, opens `Greeter.java`, and verifies covered-line decoration. Larger and mixed-language graphs remain unqualified.

Java Run saves the last ten completed JaCoCo measurement summaries locally for each workspace. The measurement and baseline selectors display the test filter passed to the build tool, including the captured selection for a discovered test or failed-test rerun. They show up to three selectors, the count of additional selectors, and the synchronized Gradle source set when the planner explicitly mapped its test task. A run without an IDE filter still follows the build tool’s test settings. Previously saved measurements display unavailable selection details. Reopening the same workspace restores its own history; changing workspace loads the selected workspace history while stale execution replies remain rejected by workspace generation. Stored summaries are limited to 128 KiB, validated before use, and contain counters and descriptive metadata rather than source text or live execution authority. Malformed, oversized or unsupported saved data produces an explicit restoration error. If saving fails, the current measurements remain available in memory and the IDE reports that they were not saved. Each entry records its configuration name, coverage operation, completion time, build-tool outcome, report and source-file counts, test count when available, and measured line, branch and instruction counters. Completed failed tests can still supply measurements; partial results remain visibly partial and cannot be compared. Running, stopped and unavailable results do not create history entries. History survives new runs, panel changes and application restarts, but never grants source links, editor decorations, workspace trust or a restored execution session. Distinct runs remain separate after an application restart even when native execution numbers are reused. **Clear saved coverage history** removes the summaries from memory and local storage; repeated updates for the cleared completed run cannot recreate it. A failed deletion is reported because saved data may return on reopening.

The coverage history panel compares two complete measurements from the same project directory, build tool and coverage operation. It shows both covered/total counts and percentages, plus changes in percentage points; an empty denominator has no percentage or delta. Different test selections, modules, compiler inputs and compiled code can affect these measurements, so the panel does not present a percentage change as proof of a regression. Focused production-hook and panel tests cover bounded retention, immutable summaries, workspace retirement, partial results, baseline filtering and percentage calculations. The Linux release/no-bundle native JaCoCo profile verifies Maven 3.9.11 and Gradle 9.8.1 with JDK 21: single-test and full-test runs produce 50% and 100% branch measurements, and the history panel shows +50 percentage points. Both scenarios also verify failed-test measurements, saved-draft reruns, interruption without a new complete history entry, preserved source/build inputs, normal window closure, restored scenario environments and no surviving processes after runner cleanup. Both native scenarios also close and reopen the application, restore the four measured runs without restoring a current report or execution trust, compare saved measurements, add a fifth run after the native execution numbering restarts, and verify that explicit deletion remains effective after another restart. The same Maven and Gradle scenarios pass on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland. The history shows the single-method selector for the initial run and captured repetitions, identifies the run without an IDE filter, and retains those details after restart. A separate packaged Gradle case on Wayland verifies the mapped integrationTest source set in the history. Comparison is scoped to the recorded project directory, build tool and operation.

Each saved Java configuration can specify optional minimum line, branch and instruction coverage percentages from 0 to 100 with up to two decimal places. An empty value disables that counter. Coverage runs capture the selected thresholds before source-save preparation; failed-test reruns retain the original execution thresholds even after configuration changes. Discovered-test coverage captures and validates the thresholds from the currently selected configuration before saving sources. Test execution still uses the launch settings captured during discovery. Invalid or incomplete percentages prevent a coverage launch while ordinary build and test operations remain available. The IDE checks complete JaCoCo counters automatically using unrounded ratios. Partial, unavailable, interrupted and zero-denominator measurements cannot pass an enabled check. Build-tool results retain their actual execution state and exit code; the coverage threshold result is shown separately with its captured requirements and measured counts. Thresholds are IDE configuration settings and do not modify project build descriptors. Unit tests verify validation, storage and duplication, captured execution settings, failed-test reruns and source-save admission. The Linux native Maven and Gradle coverage scenarios verify a 75% branch threshold failing at 50%, passing at 100%, retaining 75% during a failed-test rerun after the form was changed to 40%, and becoming unavailable after interruption. Other project layouts, packaged applications and operating systems remain unqualified.

**Discover tests** compiles the selected Maven or Gradle project and presents runner-provided class and method identities before test-body execution. It uses the same explicit trust, save-before-execution, selected JDK, environment, Stop and workspace/session guards as other Java tasks. Discovery has its own status and console; it does not present skipped dry-run reports as passing test execution. Choosing **Run class** or **Run method group** saves current edits and uses the still-current completed discovery session's project, tool, JDK, environment and test JVM options. Later form edits do not replace these captured settings. A new task retires the previous discovery selections. A method selection matches its name rather than a Java parameter signature. The panel identifies it as a method-name group: Run, Debug and Coverage target every matching overload and parameterized invocation, not one display label. Distinct runner display names sharing that selector are retained in deterministic order; the panel shows and searches at most 32 names per group and discloses the total when more were returned. These are discovery labels, not an execution count. Manually entered `class#method` filters have the same name-based scope. Individual parameterized or dynamic invocations are not independently selectable here.

For a conventional Maven launch, the IDE invokes `test-compile` and obtains the resolved test classpath from the pinned Exec Maven Plugin 3.5.0 using its [test classpath scope](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/examples/example-exec-or-java-change-classpath-scope.html). Maven supplies the effective `testOutputDirectory` as the only discovery root for that conventional launch. A launch captured from that discovery remains nonrecursive for tests, debugging, coverage and subsequent reruns. A new manual reactor test session retains Maven's recursive lifecycle. Main classes and dependencies remain on the test classpath for loading and linking. A synchronized Maven launch uses the provider's revalidated test runtime classpath and selected module output roots. The Maven and plain-JDK paths compile the IDE's helper in private storage using the selected project JDK, then launch it on that JDK to query public [JUnit 4 runner descriptions](https://junit.org/junit4/javadoc/latest/org/junit/runner/Request.html), [JUnit Platform engine discovery](https://docs.junit.org/5.12.1/api/org.junit.platform.engine/org/junit/platform/engine/EngineDiscoveryRequest.html) and [TestNG method interception and dry-run](https://testng.org/documentation.html). Only workspace-contained compiled directory roots on that resolved classpath are scanned; dependency JARs provide frameworks, not extra project test roots. TestNG's public test context supplies enabled method identities and their concrete test classes, including dependent/inherited methods and class-level annotations. The helper returns an empty intercepted execution list and enables TestNG's documented dry-run to collect metadata without calling test bodies. An identifiable TestNG version of at least 6.14 is required before initializing its runner. This is compiled-classpath discovery: Surefire include/exclude patterns, groups, suite XML, engine configuration and `argLine` are not applied. The discovery JVM receives the IDE's test JVM options directly; successful discovery does not prove Surefire will honor them during a later Run tests. Missing compatible providers or a failed helper return unavailable discovery rather than a fabricated list.

Running a Maven TestNG selection from this list supplies a private suite XML through [Surefire's TestNG suite configuration](https://maven.apache.org/components/surefire-archives/surefire-3.5.3/maven-surefire-plugin/examples/testng.html). It identifies the concrete class and escapes literal method names, including `$`; inherited methods therefore retain their executable owning class. The native completed discovery session chooses this route, and client requests cannot select a different provider. The generated suite contains no document type declaration and does not edit the project's descriptor or suite files. It replaces an overridable `surefire.suiteXmlFiles` property and omits the competing `test` property. Fixed project suite configuration, suite parameters, groups and arbitrary provider combinations remain outside this focused qualification. Manually entered filters retain the ordinary build-tool selector path.

Gradle discovers through its configured default `Test` task's public [dry-run support](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/java_testing.html#sec:test_dry_run), retaining task dependencies, runtime classpath, include/exclude settings and test JVM configuration. The task is rerun to avoid an earlier cached result. The IDE finalizes the dry-run property before task execution; a project attempting to change it is refused. Public [test descriptors](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/api/tasks/testing/TestDescriptor.html) supply JUnit labels and class names; Gradle 9.4 or later can supply public [method sources](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/api/tasks/testing/source/MethodSource.html). Earlier descriptors support method selection only when the runner gives a literal method name; descriptive names receive class selection, without guessing a method from display text. For TestNG, a temporary listener is compiled against the task's existing test classpath through the public JavaCompile task and added through [TestNGOptions.listeners](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/api/tasks/testing/testng/TestNGOptions.html). Public TestNG callbacks provide actual class/method identities even when Gradle displays parameterized case labels. The listener confirms TestNG's version and dry-run property; [Gradle requires TestNG 6.14 or later](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/api/tasks/testing/Test.html#getDryRun%28%29). Gradle's TestNG dry-run can initialize data providers. Constructors, factories, project listeners and custom runners can also initialize project code during discovery; trust remains necessary. Discovery does not replace RefactorKit's semantic project model.

Private discovery output is correlated to its owned session and bounded to 2 MiB and 10,000 selectable entries. Linked output, malformed/oversized data, missing output even after tool exit zero, and stale sessions are refused. The UI preserves the actual tool exit, distinguishes collecting, complete, partial and unavailable discovery, and disables automatic selection from incomplete discovery. Unsupported sources or class names make discovery partial. Helpers, listener classes, metadata and selected TestNG suite files use private directories and remain owned until their task finishes; cleanup removes those owned paths without following redirected output directories. Crash leftovers have the same limitation as launch settings below. Other test tasks, complete reactor/framework configuration, additional runner versions, coverage and the OS matrix remain M4 qualification work.

Automatic detection checks build descriptors in the selected directory; it is not full project import/synchronization. A Unix project wrapper is preferred, searching ancestor directories only within the authorized workspace, otherwise installed tools are used. External project directories and escaping wrapper symlinks are refused. Selecting a Maven module does not build or install its reactor dependencies automatically.

When a synchronized Gradle project exposes additional Java source sets, **Build**, **Run** and **Debug** can target the selected set. The build uses its provider-declared `classesTaskName`; Run and Debug also use that set's runtime classpath. For **Run tests**, **Discover tests** and **Run tests with coverage**, the native service accepts a custom set only when exactly one Gradle `Test` task uses the selected set's compiled class directories and that task's classpath contains its provider-declared runtime classpath. The selected test filter and test JVM options are applied to execution; ambiguous task mappings and mismatched classpaths fail closed. The selected task runs on every invocation so its reports or discovery data belong to the current request. Discovery uses Gradle's dry-run support and does not run JUnit test bodies; coverage attaches JaCoCo to the mapped task and reports against the selected source set. For Maven, the IDE requests context v4 before integration-test execution and requires the provider's one complete Failsafe execution and concrete report directory; other operations for this source set and arbitrary Maven `custom` source sets remain refused. The IDE rechecks the selected project context after compilation before launching Run or Debug. Real-tool checks use a Gradle multi-project, RefactorKit context and JDK 21: the `smoke` source set verifies Run and a JDI source breakpoint, while `integrationTest` verifies one filtered JUnit method, its JVM option and environment, a repeated invocation with fresh results, discovery of both methods without executing either body, selection of one discovered method, positive JaCoCo instruction counts for `SmokeTest.java` while excluding its companion method, and refusal of ambiguous or mismatched tasks. These checks exercise the native execution service. A focused Linux GUI scenario verifies **Build** through `:app:integrationTestClasses`, **Run** using `pkg.IntegrationRunner` compiled in that source set, **Discover tests** reporting its one selectable method without running the test body, and **Run tests** for one `integrationTest` source set. The workflow synchronizes the selected project context after compilation before the next operation; section 10.1 records its scope. A separate GUI scenario verifies custom-source-set coverage. A companion JDI GUI scenario sets a breakpoint in `IntegrationRunner.main`, verifies suspension and continuation, checks the selected JDK and runtime classpath, and confirms debuggee exit. Together, these stories qualify one `integrationTest` source set only; other task mappings, project layouts and operating systems remain unqualified. RefactorKit's Build Model SPI defines the `INTEGRATION_TEST` and `CUSTOM` kinds and typed source-set DTOs. The effective Maven provider classifies `INTEGRATION_TEST` only for the qualified same-scope Build Helper/Failsafe shape. Its context-v4 acceptance covers configured execution, selector and report metadata plus partial, ambiguous and inactive cases. The synchronized Maven GUI story for one Build Helper/Failsafe source set passes with a v4-capable daemon; broader provider accuracy and project layouts remain unqualified. The [Java project execution interaction](docs/c4/runtime-java-project-execution.md) shows the boundary.

For a Gradle composite, the IDE uses the build root and project path supplied by RefactorKit to target the selected project, including a project whose source directory lies outside the included build root. It uses that identity for Run, test discovery and execution, coverage, debugging, Clean and Rebuild. If the provider omits the project or either part of its identity, the IDE cannot select it for execution. Both omissions occurred with earlier provider builds. See [section 6.8](#68-java-project-context) for task selection and [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope) for the tested combinations.

Gradle owns build-script evaluation. The native GUI acceptance also passes for a conventional two-module Java project configured with `settings.gradle.kts` and root, app and library `build.gradle.kts` files. After explicit Gradle evaluation, the synchronized module selector includes `library / main`; Java Run selects `app / test`, whose task compiles and runs against the library project dependency. This does not qualify arbitrary Kotlin DSL logic, plugin combinations or project layouts.

**Launch settings** accepts literal application arguments, application and test JVM options, child-process environment overrides and an optional absolute full-JDK directory. Each argument has its own row, preserving empty values, spaces, quotes, backslashes and line breaks. Arguments apply to Run and Debug; no rows preserve build-tool argument defaults except Maven Run with explicit JVM options or an application working directory. Environment values, including empty values, apply to the child compiler/build tool/application/debugger and inherit other IDE environment values. Names must be valid and unique; `JAVA_HOME` and `IDE_JAVA_HOME` overrides are refused in favor of the JDK field. The resolved selection is shown in the panel and frozen when the native session starts. Plain-JDK compiler/runtime/debugger paths and the build-tool launcher `JAVA_HOME` follow that selection; build-tool project toolchains can select a different compiler/runtime. The chooser does not synchronize JDT LS or RefactorKit project metadata. Argument-file secret management remains planned.

**Application working directory** sets where application Run, Run with JFR and Debug resolve relative files. Leave it blank to use the selected project/module directory, enter `.` for the workspace root, or enter an existing workspace-relative directory. Spaces, quotes and Unicode are preserved. Absolute paths, traversal and links outside the active workspace are refused. Build, tests, coverage and discovery retain the project directory, so an unfinished application-directory draft does not block them. Saved configurations and captured-session Rerun/Restart retain this setting. The native service resolves the directory before preparation and rechecks it before application launch; a changed selection refuses execution.

Plain-JDK and debugger application processes start in the selected application directory. Manual Maven Run with an explicit directory compiles first, rechecks the directory and then forks the selected Java executable through the Exec plugin; it no longer uses Maven's in-process `exec:java` route for that case. Manual Gradle Run configures the selected `JavaExec` task and rechecks the directory immediately before its actions. Project plugin/task configuration can still affect execution; the qualified conventional layouts are described in section 10.1. Synchronized-project launch applies the directory to the JVM after build and fresh provider-context validation, without changing RefactorKit's semantic project model. Its real-provider and focused Linux native GUI qualification is described in section 10.1.

**Application JVM options** applies each row as one literal option to Run and the debuggee JVM, for example `-Xmx512m`, `-Dmode=local` or `--add-opens=java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED`. Values containing spaces, quotes, backslashes, Unicode and line breaks stay within their option; empty system-property values are supported. Options requiring values use a single `--option=value` row. Incomplete rows remain editable in stored drafts and refuse Run/Debug before source-save preparation; their application-only syntax does not block Build or Run tests. Text and size limits still apply to all operations. Main-class, classpath and alternative-entry launcher selectors are refused in favor of the dedicated controls; the selected JDK validates other supported options. Build retains its project JVM settings; Run tests uses the separate test JVM configuration below. Gradle combines the public [`JavaExec.jvmArguments`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/dsl/org.gradle.api.tasks.JavaExec.html#org.gradle.api.tasks.JavaExec:jvmArguments) property with the additional options, preserving project defaults. Maven uses a separate selected Java process whenever JVM options are present; application arguments then come only from the IDE rows, rather than the Exec plugin's configured argument defaults. With neither application arguments nor JVM options, the existing Maven `exec:java` path remains. Broader version/project qualification remains planned.

**Run with JFR** starts the selected main application with the selected JDK's `profile` Flight Recorder configuration and dumps the recording when the JVM exits. It is available for JDK 11 or later when that JDK provides `profile.jfc` and the `jfr` tool. Plain-JDK, manual Maven/Gradle and synchronized main-source launches use the same application JVM option; test source sets, test JVMs, external attached processes and debugging are not profiled by this action. The IDE creates a unique, workspace-contained `.ide/flight-recordings/<id>/recording.jfr` path under the selected project and displays it in the session after launch. The JVM filename is relative to the actual application working directory, so a separate application directory does not relocate the recording or prevent JVM startup. JFR filename syntax is separate from Java process argument syntax: paths containing commas or one quote style are quoted for JFR. If the relative destination contains both quote styles, control characters or the [JFR filename substitutions](https://github.com/openjdk/jdk/blob/master/src/java.base/share/man/java.md) `%p` or `%t`, Run with JFR refuses before application launch. Choosing a working directory inside the project avoids incorporating ancestor names in that relative destination. A completed session reports the path only if a nonempty recording was written. For the current trusted Run session, **Analyze recording** invokes `jfr summary` from the selected JDK and displays recording version, chunk count, start time, duration, and each event type's recorded count and byte size. The table can be filtered by event type name. For a selected type, **Inspect** invokes the selected JDK's `jfr print` and shows event start time, duration and thread name when present, plus selected non-metadata payload fields. Each event returns at most 16 fields, with serialized values bounded to 256 UTF-8 bytes and 4 KiB total payload per event; shortened or omitted values are identified. When the event records a stack trace, the row shows at most 32 frames with class, method, line number and frame kind; shortened traces are identified. Timeline output is limited to 16 MiB and 20 seconds, and the UI shows at most 1,000 events; the timeline read is rejected if the workspace or session changes. Native summary and timeline commands dispatch filesystem and tool-process work to the blocking worker pool, keeping those waits off Tauri’s main and asynchronous executor threads. Summary reads retain a 15-second deadline and timeline reads a 20-second deadline. A read already issued can finish or reach its deadline after Rerun; the service rechecks the workspace and exact session before returning its data and refuses results for a replaced session. The recording remains readable with the selected JDK's `jfr` command or another JFR viewer. Rerun and Restart retain the captured profiling choice and allocate a new recording destination for the replacement process. Once a new session is adopted, the controller clears the previous summary, timeline and their pending state; late responses from the replaced session cannot replace current recording data. Real JDK 21 checks pass for plain-JDK and manual Maven/Gradle launches, and synchronized Maven/Gradle main-source launches with RefactorKit project context. A focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario verifies trusted launch, readable recording metadata through `jfr`, the in-IDE event summary, filtering, a bounded per-type timeline, event payload fields, sampled stack frames and clean application shutdown. Installer and other-operating-system qualification remain separate.

The JFR summary and timeline use the selected JDK's `jfr` executable. On Linux, their subprocess launcher removes a Python home that points inside the running AppImage and filters AppImage entries from the Python search path. This allows a JDK launcher wrapper to use the host interpreter while preserving external Python search directories.

**Test JVM options** configures the selected build-tool test process independently of application Run/Debug options. Rows preserve literal values with the same text and size bounds as application JVM options. Incomplete test-option drafts refuse Run tests and Discover tests before source-save preparation and remain unused by Build, Run and Debug. With no rows, project defaults remain. Gradle adds the options through the public [`Test.jvmArgs`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/dsl/org.gradle.api.tasks.testing.Test.html#org.gradle.api.tasks.testing.Test:jvmArgs%28java.lang.Iterable%29) API, retaining other project settings; explicit heap or property options can override their corresponding defaults. Maven supplies a private Java argument file through Surefire's [`argLine`](https://maven.apache.org/surefire/maven-surefire-plugin/test-mojo.html#argLine) user property. This replaces an overridable project `argLine`; required agent options must be included explicitly. Fixed plugin configuration and in-process tests can ignore that property. The IDE confirms the argument file's identifying system property in every fresh populated Surefire suite before admitting the requested configuration. Missing, stale, malformed or incomplete reports, or omitted properties, leave that configuration unconfirmed. The activity then shows a configuration failure while preserving the build tool's actual exit code and readable test results; passing cases remain observations of that tool execution. Automatic failure rerun refuses an unconfirmed configuration. For confirmed configurations, rerun retains the original test JVM options rather than later form edits. This report check is for trusted build-tool execution, and does not override fixed Surefire configuration or implement test discovery.

The Maven test and coverage route that supplies explicit Test JVM options through `argLine` requires a test JVM that supports Java launcher argument files. Temurin 8 treats the argument-file reference as a class name and the affected test suite never starts. Offline checks with Maven 3.9.11 on JDK 21, Surefire 3.5.3 and Failsafe 3.5.4 verify this for a fork selected through either `jvm` or `jdkToolchain`. The default fork runs on JDK 21. An explicit `jvm` pointing to JDK 21 also takes precedence over a Java 8 toolchain in these fixtures, and both JDK 21 cases accept the argument file. In the integration fixture, `verify` can pass Surefire on JDK 21 and fail when starting Failsafe on Java 8 in the same module. The control executions pass with a Maven user property and preserve the original POMs and tests. The fixtures use a separate Maven toolchains file and impose no Java 8 limitation on project-default testing.

RefactorKit 0.8.0 returns complete fork-mode and empty `argLine` facts under v7 for these fixtures. Effective JVM selection remains unavailable in those facts. The IDE needs it for each execution because the build JVM and successive test forks can use different Java versions. JVM selection needs provenance for explicit `jvm` and toolchain inputs, plus an unavailable result when Maven's selection cannot be resolved. A command-line `-Djvm` also fails to replace a fixed plugin `jvm` in the explicit-JVM fixture.

When RefactorKit advertises the experimental `project.context.v7.testJvmSelection` capability, synchronized Maven test, test debugging and coverage launches with IDE test JVM options request execution-specific JVM facts. The supplemental response must match the ordinary v7 context, including its execution identities and snapshot. Java Run checks the installed Java release of the build JVM or the explicit fork executable for each relevant execution in the reactor scope. Providers without the supplemental method use the existing v7 settings and report verification. If the provider reports complete `jdkToolchain` criteria without an executable, Java Run lets Maven resolve the criteria immediately before the affected execution. The provider can also identify a build-level selection declared by Maven Toolchains. Java Run asks Maven for the active build toolchain immediately before each test execution. If the selecting goal has not run in the requested lifecycle, the test uses the JVM running Maven unless another test-level selector applies. The IDE refuses unqualified selector metadata before starting Maven. Failsafe can require a matching toolchain before it uses an explicit `jvm`, even when that explicit executable takes precedence for the fork itself.

On Unix with Maven 3.9, Java Run uses a private Maven [EventSpy extension](https://maven.apache.org/ref/3.9.11/maven-core/apidocs/org/apache/maven/eventspy/EventSpy.html) when the synchronized reactor has a confirmed Java 8 fork, a project-defined `argLine`, or a test JVM selected by a plugin or build-level toolchain. The extension checks the module directory, plugin version, execution ID, goal and active fork selector. For a plugin-level `jdkToolchain` it checks that the effective criteria still match the provider's result. It obtains both plugin-level and build-level toolchains through Maven's toolchain manager. If Maven finds no match, the affected tests stop before their fork. Earlier Maven phases can already have produced outputs. For Java 8 it substitutes a private launcher that passes the IDE options as separate JVM arguments. For Java 9 and later it appends a private argument file to that execution's `argLine`, while Maven retains the original executable and fork command. Both paths preserve project options and support late property expansion in the Maven plugins. Session-owned launch files are kept in private temporary storage. A stale or unexpected execution fails before its tests start. Existing Maven extension class-path overrides remain unsupported for this route.

Linux service verification uses an isolated RefactorKit 0.8.0 preview, offline Maven 3.9.11 and 3.9.16, Surefire 3.5.3 and Failsafe 3.5.4. The checks cover a JDK 21 Maven build and Surefire fork with an explicit Java 8 Failsafe fork, both forks inheriting Maven's Java 8 JVM, and integration coverage on Java 8 and JDK 21 with a project-defined `argLine`. The JDK 21 case exercises late property expansion alongside the IDE options and the JaCoCo agent. The Java 8 fork observes the requested heap limit, a literal JVM property containing whitespace, quotes, a backslash and Unicode, and the project's JVM property. A separate case verifies that Maven reports a missing toolchain before Failsafe starts, even when Failsafe has an explicit JDK 21 executable. Toolchain-only Failsafe cases verify Java 8 under Maven running on JDK 21 and, with Maven 3.9.11, JDK 21 under Maven running on Java 8. A missing match stops before Failsafe writes a report. With Maven 3.9.16 and [Maven Toolchains 3.3.0](https://maven.apache.org/plugins/maven-toolchains-plugin/toolchain-mojo.html), the service test also verifies both test forks using Java 8 from an active build toolchain. If selection is bound to `install`, a `verify` invocation instead runs the tests on JDK 21, the JVM running Maven. With JDI hosted on JDK 21, Debug Integration Test reaches a saved source breakpoint in the explicit Java 8 Failsafe fork, resumes the selected method, and confirms its JVM options in a fresh report.

The Linux x86-64 AppImage passes the six-module Maven scenario on X11 and on KWin Wayland with XWayland disabled using the locally packaged RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime built from the integrated source. The application runs its Surefire and Failsafe tests on Java 8 after Maven Toolchains 3.3.0 selects the build toolchain in `validate`. Both executions receive the IDE JVM option, and Failsafe also receives its POM options. After resynchronization, the library's explicitly configured JDK 21 fork passes with a matching Java 8 toolchain prerequisite and verifies both its own POM option and the IDE option. Both invocations produce fresh reports in their declared directories, preserve project inputs, and close without surviving processes. The scenario then debugs the Java 8 Failsafe method from a saved breakpoint and resumes it to produce a fresh test report. After the selector changes, the captured rerun still reaches the same breakpoint. Stop terminates the owned fork before the next proof write. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:maven-test-jvm-selection:appimage` or its `:wayland` variant with Maven 3.9.16, cached Maven Toolchains 3.3.0, JDK 21 for Maven, `IDE_TEST_JAVA8_HOME` for the application toolchain, and a RefactorKit runtime advertising execution JVM selection and the toolchain prerequisite. The separate Maven Failsafe context scenario also passes with the base v7 RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate.

When Maven's test plugin or the IDE fork launcher reports that no JDK toolchain matches a test execution with IDE JVM options, Java Run asks the user to configure a matching Maven toolchain. This covers a Failsafe execution with an explicit Java executable and a separate toolchain prerequisite. The native library scenario removes the matching toolchain, observes the refusal before the fork can update the previous report, then restores the toolchain and verifies a fresh result after synchronization. When the launcher reports the current session's private argument-file reference as the main class, Java Run explains the argument-file incompatibility and points to the project's test JVM configuration and the option to use project defaults. If Maven reports that a build plugin or one of its dependencies could not be resolved because the repository is offline, Java Run identifies the offline plugin failure and points to explicit Maven project verification with the selected repository. This covers the direct repository refusal and the refusal nested in Maven's unresolved-artifact detail. The message takes precedence over the generic missing JVM option confirmation. The session retains Maven's exit code and any observed report results. The offline-plugin diagnosis has a real Maven 3.9.16 service test with a deliberately unavailable plugin version.

On X11 and KWin Wayland, the packaged six-module scenario removes the Toolchains plugin JAR and its parent POM in separate runs against a private copy of the selected repository. Java Run shows the offline-plugin diagnosis for each failure and preserves the previous application report without presenting it as current. Restoring the cache and synchronizing again produces a fresh passing Failsafe report from the Java 8 fork. Both sessions preserve the project inputs and close without surviving processes.

Integration testing and integration coverage invoke Maven `verify`, which can run Surefire before Failsafe. With IDE test JVM options, Java Run checks the marker in fresh Failsafe reports and in any fresh populated Surefire reports under the build's conventional `target/surefire-reports` directories. If either set contains fresh test cases without confirmation, the session reports a configuration failure and prevents automatic rerun while retaining the observed Failsafe and coverage results and Maven's exit code. Skipped Surefire executions can leave no fresh reports. Unchanged reports from earlier runs do not invalidate the current run. Custom Surefire report locations are outside this supplementary inspection.

The mixed-JVM AppImage scenario also runs integration coverage separately for app and library on X11 and KWin Wayland. With Maven 3.9.16, the app uses the Java 8 build toolchain and the library uses the explicit JDK 21 executable with the toolchain prerequisite satisfied. Each new session displays the fresh Failsafe report for the selected module, verifies its JVM options and shows covered production instructions for that module in JaCoCo.

The mixed-JVM scenario also passes on both display backends on the AppImage that adds saved-file recovery, with the RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate used for that verification. It also passes with the earlier AppImage and RefactorKit candidate used for the managed Jakarta `@NamedQuery` profile in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope). Run it with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:maven-test-jvm-selection:appimage` or its `:wayland` variant. Set `IDE_TEST_JAVA8_HOME` to a full JDK 8 and use a populated offline Maven repository that includes Maven Toolchains 3.3.0 and its dependencies. The same mixed-JVM scenario passes on KWin Wayland with Maven 3.9.16 and the AppImage that retains the verified Maven launcher. It exercises test runs, JaCoCo coverage, JDI debugging and recovery after restoring the missing toolchain.

**Configured Java commands** are available from Commands and Search Everywhere when their operation is currently admitted. Build, Run, Debug, tests, integration tests, discovery, coverage, JFR and Attach use the same selected saved configuration and controller as Java Run. The palette also offers Stop/Detach, captured-session Rerun/Restart, failed-test rerun and current structured-debugger controls. Failed-test rerun retains the failed session’s captured settings even after the visible configuration changes; it requires current trust, an eligible failure result and no execution or preparation in progress. Shared presentation checks keep tool, trust, module/source-set, Failsafe metadata and pending-operation admission consistent with the panels; native execution remains responsible for validating current authority. Invoking a command opens Java Run so preparation, output and failures remain visible. Execution targets come from the selected configuration.

With a Java editor, Java Run or a current Java task active, **Ctrl/Cmd+F5** runs the configured application; **F5** starts configured Debug or continues a suspended structured JDI session. **F10** steps over, **F11** steps into and **Shift+F11** steps out when the current top frame permits stepping. **Shift+F5** stops the owned Java task or detaches an external debugger connection; **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F5** repeats the captured Run/Debug session. These keys preserve modal, form and terminal input and ignore repeated/composing events. When Run, Debug or captured-session repeat is unavailable, its function key opens Java Run for configuration without starting execution. Step keys remain unhandled without an admitted step. Source saves, explicit trust and stale-workspace guards are the same as for the panel controls.

**Saved configurations** provides up to 16 named settings collections per workspace, with selection, creation, independent duplication, renaming and deletion. A new configuration starts with automatic tool detection and empty application/test settings. Each configuration keeps its project directory, build tool, main class, test selector, classpath, report directories, application arguments, application JVM options, test JVM options, environment, JDK selection and debugger choice. Existing configurations retain the jdb default; the **Debugger** control selects structured JDI explicitly. Actions use the selected configuration. Names are unique without regard to case, trimmed and limited to 128 UTF-8 bytes; at least one configuration remains. Changes are disabled during source-save preparation and native execution. Results show the configuration name captured when the session started; failed-test reruns retain that session's settings even after selecting another configuration, renaming it or deleting its saved entry.

Settings and the selected entry are stored in local application storage, with a 2 MiB aggregate limit in addition to each configuration's limits. A previous single configuration is restored as **Default** when no named collection exists. Incomplete settings drafts remain editable after reopening. Launch settings, including environment and JVM option values, are stored unencrypted, and workspace trust is never persisted. Invalid or oversized saved collections restore an untrusted default; storage failure is visible while in-memory settings remain usable. Configuration controls and launch callbacks from an obsolete workspace are refused. Portable project configuration files and shared/team configuration management remain planned.

Application launch arguments remain separate from shell commands. Plain-JDK Run uses separate native process arguments. Synchronized classpath Run with a Java 8 launcher also passes JVM options, the resolved runtime classpath and application arguments as separate native arguments. Other synchronized application launch paths use a private Java argument file. On Unix with a Java 8 launcher, console jdb starts the application with separate native arguments and attaches to its suspended JVM over a temporary IPv4 loopback listener. The IDE owns both processes, stops them together and retains the application exit status. The same route serves manual and synchronized application debugging. For a Maven project without a synchronized context, explicit application arguments, JVM options or an application working directory cause Maven Run to delegate runtime-classpath resolution to the [Exec plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/exec-mojo.html) and forks the selected Java executable. For Java 8, a private compiled launcher passes the IDE's values as separate native arguments alongside the resolved classpath. Newer manual Maven launches and jdb use a [Java argument file](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/java.html#java-command-line-argument-files) to preserve application values. Gradle configures the selected project's `run` task using the public [`JavaExec.setArgs`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/api/tasks/JavaExec.html#setArgs%28java.util.List%29) API in an owned initialization script. Private temporary launch files use exclusive creation and, on Unix, owner-only directory/file permissions; normal completion, failure and Stop attempt to remove them. An abrupt IDE termination can leave temporary files. Unsupported debugger temporary-path connector characters refuse launch. Application arguments, application JVM options and test JVM options are each bounded to 128 entries, 4 KiB per value and 16 KiB aggregate; environment overrides to 64 entries, 4 KiB per value and 32 KiB aggregate; the serialized configuration to 128 KiB. Text and size violations produce explicit errors before source-save preparation; Rust also checks the actual selected JDK and workspace paths before execution.

The **JDK console (jdb)** option provides line breakpoints, continue, step into/over/out, stack, locals, threads and expression evaluation in the console. **Structured Java debugger (JDI)** provides typed suspended/running/terminated state, source-line breakpoints, continue, pause, stepping, thread and frame selection, local variables, object fields, array pages, persistent watches, one-time read-only evaluation, bounded conditional logpoints and caught/uncaught exception breakpoints. **Run Java to Cursor** is available for a live suspended session with a current captured source: it installs a one-shot source breakpoint on an existing line without another breakpoint, resumes the JVM, and removes the temporary breakpoint at the next stop, pause or termination. The action does not save or alter the source. Pending breakpoints are installed when the corresponding class loads; unavailable executable lines remain visibly unverified. Stepping requires the top frame of the selected suspended thread. Exception breakpoints can match all exception classes, one exact binary class name, or that class and its subclasses, independently of caught/uncaught mode. The class filter is explicitly applied and the panel displays the acknowledged setting; a new debug session starts with exception breakpoints disabled and no class filter. Matching reads the thrown object’s JDI class and superclass metadata, including classes loaded after configuration, without invoking application methods. Names match across class loaders; selecting a particular loader is unavailable. Unrelated exception events resume automatically, but broad JDI exception requests can briefly suspend the JVM before the helper filters them. These settings are session-local and are not persisted with source breakpoints. Watches, one-time evaluation, conditions and logpoint placeholders read locals, `this`, fields, initialized loaded-class static fields and array indexes without invoking application methods or `toString`; the bounded evaluator supports selected primitive arithmetic, comparisons, logic, bitwise and shift operators, lazy conditional `?:` expressions, `instanceof` checks against loaded reference types, and selected java.lang.String operations computed locally from captured JDI values, including `indexOf` and `lastIndexOf`. In primitive contexts, it applies [Java unboxing conversion](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-5.html#jls-5.1.8) to captured bootstrap `Boolean`, `Character` and numeric-wrapper values by reading their primitive fields; equality between two wrapper references retains object-identity semantics. Full Java expression evaluation and application method calls remain unavailable. A one-time result is scoped to the selected stop and frame and does not consume or modify persistent watch slots. A nonempty log message resumes without suspending; `{expression}` placeholders use the same read-only evaluator, and object values display type and identity. The structured debugger runs in a full JDK 17 or later with readable release metadata bounded to 16 KiB and the [public debugger module](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/jdk.jdi/module-summary.html). For application or test debugging on an older project JDK, set `IDE_JAVA_DEBUGGER_HOME` to the debugger JDK before starting the IDE. The IDE also accepts its compatible default JDK as the debugger host when the variable is unset. The application and compiler retain the selected project JDK. The helper passes application JVM options and arguments directly to the selected Java executable and owns the child and its temporary loopback JDI listener. For test debugging, the debugger host reserves the loopback endpoint while the selected build tool or plain JDK owns the test JVM. External socket attachment uses the compatible JDK selected for that operation. See [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope) for the tested combinations. The JDI capability check accepts `jdk.jdi` in the installed runtime image as declared in bounded JDK release metadata. JDKs with older metadata can still identify the module through the JMOD file.

**Mute line breakpoints** temporarily disables the current session's ordinary line breakpoints and logpoints without deleting their conditions or changing matching-hit counts. Breakpoints added or reconfigured while muted stay muted, including locations installed when a class loads later. Unmute restores eligible requests but does not reactivate breakpoints whose matching-hit count is already exhausted. Exception breakpoints, stepping, Pause and the temporary Run to Cursor breakpoint remain independent. The control displays the helper's acknowledged state and is unavailable when that state is absent. Each new debugger session starts with line breakpoints active; this setting is not a saved launch preference.

**Step exclusion patterns** let a person skip selected class names during structured Step into, over and out, including the function keys and command palette. The current session accepts up to sixteen patterns of at most 512 UTF-8 bytes each and 1,536 UTF-8 bytes combined after duplicate removal: an exact class name, or one wildcard at the beginning or end, such as `java.*`, `*.Helper` or `example.Main$Nested`. Empty input keeps ordinary stepping. The native service validates the request and the helper applies JDI [class exclusion filters](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/jdk.jdi/com/sun/jdi/request/StepRequest.html#addClassExclusionFilter(java.lang.String)) before counting the next admitted step event. Explicit breakpoints remain independent of these step filters. The draft clears on a new session or workspace activation and is not a saved launch preference. Pattern matching uses JVM class names rather than inferred source ownership. If execution stays inside excluded classes, the next stop may be an explicit breakpoint or termination; Pause and Stop remain available. Invalid patterns refuse stepping while Continue remains available.

**Clean build outputs** delegates to Maven's `clean` lifecycle phase or Gradle's `clean` task through the owned execution service. It uses the selected build root, module selector, JDK, wrapper and provider settings, with the same trust, saved-buffer preparation, workspace identity and process controls as Build. The native runtime must explicitly advertise this operation; it is unavailable for plain-JDK projects. Clean does not compile, run the application or run tests. The build tool and project plugins determine which outputs to remove; the IDE does not delete inferred output directories. A successful result requires the owned tool process to exit successfully, and a failed clean is reported as a failure.

**Rebuild** runs the build tool's clean phase and the selected Build compilation mapping in one owned invocation. Maven runs `clean` before `compile` or the mapped test-compilation phase; Gradle runs the selected project's `clean` task before its compilation task, including provider-qualified included-build paths. The job captures one JDK and project selection, uses normal trust and saved-buffer preparation, and can be stopped through the existing process control. Compilation failure after cleanup is reported as a failed Rebuild; previous compiled outputs are not presented as a successful result. Rebuild does not launch the application or execute tests. It requires a separate runtime capability and is unavailable for plain-JDK projects. Build's source-set admission rules still apply.

**Restart session** saves editor changes, stops the IDE-owned Run or Debug process and rebuilds and launches the same session configuration. After completion, the control becomes **Rerun session**. Both actions use the native session’s captured main class, project selection, application working directory, JDK, arguments, JVM options, environment and profiling choice; later form drafts do not replace them. The provider must advertise restart support. Workspace trust, session identity and the saved-buffer review are checked before the request. A failed save leaves the previous process running. Stop cancels pending preparation, and a replacement returned after session or workspace retirement is stopped rather than adopted.

**Rerun session** is also available for completed unit and Maven integration test sessions. It runs the original test scope with the captured JDK, build tool, environment and test JVM options after saving current edits. If the previous session ran only a discovered selection or a set of failed tests, that scope is retained. **Rerun failed tests** continues to select failures from the current report. When a new test task cannot start, the previous completed report stays available.

For a completed coverage session, **Rerun session** measures the captured test scope again and evaluates the original coverage thresholds. A new complete measurement records a separate history entry. For synchronized projects, coverage navigation uses a fresh review of the current saved sources and refuses locations when the reviewed source changes during measurement.

For a synchronized project, the native executor revalidates the retained provider settings and reacquires facts for the saved sources through the repeated-execution path. Changed provider settings or a lost session require starting a new Java session. Debug uses the current explicitly bound saved source breakpoints; changed source fingerprints still require review and **Rebind active file** before restart. The native executor waits for the old owned process to exit before replacing its exact session. A failed rebuild or launch is reported as a failure; stopping the old application does not prove its replacement started. This control applies to IDE-launched Run and Debug, including completed sessions; socket Attach remains an externally owned application connection.

**Drop frame** removes the selected suspended JDI frame and all younger frames, leaving its caller suspended at the invocation. Continue or Step into can call the method again; changes to the called method’s arguments remain in effect. This is not application rollback: field changes and external effects remain, acquired monitors are released and `finally` blocks in removed frames do not execute, as specified by [JDI `ThreadReference.popFrames`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/jdk.jdi/com/sun/jdi/ThreadReference.html#popFrames(com.sun.jdi.StackFrame)). The panel explains these consequences beside the action. JDI must advertise support in a modifiable VM, and every removed frame and its surviving caller must be non-native and present in the bounded captured stack. A missing or unsupported capability leaves the action disabled. Both the requested suspension and selected frame are checked again before removal; success produces a new suspension identity and rebuilds frames, variables and evaluation state. Old frame and object references cannot be reused. The operation does not compile, redefine classes or change source files. Verification scope is described in section 10.1.

**Attach** connects the selected full JDK helper to an already started JVM through the JDI [socket attaching connector](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/jpda/conninv.html). The target must expose a listening JDWP socket; the IDE does not start it or discover endpoints. **JDWP host** and **JDWP port** default to `127.0.0.1` and `5005`. Named launch settings retain these bounded fields, including incomplete drafts; Attach requires a host and decimal port from 1 to 65535, structured JDI mode, explicit provider capability and current workspace trust. Trust is not restored. The connector has a ten-second connection timeout; DNS and network behavior still depend on the platform.

Attach does not build the project, launch an application, save editor drafts or install saved source breakpoints. Application arguments, JVM options, project paths and classpaths belong to launch; they do not select the external target. The selected JDK and child environment apply to the helper. Class-name breakpoints, conditional controls, threads, frames, read-only values, watches, stepping, Pause and exception controls use the connected runtime. External artifacts cannot yet be verified against local editor files, so Attach does not enable Monaco source-margin binding or selected-frame source annotations. The panel reports this limitation and keeps runtime class controls available.

**Detach** closes the debugger connection and stops only the owned helper; the external JVM continues, including after a debugger suspension. Connection EOF and malformed input also dispose that connection without terminating the target. An orderly EOF completes the connection with helper exit zero; malformed command transport exits the helper with a failure. An attached connection can begin with a running state, whereas a launched JDI session must observe its suspended entry. Workspace/session retirement uses the same ownership boundary. The panel labels connection state and helper exit separately: they do not establish the external application's exit code or success. External stdout/stderr stay with the process that launched it. Connection failure is visible and never fabricates a debugger state. Real-tool and native UI qualification are described in section 10.1; remote hosts, network failure modes and other operating systems need separate qualification.

**HotSwap compiled classes** reloads explicitly selected `.class` files into the connected JDI runtime. The [runtime interaction diagram](docs/c4/runtime-java-class-reload.md) shows its process and transfer ownership. **Build and reload classes** saves dirty editor buffers, compiles with the selected JDK or configured project build tool in a sidecar task, and keeps the active JDI session connected. A successful build result is shown before the selected workspace-relative class files are sent for redefinition; the compiler result does not imply JVM acceptance. In a synchronized Java project, the class-file field suggests outputs from the selected source set and its provider-declared runtime project dependencies; a unique candidate is filled automatically, while ambiguous candidates remain for explicit choice. Native Linux project-debugger qualification verifies provider-suggested `pkg.Runner` output selection and HotSwap for one synchronized Maven project and one synchronized Gradle project; see section 10.1. For project-launched sessions, Rust admits files only beneath materialized workspace directories on the selected source set’s synchronized runtime classpath and revalidates those roots before and after a sidecar build and before reload; changed roots require restarting the debugger. This binds the chosen file to a runtime-classpath directory, but does not prove it supplied the bytes loaded by the JVM. Manual attach retains explicit workspace path selection because the IDE cannot identify a stable output directory for an external VM. Stop/Detach cancels an active sidecar build, and a second execution is refused until it finishes. **Reload compiled classes** continues to use existing outputs without saving buffers or compiling. Exhaustive discovery beyond the captured JVM list, verification of a loaded class's source/output provenance, automatic redefinition and reload after arbitrary external builds remain planned.

Before transfer, a synchronized project-launched session must select a class file beneath a materialized workspace directory on the selected source set's captured runtime classpath. The IDE re-resolves that project context before and after a sidecar build and before reload, and refuses changed runtime-output directories. A sidecar build reacquires provider facts for the saved edits while retaining the launched session’s runtime-output directories as its boundary. Rust also parses the selected class file's constant pool and refuses it when its declared binary name differs from the selected name. These checks establish the file's project classpath location and declared type; they do not establish that the JVM loaded those exact bytes. Manual attach remains an explicit path choice.

**Build and review changed classes** saves dirty buffers and builds beside a suspended, launched JDI session, then proposes compiled files whose bytes changed around that build. It uses the last class-name list explicitly read from the JVM and existing, unambiguous output files: plain-JDK launch uses its compiler output, while synchronized Maven/Gradle launch uses the captured runtime output directories. Names loaded by several class loaders and names present in several output directories are excluded. A truncated JVM list is disclosed; absence from the proposal list does not prove an application class was unchanged. Manual attach and unsynchronized build-tool launch retain explicit file selection. The comparison does not establish which bytes the JVM loaded or prove that the build alone produced a change.

The person reviews the proposed names and paths, chooses **Use changed classes**, then explicitly requests **Reload compiled classes**. Compilation and review alone never request redefinition. Each proposed file carries its reviewed content hash; Rust refuses changed bytes before capturing the transfer. Each selected row retains its suspension identity, so changing or removing one row cannot admit other retired rows. Manually editing a row makes that row an explicit manual file choice. A failed build, unsupported provider, changed session or suspension, unavailable output mapping or comparison limit produces no automatic selection. Build success remains separate from comparison availability and actual JVM acceptance. The comparison reads at most 8 MiB per pass, probes at most 65,536 paths across at most 256 output directories, and checks a cooperative two-second budget; a blocked filesystem call cannot be interrupted by that check. At most 32 changed classes can be proposed.

The form pairs each binary class name with a workspace-relative compiled file. **Refresh loaded JVM classes** asks JDI for a bounded list of prepared binary names accepted by the current class-name validator and reports duplicate names across class loaders. The visible prepared-class selector fills the chosen binary name; selecting it also applies any unique compiled-output suggestion from the synchronized project context. Names outside that validator or beyond the result limit are omitted and mark the list as truncated. This list identifies classes in the running VM, not the workspace file that produced them. The compiled-file field still requires an explicit project output selection, and JDI refuses to redefine a name with multiple loaded definitions. The form accepts at most 32 distinct classes/files, 1 MiB per file and 8 MiB aggregate. Only regular workspace-contained files without symlinks or hard links are admitted. Captured byte arrays travel through a private bounded file with an integrity check; later replacement of the original compiled path does not change that transfer. These are selected compiled bytes, not proof of an atomic build or of matching editor source. The queued result means only that input was accepted; **applied** requires the actual JVM redefinition result. The selected helper must report the connected VM's capability. Older providers, an unsupported/read-only VM, missing or duplicate loaded types, obsolete workspace/session/suspension, malformed bytes and unsupported changes refuse visibly. Reload cannot select between multiple class loaders sharing a binary name.

The JVM's public [class redefinition API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/jdk.jdi/com/sun/jdi/VirtualMachine.html) determines accepted changes. On the qualified JDKs, method-body changes work and structural additions are refused. New method invocations use the accepted definitions; existing active frames may keep obsolete code, which the frame list identifies. Existing fields retain their values and initializers are not rerun. A successful suspended reload creates a new stop identity and revokes old frame/object actions. Reload preparation retires captured local source binding, and successful redefinition removes all source-bound runtime breakpoints and runtime class points in reloaded types. Saved preferences remain available for a later Debug launch. Review runtime breakpoints before continuing; source-margin binding and source annotations are unavailable for this revised session. Stop/Detach remains available while preparing or awaiting a reload; an ended connection without its result is a failed reload, never inferred success.

JDI source and class breakpoints accept an optional **condition**, **matching-hit count** and **log message**. An empty condition accepts every occurrence. A breakpoint without a log message stops on every true result when the count is zero; with a nonempty message it logs without suspending.
