A positive count stops or logs once on that many true results, then disables that logical breakpoint's runtime requests. Log messages are limited to one line and 512 UTF-8 bytes, with at most 16 `{expression}` placeholders; failed evaluation visibly suspends with an error. Counts combine installed locations and types, so they are debugger events rather than a guaranteed loop-iteration count. A new Debug session resets all counts. Setting a runtime class breakpoint again also resets and re-enables it. Java Run displays the condition, message, observed matches and whether a positive target has been reached; skipped events update the next published debugger view rather than streaming a view for each occurrence.

Conditions evaluate the event thread's top frame while the application is suspended. They use the same bounded, read-only expression evaluator as watches, one-time evaluation and logpoint placeholders, described below. Reference equality compares JDI object identities; field lookup follows the object's runtime type rather than reproducing Java's lexical field-hiding resolution. Field and array-length reads can follow computed indices or parenthesized references. A selected String operation can use a String field reached through the same expression, without invoking application code. Arbitrary method calls, assignments and general Java expression evaluation remain unavailable. Conditions are limited to 512 UTF-8 bytes on one line, 128 tokens, nesting depth 32 and 32 field/index path steps; matching counts and observed matches are bounded to one billion. Invalid syntax refuses a runtime change before mutation or a saved-point launch before application code executes. Missing values or debug information, incompatible operand types and arithmetic errors suspend with a visible error, leaving the person to repair or remove the condition before continuing.

Each suspension has a new identity. Resume, Stop and termination revoke frame/value references; actions captured for an older stop or workspace cannot inspect a later one. This follows the JDI [stack-frame lifetime](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/jdk.jdi/com/sun/jdi/StackFrame.html). Views contain at most 128 threads, frames, locals or breakpoints, 32 watches and 32 children per page, with at most 1,024 retained object references and only the latest child page. Limits and missing debug information are visible. String previews inspect at most 256 UTF-16 units for display and remain bounded to 512 units after escaping; control characters are escaped and truncation is marked. Valid Unicode supplementary characters are preserved. On the qualified JDK 21 and 25 installations, JDI's string-value API replaces isolated UTF-16 surrogates with U+FFFD; this inspector cannot recover the original code unit. Runtime state frames are bounded to 512 KiB, and malformed or incomplete helper output refuses the session rather than admitting tool exit zero as success.

Clicking Monaco's glyph margin or pressing **F9** records a source-line breakpoint for the active Java file, including before Debug. The editor distinguishes saved/pending, disabled and runtime-verified points. In a live JDI session, the same action updates the owned debugger and its saved choice. The editor highlights/reveals the selected suspended frame's line when its runtime source path identifies a unique captured file. For Attach, the configured manual project path supplies the saved Java source inventory; the on-disk file and exact editor text must still match the captured source fingerprint. Attaching does not save or build local source, and saved breakpoints are selected explicitly rather than loaded automatically. A runtime source path may differ in its path prefix from the local path, but it must map uniquely to a captured Java file; the breakpoint is sent using the runtime path so JDI can verify the line. This association does not prove that the external JVM loaded bytecode built from the captured local file. JDI's [source paths and line locations](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/jdk.jdi/com/sun/jdi/ReferenceType.html) establish the runtime association, including multiple types in one source file. A pending [class-prepare request](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/jdk.jdi/com/sun/jdi/request/ClassPrepareRequest.html) installs source breakpoints when their types load. Non-executable lines and ambiguous source paths remain visibly unverified. Class-name controls remain available separately; a class breakpoint associated with the selected frame can also be cleared through its source margin.

**Saved source breakpoints** are workspace preferences, separate from launch configurations and runtime verification. At most 128 points are stored in local application storage, bounded to 256 KiB, with workspace-relative Java paths, line numbers, enabled state, optional conditions, matching-hit targets and log messages, and SHA-256 fingerprints of the exact UTF-8 editor text. A point may also retain a SHA-256 hash of its trimmed preceding, current and following lines to support bounded relocation suggestions; no source text is stored. Preferences without context hashes remain supported. They contain no source bodies or runtime counters. Existing preferences without conditions remain unconditional. **Edit condition** changes a saved point's condition, hit target and log message before Debug; these settings survive reload, restart, disabling and reviewed source rebinding. Enabling a disabled saved point through the editor during a live JDI session installs and retains its condition, matching-hit target and log message, preserving non-suspending logpoint behavior. Runtime class controls can change breakpoint settings during a session; live editing of saved source settings is not provided. Web Crypto supplies asynchronous hashing; unavailable hashing refuses source binding visibly. Storage errors retain in-memory choices with an explicit warning; invalid stored data is preserved and not treated as a usable collection. Explicit clear replaces it. Workspace changes, buffer retirement and obsolete suspension actions revoke pending writes.

After editing or an external source change, old fingerprints do not authorize a breakpoint in the revised source. Typing removes its old marker; subsequent inspection and launch checks report changed source. The person reviews line positions and chooses **Rebind active file**, repositions or removes the points. Rebinding moves a point only when its three-line context hash has exactly one match in a file of at most 5,000 lines; ambiguous matches are refused, while unmatched or unscanned points keep their existing line for the person's explicit review. Source Save remains part of the existing launch preparation. JDI checks enabled choices against captured disk source before compilation and again before application launch; a changed captured source refuses Debug. Points outside the selected project's captured inventory are omitted with a visible console explanation, without claiming runtime verification. A bounded private startup file installs accepted points before application code executes, independently of the interactive input queue. Stop removes runtime verification while retaining saved choices. The jdb console option requires switching to JDI to use saved source breakpoints.

Before compilation, the native worker captures bounded source-file fingerprints under the selected project. Source annotations require both the current disk file and the exact editor text to match that capture. Typing immediately clears decorations; changed source receives a visible refusal while the draft is preserved. Returning to identical captured text permits inspection again; this does not clear the editor's dirty flag or save the file automatically. Source requests are bound to the active workspace, session, suspension/frame, model version and buffer lifetime. Queued helper actions recheck their suspension/frame before changing a breakpoint. Resume and termination remove the suspended-line marker. Event polling continues while a launched session is active even if its activity is hidden.

Inspection admits at most 2,000 Java files, 20,000 visited entries, traversal depth 32, 2 MiB per source and 64 MiB aggregate, with bounded UTF-8 paths. Conventional output/private directories and symlink entries are excluded by the source traversal. Source reads run on blocking workers; one inspection holds a job's source map, competing inspections refuse, and Monaco serializes requests while retaining only the latest edit. **Retry source binding** requests a fresh inspection after a temporary refusal. A stalled filesystem call cannot be cancelled by these guards. Limits or unavailable source inventory leave ordinary JDI controls available. These fingerprints are not an atomic build-input snapshot or proof of artifact provenance for every custom build. Effective module/source-set roots, library sources, custom generated outputs and source mappings remain project-system integration work. For Attach, a runtime source path maps only when it identifies exactly one captured local Java file; missing or ambiguous matches are refused rather than inferred from a guessed package/class name.

Additional classpath entries apply to plain-JDK compilation/Run and both debugger launch modes; Maven/Gradle Run uses project-configured dependencies. Debugger runtime libraries still require explicit configuration. The shared JDI expression evaluator reads current-frame locals, `this`, object fields, initialized loaded-class static fields and array elements selected by literal or computed `int` indexes. It supports decimal, octal, hexadecimal and binary integer literals; decimal and hexadecimal floating-point literals; booleans, strings, characters and `null`; arithmetic, comparisons, logical, bitwise and shift operators; lazy conditional `?:`; primitive casts; and runtime `instanceof` checks for loaded reference types. Runtime type checks accept loaded array types such as `int[][]` and `java.lang.Object[]` and use JDI type identity and component assignability. The check uses loaded type metadata and follows [Java array subtyping](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.10.3). It applies Java unboxing conversion to captured bootstrap `Boolean`, `Character` and numeric-wrapper values in primitive contexts, while equality between two wrapper references retains object identity. String concatenation and selected `java.lang.String` operations—`length`, `isEmpty`, `charAt`, `substring`, `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf`, equality, and search/prefix/suffix checks—are computed from captured values without invoking application code. A supported call can use a string literal, a parenthesized expression that yields a string, or the string result of a previous supported call. Quoted strings and characters can contain operator or delimiter characters, including in conditions and logpoint expressions. The evaluator requires unquoted operators and delimiters to form valid syntax. The explicit **Set local** action changes one visible local in the selected current, non-obsolete frame. Its input is bound to the suspension and frame in which it was written. Polling the same frame preserves the draft; resuming execution, changing the selected stop or frame, losing the frame or marking it obsolete clears the draft and disables submission until a new assignment is entered. Returning to an earlier frame does not restore its retired draft. Focused component tests verify these transitions without dispatching a mutation. Its right-hand side uses the bounded evaluator. For primitive locals, it preserves identity conversions and permits Java primitive widening, including widening after unboxing a captured standard wrapper. Unboxing reads the wrapper's value without running a method in the debuggee. An explicit cast is required for narrowing, and null cannot be assigned to a primitive local. Reference values must be assignable to the declared local type. See the Java Language Specification's [widening primitive conversions](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-5.html#jls-5.1.2). Arbitrary method calls, field or array writes, compound assignments and general Java expression evaluation remain unavailable, and stale stops or frames are refused. Automatic dependency resolution and unprompted breakpoint relocation remain planned; explicit rebinding can apply a unique hashed-context suggestion, but it is not integrated with RefactorKit edit results. Build-triggered compilation beside an active JDI session is implemented for explicitly selected class files; exhaustive output discovery, HotSwap after arbitrary compiler runs and source rebinding after HotSwap remain incomplete. Attachment source provenance and remote-network qualification remain incomplete. Debugger process-group ownership and availability are currently Unix-only.

Debugger commands are bound to the active running session. Retired callbacks cannot submit input after workspace changes, unmount or Stop, and a delayed rejection cannot replace the error state of a newer session or JDI suspension. The JDI sender checks the helper's 3,072-byte encoded-command limit before acquiring the input pipe; an oversized request refuses without writing bytes or changing the current suspension. Native input writes are nonblocking and atomic within the platform pipe limit: a debugger that stops reading produces a visible queue-full refusal without holding the process lock needed by Stop. Acceptance into that pipe is not evidence of execution; the jdb console or subsequent JDI runtime state and actual session outcome supply that evidence. Both modes retain JVM stepping behavior, including a return to the call-site line before the caller stores the returned value.

The native JDT LS protocol reader enforces its 8 KiB aggregate header limit while reading, including a single line without a newline; it stops consuming at the first byte beyond that limit. The existing 4 MiB message-body limit remains. Malformed non-header stdout still fails the connection and now includes an escaped preview of at most 96 input characters for diagnosis. Unit tests verify exact-boundary admission, oversized individual and aggregate headers, partial reads, duplicate lengths and bounded failure previews.

### 6.4 Refactoring and Agent Flows

RefactorKit preview does not grant write permission. Apply requires the exact reviewed plan and current authority. The native engine rechecks the plan before transformation. Rollback is offered only when the provider supports it. Clipboard import requires advertised directory targeting, preview, apply and rollback support before reading clipboard text, and never intercepts normal editor paste.

After closing an applied saved-source Java review, **Commands > Review Last Applied Java Refactoring** reopens the most recently retained transaction in the current workspace session. The view retains the original plan, result, transaction identity and applied snapshot; reopening does not preview or apply again. Rollback still requires the original workspace activation, provider capability, project settings and applied-source snapshot, and can refuse changed build outputs. A typed refusal that confirms rollback did not start can be closed and reopened for a later guarded retry. Only one closed applied review is retained in memory. Workspace reset, provider replacement and application closure retire it; successful rollback consumes it. This is not transaction history or recovery after restart. Editor-owned draft transactions continue to use their separate recovery flow.

The Java Refactor dialog collects the requested new name, current local-variable name, destination package, or current/new parameter names. The signature operation can rename one parameter or accept a comma-separated order containing every method parameter exactly once when the selected provider advertises `reorderParameters`. The editor context menu and command palette offer cursor-based parameter rename and parameter-order review only when saved-source selection and managed project-context preview are advertised; each request is bound to the method selected by RefactorKit, and parameter rename locks its target to the cursor. The installed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 daemon qualifies parameter rename for one package-private method in the Linux release/no-bundle Maven GUI (section 10.1); overload, hierarchy, public/protected, Gradle and other operating-system cases remain unqualified. RefactorKit refuses parameter-order call sites whose argument evaluation effects it cannot prove safe. Add Parameter follows the saved-source cursor path above. Add, Remove, Reorder and Change Parameter Type offer API scope controls that request the source override hierarchy and acknowledge the risk to callers outside the workspace; both choices default off, and hierarchy expansion requires explicit acknowledgement before preview. The native boundary preserves and validates both choices. RefactorKit decides whether the editable override family and its bound calls form a safe plan; callers outside the workspace cannot be updated. Change Parameter Type is offered only when the selected provider advertises stable managed authority. The locally rebuilt 0.7.0 package passes the bounded native GUI case in section 10.1; other provider distributions and broader project layouts remain unqualified. Remove Parameter is offered only when saved-source selection and stable managed project-context authority are advertised; the dialog requests the parameter name and RefactorKit decides whether the method and call sites are safe. Missing or incomplete change parameters remain editable and refuse the provider call. Changing the operation clears the previous parameters. Apply reuses the parameters captured by the reviewed preview and refuses altered plans, backend blockers, stale authority or withdrawn apply capability.

When RefactorKit refuses to remove a parameter because its argument has side effects, the Java Refactor dialog explains the risk and keeps Apply disabled. The IDE uses the provider's specific refusal code when supplied and recognizes the exact message from older runtimes. Both paths display a fixed explanation while filtering other refusal details for paths and sensitive data.

Add Parameter offers explicit adaptation of supported method and constructor references to lambdas. The IDE describes the bounded `this::method` case when RefactorKit advertises `thisMethodReferenceMigration` for Add Parameter. This case uses a private instance method, unqualified `this`, an explicitly typed local functional-interface initializer and a literal default value. The option defaults off, retains the functional-interface arity and asks RefactorKit to insert the new argument in each bound lambda and ordinary call. The constructor case uses the exact saved declaration selection and preserves unrelated overloads; the isolated corrected provider candidate has bounded Maven GUI qualification. The consumer validates the boolean and refuses use by other operations or combined hierarchy migration. A direct Maven daemon replay with a saved JDT selection verifies that an earlier RefactorKit candidate refuses the bound instance case before planning. The candidate with the new discovery flag previews both the static and instance cases. The same candidate refuses an unbound instance reference such as `Type::method` with `java.changeSignature.functionalReferenceUnsupported`, preserving the saved sources. Both candidates preserve the saved source bytes during preview. Focused contract, dialog and native-boundary tests verify option preservation and refusal of unsupported combinations. Section 10.1 records the bounded native GUI qualification.

The native consumer accepts provider-attested constructor selections for parameter rename, addition, reordering, removal and type change. It preserves the exact constructor symbol and binding identity after validating saved-source and project-context authority; method-only operations still refuse constructors. Production-boundary unit tests cover all five signature operations and validate authority before explaining an incompatible target. The isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate with the corrected Java selector passes the bounded Maven GUI workflows recorded in section 10.1. A separate same-compilation-unit fixture also qualifies each signature operation on a package-private constructor reached through both `this(...)` and `super(...)`; RefactorKit supplies the bound call updates, while the IDE retains the reviewed transaction lifecycle. The earlier sealed candidate still refuses constructor targets in saved-cursor mutation selection, even when its direct constructor-symbol planner can produce a preview. A correlated `java.selection.constructorUnsupported` result receives a fixed explanation that no refactoring plan was created; the IDE does not substitute a method or type identity. Other malformed, stale or unknown selection responses retain the protocol refusal. Constructor references in signature operations other than the bounded Add Parameter case, constructor call-site selection, cross-file or longer delegation chains, varargs, broader overloads, Gradle, packaged installers and other operating systems remain unqualified; the default provider installation has not been replaced.

**Introduce Parameter Object** is available from the Java editor context menu and Commands when RefactorKit advertises the operation and saved-source mutation selection in the synchronized SDK context. The person places the cursor on a saved method and enters a type name and two adjacent parameter names in declaration order. RefactorKit checks the bindings, call sites and evaluation order and supplies a reviewed plan. The IDE binds the ordered names and saved method selection to Apply and supports exact rollback.

**Extract Delegate** is available from the Java editor context menu and Commands when RefactorKit advertises the operation and saved-source mutation selection in the synchronized SDK context. Place the cursor on a saved method in the group and enter the name of the delegate type and the member names. RefactorKit resolves the group and its dependencies and retains the selected method in the preview. The tested Maven and Gradle cases move two private static helpers and one private static integer constant into a nested delegate while retaining the public caller. An omitted dependency leaves Apply unavailable. Gradle retains the evaluated context for this refusal, so the person can correct the member group and preview again without synchronizing. A stale snapshot or a lost session still retires that context. The same review, Apply and rollback flow protects saved inputs and reconciles open editors.

The experimental Gradle module-rename consumer selects an existing provider-qualified project in Java Project and collects a new canonical Gradle project path. The selected build root and settings file are fixed for review; duplicate module coordinates or ambiguous settings files withhold the action. Its complete method contract must advertise preview, rendered diff, Apply, rollback, literal settings, preserved physical directories, explicit synchronization and a guarantee covering inbound dependencies. Native validation binds the settings path and build root to the synchronized SDK project and passes the old/new project paths to RefactorKit through structural context authority. The provider owns parsing, model projection and edits. The controller captures editor-buffer authority and refuses Apply while open edits are unsaved; unit tests and native GUI acceptance cover this guard. The logical project path changes while its physical directory is preserved. The independently tested provider upgrade accepts the conventional Groovy and Kotlin multi-literal settings fixtures through managed Apply and exact Rollback, with offline tests on independent copies of the applied sources. The expanded contract advertises literal inbound project dependency updates together with refusal of unqualified dependency declarations. The IDE displays that support only when both properties are present. Earlier runtimes continue to use the settings-only contract. RefactorKit verifies the dependency origins and supplies the edits for review. The verified candidates support a closed set of literal references in Java and application plugin scripts. RefactorKit refuses references whose origins it cannot verify. Section 10.1 lists the tested application configurations.

Change Field Type is available from the Java editor context menu and Commands when RefactorKit advertises stable managed `changeType`, saved-source mutation selection and synchronized SDK authority. The person places the cursor on a saved field and enters its requested type. The native service acquires and validates a provider-attested field selection, then passes the exact symbol, declaration path, binding key and requested type to RefactorKit. The IDE does not infer the field from its spelling or rewrite Java locally. Unsaved project edits, moved cursors, stale context and unbound or non-field selections refuse preview. The tested provider supports one private mutable primitive `int` field changed to `long` in an ordinary top-level class without a declared hierarchy or type parameters; static, final, annotated and non-private fields, other type pairs and newly introduced compilation errors refuse the plan. The provider owns those semantic limits. Apply and Rollback use the existing reviewed transaction flow. Section 10.1 records the bounded native qualification; Gradle, broader field shapes, recovery across restart, default or released providers, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

Make Public is available only for a saved cursor-selected method in a synchronized SDK project when RefactorKit advertises stable managed `changeVisibility`. The action delegates the exact method selection to RefactorKit; a refusal leaves Apply disabled and preserves source. Its current qualification status is recorded in section 10.1.

The locally rebuilt RefactorKit development server exposes experimental LSP `refactorkit.changeVisibility`, currently limited to promoting one exact JDT-selected final private method in a dirty Java buffer, `refactorkit.extractParameter` for a bounded primitive-integer expression with one unique same-file call site, and `refactorkit.extractSuperclass` for a JDT-selected type. Focused source-built Cucumber scenarios cover Change Visibility and Extract Parameter, and a packaged-server stdio smoke verifies all three advertised commands and their response shapes while leaving saved sources unchanged. These commands return client-managed versioned edits and do not retain plans or support RefactorKit-managed Apply/Rollback.

The desktop starts a native stdio client when a provider advertises these operations. Capability discovery and previews bind the active workspace generation. Each preview starts the LSP at the currently synchronized Java project root, relative to the IDE workspace, and passes the selected project JDK for analysis; the launcher uses the host Java runtime configured for the application. Requests include only saved Java documents in the selected project, with current open Java-buffer overlays; non-Java tabs, unsaved new-file drafts and Java documents from other projects are excluded. The native client maps workspace-relative editor paths to the selected project root for analysis, then maps proposed edits back to workspace-relative paths. It accepts only provider-attested client-managed edits whose document versions, paths and operation-specific shape match the captured request. The review shows before/after content, and Apply rechecks the workspace generation, selected project root, project JDK and every captured buffer before committing the exact proposal to editor buffers without writing saved files. Extract Superclass `CreateFile` becomes a dirty unsaved Java tab; its first save refuses to overwrite a destination created after preview and refreshes the file tree after a successful save. The [runtime interaction](docs/c4/runtime-java-refactorkit-lsp.md) describes this client path.

Rust and TypeScript adapter/transaction/component tests and the desktop production build cover the client. An opt-in Rust integration test exercises the production stdio transport against a source-built LSP server: it checks advertised commands, previews a bounded Java visibility change, validates the returned edit and confirms that the saved source remains unchanged. One native Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario with a source-built LSP now qualifies Change Visibility: Apply updates only the editor buffer, offline Maven `verify` succeeds on a copy with the selected JDK 21, the saved source remains unchanged, and discarding the draft restores a clean buffer. This does not qualify other LSP operations, a packaged application, the default cached RefactorKit 0.7.0 bundle or other operating systems. That default bundle does not advertise these commands. The SDK-context Make Public action remains the managed visibility path.

The dialog enables only preview operations advertised for the active route: general CLI operations when no synchronized SDK project context is used, saved-project previews when the selected SDK context is synchronized, or immutable editor previews for supported cursor and draft operations in that project. Whole-file `format-file` and `organize-imports` may use the general CLI route when no synchronized context is available or that context does not advertise the operation; this fallback is limited to saved files and carries no project-wide authority. Their capability-advertised editor actions remain visible on dirty workspaces, but preview refuses until all buffers are saved. Each operation is bound to its matching target kind—type, member, local binding, source root or file—and the controller refuses mismatches before contacting the provider. Safe Delete currently accepts type targets only, matching RefactorKit's supported declaration scope. RefactorKit's bounded workspace text-scan result is displayed with file and byte counts for the captured snapshot, but it does not establish complete project closure or Apply authority. Apply still requires an explicit provider capability for complete project-wide reference analysis, including build and resource files; a Java-only or unqualified search remains review-only. Other operation choices remain visible as unavailable, and Preview is disabled for them. Operations without managed Apply authority are labeled preview-only; Apply remains disabled until both the provider authority and exact plan eligibility pass. The engine bridge reports managed Apply authority per operation from RefactorKit capability metadata and the adapter binds it to the advertised operation; selected-project Apply continues to require the separate language-kernel authority. These are user-interface gates; the controller and native adapter still validate provider capability, workspace and project context before making a request. For Extract Method, Monaco adds a context-menu action for a non-empty selection in a saved Java file when the synchronized project advertises stable managed `extractMethod`; the dialog collects the method name. The Rust bridge accepts only complete contiguous statement lines, maps the UTF-16 selection to the provider’s inclusive line range, and refuses partial lines or invalid Unicode boundaries. The controller rejects dirty buffers and stale workspace authority, and RefactorKit’s JDT-bound planner refuses unsupported bindings or data flow before Apply. The qualified managed shape captures resolved enclosing parameters and read-only preceding direct-local reads, returns exactly one selected local used after the range, supports selected conditional assignments and propagates checked exceptions from extracted calls. JDT LS `refactor.extract` remains an independent code action. Native GUI evidence and the bounded syntax are recorded in section 10.1 and the capability matrix.

For the active Java file, **Review Java formatting** and **Review Java imports** open that same RefactorKit dialog with a whole-file target. Monaco's **Command Palette** (`F1`) and editor context menu expose these reviewed actions. They appear only for operations advertised by the installed engine; the native bridge requires stable managed Java capability metadata and the corresponding CLI command. Supported subsets remain valid advertisements, so an older provider's semantic operations do not imply file-operation support. A file target contains its exact workspace-relative path, without guessing a class or member identity. Retired models/workspaces and withdrawn capabilities cannot run a retained action. The conventional CLI route refuses unsaved buffers and preserves them; saving is an explicit person action. The selected-SDK route can review immutable drafts as described below. Monaco's separate **Format Document** command invokes the JDT LS formatter on the active buffer, as described in section 6.2.

When the selected SDK project is synchronized and the provider advertises immutable editor-selection preview, the Monaco context menu offers **Review type rename at cursor** and **Review member rename at cursor**. `Shift+F6` opens type rename and `F2` opens member rename while the Java editor has focus. Each action captures Monaco's exact cursor for RefactorKit. When all captured buffers are clean and the provider advertises saved mutation selection and saved-project member-rename preview, member rename resolves the cursor against the saved snapshot. This route can review changes to Java files that are closed in the editor. Draft rename uses the immutable editor preview and preserves unsaved changes. Focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios verify both shortcuts against a Maven fixture; installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

Java Project class rows offer **Move** and **Delete** only when the synchronized provider advertises `moveClass` or `safeDelete` preview. The IDE first opens the engine-reported declaration, then targets its exact qualified type and source path in the shared review dialog; move collects a destination package, while safe-delete Apply is enabled only when RefactorKit advertises complete project-wide reference analysis, including non-Java build and resource files. A dirty Java buffer in the selected project blocks these saved-source actions and asks the person to save explicitly. The action does not save source, and workspace changes during navigation prevent opening a stale review. Production panel/controller tests cover the action handoff, target-scope refusal and capability refusal. The native Maven story moves a referenced type, verifies an applied-source copy with offline Maven `verify`, and rolls the live transaction back. The native Gradle story now moves one unreferenced type after v3 context attestation, verifies an applied-source copy with offline Gradle `test`, and rolls the live transaction back. The native Maven story refuses a Java-referenced deletion without changes. In the native run with the pre-fix isolated daemon, a type referenced only from the reactor root POM fails to produce an eligible preview: the provider reports the reference at `maven/pom.xml:12` and suggests `--force`; the Java file and POM remain unchanged. RefactorKit's source BDD and a Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario now verify that the captured-context proposal remains review-only, Apply stays disabled, and the source and POM remain unchanged. Project-wide build and resource reference coverage remains unqualified. Generated code, reflection, framework configuration, external configuration, broader Gradle class and delete cases, other source layouts, installers and other operating systems also remain unqualified.

Java Project symbol rows offer **Encapsulate** only for RefactorKit-reported `FIELD` symbols when the selected SDK context and the provider's `encapsulateField` preview capability are available. The action passes the exact provider symbol identity to the shared review flow, refuses dirty Java buffers in the selected project, and rechecks workspace identity after opening the source. RefactorKit owns field resolution and source changes. A Linux X11/Tauri/WebKit release/no-bundle GUI run with locally source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 qualifies a public final `List<String>` field in a Java 17 Maven reactor using JDK 21: preview shows the bound declaration and client read, Apply updates both, a copy of the applied sources passes offline `mvn verify`, and Rollback restores both original files. Editor inputs remain unchanged and the IDE exits cleanly. The run is not a packaged application and does not qualify other field types, providers, installers, operating systems, or broader projects. RefactorKit daemon capability metadata advertises public final primitive-`int`, `String`, `List<String>` and `int[]` fields, preserving the bound type and refusing field declaration annotations and dimensions written after the field name; its original MCP acceptance remains limited to the integer shape. Mutable, static and unresolved fields still refuse. Production panel/controller and Rust request tests cover the integration and refusal boundaries.

For each non-generated source root in the synchronized Java project context, the panel offers **Review move** only when the selected SDK context is available and RefactorKit advertises `moveSourceRoot`. The developer supplies a destination relative to the selected project. The IDE binds the source root to its exact workspace path, refuses dirty Java buffers in that project, and uses the same provider preview, Apply, and protected Rollback flow. Context schemas v3–v7 already supply workspace-relative source-root paths; the review preserves those paths, while legacy v1/v2 paths receive the selected project prefix. A focused unit regression verifies the v7 conversion for a nested Maven project; it does not qualify a native v7 source-root move. RefactorKit owns source-root recognition, package and byte preservation, collision checks, and post-image diagnostics. The Maven Build Helper and Gradle source-root scenarios qualify this route within the bounds described in section 10.1. A real Gradle fixture passes preview, Apply, and Rollback; an applied-source copy passes offline `gradle test`, including a module test that imports the moved `Extra` class. This qualifies one same-module Gradle source-root move and its module test on Linux. Other root layouts, cross-module moves, installers, and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The Java Project view offers **Review Maven module rename** only when its synchronized Maven model and the daemon's experimental preview/diff capability are available. Runtime behavior and limitations are described in [section 6.8](#68-java-project-context).

Formatting and import organization are separate reviewed changes. RefactorKit's current Java formatter source reads hash-bound module `.settings/org.eclipse.jdt.core.prefs` when present and otherwise uses its versioned Eclipse JDT default; this source behavior is not yet qualified in the installed IDE package. The IDE now passes a selected workspace Eclipse formatter XML profile to managed RefactorKit `formatFile` preview. Native workspace code reads and validates the XML, then binds the provider-attested path, profile name and content hash through saved Apply and dirty-editor prepare/confirm; a changed profile invalidates the reviewed plan. Focused Rust, adapter, controller and dialog tests cover this consumer contract. The focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI profile now qualifies the selected workspace profile through saved format-file preview and Apply with the installed RefactorKit daemon; broader project/style combinations remain unqualified (section 10.1). When no profile is selected, the dialog identifies that RefactorKit used project preferences or its default and asks the developer to compare the diff with the workspace style. The IDE does not write project preferences as a side effect. Import organization retains wildcard and unresolved imports where the engine cannot establish safe usage. Preview must contain actual affected files, a rendered patch and engine review evidence; the dialog displays each evidence item's kind and summary, with available file and detail context. This is the provider's reported basis, not an independent IDE verification of semantic completeness. Both saved-source Apply routes keep plans with explicit lexical or absent semantic evidence review-only. A file operation may affect only its requested compilation unit. Apply repeats the engine's read-only preview and refuses a changed artifact before writing. No-patch output currently receives a visible refusal: the installed CLI does not distinguish an unchanged request from every unsupported source-layout case, so the IDE cannot report a verified no-op. The conventional CLI route has real-engine qualification for saved Maven source layouts. It does not authorize the selected SDK or an effective multi-module context; the separate SDK route below owns that boundary. Arbitrary plain-JDK roots and unsaved mutation remain incomplete.

Saved-source Java refactoring requires all editor buffers to be saved and file loads/saves to finish. Buffer revisions and lifetimes are captured before preview; edits, including edits restored to identical saved text, tab replacement and workspace changes require a new preview. A stale-snapshot refusal from `project.open` or `refactor.preview` is surfaced as a synchronization request and retires the selected project context before another review can be applied. Other provider preview refusals retain a sanitized reason, include the provider's JSON-RPC error code when supplied, and state that no source changes were made; they do not recommend retrying an unsupported operation after synchronization. During Apply or advertised Rollback, the editor prevents typing, opening source files, source saves, disk-buffer replacement and recovery replacement. Closing the dialog or cancelling an ordinary file-open intent does not release that protection before the provider write finishes. A workspace switch invalidates the old editor authority.

After confirmed saved-source Apply or Rollback, affected clean open files are read from disk and adopt their new save revision while the write guard is held. A clean open tab for a provider-reported move is loaded from the actual destination, rebound to that path and its fresh save revision, and its Java language document is closed and reopened at the new URI. If the moved file was selected in the explorer, selection follows it to the destination. Destination collisions, unreadable files and other reconciliation failures retain the old tab with a visible warning; unrelated buffers remain untouched. The native CLI bridge retains the applied transaction's affected files and returns their inverse changes after confirmed rollback, because the CLI's rollback message does not list restored paths. Language synchronization, affected explorer directories and an already-loaded Java project view are refreshed. Explorer refreshes reload missing children of already expanded folders when a bounded native listing ends at those folders, so an unrelated open source branch remains usable after a transformation. The IDE never reconstructs Java text from a rendered diff. Late reads cannot replace reopened buffers or update a newer workspace. Refresh failures are reported separately from the provider's confirmed write outcome. Deleted or unreadable source buffers remain open with warnings. Production unit coverage is supplemented by focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI acceptance for a same-module class move and rollback, where the open tab follows the moved path and returns to the original path (section 10.1). Destination collisions, unreadable-file recovery, other transformations and other operating systems remain unqualified. The separate editor-owned draft route is described below. Unit tests exercise the production controllers, editor/file-tree view models and reconciliation helper with provider doubles.

The CLI's reviewed plans and transactions survive an unavailable or restarted daemon in the same workspace. Daemon-owned previews and transactions retire with its session. Workspace shutdown clears both sets of authority. Availability of the separate daemon does not authorize or disable a CLI operation that has passed its own capability and review checks.

With an explicitly selected project SDK, the Java refactoring consumer requires an available saved project context and the daemon's separate `javaContextRefactoring` operation advertisement. It captures the project directory, SDK, Maven repository and profiles with the provider's snapshot and context identities. Unsynchronized or partial context, a target outside that project, changed settings and uncorrelated preview evidence refuse the offer. Package actions originate from RefactorKit package groupings and bind a representative source path inside the selected project, including when the workspace model also contains the same package under another build. The reviewed request carries the exact `fromPackage` and `toPackage` intent to the typed `movePackage` operation. Editor file actions use the SDK advertisement when an SDK is selected, including when the legacy CLI is unavailable. Selecting an SDK never falls back to CLI analysis or mutation.

The editor menu and command palette also expose **Review Java Inline Method at cursor** only when a synchronized Java project advertises stable managed `inlineMethod` through the project-context route. The IDE binds the saved cursor to RefactorKit selection, sends no replacement intent, and has no general CLI fallback. The installed provider does not advertise this operation, so it offers no action. An isolated source-built RefactorKit candidate now accepts the cursor-resolved method selection, and the focused Linux native profile passes preview, Apply and Rollback for the bounded case recorded in section 10.1. The candidate fix is not yet in an installed or released provider package; broader method shapes and other platforms remain unqualified.

The IDE also provides a capability-gated **Review Java interface extraction at cursor** action in the editor menu and command palette. It binds the saved class cursor to RefactorKit’s exact JDT class selection and asks for the interface and method names. The current provider cell supports one public concrete instance method with primitive parameters and primitive or `void` return type on a top-level class without an existing hierarchy or type parameters; it creates a same-package interface and makes the class implement it. Other signatures and class shapes must be refused by RefactorKit. Contract, controller, editor action and native request-payload checks pass. The locally source-built 0.7.0/API 0.2 daemon and CLI used for GUI qualification advertise `extractInterface`; a focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI run has completed preview, Apply, offline Maven verification on a copied source tree, and Rollback successfully (section 10.1). Cached provider builds that do not advertise the capability continue to hide the action. Installed or released packages, broader project contexts and method shapes, and other operating systems remain unqualified.
The editor menu and command palette offer **Review Pull Up Method** from a saved Java cursor only when the selected SDK context, mutation-selection query and stable managed `pullUpMember` capability are available. The developer enters the fully qualified direct superclass; RefactorKit resolves the method with JDT bindings and owns preview, Apply and Rollback. The preview marks this bounded operation high risk and warns that reflection and external or resource-shaped consumers are not analyzed, so the developer reviews the warning before explicit Apply. The qualified provider shape and its limits are recorded in section 10.1; unsupported declarations refuse.

The editor menu and command palette also offer **Review Push Down Method** only when the selected SDK context, mutation-selection query and stable managed `pushDownMember` capability are available. The developer enters the fully qualified direct child; RefactorKit resolves the saved method with JDT bindings and owns preview, Apply and Rollback. The first qualified high-risk provider cell requires a package-private abstract parent, one package-private final direct child and a single compilation unit in an available non-generated source set; every method use must be a complete binding-resolved invocation inside that child. RefactorKit warns that reflection and external or resource-shaped consumers are not analyzed, so the developer reviews that warning before explicit Apply. Unsupported hierarchy, declaration and invocation shapes refuse.

**Review Move Member** uses the saved method cursor and the same guarded review flow. The dialog searches JDT LS class declarations in the current source file; RefactorKit resolves the chosen declaration to a saved JDT binding and checks the requested move. The dialog states the current provider limit of exactly two top-level classes in that file. RefactorKit owns the method and invocation edits, rejects unsupported shapes, and supplies the plan for explicit Apply and guarded Rollback. Dirty Java buffers require explicit saving before review. Native qualification for the supported method and an unsupported instance method is scoped in section 10.1.

The native SDK route retains the exact provider plan, target, mutation intent and workspace selection in a bounded daemon session. Maven opens an owned session for the SDK operation; an evaluated Gradle project reuses the active project-context session and binds its plan and transaction to that session identity. The route requests `refactor.preview` with the selected context, requires its attestation and the provider's actual rendered text diff, then invokes `refactor.apply` for the approved retained plan with the same context. The SDK advertisement must explicitly offer rendered diffs, and the returned diff must include completeness evidence. Apply and rollback also require the exact Java operation's language-kernel entry to declare stable maturity, managed-stable mutation authority and non-lexical evidence; the aggregate operation list alone does not authorize writes. Proposal-only or lexically evidenced operations remain reviewable when preview is advertised, but their plans are visibly ineligible for Apply. A truncated preview stays readable but cannot be approved, including through a direct native Apply request. The current upstream Apply contract does not bind and recheck mutation authority per operation; IDE-side admission therefore does not prove provider-side enforcement, and the operation-specific authority contract remains open. SDK, snapshot and context validation remain RefactorKit's responsibility. Native preview, Apply, Rollback and discard run on blocking workers; workspace activation is serialized with those calls. A confirmed Apply must report the reviewed file effects, applied context identity and committed snapshot. Transport failures or uncorrelated write responses report an unknown outcome. The editor protection remains held through completion and reconciliation, and the saved project context is retired after a confirmed or unknown write. Project settings and synchronization are disabled during the write. SDK-protected rollback requires its separate capability advertisement, the retained transaction, the original context and the exact committed snapshot. Maven rollback opens an owned daemon session with the same project settings; Gradle rollback refreshes the committed workspace snapshot and uses the retained transaction session without reevaluating Gradle. Successful restoration must confirm the original context and snapshot and the inverse file effects. Changed SDK, profiles, source or build/classpath evidence refuses restoration; ordinary or forced rollback is never substituted. The selected settings must still match, although Apply has retired the observed context. A subsequent build can change classpath evidence and invalidate this rollback; rollback after such a rebuild requires a separate provider contract and is unavailable. Transaction guards retire on workspace/session authority reset; reopening the IDE does not recover them. Verification scope is described in section 10.1.

Rollback feedback distinguishes a refusal before a write from an unconfirmed write outcome. If the native saved-snapshot check finds changed project files after Apply, the interface states that Rollback was not started and asks the developer to review the current changes and transaction. Only this confirmed pre-write refusal retains an explicit Retry Rollback action. Each retry uses the original transaction, SDK context and post-Apply snapshot, rechecks current SDK settings and workspace authority, and acquires the editor write guard again. It does not retry automatically. If the original authority or returned file effects cannot be confirmed after rollback, the interface states that files may have changed and directs the developer to inspect the project and compare open buffers with disk. Neither case is presented as a successful rollback. These messages are fixed guidance: native hashes, paths and source excerpts are not copied into them. Managed refactoring errors keep technical command identity available for diagnostics while presenting human-readable messages in the interface.

Saved-file editor reconciliation revalidates workspace authority after a moved-file read and after closing or activating its Java language document, including rejected asynchronous completions. Once the pass is retired, it stops before further document activation, buffer refresh, save notifications or view updates. The editor model also discards a late metadata-close failure after workspace invalidation instead of retrying adapter cleanup under a later activation. Errors that complete while the workspace is still current retain a visible synchronization warning. These guards govern continuations and subsequent calls; confirmed source writes retain their provider transaction outcome and recovery or rollback remains explicit.

Move Class requests provider-qualified source association when the synchronized context is still v1 or v2. Context v7 already carries that association, like v3 through v6, and opening its review dialog retains the qualified context instead of immediately starting another qualification query. Ordinary preview and Apply still perform their required provider checks.

With the separately built capable RefactorKit package, the SDK route can review class/member renames at the cursor and whole-file formatting or import changes against unsaved Java buffers. It captures the text and monotonic versions of all open Java buffers in the selected project, refuses pending file I/O, and checks buffer revisions and lifetimes again before displaying the result. Every affected existing Java source must be open and captured; missing documents receive a refusal rather than an automatic save or a guessed transformation. The ordinary installed provider has not been upgraded by this delivery.

Cursor-based draft renames use `intelligence.query` mutation selection followed by `refactor.editor.preview` in the same daemon session as project-context acquisition and navigation, preserving the provider's document-version history. RefactorKit resolves the compiler target; the IDE passes the complete `java-editor-mutation-selection-v1` selection into preview and checks its correlation to the SDK, saved base, immutable provider snapshot and every captured document. A new version invalidates the selection even when text is identical. Whole-file actions use their exact file path and do not require a semantic cursor target. The `java-editor-refactoring-v1` response supplies an actual bounded diff, diagnostics, retained plan and selection identities, and versioned Language Server Protocol workspace edits. Native checks reject uncaptured files, stale document versions, invalid UTF-16 ranges, overlapping edits, paths outside the project and renames that permit overwrite. Context and saved source evidence are checked before and after review; the TypeScript adapter checks the captured document contents against their returned hashes. No source is saved or renamed by this flow.

The dialog requests durable editor-owned previews only when the installed provider explicitly advertises mutation and every required recovery phase for the operation. Providers offering only read-only draft review keep Apply unavailable. The controller and adapter refuse submitting editor plans through the saved-source Apply route. Confidence is shown as unreported because this provider contract supplies none. Cancelling retires the IDE's local review; provider plans remain in its bounded session store until eviction or session shutdown.

The provider-neutral transaction port, native bridge and buffer orchestration now implement the separate `durable-editor-owned` preview mode and `java-editor-transaction-v1` preparation, confirmation, undo, discovery and recovery protocol. Mutation admission requires the provider's explicit operation and durable-recovery capabilities. Native preparation accepts only a retained editor plan reviewed in that mode with the same approved plan hash and original SDK context. Each mutation phase refreshes the provider's current saved snapshot through `workspace.refresh`, preserving the shared SDK session and any explicitly evaluated Gradle context. Changed saved snapshots retire observed context; synchronization must acquire fresh analysis authority before further navigation or review. The original approved context remains the authority for provider-validated undo and recovery.

The web core stages versioned LSP edits against the exact captured UTF-16 text before making changes. It refuses overlapping ranges, surrogate splits, uncaptured documents, collisions and oversized transformed buffers. An editor transaction protects typing, Save, opening and closing buffers while preparation and acknowledgement are pending. Text, paths, tab metadata and buffer lifetimes are published together; renamed documents receive a new document version lineage. After a committed rename, the desktop opening coordinator adopts the active buffer’s new path so the editor remains visible through draft Apply/Undo and saved-source Apply/Rollback. A newer pending or failed navigation keeps its own presentation; reconciliation does not replace that intent. Native file moves use Linux no-overwrite renames and retain the original saved bytes. They do not save transformed drafts. The editor adapter transfers the original save revision to each new path and rechecks the saved bytes, so subsequent Save continues to reject independent disk changes. Confirmation sends the actual transformed text and versions; Undo applies the provider's inverse to the original draft, not to the earlier saved text. Missing acknowledgements retain an unknown outcome and known transaction identity for recovery, without fabricated success or automatic source compensation.

The dialog now connects explicit Apply and Undo to this transaction service. Undo retains the original reviewed context after a source rename retires current analysis, and requires unchanged selected SDK settings. It restores original dirty flags only when the provider's inverse reproduces the exact captured text. Java tabs opened after Apply remain outside the original transaction and are preserved. Language documents receive the committed draft text; this reconciliation does not reread source content or send a save notification. An interrupted acknowledgement keeps the transformed buffers and exposes **Restore original drafts** for a known transaction, with provider revalidation before changes. View refresh cannot turn an unknown transaction outcome into confirmed success.

The **Java draft transactions** action in **Java Project** opens the provider's durable inventory after the selected project synchronizes in a new SDK session. Optional document metadata includes every originally captured Java document, including clean and unaffected companions, with its original path, approved final path and original saved-content hash. The final path describes the approved transformation and does not assert the current physical location after interruption. Journal-directed revision inspection uses the native bounded file checker independently of open-editor save baselines. If the background editor monitor is using the worker, the recovery inspection retries within its original deadline using the same workspace, path and expected revision. Missing or ambiguous paths, changed saved bytes and unavailable inspection refuse recovery. Inspection does not adopt a save revision or load text into a buffer.

Recovery review opens missing clean companions from the verified existing paths and preserves every existing buffer. RefactorKit revalidates the original SDK, plan and context against the current saved sources and the complete captured document lineage; an unknown image receives a refusal without edits. The dialog displays paired current/original draft text and the provider's inverse file moves. Cancellation leaves source files and buffer contents intact, retaining opened clean tabs and the durable journal. Private editor checkpoints remain available separately and are not automatically substituted for captured buffers.

Only explicit **Restore original drafts** can apply the reviewed inverse. A retained tab whose path differs from the verified physical source is first associated with that existing file under an editor guard; the provider's inverse then restores original paths and text. Preparation must reproduce the exact reviewed versioned edits. Changed SDK settings, workspace generation, buffer text or lifetime invalidates approval, including editing and restoring identical text. Unrelated open documents remain outside the transaction. Original dirty state after restart is derived from restored content versus the journal's original saved-content hash. Confirmation and language/explorer reconciliation follow the same guarded transaction protocol as ordinary draft Undo. If rename baseline transfer fails, subsequent Save is blocked rather than issuing a write without a revision; a fresh explicit read or issued disk comparison is needed before saving. Restart recovery is implemented; its native GUI verification scope and remaining limitations are maintained in section 10.1.

Separate opt-in native-library checks have passed against installed RefactorKit 0.7.0 (API 0.2) for a signed saved-source method selector and the two whole-file operations. Their verification scope is recorded in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope); commands appear in [section 7.2](#72-development-and-verification-commands). Arbitrary source roots in plain-JDK projects remain unqualified: the nonconventional fixture was refused before a preview. These bounded cases do not qualify all refactorings, dependency projects, cross-platform packages or editor overlays.

Pi renderer attachments remain bound to their authorized workspace. The Git Changes review and editor-navigation flow is described in [section 6.12](#612-read-only-git-review).

An interrupted RefactorKit transaction on saved files can prevent Java project synchronization. When the daemon advertises saved-file recovery, **Java Project** offers a review for the selected project. Explicit confirmation calls RefactorKit's journal recovery for that project. The IDE refuses obsolete requests and uses the workspace write guard to protect open drafts. The native command stops the managed JDT LS session before journal recovery and keeps it from starting during the operation. After the provider returns, the IDE refreshes the explorer and clean open files from disk, retaining any buffer it cannot reconcile. After confirmed recovery it resumes a previously active JDT LS session, including when recovery succeeds on a retry. A successful recovery clears the offer and requires a new synchronization. RefactorKit remains responsible for reversing its saved-file changes and refusing conflicting disk state. The Linux AppImage qualifies recovery from a partially moved Maven module on X11 and KWin Wayland, as described in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).

### 6.5 Editor Recovery and Local History

The desktop **Recovery and history** control lists earlier/other-session drafts and checkpoints for the active file. A provider-neutral port delegates persistence to native, workspace-isolated journals; see [ADR 0018](ADR.md#adr-0018--workspace-scoped-editor-recovery-and-checkpoint-history). The browser provider reports unavailable rather than claiming durable native recovery.

Dirty buffers are checkpointed after a fixed 750 ms scheduling delay, including continuous typing. Save, save-before-Java execution, dirty-tab close and explicit disk-buffer discard attempt an immediate checkpoint first. Storage failure remains visible but does not become an unrelated source-save permission gate. The status becomes current only after a successful acknowledgment; recent unacknowledged edits can still be lost if the process is terminated. Initial inventory reads remain loading until they complete. Refreshing readable inventory does not acknowledge a failed draft checkpoint or hide its error. After storage is explicitly repaired, **Checkpoint now** revalidates it even if the current draft set has not changed, without forcing a journal or source write. A repaired empty-draft session can therefore return to ready; unacknowledged dirty content still requires a successful checkpoint.

Native sessions are issued for the actual main window and registered workspace, with generation/session checks and revocation on workspace switch or application exit. Journal operations run on native worker threads. Persistent data is keyed by canonical root beneath `IDE_HOME/editor-recovery`, not written into project sources. File locks coordinate processes; same-directory temporary publication, flushing and Unix directory synchronization protect the previous committed journal from interrupted writes. Corrupt journals are refused rather than overwritten. These controls are not a guarantee against every same-user filesystem race, disk failure or power loss.

When source storage is full, Save reports failure while retaining the current dirty buffer, the saved source and acknowledged recovery data. Its message includes checking available disk space. After freeing space, the person can retry Save using the existing revision. A full recovery filesystem retains the previous journal and current buffer, reports that the newest edits may lack a durable checkpoint, and still permits explicit source Save when its separate filesystem is writable. **Checkpoint now** retries recovery after space is released. Temporary writes that fail before publication are removed. Focused Linux qualification uses separate bounded filesystems for these two failures; it does not cover every filesystem, quota, inode or post-publication durability failure.

**Retention and privacy:** each buffer is limited to 1 MiB UTF-8, with at most 64 pending drafts, 100 historical versions and 16 MiB of retained source content per workspace. Older history is trimmed first; pending drafts are not silently evicted. Exceeded capacity preserves the previous checkpoint and reports failure. Unix directories/files use private permissions. Checkpoints contain unencrypted source text, which may include sensitive data; encryption, exclusion policies and configurable retention remain future work. Only persisted checkpoints and checkpointed pre-save/pre-discard buffers enter this history—not every keystroke, source save or external Git/Pi write.

**Restore:** choose a checkpoint, review the current buffer and selected version, then explicitly replace the reviewed buffer. It becomes dirty and retains its existing disk-save revision, so a later external write still makes normal Save refuse. Concurrent edits, pending saves, workspace changes and tab lifetime changes reject stale reviews. Other dirty buffers are preserved. The original recovery entry remains available subject to the workspace retention limits or separately confirmed removal. Missing/deleted files expose the checkpoint for selection/copying; automatic file recreation is deliberately unavailable. This is buffer recovery, not RefactorKit multi-file transaction rollback.

### 6.6 Java Cursor Navigation

**Java Structure** is a persistent activity for the active workspace Java source. **Show Java File Structure** in Commands opens it and reveals the sidebar. It displays JDT LS document symbols, including nested types and members, with per-branch and whole-outline expand/collapse controls. Source order is the default; the Order control can instead sort sibling declarations by name while retaining their parents. Name sorting ignores case, compares embedded numbers numerically and keeps provider order for equal names. The chosen order remains active while the view is mounted. Sorting and filtering change only presentation and never rewrite provider identities, ranges or source text. The local filter matches names, details and symbol kinds while retaining matching declarations' ancestors; filtering never starts a new semantic query. Selecting a declaration uses its provider selection range through guarded document navigation and participates in Back/Forward history. It does not save the buffer.

The structure view uses the exact synchronized editor version, including unsaved text. It queries only while active, debounces updates by 250 milliseconds and cancels replaced or hidden requests. Workspace activation, source text, buffer lifetime, language-session identity and document version bind each response and later navigation. Results with mismatched metadata or ranges outside the captured UTF-16 source are refused. Presentation is bounded to 2,000 declarations and 33 nesting levels; provider or presentation truncation is identified as partial. A missing symbol capability, unsynchronized source, library preview or provider failure remains unavailable rather than an empty successful outline. This is a document-local projection of the existing language-service contract, not an additional semantic project model. It does not supply inherited members, project-wide structure or a library-source outline.

The Java Intelligence panel keeps RefactorKit position-query results independent of JDT LS cancellation callbacks. A language-service callback change does not silently discard a pending RefactorKit response or leave its controls permanently busy. A different workspace activation, active source or project-context identity clears those results and rejects late panel publication; disposing the panel also retires its pending display. Provider authority and location validation remain the navigation controller's responsibility.

When a project SDK is selected in Java Project, cursor navigation requires its current available effective context. The controller carries the same project directory, SDK, local Maven repository, profiles, snapshot, context identity and provider platform identities into the navigation request. A missing or partial context, a source outside the selected project, or changed settings refuses navigation. A configuration/context change also revokes an already returned location before opening or revealing it.

The native service uses the same daemon session as the selected project-context acquisition and supplies RefactorKit's `javaContext: {sdkHome, expectedContextHash}` query authority. Context acquisition, navigation and draft preview are serialized under the session lock. Before and after SDK-bound navigation, the consumer reuses the successful versioned context method and its provider, module and source-set selectors, pins the snapshot and context hashes, and requires the same schema and JDK identities. If that selection cannot be revalidated, synchronization is required. It neither reopens the project nor evaluates build code during navigation; a retired session requires synchronization again. The workspace, SDK, project settings, saved context and platform identities must match before the session can be used. Ready results must attest the same saved snapshot, exact context schema version and hash (v1 through v7), and platform identities. A provider that ignores the authority cannot return an accepted result. Workspace-relative editor paths are converted to the selected project's relative paths for the engine, then validated source locations and preview paths are converted back for the editor. No dependency graph is reconstructed in the IDE. Without a selected project SDK, the existing saved-source path remains available and makes no configured-SDK claim.

The desktop derives the Java editor model URI from the workspace path when the file opens. The editor keeps that model when JDT LS binds to the file. Monaco registers the navigation provider for the active model and workspace generation. A pending request keeps its cancellation callback while subsequent requests use the current callbacks. The native adapter validates source locations against the selected daemon project root and converts those paths to workspace-relative paths before the IDE opens a source file. Monaco uses the destination file extension to select syntax highlighting for the immutable navigation preview. A correlated query refusal that reports a changed snapshot retires the selected context and asks for synchronization. The refusal carries no definition, selection or edit authority.

Java definition navigation uses F12 or Ctrl-click; RefactorKit references use Shift+F12 and Monaco's reference preview. When RefactorKit returns an unavailable or empty definition result, or the typed refusal `java.context.sourceAnalysisUnqualified`, F12 and Ctrl/Command-click try the JDT LS definition capability only if its active workspace, document path and URI, and buffer version still match the current editor request; it never bypasses a retired RefactorKit project context. The fallback accepts only a current, correlated JDT LS result and opens it through guarded application navigation. Keyboard and modified-click navigation use the same guarded opener; late fallback replies cannot navigate or replace the current status after a buffer or workspace change. If no current target can be opened, the editor preserves the provider or language-service reason. An empty result across the available routes reports that no definition was found. If the provider has retired the project context, the editor reports that reason before any dependency lookup or JDT LS fallback. The Java Intelligence panel also queries type definitions, supertypes, subtypes, callers, calls made and implementations at the current editor cursor. The RefactorKit implementation query is a separate panel action from JDT LS Go to Implementation. It resolves source type and method declarations to concrete workspace-source implementations through exact JDT bindings; the result identifies whether the selected target is a type or method and reports completeness, warnings and truncation. The native service discovers RefactorKit's API 0.2 capability for each query and submits its exact path, editor text, version, optional hierarchy direction and zero-based UTF-16 position. Implementation lookup is offered only when saved-snapshot, position and bounded-query capabilities are advertised; dirty-buffer queries additionally require an available SDK-bound context and the immutable-overlay implementation capability. RefactorKit owns overload resolution and project analysis. The IDE accepts compiler-backed, snapshot-correlated locations and validates their source ranges; it does not infer symbol identity from token spelling. Canceling an in-flight cursor query removes its pending UI approval and sends RefactorKit `intelligence.cancel` with the same request ID. An acknowledged cancellation keeps the daemon and project session available for later queries; if the provider does not acknowledge within one second, the owned daemon process is stopped. Controller, adapter, cancellation-registry and Rust transport tests cover the bounded wait. A Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario against installed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 verifies a cancellation response and successful later queries on the same daemon session; broader query loads and providers remain unqualified.

The Java definition request can opt in to RefactorKit’s Kotlin source resolution for a saved Java cursor in a synchronized Gradle project. The desktop sends the selected JDK and explicitly configured compiler JARs only when the daemon advertises `kotlinDefinitionToolchain`. Set `IDE_KOTLIN_DEFINITION_COMPILER_JAR` and `IDE_KOTLIN_DEFINITION_COMPILER_CLASSPATH` before starting the desktop. Use an absolute compiler JAR and a platform-separated list of absolute dependency JARs for the same Kotlin compiler. RefactorKit checks the evaluated Gradle source ownership and compares the resolved class bytes against a disposable compilation before returning a Kotlin location. The IDE reads and validates that destination through the ordinary workspace navigation path.

Shift+F12 also uses JDT LS after the typed source-analysis refusal. Reference occurrences in the same file share one immutable Monaco preview model so the results are grouped by file and show real source text. The IDE reads open draft buffers first and uses read-only disk inspection for closed files, without opening tabs or adopting save baselines. Accepted preview text is limited to 200 files, 1 MiB per file and 8 MiB in total; unavailable or oversized source text produces an explicit unavailable result. Ranges outside the loaded source text are refused. Opening an occurrence rechecks the source request and target text before guarded workspace navigation. Preview snapshots describe displayed text, not additional semantic authority. Retiring a result or its editor disposes its preview models. Focused unit tests cover source inspection, grouping, target changes and model disposal. The Maven Java 27 native scenario in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope) verifies read-only previews and call-site navigation with open sources and, in a separate execution, with the declaration tab closed. Inspecting the closed declaration does not open a tab. The complete native runner invocation also passes, including source preservation, normal application closure, environment restoration and no surviving scenario processes.

The native navigation boundary retains a bounded RefactorKit refusal code alongside its explanation. This distinguishes a typed `java.context.sourceAnalysisUnqualified` result from generic unavailability when JDT LS supplies a guarded definition target; metadata-only project context still carries no RefactorKit semantic authority.

**Find references with JDT LS** is a separate, explicit workspace query in the Java Intelligence panel. The editor action `Find References with JDT LS` is available from the Java editor context menu and `Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+R`; it opens the Java Intelligence panel and searches from the current cursor.
