The query sends the current synchronized Java document and UTF-16 cursor position through LSP `textDocument/references`, including the declaration. The native service checks the active session capability and current document version, restricts returned locations to canonical Java files inside the workspace, and bounds the response to 100 locations. The panel identifies JDT LS as the provider and labels truncated results as partial; selecting a location opens it through workspace-generation-guarded navigation. This command does not silently replace RefactorKit's `Shift+F12` operation. Rust sanitizer, Tauri adapter, production-controller and panel tests cover workspace confinement, exact request policy, stale replies and partial-result presentation. A Linux native GUI scenario qualifies the keyboard shortcut and panel query for one basic Java project; section 10.1 records its scope. Packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

**Go to Type Definition** in the Java editor context menu resolves the type at the cursor through the capability-gated RefactorKit query also used by Java Intelligence. It requests one workspace-source declaration at the current UTF-16 position. The workspace, model version and project authority must remain current through navigation. Availability follows the advertised saved-source support and, for supported unsaved buffers, immutable editor overlay support. The editor also admits the action for a synchronized workspace document when JDT LS advertises `typeDefinitionProvider`. It uses JDT LS when RefactorKit has no type-definition capability or gives the typed `java.context.sourceAnalysisUnqualified` refusal for a current project. The native language service restricts the result to workspace Java source. The editor checks workspace generation, document identity, buffer version, cursor position and request correlation before opening the result. Java Intelligence also offers an explicit **JDT LS type definition** query for the current buffer. It lists the workspace locations for review and clears the list when the active document, language session or cursor changes. Selecting a location rechecks the source and workspace before opening it.

Go to Implementation sends a JDT LS request over the current synchronized Java document. The desktop client advertises dynamic registration and enables the action while JDT LS reports the implementation capability. Responses are bounded to 100 locations and restricted to canonical `.java` files inside the workspace. The IDE verifies the source model version and workspace generation through the file switch and reveals the returned declaration range. The Java Intelligence panel also offers a RefactorKit implementation query with a limit of 200 workspace-source results. Section 10.1 describes the native verification of both workflows.

Without an explicitly selected SDK, all open buffers must be saved and file operations finished, and the requesting text must match the UTF-8 source on disk. With an available SDK context, unrelated non-Java drafts remain unsaved and are monitored for changes throughout the query and target opening. Java drafts use the provider's separately advertised immutable-editor query contract. The controller captures every open Java buffer in the selected project when any of them is dirty, including the queried source, and sends exact text and process-local document versions without saving. RefactorKit closes its analysis over the saved project plus those replacements. The native bridge requires the saved base/context, provider snapshot, overlay identity and every supplied document's path, version and content hash; navigation locations use the captured dirty text where applicable. It retains the same daemon session so document-version checks survive successive queries, validates the SDK/project context before and after each query, and confirms that supplied documents' saved bytes have not changed. The ordinary route still reopens its saved project after queries. Transport, protocol and oversized-request failures retire the selected session. A complete JSON-RPC `INTERNAL_ERROR` response refuses only that query and preserves the synchronized project context for retry; other provider errors retain their existing recovery behavior. When the native bridge confirms that the selected session was retired, the result carries an explicit retirement marker and the IDE clears the observed Java project context, so the Project panel no longer presents it as synchronized. Preflight refusals that do not enter and retire the selected session leave that context intact. Rust, adapter and controller tests cover this state transition; native GUI failure presentation has not been qualified. It does not silently retry a lost session or repeat Gradle evaluation; the user must synchronize again before another project-context query. Edits, including edits restored to identical text, replaced tabs and workspace changes invalidate a request or selected result. When a selected target opens, its buffer must match the returned source text and the original buffers must retain their reviewed revisions. An obsolete result cannot authorize a cursor reveal or replace local edits.

Monaco previews use separate source models and read-only preview editors. Selecting a result opens the real workspace buffer through the application navigation controller. Preview models are bounded, disposed with their registrations and never copied into a live editor buffer. Source files are limited to 1 MiB UTF-8 each and 8 MiB in aggregate; reference and call-hierarchy queries return at most 1,000 references or 500 related methods, and type hierarchy and implementation queries return at most 200 items each. Hierarchy and implementation responses are limited to 10,000 validated source locations. RefactorKit does not currently impose an aggregate call-site or response-byte cap, so the IDE refuses call-hierarchy responses above its location limit. Type hierarchy and implementations cover workspace source only. Call hierarchy reports direct method and constructor calls, and includes exact identities for resolved classpath targets; binary-only targets have no source location and cannot be opened as source. It remains partial and excludes dynamic dispatch and method references. Semantic completeness, analysis warnings and truncation of returned results remain distinct and are presented honestly. Editor cancellation suppresses late presentation; native RPC calls retain the transport's bounded timeout rather than claiming cooperative engine cancellation.

**Dependency and JDK sources:** the Java editor's **Open source** action and F12 use the selected SDK and effective project context. When Java buffers are dirty, navigation first selects their complete immutable editor frame, then repeats that frame and provider identity through source lookup and guarded read. Missing frame support or changed documents refuses opening without saving. Automatic definition previews cannot replace a pending explicit source lookup/read; workspace, SDK and buffer changes still invalidate it. Clean Java buffers use saved-source authority and preserve unrelated drafts. RefactorKit resolves dependency sources to an exact JVM binding, scoped binary owner and locally attached source. The native consumer checks provider/module/source-set/classpath ownership and reads through the same daemon session using the returned association identity. Missing attachments, ambiguous binary owners and changed associations produce explicit unavailable, ambiguous or refused results. Queries neither evaluate Gradle nor download sources; Gradle source variants must already belong to an explicitly synchronized context.

JDK sources use a separate read-only platform-source contract. After validating the selected project context and current editor frame, the native adapter returns an explicit unavailable result when the selected SDK lacks its standard `lib/src.zip`, without waiting for a provider lookup. When the archive exists, the provider verifies the selected SDK's current JRT module/class, its matching source file in that archive, and the current platform identity; historical signature archives cannot attest source for the current platform. The native commands, provider-neutral contracts, web-core port, TypeScript adapter, Monaco read-only model and editor-controller fallback are implemented. Adapter and controller tests cover selected SDK/context identities, JRT/source correlation, stale associations, complete editor frames and the separate 512 KiB UTF-8 source limit. Real production-path native tests pass with current JDK 25 sources and report JDK 21 sources unavailable when that SDK has no standard source archive. Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios now cover both states: JDK 25 F12 selects the exact `StringBuilder.toString` declaration, **Open source** reopens it, typing and Save are blocked, an unrelated unsaved text draft remains intact, and source archive/project inputs and application state pass clean-exit checks; JDK 21 displays the missing-source result without creating a source tab and preserves both a dirty Java editor frame and an unrelated text draft. Both JDK 21 windows close normally with no remaining runner-owned processes. GUI qualification for an available archive still uses saved-source authority; dirty JDK-source editor-frame GUI, other operating systems, installers and broader SDK packaging remain unqualified.


The native SDK-source consumer distinguishes an explicit `--release` restriction from source/target syntax. A source/target 8 source set can accept current SDK source evidence only when its returned API profile, platform identity, source ownership and archive evidence match the selected context; an explicit release 8 still rejects current-platform evidence. Focused native tests cover this admission and refusal boundary. The isolated RefactorKit candidate used for Java-only context projection also passes the production-path Maven release-21 and release-25 fixtures with selected JDK 21 and 25 and their actual v2 context schema: lookup, declaration, source reading and dirty-companion editor frames preserve the saved inputs, compiled output and live session. The production TypeScript SDK-source decoder accepts the returned evidence. A subsequent isolated RefactorKit candidate corrects the SDK-source API selector. Independent native-service checks now pass source/target 8 with selected JDK 21 and 25, including saved-source lookup, declaration and source reading, independently modified companion buffers, exact document correlation and production TypeScript decoding. Saved sources, build inputs, compiled output and the live session remain unchanged. Position requests and captured editor buffers can use independent document-version counters; exact text and response identity remain required for both. Compiler checks use the captured buffer version directly. The [native SDK-source regression](apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/refactorkit_daemon/java_platform_source_real_tests.rs) checks the shared guard on JDK 21 and 25. These checks qualify the tested Maven service path; they do not qualify that candidate through the native GUI or replace the default provider. The corrected diagnostic candidate also passes the real saved-source and dirty-companion SDK-source fixtures on JDK 21 and 25. Historical release-8 source availability and SDK installations without source archives retain their existing limitations.

Library and JDK source tabs are immutable in-memory snapshots, separate from workspace buffers, Save, recovery and filesystem navigation. Their labels identify the dependency component or JDK release/module and owning source file. Typing and the active-file save shortcut are blocked; an explicitly requested Save All still saves actual workspace drafts. Opening a source preserves unrelated drafts and rejects changed buffers, tab lifetimes, workspace or SDK/context authority before presenting either response. Workspace opens and tab selection cancel late source presentation; SDK/context changes retire all source tabs. The application retains at most eight source documents: dependency sources are bounded to 128 KiB UTF-8, and JDK sources to 512 KiB. Displayed content is the captured snapshot. F12 and definition navigation use the provider's declaration API and guarded read when ordinary project navigation has no source target; the consumer checks returned ranges against guarded text. Monaco uses a separate immutable model, and selecting a declaration revalidates its association before opening and selecting it. No source line is inferred from a JVM name or descriptor. Dependency navigation with dirty Java buffers uses the immutable frame attested by workspace definition selection, including every open Java buffer in the selected project. Changes to the inventory, buffer revisions or SDK/context revoke that selection. A provider without the immutable-editor source methods returns unavailable; the IDE does not switch to saved-cursor authority or save drafts. Matching a binary identity to source metadata does not establish source/binary implementation equivalence.

Unit tests exercise the production adapter, Monaco provider registration and controller with public API/provider doubles, including stale responses, UTF-16 validation, buffer lifetime changes, read-only previews and refusal without writes. An opt-in native library test has passed with installed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 for an overloaded Java method in a minimal Maven source layout, an astral character before the call, declaration inclusion and bounded references.

The added type-definition, type-hierarchy and call-hierarchy paths pass focused native Rust normalization/capability tests, TypeScript adapter tests, controller tests and Java Intelligence panel tests. RefactorKit's immutable-editor overlay BDD scenario also passes for these query forms. The IDE's opt-in production Rust test passes against the RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 package built from the current source, exercising all three query forms through the native service. The complete native GUI result and its limits are recorded below.

Section 10.1 records the current native cursor verification. An earlier run of the two-module fixture with the user-installed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 daemon used a one-second bounded cancellation-acknowledgment wait. The trace records a written `intelligence.cancel`, a matching JSON-RPC `-32800` response, and later successful definition and implementation queries on the same session. A prior 250 ms wait expired while the child process was still running and caused context retirement; the reason for that longer response remains unknown. The tested scenario qualifies cancellation continuity for this Linux Maven fixture, not a general provider latency bound. The source-built scheduler regression verifies that a non-fatal query-handler error returns JSON-RPC `INTERNAL_ERROR` and the same worker serves a later request. A source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon package also passes a direct two-module Maven session check: project.context v2 followed by definition and implementations queries returns the expected declarations while the daemon stays alive. The native Linux release/no-bundle project-context scenario passes with this package. The installed RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon also passes a direct two-module Maven check: project-context v2 acquisition followed by definition and implementations queries returns the expected declarations while the daemon remains alive. The native Linux project-context GUI scenario passes with the installed daemon. These runs qualify ordinary query continuity for the tested fixture; non-fatal error-handler recovery remains qualified only with the source-built daemon. A separate library-navigation profile verifies exact dependency overload identities and navigable workspace call sites across Maven and Gradle, saved-source and editor-frame cases. These scenarios run as Linux release/no-bundle GUI tests with explicit provider paths; other runtime selections remain unqualified for these queries. Shared installation-discovery verification is described in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope). The [native cursor requirement](features/refactorkit/native-java-cursor-navigation.feature) and broader Java navigation requirement remain partial. Run the scenario with `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON`, `IDE_JDTLS_HOME`, `IDE_JAVA_HOME` and `IDE_JDTLS_JAVA_HOME` set to qualified tool paths using `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-cursor-navigation-native-001`. The matching `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-cursor-navigation-native-001:appimage` profile builds and runs the Linux x86-64 AppImage. Remaining qualification includes broader build layouts, complete call-graph semantics, automatic runtime discovery and other operating systems. A browser without a conforming provider reports Java navigation as unavailable.

### 6.7 Interactive Workspace Terminals

See the [implemented terminal runtime interactions](docs/c4/runtime-workspace-terminal.md).

The desktop provides real general-purpose shell sessions independently of Pi and Java Run. Before **New terminal**, the person confirms workspace shell trust and chooses an executable shell and an initial directory inside the registered workspace. Trust is local to the current interface/workspace and is not restored. The shell operates on saved disk files; terminal commands do not save, discard or replace editor buffers. Ordinary external-change detection and disk comparison continue to protect unsaved edits.

Each terminal retains its own working directory, environment, shell history, prompts and job control. xterm forwards raw keyboard and paste bytes, including Ctrl+C, and native resize changes the actual PTY. There is no IDE command parser, synthetic prompt or ten-second task timeout. Up to eight sessions are retained, with independent selection, Stop, Close and display clearing. Hiding the bottom panel or selecting another activity leaves the sessions running and replays retained output on return. **Clear terminal display** only clears renderer presentation, not shell history or native output ownership. Commands also offers **Show workspace terminal**, **New terminal at workspace root**, and Stop, Close and Clear for the selected session. New terminal uses the provider's default shell in the workspace root, independently of the panel's directory and shell drafts, and requires the same trust and provider availability. Session commands remain bound to the selected session and workspace context; a captured command cannot act on a replacement selection or workspace.

A provider-neutral port connects the renderer controller to typed native commands; UI and web core do not import Tauri. Requests and responses carry registered-workspace, generation, renderer and session identities. Old reads, pending launches, input and resizes cannot update a replaced workspace. Resize requests are serialized with the newest geometry retained. Native input writes are nonblocking, limited to 4 KiB per call and acknowledged by the exact accepted byte count; the renderer retries only unaccepted bytes and bounds queued input to 64 KiB. Native and renderer replay transcripts each retain at most 1 MiB per session. Reads deliver at most 64 KiB of raw bytes with checked cursor ranges; discarded native history explicitly resets the display. xterm supplies ANSI rendering and a screen-reader view.

Implemented native availability is **Linux only**. The selected shell must be an existing executable absolute path; the default is an available configured shell, Bash or sh. Initial directories are canonicalized and restricted to the workspace, including symlink destinations. Startup, reads and process cleanup run on native blocking workers. Stop identifies foreground and background jobs in the owned Linux OS session, checks captured process start times and the original or revoked controlling terminal, pins each signal target with a Linux process file descriptor, sends termination/continue signals and escalates within bounded waits. Hosts without that process-handle support refuse terminal availability. Natural shell exit retains its real exit status and also stops remaining owned jobs. Process errors remain visible; they do not become a successful fake session.

Workspace switching and normal application exit close the native sessions. A fresh renderer claims a new identity and stops the previous renderer's general terminal sessions, so interface reload starts untrusted with no attached shells. Pi keeps its separate attachment and process lifecycle. Shell execution is not confined to the workspace and deliberately detached processes that create another OS session are outside terminal cleanup. Uninterruptible kernel operations and abnormal application death require separate lifecycle qualification. Windows, macOS and browser terminal execution are unavailable; the browser explicitly states the missing native provider. Rationale: [ADR 0022](ADR.md#adr-0022--workspace-owned-interactive-shells-through-native-ptys).

The focused requirement is [REQ-IDE-WORKSPACE-TERMINAL-001](features/workspace/native-workspace-terminal.feature). Verification scope is maintained in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).

### 6.8 Java Project Context

When RefactorKit reports `java.context.compilerOptionsIncomplete`, Java Project retains the provider's reason and asks the user to declare the intended Java release or make the compiler configuration explicit. It directs the user back to the synchronization action they used. The project context stays unavailable until the provider accepts it.

For a Maven project with an empty local repository, **Open Java Run for Maven verification** in Maven settings opens the execution activity. When the effective Maven provider reports `offline-missing`, Java Project shows the action next to the diagnosis. With workspace execution trust, **Verify Maven project** starts [Maven's `verify` phase](https://maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-the-lifecycle) from the selected Java Project directory and uses its JDK, local repository and active and inactive profiles. It prefers the workspace's Maven wrapper and falls back to an available Maven executable. Maven can resolve dependencies and plugins and builds and tests the reactor according to its POMs. The console reports the result, and Maven leaves its normal build outputs. Preparation retires the current context. After verification, **Open Java Project** returns to the selected settings for explicit synchronization against the populated repository.

For a Gradle project with an empty cache, **Prepare Gradle dependencies** in Java Run starts an explicit build-tool session after workspace execution trust and saved-buffer review. It uses the project directory, Gradle executable, Gradle user home, project properties and JDK settings selected in Java Project. It evaluates the build with repository access and resolves the compile, runtime and annotation-processor classpaths of Java source sets, including tests. For a [Gradle composite](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/composite_builds.html), preparation follows the included builds in the same invocation, including nested builds. Each build is scheduled once, including when another build refers back to it. This preserves Gradle's composite dependency substitutions. The IDE requests only preparation tasks. Gradle owns plugin and build-logic execution, including any outputs those produce. Preparation retires the current project context. Select **Evaluate Gradle project** again to acquire fresh metadata through the provider's offline evaluation. The Java Run console shows progress, failures and cancellation.

When the workspace terminal is available and a Gradle executable is configured, **Open Gradle project terminal** opens the terminal form with the selected project directory filled in. Starting a shell requires workspace shell trust and **New terminal**. The terminal uses its normal shell environment.

A Gradle export refusal leaves the effective context unavailable. The IDE preserves the provider's bounded human-readable message and primary `gradle.sync.exportFailed` code. An isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 diagnostic candidate adds fixed cause messages based on Gradle process output, including denied cache access, unavailable offline dependencies and an unknown cause when the output lacks recognizable evidence. It collects stack traces internally without returning raw logs, paths, URLs or credentials. Classification reports the process output. For an unavailable offline dependency or plugin, **Open Java Run for Gradle preparation** opens the execution activity. Starting Gradle still requires workspace execution trust and a separate **Prepare Gradle dependencies** action. When preparation succeeds, **Open Java Project** returns to the existing settings for another explicit offline evaluation. For a plugin failure, Java Project also asks the person to check the plugin version and repositories. For an unknown export failure, including generic refusals from older providers, Java Project suggests running Gradle in a trusted shell with the selected settings to see the original error. Candidate qualification is described in section 10.1.

For plain Maven and Gradle projects, the starter wizard offers Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, 26 and 27. Context synchronization depends on the configured RefactorKit runtime. With the locally packaged runtime built from integrated RefactorKit 0.8.0 source, the Linux AppImage synchronizes both build tools, supports the tested Java 26 rename workflows and uses Java 27 contexts for project metadata. Java 27 source analysis and semantic refactoring remain unavailable through that runtime. Section 10.1 records the provider and platform scope. The wizard creates project files, and separate Linux native acceptance covers explicit build, test and run for Java 26 and Java 27 starters.

Project-aware Java test templates use the active file's provider-declared test source root and resolved test compile classpath. The editor offers framework-specific JUnit 4, JUnit Jupiter and TestNG test and assertion snippets only when the owning provider and all classpath entries are available; this can still work when an unrelated provider makes the aggregate context partial. Mockito and Spring Boot test snippets appear when their dependencies resolve. Templates use fully qualified names and sort ahead of word-based completions. They assist typing only; test execution remains the build tool's responsibility. Linux native GUI verification for Maven and Gradle is scoped in section 10.1.

The Java Project panel synchronizes saved project inputs with an explicitly selected full JDK. It presents RefactorKit's modules, source sets, source and generated roots, output directories, module dependencies and ordered compile/runtime classpaths. Annotation processor details include their reported status; unresolved inputs trigger a notice that remains visible while processor details are collapsed and explains that generated-source roots may be missing. The status describes provider-resolved inputs, not successful compilation or processor execution. Independent probes of the isolated providers return unavailable when a reactor processor output directory is absent and complete when that directory exists but is empty. Opening a Java source can let JDT LS create declared output directories; the initial warning check therefore runs before source import. Generated-source availability is verified separately after explicit build-tool execution. Maven settings include a local dependency repository and active/inactive profiles. Gradle settings include an absolute executable, optional user home and provider project properties. The desktop provides native path selection for the project directory, JDK home, Maven repository, Gradle executable and Gradle user home; cancellation preserves the current setting, results from a retired workspace are refused, and project selections outside the active workspace are rejected before the provider revalidates canonical containment. The selected project path is stored relative to the workspace. Provider-qualified Gradle v3 rows preserve three separate values: the workspace-relative evaluated build root, Gradle logical project path and evaluated workspace-relative module directory. The IDE displays them independently, resolves module/source/output paths from the workspace root, and dispatches Gradle tasks from the build root using the logical project path; it does not derive a filesystem directory from Gradle’s logical path. For provider-qualified Gradle modules, the adapter requires both `buildRoot` and `projectPath` and refuses incomplete or ambiguous identities, with a specific diagnostic when either identity field is missing. The native GUI can select an included project when the provider returns both fields. [Section 10.1](#101-verification-scope) records the provider and Gradle combinations exercised. Before project-based execution, the IDE saves the open editor buffers and captures their saved revisions, then verifies those revisions before and after context acquisition. If the save changes the source snapshot and retires the current context, this execution path reacquires the selected provider/module/source-set without reusing the previous snapshot hash; ordinary context refreshes remain pinned to the observed snapshot. Workspace, generation, settings and returned module/source-set ownership are revalidated. The IDE then adapts context paths relative to RefactorKit's opened project to workspace-relative paths before resolving files. The Linux GUI exercises one composite with project directories outside the included build root and another with the same project path in two included builds. See [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope) for the operations verified in each. Adapter and panel unit tests cover selected paths, cancellation, invalid responses, workspace boundaries and workspace changes; OS dialog interaction has no separate native GUI acceptance yet.

**Find in Java Project** performs literal, optionally case-sensitive search across saved Java source and supported project text files, including Maven/Gradle descriptors and common text resources such as XML, properties, YAML, JSON, SQL and plain text. It also overlays currently open dirty buffers in those formats; a dirty buffer replaces the saved view at its path, and search never saves or changes it. Results include every non-overlapping literal match with a workspace-relative line and one-based UTF-16 column, so opening a result reveals that occurrence in Monaco. The disk search skips version-control and build-output directories and does not follow symbolic links. The editor overlay admits at most 128 dirty buffers, 2 MiB per buffer and 8 MiB total; omitted or oversized buffers make results explicitly incomplete. Disk traversal, total bytes, per-file size and returned matches are also bounded, and reaching a result limit marks the result as truncated. In-flight results are discarded when the workspace or a participating buffer changes. Search results do not provide semantic references or a coherent source snapshot. Rust, adapter, controller and panel tests cover the production search path. Focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI acceptance verifies saved Java, build-descriptor and resource matches, unsupported binary and generated output exclusion, dirty Java and resource-buffer replacement, editor navigation, source preservation and clean exit. This does not qualify search limits on large projects, other operating systems or packaged installers.

The panel can create Maven or Gradle starters in either a single-module layout or a two-module application/library layout. Both include Java sources, JUnit tests, `.gitignore` and README; the multi-module layout adds a root aggregator and a project dependency from the application to the library. Maven starters include Maven Wrapper 3.3.4 pinned to Maven 3.10.0 with distribution checksum verification. Gradle starters include the Gradle wrapper launcher and select a checksum-verified Gradle 8.14.6 distribution for build JDKs 8–24 or Gradle 9.8.0 for JDK 25 and later; both generated wrapper variants allow up to two minutes between network reads while downloading. First use requires network access unless the distribution is already cached. Gradle starters offer Groovy or Kotlin DSL and use the [application plugin](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/application_plugin.html), [`JavaCompile.options.release`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/toolchains.html) and [JUnit Platform](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/java_testing.html), including its runtime launcher dependency; the selected DSL determines the `.gradle` or `.gradle.kts` build and settings files. The selected Java release can be 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, 26 or 27; the default is 25. Java 26 and 27 are generally available ([JDK 26 release notes](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/26all-relnotes.html), [JDK 27 release notes](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/27all-relnotes.html)). The native Java 26 build profile creates one plain Maven and one Groovy Gradle starter, confirms both are initially unbuilt, then explicitly builds, tests and runs them with JDK 26; section 10.1 records the host and tool scope. The pinned Gradle 9.8.0 distribution supports running on JDK 26; Gradle 9.4.0 is the first release qualified for that runtime in the [compatibility matrix](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/compatibility.html). The installed RefactorKit provider's context synchronization remains limited to Java 25 and lower, including for Java 26 starters. The scaffolder's separate real-tool qualification builds, tests and runs all six Java 27 Maven and Gradle starter shapes. The native scaffold GUI story creates the Java 27 Maven and both Groovy/Kotlin Gradle starters; its harness builds, tests and runs all three with JDK 27 and checks class-file major version 71. These build commands use installed Maven/Gradle tools; first-use wrapper execution is qualified separately. The managed JDT LS 1.62 bundle requires JDK 25 to run, and its [release notes](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) add Java 27 source support. Its checksum-verified installation passes the real-server semantic smoke with server JDK 25. An opt-in service integration test imports a Maven project configured for release 27. JDT LS reports Maven nature, compiler source and compliance 27, and preview features enabled; it accepts a [Java 27 primitive-type pattern in a switch](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/language/type-patterns.html), which also compiles with `javac --enable-preview --release 27`. JDT LS runs on JDK 25 with JDK 27 selected for the project. This qualifies service-level Maven compiler settings; separate GUI evidence covers editor import and semantics for one Maven fixture, not Java Project synchronization through RefactorKit. The selected-SDK-switch test still uses JDK 27 with Java 21 source, a separate scope. Running Gradle on JDK 27 requires Gradle 9.8 or later according to its [compatibility matrix](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/compatibility.html). Names are validated, existing paths are refused, and failed writes remove the newly reserved project directory. The generator writes project files only; it does not run a build or evaluate Gradle build scripts. The separate scaffold build profile invokes installed Maven and Gradle explicitly and does not exercise the generated wrappers. The returned workspace-relative path becomes the selected project. For Java 26 and 27, the wizard explains how to select a full project JDK and that analysis depends on the configured RefactorKit version. After refreshing File Explorer, the IDE synchronizes only while the original workspace activation and selected project settings are current. Gradle build-script evaluation requires a separate explicit action. These simple Kotlin DSL templates do not qualify RefactorKit's effective context for arbitrary `.kts` scripts, plugins or generated DSL accessors. Larger module layouts and broader template choices remain planned.

The project-type selector also generates a single-module Spring Boot 4.1.2 MVC starter for Maven or Gradle Groovy/Kotlin DSL, targeting Java 17, 21 or 25. It includes a runnable application, `GET /api/hello` endpoint and an integration test that starts an embedded server on a random port and checks the HTTP response. Maven Central access is required on the first build. The Linux native scaffold acceptance has built and tested the generated Maven project with its Maven wrapper on JDK 21 and both Gradle DSL projects with installed Gradle 9.8.0 on JDK 25; each test passed its HTTP response assertion. This scenario does not exercise the generated Gradle wrappers. This is framework project bootstrapping only: Spring-aware navigation/refactoring, Jakarta features, JPA and framework-aware database integration remain unavailable or planned. The separate JDBC console is described in section 6.10. See the official [Spring Boot system requirements](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/system-requirements.html), [Maven plugin guide](https://maven.apache.org/guides/mini/guide-using-plugins.html) and [Gradle plugin guide](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/plugins.html).

The Spring Boot Gradle starter writes a settings file in the selected DSL and sets the root project name to the chosen folder name. This establishes an independent build when the starter is created inside an existing Gradle workspace.

Java Run consumes this provider-owned context for synchronized module execution as described in section 6.3. It refreshes saved metadata after Save All and retires the displayed context before a build can change generated files or compiled outputs. This presentation change does not close the owned provider session. Gradle launch metadata reuses an explicitly evaluated session with the same settings. Ordinary synchronization refreshes the saved-source snapshot in that session, retaining the provider's original evaluation result; its snapshot describes the evaluation, while the returned project context describes current saved inputs. Explicit evaluation still requires matching snapshots. The provider refuses obsolete build metadata when build inputs change. Ordinary execution never performs an implicit Gradle metadata evaluation after session loss.

When Gradle runs on a JDK different from the selected project JDK, the IDE passes the selected JDK home through Gradle's `org.gradle.java.installations.paths` property so toolchain discovery can find the compiler, while Gradle itself continues running on its selected runtime JDK.

**Synchronize project** opens the selected workspace-contained project with dependency resolution disabled and acquires read-only metadata. Maven’s bounded effective-model parser does not invoke lifecycle goals or build plugins; dependency resolution remains disabled unless separately authorized. Maven can supply an effective context; an unevaluated Gradle response remains partial and disables source ownership. **Evaluate Gradle project** is a separate explicit action that authorizes evaluation of the project's build and initialization scripts. The panel explains that offline dependency resolution does not prevent scripts from accessing the network or credentials. The action requests the provider's bounded metadata exporter with the selected SDK, executable, user home and properties, without requesting a compilation task or automatic toolchain downloads. It requires the daemon's explicit Gradle capability advertisement and accepts only the versioned, SDK-correlated synchronization result. Ordinary synchronization, source inspection, navigation, restored settings and session loss never implicitly execute or repeat this action.

For a standard Maven 3.9 installation selected from `PATH`, the desktop can supply the canonical Maven Core JAR and its expected digest to a RefactorKit daemon that advertises `project.open.features.mavenRuntime`. RefactorKit reads the default compiler binding from the distribution. The desktop keeps the project JDK separate and retains the launcher, bootstrap configuration and Core JAR identities for synchronized operations. Java Run uses that canonical launcher for Maven build and coverage commands and checks the identity again before starting a process. A changed identity requires synchronization again. Project wrappers and unqualified Maven installations continue to use the existing explicit compiler-configuration path. Synchronization does not invoke Maven.

When read-only synchronization of a configured Gradle project receives a source-level refusal before evaluation, the IDE shows the provider's reason and points to **Evaluate Gradle project**. The effective Gradle metadata fallback requires a successful explicit evaluation in the current session.

If the provider reports denied access or a read-only filesystem for Gradle’s selected user home, Java Project offers **Edit Gradle user home**. The action opens Gradle settings and focuses the path field. After choosing a writable location, the person explicitly evaluates again before Java analysis can use the context. The action is offered only when the provider identifies the user home as the affected location.

The Commands palette exposes **Synchronize Java Project** and, when valid Gradle settings are present, **Evaluate Gradle Project and Synchronize**. Both use the current Java Project settings and the existing acquisition controller. The commands are unavailable without a selected JDK, during workspace loading or switching, during a Java refactoring or recovery write, or while synchronization is busy. A retained command rechecks workspace identity, generation and settings before starting. The action opens Java Project and releases the palette immediately so progress, errors and Cancel remain accessible. Neither command saves editor buffers. Ordinary synchronization does not evaluate Gradle; the separate evaluation command explicitly authorizes build-script execution as described above.

The native service discovers the experimental `project.context` capability and requires its typed, snapshot-bound, configured-SDK and shared-JDT-analysis features. The SDK must provide `javac`, release metadata and platform signatures. The IDE validates workspace, generation, request, saved-source snapshot, provider policy and ordered context response; it does not reconstruct dependencies or infer successful import. Read-only providers must deny build-code execution, credentials and network access. An effective Gradle provider may report explicitly allowed build execution, build-controlled credential access and offline resolution only when the same native session retains a successful synchronization with unchanged selected settings. The typed adapter also requires that synchronization evidence. An older daemon without the necessary capabilities reports unavailable. Versions v1 and v2 omit provider identity from selected-source associations, so the IDE accepts those associations only when the module/source-set pair resolves to one provider. When the daemon advertises both `typedSchemaV3` and `providerQualifiedSourceAssociation`, an explicit provider/module/source-set selector uses v3 and the adapter verifies the echoed provider against the selected scope. Colliding legacy requests remain refused. A source association is accepted only for a requested path or type and must match that module's declared source root; project-wide queries cannot return unsolicited source ownership. In schemas v2–v5, the SDK API selector `sourceRelease` admits 8–25 or 27, while source-language and explicit release levels remain limited to 25. API profile 26 is excluded from those legacy schemas. Schemas v6 and v7 represent source/release levels through 27 and distinguish their semantic-analysis qualification explicitly; accepting metadata does not establish qualified source analysis.

Available effective Maven and Gradle providers with JDT analysis enable source ownership inspection. The person selects a module/source set and inspects the owner of a source-relative path or qualified type. Each request carries the prior snapshot and context identities. On the first context acquisition only, a stale refusal that includes a new valid snapshot hash is retried once with that hash; explicit snapshot/context identities are never rebased, and a second refusal is returned unchanged. RefactorKit owns source association, including secondary top-level types and same-path main/test sources. Acquisition, source inspection, configured-context navigation, draft preview and the editor transaction bridge share one serialized daemon session, preserving evaluated Gradle metadata and editor document-version history. For an explicitly evaluated Gradle project, saved-source refactoring preview, Apply and rollback also use that session; rollback checks the committed source snapshot without another project evaluation. A changed descriptor, source, dependency, SDK or selected configuration can refuse the request. The panel retires previous evidence before every query; a refusal cannot leave the previous context presented as current. Reopening or retiring the daemon loses Gradle evaluation evidence and requires another explicit evaluation before effective Gradle analysis.

**Add Maven Module** resolves its parent POM from the provider-reported module root. Context schemas v1 and v2 express that root relative to the selected project; v3–v7 express it relative to the workspace. The panel applies the corresponding path base once, labels workspace-relative roots explicitly, and offers the selected project root as an extra parent only when the provider did not already return that root module. For a synchronized Maven integration-test source set, Java Run and the configured execution commands require one complete Failsafe execution before offering integration tests or their coverage in schemas v4–v7. Missing, partial or ambiguous facts keep those actions unavailable; the native execution boundary repeats its authority and report-location checks.

When the synchronized context contains available `maven-effective-v1` modules and the daemon advertises `java.renameMavenModule` with preview and rendered-diff support, **Review Maven module rename** requests a read-only provider plan. The operation uses its provider-qualified module list and can remain available when another part of the aggregate project context is partial; that does not make the overall project context complete. The request carries the current snapshot and context hashes, uses module paths relative to the selected Java project, and accepts affected files only when they remain inside the workspace. The preview is bound to the active project session and can be discarded through its dedicated route; its request fields stay fixed while the provider plan is visible, and closing the dialog discards that plan. When the provider also advertises managed Apply and rollback, the panel offers Apply and refuses it while editor buffers are unsaved. Apply takes the editor external-write lock, submits the reviewed plan and retains the returned transaction only for the active workspace generation and daemon session. The old project context is retired and changed files are reconciled with open documents and the file tree. Rollback is available only while that same session retains the transaction; it uses the returned transaction identity and reconciles its changed files. Session loss removes the IDE transaction handle, so this flow does not provide crash recovery. An Apply error after mutation may have started remains visible with guidance to inspect the project, with provider diagnostics available in a disclosure, even after context retirement. Rust and component tests cover preview correlation, dirty-buffer refusal, retained Apply errors and admission when a partial aggregate still has a current Maven provider and selected module. Native GUI requalification for this partial-context case remains pending; the production desktop build passes. One focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario passes against a source-built RefactorKit package. It verifies the rendered review, dirty-buffer Apply refusal, explicit draft discard, provider Apply, offline Maven `verify`, generated-output cleanup, rollback and restoration of the original descriptors, Java source and module path. A separate temporary Maven fixture confirms that `mvn -o verify` after module rename creates outputs under the renamed module's `target` directory and RefactorKit refuses rollback while those files remain; removing only those generated outputs allows rollback and a subsequent verification to pass. The GUI workflow cleans generated outputs before rollback, so it does not qualify rollback across a build without cleanup. The provider's rolled-back transaction record and released workspace lock remain; no IDE transaction handle survives session loss, so this does not provide crash recovery. The scenario uses the selected source-built package and fixture. The standard user-installed runtime now provides `project.context`, but has not been exercised for this rename flow. RefactorKit exposes module creation and rename through the daemon with managed Apply/Rollback capability; CLI-v2 JSON remains catalog-only for create-module and move-across-Maven, and preview-only for rename. The stable daemon `java.createMavenModule` route is integrated into the Java project panel through the SDK-bound refactoring flow. The panel offers a synchronized Maven parent only when the daemon advertises the complete stable lifecycle; the flow checks open editor buffers and binds the request to the current project/session, then uses the shared preview, Apply, rollback and changed-file reconciliation path. Contract, component, TypeScript and Rust tests cover the consumer. Native GUI acceptance for Maven Add Module is qualified for one bounded fixture as described in section 10.1; the CLI-v2 route remains catalog-only. The Java project panel also implements a capability-gated Add Gradle Module consumer for an explicitly synchronized build. It requires the stable top-level `java.createGradleModule` method with preview, rendered diff, Apply, rollback, workspace-relative build-root, canonical nested-project-path and settings-DSL features. It binds the request to the exact unique `settings.gradle` or `settings.gradle.kts` file and the selected Gradle `buildRoot`; Apply remains blocked for unsaved Java buffers. The IDE transport re-bases the workspace-relative build root to the selected project root expected by the daemon, and rollback checks the committed snapshot on the same daemon session after Gradle evaluation evidence is retired. Contract, component, controller and Rust tests cover this path. Section 10.1 describes the focused native GUI qualification for the Groovy and Kotlin settings DSLs. An isolated source-built CLI fixture also confirms that rollback refuses while generated build outputs remain inside the moved module; removing those outputs allows the original POM/source bytes to be restored. The Maven native scenario verifies reactor `verify`, not test execution. Do not extrapolate this route to other project layouts or build tools.

Maven module rename pauses the owning JDT LS session before sending Apply or Rollback to RefactorKit. Preview leaves the language session available. The native command holds the lifecycle lock across the provider mutation so queued language-service requests cannot start an import during the directory change. After a confirmed result, the IDE refreshes the language-service state, reconciles the editor paths, and resumes a previously active service for the current workspace. The workspace retains the transaction when the user switches activities, so Rollback remains available when they return to Java Project.

JDT LS import can materialize empty `target/classes` and `target/test-classes` directories before the first build and in the renamed module after Apply. The corrected RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate accepts the tested Maven rename with those directories present at both paths. Linux AppImage verification on X11 and KWin Wayland covers a saved reactor, dirty-buffer Apply refusal, a fresh preview, Apply, offline Maven verification, and exact rollback after cleanup of only the generated build entries. Both original output directories are restored and the renamed module is removed. A direct daemon replay separately verifies that compiled files still cause a rollback refusal and are preserved. The IDE explains an unverified reactor and reports a rollback conflict with review and retry guidance.

Workspace/generation and configuration changes, cancellation and replaced requests suppress late results. Session retirement is serialized before the next synchronization, so rapid settings changes cannot let an older stop close a newly queried session. If a later consumer finds that the daemon has already exited, the SDK context is retired and the operation asks for explicit resynchronization; the IDE does not reopen the provider session or reevaluate a build silently. Native calls run on blocking workers with bounded daemon transport. Cancellation immediately revokes presentation; helper termination waits for an in-flight bounded RPC to finish. Gradle synchronization allows 135 seconds for the provider's 120-second metadata export and protocol completion; ordinary calls retain the 15-second bound. Transport admits at most 2 MiB per response. The typed consumer further bounds modules, source sets, roots and classpath entries, and paginates large classpath views. A transport or decoding failure remains visible.

The nested **Saved source structure** view is a separate read-only RefactorKit scan and symbols result. Refresh waits for an in-progress capability check and retries discovery when the engine is reported unavailable or does not advertise `scan` and `symbols`; the view remains unavailable unless the real engine advertises that surface. Selecting a reported type or member opens its engine-reported path and line through the guarded Java navigation controller, without changing source. The focused Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario verifies navigation to the reported line, preservation of an unsaved draft, distinct Maven main/test source ownership, refusal of a changed descriptor, and partial plus explicitly evaluated Gradle contexts. It also compiles a new Maven test output after context acquisition, verifies that the old ownership request is refused and the context retired, then explicitly synchronizes again and resolves ownership from the new context. The scenario creates a Java module descriptor from a synchronized Maven source root, keeps it as an unsaved editor draft, and saves and compiles it. Changing the project JDK restarts JDT LS, preserves the dirty buffer and makes navigation with the old project context refuse. This does not qualify an installer or another operating system; the wider project-system requirement remains `@partial`.

The selected Java Project JDK also configures JDT LS through its published [project runtime settings](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/wiki/Running-the-JAVA-LS-server-from-the-command-line). The native service probes the explicit full JDK and supplies consistent settings during initialization, configuration notifications and server configuration requests. It associates compatible Java execution environments with the selected JDK, so a project requesting an older compiler level does not silently select the server's JDK instead. Its Java process runtime remains separately discovered; Java Intelligence displays the server runtime and project JDK separately. Persistent JDT LS state is separated by selected JDK installation/version to prevent another SDK's remembered runtime associations from being reused. An invalid explicit selection fails without substituting another project JDK. Changing the selection retires prior document semantics and diagnostics immediately, waits briefly for editing of the settings field to pause, and replaces the session in submission order. The controller reopens synchronized documents with their current editor text, including unsaved changes, without saving them. Workspace and generation checks protect lifecycle operations, and a workspace change during server initialization retires the newly started process. Native lifecycle work runs outside the UI thread.

JDT LS autobuild is disabled in the managed session, and generated Eclipse project metadata is redirected away from the project root. This prevents background language-server builds from changing Maven or Gradle outputs while RefactorKit holds classpath-bound project evidence; compilation remains owned by the selected build tool or JDK. See [ADR 0024](ADR.md#adr-0024--jdt-ls-project-metadata-and-build-ownership).

JDT LS Gradle import is disabled by default. Buildship can run a project wrapper while importing Gradle projects, so the Java Project panel offers a separate session-only authorization and explains that build scripts can access the network and credentials ([Gradle support](https://github.com/redhat-developer/vscode-java/wiki/gradle-support)). The grant is held in renderer memory, scoped to the active workspace generation and selected project path, and is cleared on a workspace/project change or application restart. Changing or revoking it replaces the language-server session and reopens current editor buffers, including unsaved text. This permission controls JDT LS import independently from RefactorKit's **Evaluate Gradle project** action; neither authorization implies the other.

When JDT LS import is authorized and Gradle project settings are present, the language-service session passes the configured Gradle user home, project properties and project JDK to JDT LS. Changing these settings replaces the session and requests a forced Buildship update for already imported Gradle Java projects, so the retained classpath can be recalculated from the new values. An executable under a Gradle installation's `bin` directory selects that installation and disables wrapper use. A selected project wrapper is accepted only when it is inside the workspace and belongs to the selected project or one of its parents. An unsupported executable path fails the session before replacing the current one instead of silently importing with a different Gradle installation. When no Gradle executable is configured, explicit import authorization retains JDT LS's normal wrapper behavior. JDT LS discovers Gradle roots across its workspace; the selected project path does not limit this importer. With wrapper use enabled, other discovered roots may run their own wrappers under the same workspace-scoped authorization. RefactorKit reports bounded, ordered literal `JavaCompile.compilerArgs` with compile-task and source-set origin and redaction. Argument providers, custom task actions, missing inventories or export bounds make compiler options partial, and a request requiring complete options refuses rather than inferring values. The IDE consumes these records and shows their origin and redaction. In the qualified Gradle 9.6.1/JDK 21 fixture, source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 returns the typed `compilerArg` value `--enable-preview` for both main and test source sets. The IDE applies preview settings to an imported Gradle module only when its non-empty source sets have complete, consistent compiler options that enable preview and the release matches the selected project JDK. The JDT LS runtime must also use that release, and the imported project roots, Gradle settings, workspace generation and context hash must match the synchronized project. The service sets and reads back JDT LS source, compliance, target and preview settings, refreshes diagnostics for open files in the affected modules, and restores the previous settings when the context is cleared or the session stops. The focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI profile verifies the applied outcome and removal of the Java 21 preview diagnostic for this fixture; section 10.1 records the verification scope. This does not qualify a packaged application, other JDT LS/JDK/Gradle combinations or other operating systems. The standard installed provider remains limited to Java 25 in the tested package; a source-built v7 candidate passes metadata-only Java 27 project-context synchronization and, on Linux, applies the Gradle-verified Java 27 preview setting to JDT LS. This does not qualify source analysis, the installed provider, packaged applications or other operating systems.

Compiler-setting application to JDT LS requires the still-current published Java project context. The controller binds each request to that context’s synchronization revision, workspace activation and adapter, then checks the same authority after the asynchronous response. Retained callbacks from cancelled, retired, replaced or unmounted context views do not invoke the adapter. Replies must match the project path, context schema, snapshot and context hashes as well as workspace identity; a mismatched or late reply cannot be returned as a current result or publish a success message. This is consumer lifecycle coordination; RefactorKit still supplies the compiler facts and the native language service applies them.

A separate Linux release/no-bundle GUI story imports an isolated Maven project configured for release 27 and preview features under JDK 27. JDT LS 1.62 resolves the preview pattern variable as `int matched` in Monaco with no error marker in that source. A deliberately unresolved type in a sibling source appears in Problems, confirming that project diagnostics are active. The POM and both source files remain unchanged, JDT LS stops, and the native window exits cleanly. This qualifies the Maven import and editor path for this fixture; it does not qualify a packaged application or another operating system. Project-context synchronization and Gradle preview-setting application are qualified separately against a source-built RefactorKit v7 candidate on Linux; the standard installed provider remains limited to Java 25, and packaged or other-operating-system behavior remains unqualified.

The Java language-service session also receives the Java Project panel's selected workspace-relative project path, Maven active/inactive profiles and local repository. The native service resolves the project path inside the canonical workspace, asks JDT LS for its Java project roots and nature identifiers, and applies profile selections only to Maven Java projects at or below the selected project root through JDT LS's `java.project.updateSettings` command. When profiles are selected, it waits for a matching Maven project within the initialization deadline and fails visibly if the selection cannot be applied. When a local repository is selected, the native service gives JDT LS a temporary derived user `settings.xml`: it copies the default user settings, changes only `<localRepository>`, restricts file permissions on Unix, and removes the copy after the language server stops. The user's settings file is never rewritten, so mirrors, proxies and credentials remain available. With no selected repository, Maven keeps its default settings. This aligns the repository location; it does not attest that JDT LS's effective compiler, toolchain or dependency classpath matches RefactorKit's full effective project context. Gradle evaluation and metadata remain owned by RefactorKit and the build tools. The rationale is recorded in [ADR 0023](ADR.md#adr-0023--session-scoped-maven-settings-for-jdt-ls).

The project-context view grants no source mutation authority by itself. Configured-context navigation is described in section 6.6, and SDK-bound refactoring in section 6.4. Saved-source refactoring for an evaluated Gradle project reuses the RefactorKit session that retains its Gradle context: preview and Apply use that session, while rollback checks the committed workspace snapshot on that same daemon session before using the retained transaction. If a build-file change retires Gradle evaluation evidence, the IDE refreshes the saved snapshot in the original session before rollback; it does not reopen or reevaluate the Gradle project. An indeterminate write still invalidates the Gradle evaluation receipt. A RefactorKit preview refusal that identifies a stale project snapshot also retires the displayed context and requires explicit resynchronization. Rust compilation, the focused SDK-refactoring and project-context unit suites, and the real Gradle formatting and cross-module class-rename preview/Apply/rollback scenario pass with selected JDKs 21 and 25; the scope of that native-library qualification is described in section 10.1. JDT LS receives the selected project JDK and Maven profile intent, but consuming and attesting the full effective project context remains incomplete. A selected JDK and profile list alone do not prove alignment with Maven/Gradle compiler release, explicit toolchains, all effective profile effects or dependency classpaths. The native desktop starts recursive monitoring after a context is acquired. Changes to Java/Kotlin source files and Maven/Gradle build descriptors invalidate the provider snapshot and Gradle evaluation evidence, retire the displayed context and prompt explicit resynchronization; generated outputs, build caches and unrelated files are filtered. Monitoring does not save editor drafts, run builds or automatically reevaluate Gradle. If the native watcher is unavailable, the panel keeps manual synchronization available and reports that automatic tracking is unavailable. Its current host and scope are described in section 10.1. Unsaved Java mutation remains incomplete. The current project-context schema does not expose binary-to-source attachments for dependency JARs. The IDE consumes the provider's separate context/SDK-bound lookup and guarded source-read methods, as described in section 6.6, rather than deriving another dependency model. Verification scope is maintained in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope); the focused [native project-context requirement](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) remains partial.

A Gradle class-move preview can refuse because compiler outputs needed for binding analysis are missing. When RefactorKit returns the typed `java.moveClass.gradleCompilerOutputsMissing` refusal, the IDE displays which source sets need compilation and leaves Apply disabled. The IDE discards retained refactoring plans and keeps the evaluated Gradle session so Java Run can build or test the configured project. After that explicit execution, the developer synchronizes and requests a new preview. A stale snapshot, malformed reply or lost session still invalidates the context.

For a generated root in an available source set, **Reveal in Files** opens and focuses the corresponding workspace directory in the File Explorer. The IDE uses the root supplied by RefactorKit and loads only the required branch through the existing directory reader when a build-output folder is still collapsed. The action does not run a build or open an editor tab. A missing directory or a context change during lookup leaves the current editor in place.

When starting or restarting JDT LS after synchronizing an authorized Gradle project, the desktop can include materialized generated roots in Gradle's Eclipse tooling model. The native service uses the current RefactorKit context for the same workspace, Gradle settings and selected project JDK. A generated directory must resolve inside its owning module. The importer adds it only when the corresponding ordinary source folders agree on the Eclipse output, Gradle scope attributes and test-source classification. The private initialization script applies only to model requests with no Gradle tasks. It leaves Gradle source sets, compiler inputs and build descriptors unchanged. JDT LS data for an import with generated roots is separate from data for the ordinary import. After a build materializes new roots, synchronize the project and restart the language service to acquire the new model.

The editor identifies a Java file under a generated root when the current project context attributes it to one source set. It warns that a build may overwrite edits. **Reveal generated root** focuses the provider-declared directory in Files and keeps the generated document open. The action needs a unique, nonempty workspace-relative root. The notice and action are withdrawn when the project context is retired. The Linux AppImage checks for Maven on X11 with JDK 21 and for Gradle on KWin Wayland with JDK 27 verify the notice, the focused directory and the unchanged active generated document. The Maven scenario also checks the notice after F12. Both scenarios confirm that the notice is absent in the handwritten caller.

For Maven test and integration-test source sets, Java Project shows the fork configuration reported by RefactorKit v7. If the synchronized context did not include these facts, **Request Maven test JVM details** queries the selected source set against the current saved snapshot. The details show availability, refusal codes, plugin and execution identity, fork mode, settings and their origins. For `argLine` the panel shows whether a layer is empty, configured, incomplete or redacted. The inspection uses provider metadata and does not start Maven, choose an executable for the fork or change test settings.

The effective Maven provider reports main and test source sets and defines distinct `CUSTOM` rows for recognized Build Helper roots. It classifies a root as `INTEGRATION_TEST` only when one complete Build Helper `add-test-source` declaration and exactly one Failsafe `integration-test` execution share the same effective build/profile scope; ambiguous provenance is refused. Provider acceptance covers active/inactive profiles, module/source-set selection, root provenance, classpath visibility, stale-snapshot refusal and duplicate-root refusal. Contexts v4 and v5 carry typed Failsafe execution, selector and report settings; v5 additionally carries the complete standard JPMS directives. The RefactorKit v4 acceptance checks complete, partial, ambiguous and inactive execution metadata. The IDE contract and adapter validate the v4 shape, while the native execution service requires one complete Failsafe execution and uses its concrete report directory for fresh-result collection. Operation attestations preserve the exact v1–v5 schema version. The native mutation boundary requires an explicit project-context schema version and refuses omitted versions rather than defaulting to v1. For v3, v4 and v5, the adapter resolves the selected source only within the echoed provider. The project panel sends a provider-qualified selector only when the daemon explicitly advertises it, while legacy source associations still require a unique provider owner. The IDE consumes `requires`, `exports`, `opens`, `uses` and `provides` from JPMS descriptors. RefactorKit source acceptance now covers recognition of `module-info.java` by compilation-unit name and Maven descriptors containing `opens`, `uses` and `provides`, with the descriptor content hash checked exactly. When a descriptor contains directives not represented by context v2, RefactorKit preserves supported facts, marks JPMS partial with `java.context.jpmsDescriptorIncomplete`, and refuses requests requiring complete JPMS facts. A separate provider story changes `module-info.java` after `project.open`, then confirms that a JPMS request using the old snapshot returns `java.context.snapshotStale` without publishing module records. Another Maven provider story compiles a real `fixture.dependency` modular JAR and checks the exact module-path name/fingerprint, descriptor identity/hash, `requires static transitive` and qualified exports; the JPMS required fact is accepted although that metadata-only response remains partial and has no selected source. A Gradle provider story exercises explicit synchronization, `module-info.java` and a modular JAR supplied through `JavaCompile.options.compilerArgs --module-path`, then verifies the complete JPMS fact, exact module/fingerprint and descriptor hash, and unchanged project inputs. That acceptance exposed and closed the scanner's missing `ClasspathEvidence` capture for Gradle module-path artifacts; fresh `compileKotlin` and `compileTestKotlin` runs pass. A second Gradle story changes the literal module-path JAR after synchronization and confirms `java.context.snapshotStale`, a changed hash and no module records; the mutated fixture remains preserved. Follow-on provider acceptance now covers semantic resolution and metadata availability for both Maven and Gradle. RefactorKit’s JDT resolver receives the snapshot-bound module path separately from the classpath, maps `module-info.java` to its exact source root, and honors `requires`/`exports`. Stories resolve exported APIs with JDT binding, refuse hidden packages, and return available contexts with complete JPMS and no implicit source selection when JPMS is required. The Gradle semantic fixture also leaves one warning for a non-exported package. Original project inputs are preserved; IDE-native JPMS navigation remains unqualified. A bounded Gradle annotation-processor story explicitly synchronizes offline and reports the selected main source set’s local processor path, service provider name read statically from the JAR descriptor, and snapshot-bound fingerprint in `buildEvidence`. Its processor would generate a marker, but synchronization leaves the marker absent and fresh `compileKotlin`/`compileTestKotlin` checks pass; this demonstrates static metadata inspection without compiling or executing the processor. In the six-module Maven Failsafe fixture, app declares an annotation processor from the reactor, but v7 reports its processor path unavailable and no generated source roots; Maven still compiles and runs code that uses the generated type. This qualifies a pre-build project-context gap, not a Maven build failure. The response marks top-level `semanticAnalysis` available while processor-path availability is unavailable; these are separate facts, and the former does not establish complete generated-source roots. The IDE adapter decodes processor path, provider name and build-evidence fingerprint, and the panel displays processor path/name/options; focused tests cover these consumer facts. A focused native Java 27 Gradle scenario now checks the materialized processor path and generated source root after Build and resynchronization; this GUI path remains unqualified until the scenario passes. Presentation of a real modular JAR and IDE-native JPMS navigation also remain unqualified. The adapter preserves provider refusal codes; it also downgrades a nominally complete legacy response when `opens`, `uses` or `provides` are omitted and identifies those omissions. For v5 it requires all three arrays and the provider's closed directive fields. Focused adapter, controller, UI, and Rust tests verify the consumer path. A separate Linux native run confirms Maven artifact-coordinate presentation and refreshed source ownership after a generated-output change, but later times out while waiting for the editor model to match the JDT LS document URI. The dedicated Gradle context-v5 GUI scenario above verifies display of all standard JPMS directives for its fixture; native Maven display and broader descriptor layouts remain unqualified. Broader Maven/Gradle module-path resolution and ownership, stale-artifact cases outside the tested Gradle snapshot path, processor custom-task/override shapes and module-coordinate dependencies, Maven compiler-plugin ownership, additional Gradle named-module shapes, IDE-native consumption and broader semantic navigation remain open. A Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario also exercises one synchronized Maven Failsafe source set through Run and report collection; broad provider accuracy remains unqualified until acceptance exercises additional real project shapes. Source roots, a compiler release and artifact paths alone do not establish the exact compiler configuration, dependency mediation identity or processor setup. RefactorKit owns provider projection and acceptance; the IDE owns versioned consumption and build/test task invocation.

JDT LS resolves Java 26 preview primitive type patterns in an Eclipse Java project when the project compiler settings explicitly enable preview features, and resolves a Java 27 preview primitive pattern in an imported Maven project. Focused Linux native GUI qualifications and their limits are recorded in section 10.1. The Java 27 Gradle acceptance uses JDT LS for definition and references after RefactorKit reports that source analysis is unqualified.

The IDE contract, Rust bridge and renderer retain `project.context.v6` as a metadata-only fallback. After a typed unsupported-source refusal from an earlier route, the native service can query `project.summary` and retry with a provider-qualified selector for one complete module and its `main` source set. A Linux release/no-bundle GUI profile passes this fallback with a source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 candidate for one-module Maven and six-module Gradle fixtures on JDK 27. The v6 response provides build metadata only: it does not qualify source ownership, semantic navigation, JPMS inspection or Java refactoring. Separately, the source-built v7 candidate synchronizes Java 27 Maven and Gradle metadata and has a qualified source-root-ownership lookup; v7 source analysis remains unqualified, with no JDT binding or refactoring authority. Section 10.1 records the evidence and limits. The installed RefactorKit provider does not advertise v6 or v7 and still refuses Java 26 and 27; production upgrades, packaged applications, other project layouts and other operating systems remain unqualified. The Gradle profile also verifies that JDK 27 is the project SDK while JDK 21 runs Gradle, with the synchronization receipt and snapshot attested. Gradle projects can configure a runtime JDK separately from their project SDK; the consumer passes it to project synchronization and JDT LS Gradle import and uses it for Gradle invocations, while an omitted runtime JDK defaults to the selected project SDK.

### 6.9 HTTP Client

The desktop bottom panel exposes a manual HTTP client for Java developers exercising a local or remote HTTP service. Opening the panel sends nothing. A request is sent only after the person selects a method, enters an absolute HTTP/HTTPS URL and chooses **Send**. Unsaved request drafts and response data stay in panel memory. **Saved requests and environments** offers explicit Save, selection, deletion and Reload actions. Requests are grouped by collection and name; selecting one fills an editable method, URL, headers and body without sending it. Named environments provide string variables for `{{variable}}` placeholders in URLs, header values and bodies. The resolved URL is shown before **Send**. Substitution is literal and single-pass: values are not evaluated or recursively expanded, and missing or incomplete placeholders refuse submission before the network port is called. Changing workspace or reopening the panel clears the current draft and active environment selection; explicitly saved definitions remain available.

Manual requests offer **None**, **Basic** and **Bearer token** authentication.
