[Basic authentication](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617) encodes the entered username/password pair as UTF-8 and Base64; a username containing a colon, control characters or invalid Unicode is refused. [Bearer authentication](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750#section-2.1) sends the supplied token in the Authorization header without re-encoding it. Both support the selected environment's single-pass variables. Credentials are limited to 16 KiB before Basic encoding, and a generated header cannot exceed the existing header-count limit. Conflicting manually entered Authorization headers refuse submission. Each actual send remains explicit.

The authentication fields are masked where appropriate and remain in panel memory. Their values and generated Authorization header are excluded from saved requests and collection export. Selecting another authentication mode, loading a saved request, selecting an OpenAPI operation or changing workspace activation clears the helper fields. Explicitly saved header rows and environment values retain their existing plain-text persistence/export policy; using saved environment variables for credentials does not create encrypted storage. Editor-file requests use their own declared headers and do not inherit the manual form's authentication. HTTPS is recommended for credentials. Challenge negotiation, server-specific Basic encodings, automatic OAuth refresh, persistent cookie sessions, proxy authentication and a credential vault remain unavailable.

**OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials** acquires a service-account access token using a user-supplied token endpoint, client ID, secret and optional space-separated scopes. **Get OAuth token** sends a UTF-8 form POST with `grant_type=client_credentials`; HTTP Basic client authentication is initially selected, and request-body client authentication is available when required by the server. Basic credentials are form-encoded before Base64 encoding, as specified in [RFC 6749 sections 2.3.1 and 4.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749). This workflow uses credentials issued for the selected service client; it does not register a client or embed a shared application secret.

Token acquisition requires HTTPS with normal certificate validation and does not follow redirects. An explicit local development exception permits HTTP only for numeric loopback IP addresses, not arbitrary hosts or `localhost` resolution. The request and response retain the active workspace identity; the native host checks workspace activation before and after the request, and the panel discards retired-scope replies. An already submitted network request can still complete on the server after the panel or workspace is retired. Requests retain the HTTP transport's 30-second deadline; token responses are bounded to 64 KiB and must be complete UTF-8 JSON with a supported Bearer token. Tokens are limited to 16 KiB, client values and scope to 8 KiB, and a reported lifetime must be an integral number of seconds within the supported range. Unknown extension fields and refresh tokens are not retained. Error descriptions and raw token bodies are not shown or copied into the ordinary HTTP response view.

After acquisition, the panel shows token type, scope and any reported lifetime. **Use OAuth token** selects masked Bearer authentication without sending the API request. **Send** remains a separate action. OAuth-derived requests also refuse redirects and require HTTPS, with the same explicit numeric-loopback development exception. The host must advertise its no-redirect capability before the controller sends such a request. A reported lifetime is measured conservatively from the start of token acquisition and rechecked at use and request preparation. If the server omits the lifetime, the IDE does not infer one from the token. The server remains authoritative for token validity. Editing the Bearer field manually supplies a new manual credential and clears the acquisition metadata.

Client credentials and tokens stay in memory and are excluded from saved templates, environments and collection exports. Loading a saved request, selecting an OpenAPI operation or changing workspace activation resets the OAuth form and selected authentication. **Clear OAuth credentials and request authentication** clears both explicitly. Obtaining a new token does not automatically replace the selected request authentication: review and use remain separate. Discovery, automatic refresh, token revocation, sender-constrained tokens, custom grant parameters, a credential vault and persistent account sessions remain unavailable. The authority and transport choice is recorded in [ADR 0032](ADR.md#adr-0032--explicit-oauth-client-credentials-and-protected-request-policy).


**OAuth 2.0 browser sign-in (PKCE)** supports a registered Authorization Code client with explicitly entered authorization endpoint, token endpoint, issuer, client ID and scopes. The initially selected public-client mode sends no client secret. Registered clients requiring HTTP Basic or request-body client authentication can select that mode and enter a memory-only secret. **Sign in with system browser** requests the operating system's external browser through its URL handler. The desktop WebView never renders the provider's login page or handles its password fields. A launch request alone is not successful authorization; the panel waits for a valid response and token exchange.

The native host generates independent random state and a [PKCE S256](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636) verifier, binds a temporary loopback listener and supplies the challenge, state and redirect URI to the authorization endpoint. The IDE receives the code in its native listener; the verifier never enters the renderer. Renderer completion requests contain only the captured session identity. The callback path is `/oauth/callback`. Port `0` selects an available port; a configured port must be unprivileged and available. Binding tries IPv4 loopback, then IPv6. Register the corresponding loopback URI with the provider, allowing its selected port as described in [RFC 8252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252). Existing flow parameters in the authorization endpoint URL are refused rather than allowed to override the native request.

Only a bounded GET query response for the exact listener host/path and current state is accepted. The provider must return `iss` as specified in [RFC 9207](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9207); the decoded value must equal the configured issuer exactly, including its path and trailing slash. Missing or different issuer, duplicate parameters, implicit tokens and unsupported response modes are refused. Wrong-state probes receive a generic response without consuming a valid callback; invalid attempts and incomplete headers are bounded. Callback pages contain fixed text, no code/state reflection or external resources, and disable caching and referrer propagation.

Only one browser authorization flow can remain pending in a native process. The flow has a five-minute monotonic deadline. **Cancel browser sign-in**, frontend disposal or workspace retirement revokes local authority and closes the listener; process termination also closes its socket. Cancellation does not close the system browser or reverse an authorization request already processed remotely. A token request already in progress can finish within the HTTP deadline, but its retired result is discarded. An invalid, expired or reused session cannot exchange another code.

After validated browser consent, the host exchanges the code once through the same bounded token transport used by Client Credentials, with redirects disabled. A reported token deadline is calculated when that exchange starts, so time spent reviewing consent does not consume a newly issued token's lifetime. The panel then displays type, scope and reported lifetime. **Use sign-in token** selects Bearer authentication; **Send** remains separate and retains the OAuth HTTPS/explicit-loopback and no-redirect policy. Settings and tokens are not added to saved requests or exports. Template/OpenAPI selection, workspace activation changes and explicit clearing reset the browser helper. This is OAuth API authorization, not verified OpenID Connect account identity: ID tokens and refresh tokens are not retained or interpreted. Discovery, pushed or signed authorization requests, custom URI schemes, `form_post`, automatic refresh and broader provider interoperability remain open. [ADR 0033](ADR.md#adr-0033--native-pkce-and-loopback-authority-for-browser-authorization) records the authority decision.

**Requests from editor** reads the active `.http` or `.rest` buffer, including unsaved edits. The person selects a named request, reviews its resolved URL, headers and literal body, and chooses **Send file request**. Opening, editing and selecting send nothing and do not save the source. Editing the buffer, changing its path or changing the workspace activation invalidates the selection. Submission rechecks the live editor before calling the network port. The displayed response retains the submitted file path, request name and line even when the active editor changes; this attribution is not sent to the HTTP service.

The request-file syntax is a bounded subset of the published [HTTP request syntax](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/idea/exploring-http-syntax.html) and [HTTP file variables](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/idea/http-client-variables.html): `###` request separators and names, `# @name`, comments before the body, supported method/URL lines, header lines, a blank line before a literal body, URL continuation and flat `@name = value` definitions. Referenced file variables may depend on other file variables; selected environment values take precedence and remain literal. Missing values, incomplete placeholders and dependency cycles refuse submission. Files are limited to 1 MiB, 100 requests and 64 variables with 8 KiB values; dependency expansion is bounded to 2 MiB and 10,000 substitutions before ordinary request validation. Invalid entries remain visible and unavailable while valid requests remain selectable. Explicit protocol selection supports only `HTTP/1.1`, using a backend capability and native HTTP/1-only transport; omitted versions retain ordinary protocol negotiation. Scripts, dynamic variables, external body files and response redirection are unavailable. Bodies are not interpreted as multipart instructions. This is not full compatibility with another product's HTTP client.

Collections are stored per workspace in the configured IDE home under `http-client/`, separately from project source. Only explicit Save, Delete or confirmed Import actions change collection data; loading, selection, variable resolution and HTTP responses do not write it. Saved templates remain unexpanded. Request headers, bodies and environment values are stored as plain JSON, without encryption. On Unix, the collection directory is private, files have owner-only permissions, and symlinked or hard-linked collection files are refused. The library is limited to 2 MiB, 100 requests, 32 environments and 64 variables per environment; individual values are limited to 8 KiB. Request expansion is bounded to 2 MiB and 10,000 substitutions before the native HTTP request limits apply. Unknown versions, malformed data and unsupported storage are refused. A failed save retains the editable request. Atomic replacement, a separate file lock and a revision bound to workspace activation prevent cooperating IDE instances or an old workspace activation from silently overwriting reviewed collection data. The native store releases the lock explicitly when an operation finishes, so a concurrently starting JDK process cannot keep it held through an inherited descriptor. Reload reads the current library without replacing the request draft. Collection responses are correlated with the workspace, generation and request identity, and stale results are discarded.

**Import and export collections** transfers the IDE’s version 1 library JSON by selecting a UTF-8 JSON file or by explicit copy and paste. Export contains saved request templates and environment values, including any credentials in headers or variables, in plain text; the interface explains this before export. Workspace identities, responses and the current unsaved request are excluded. Import validates the 2 MiB document and the resulting merged library before showing counts for new and matching entries. Request identity is collection plus name; environment identity is name. The person chooses to keep saved matching entries or replace them with imported entries; unrelated entries are retained. Only **Import reviewed collections** saves through the existing revision-checked native store. Editing the import, changing its conflict policy or loading a different saved revision invalidates the review. The current request draft and environment selection are preserved, and importing never sends HTTP traffic. Workspace activation changes clear transfer text and retire pending results. Selected files are bounded to 2 MiB both before reading and after the bounded read; invalid UTF-8 leaves the existing import text intact. Loading a file clears the previous review, but does not parse, save or send it automatically. A new selection, manual edit, composition start, cancellation, disabled transfer or workspace retirement aborts the owned reader and rejects late callbacks. **Export new collection file** creates the saved version 1 JSON in an explicitly chosen workspace-relative `.json` path. It rechecks the saved library revision and workspace activation in the native worker, writes a private temporary file, and publishes it atomically only if the destination does not exist. The parent directory must already exist; existing files and links are refused, so export cannot overwrite an open file or another writer’s content. On Unix the new file has owner-only permissions. Export includes saved headers, bodies and environment values in plain text and leaves the local library, unsaved request and environment selection unchanged. A native failure remains visible, including durability failures after creation. Paths outside the workspace and other products’ collection formats remain unavailable.

**Export collections as…** opens the native save dialog for a new `.json` file, including destinations outside the workspace. This separate desktop capability takes no file path from the renderer. The person chooses a destination after the interface explains that saved headers, bodies and environment values are plain text; current request drafts, responses and manual authentication-helper credentials remain excluded. Cancel creates no export. After selection, the native command rechecks the captured workspace binding, activation and saved-library revision before publishing the same bounded library JSON. It canonicalizes the existing parent directory and refuses existing files, symbolic links, hard links and concurrent creators. Publication requires a filesystem that supports the existing atomic create-only export mechanism; unsupported or unwritable destinations fail visibly. Normal export leaves the request draft, environment selection, saved library and workspace source files unchanged. The main window owns one pending chooser at a time, and retired renderer lifetimes suppress late results. The authority boundary and rationale are recorded in [ADR 0028](ADR.md#adr-0028--native-save-dialog-authority-for-external-http-collection-exports).

The **OpenAPI routes** section accepts pasted JSON or YAML and a user-selected UTF-8 JSON/YAML file up to 1 MiB and locally extracts up to 200 GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD or OPTIONS operations from OpenAPI 3.0 and 3.1. It uses the first operation-level, path-level or root server in that order (including server variables with defaults) and fills an editable request with the method, URL and an `application/json` example when available.

Local [OpenAPI Reference Objects](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1.html#reference-object) are resolved for path items, parameter definitions, request bodies and named examples using [JSON Pointer URI fragments](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901#section-6), including escaped names and percent-encoded Unicode. Resolution reads only the loaded document and never interprets a `$ref` property inside an example's payload as a reference. Missing or non-object targets, malformed pointers, cycles, external references in consumed fields and path references with local operation/settings siblings refuse import. Reference chains are limited to 32 objects, pointers to 128 tokens and 4,096 characters, and each import to 4,096 reference resolutions. Reused examples share one serialized body. An expanded example is limited to 1 MiB and all distinct serialized bodies to 4 MiB; expansion through YAML aliases cannot bypass those retained-output limits.

Operations with declared [OpenAPI parameters](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1.html#parameter-object) show a parameter form before changing the request draft. Path-level definitions apply unless an operation overrides the same location/name; header identity is case insensitive. Explicit examples, named local examples and inline schema defaults initialize editable text or JSON values; schema constraints and schema references are not evaluated. Optional parameters can be omitted. Required values must be supplied before **Prepare request** copies the encoded URL, headers and JSON body example into the editable request. Missing path declarations, duplicate definitions and undefined style/explode combinations refuse import. Missing values, malformed JSON, unsupported nested style values or output limits refuse preparation while retaining the draft. Send remains unavailable until preparation succeeds, and parameter edits require preparation again. Manual authentication entered for the selected operation remains available; changing the operation clears the authentication helper as before. Editing the specification retires its parameter form and requires explicit reload before selecting another operation.

Parameter preparation supports path `simple`, `label` and `matrix`; query `form`, `spaceDelimited`, `pipeDelimited` and `deepObject`; and header `simple`, for the scalar, array or flat-object combinations defined by the specification. Parameter `content` accepts one `application/json` or `text/plain` representation. Plain-text header content preserves literal text; style-based headers use URI-template encoding. `Accept`, `Content-Type` and `Authorization` parameter definitions are ignored as required by OpenAPI; request-body media type and manual authentication retain their existing controls. Query `allowReserved` preserves legal reserved query text and existing percent triples while protecting separators, fragments, plus signs and serialization delimiters. Values or names containing a space, pipe or bracket delimiter require the API designer’s escape convention as described in [OpenAPI Appendix E](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1.html#appendix-e-percent-encoding-and-form-media-types); preparation does not infer an additional server-specific decoder. Scalar form cookies use percent-encoded name/value pairs joined with `; ` in one explicit Cookie header; literal text/plain cookie values must be cookie-safe ASCII. This is the chosen cookie representation where OpenAPI leaves interoperability implementation-defined; JSON cookie content, array/object cookies, cookie sessions and negotiation remain unavailable.

Each operation and each declaration list are limited to 64 parameters, names to 256 UTF-8 bytes, and each value to 8 KiB. JSON values are checked before serialization for depth, size and at most 128 members per array or object; JSON integral numbers must be within the safe JavaScript integer range, while Text can retain larger integer spellings. Retained distinct parameter definitions/defaults are limited to 4 MiB. Prepared URLs must fit 8 KiB and retain valid path segments; generated and existing headers together must fit the existing 64-entry/64-KiB submission limits. Parameter preparation performs no network request or file write. Loading or selecting an operation never sends a request, and the source document remains in panel memory.

File selection uses the WebView's [File API](https://www.w3.org/TR/FileAPI/), reads at most the document limit plus one byte, validates UTF-8 without replacement characters and loads operations without selecting or sending a request. Unreadable, oversized or invalidly encoded files leave the specification and request drafts unchanged. A new selection, explicit cancellation, manual specification editing (including composition start), workspace activation change or panel teardown aborts the previous read and rejects queued late results. Source files, editor contents and editor save baselines are not changed by this import. Remote references, schema-reference expansion and example generation, authentication/security scheme application, non-JSON request-body examples and broad OpenAPI compatibility remain unavailable.

The feature controller binds each request and response to the active workspace identifier, generation and request identifier. It discards results after a workspace change or panel teardown. Captured Send and OpenAPI-load callbacks also reject a retired workspace activation or unmounted panel before parsing or network submission, including a new activation of the same workspace. The native Tauri adapter validates the correlated response before the controller presents it. The Rust command accepts GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD and OPTIONS; request bodies are accepted only for POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. It limits request bodies to 1 MiB, response bodies to 2 MiB, request headers to 64 entries/64 KiB, response headers to 128 entries/64 KiB, redirects to five, and each request to 30 seconds. Non-text response bodies are displayed as base64. Credentials embedded in URLs are refused, and transport errors omit the URL.

The implementation uses the `HttpClientPort` in web-core and the desktop Tauri adapter; neither the port nor web-core imports Tauri APIs. The browser application does not expose this feature. The [HTTP client runtime interaction](docs/c4/runtime-http-client.md) shows OpenAPI selection and the implemented request path, and the desktop/Rust components are included in the [C4 component diagram](docs/c4/components.md).

### 6.10 Java Database Tools

The desktop **Database** panel provides a bounded JDBC connection, schema inspection and explicit SQL console. The person selects a JAR already inside the active workspace, enters a JDBC URL and optional username/password, accepts the driver trust notice, and chooses **Connect and inspect schema**. The selected driver is executable Java code and runs with the user's operating-system privileges. Schema inspection lists at most 256 tables/views and 128 columns per table. **Refresh schema** repeats inspection after a schema-changing statement.

**Schema suggestions** or **Ctrl+Space** in the SQL field opens a searchable list from the last schema inspection. Selecting a table inserts its quoted schema and name; selecting a column inserts its quoted name without a table prefix. The driver supplies the delimiter through JDBC [DatabaseMetaData.getIdentifierQuoteString](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.sql/java/sql/DatabaseMetaData.html#getIdentifierQuoteString()); double quotes, backticks and bracket delimiters have explicit escaping rules. No syntax is inferred from the database product name. Missing or unsupported quote metadata makes insertion unavailable. Current-catalog filtering uses the connection's reported catalog; other or unconfirmed catalogs, control characters and names at metadata length limits are omitted. Partial metadata and the limit of 100 displayed matches remain visible, and filtering can find later entries within the captured metadata limits. This is a metadata selection tool: it does not resolve SQL aliases, joins, query scope, functions or types semantically. Refresh after schema or catalog changes.

Insertion replaces exactly the SQL selection captured when the list opened, preserves surrounding text and bound values, and restores the caret. It refuses stale metadata, changed SQL, workspace/generation changes, pending database operations and submissions beyond the UTF-8 limit. Cancel retains the draft. Opening, filtering and choosing an identifier do not connect, refresh metadata or execute SQL; **Run SQL** remains a separate explicit action.

The SQL editor accepts up to 64 KiB of SQL text per submission. **Use bound parameters** selects JDBC [PreparedStatement](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.sql/java/sql/PreparedStatement.html) execution for positional `?` placeholders. The person adds ordered values and selects string, signed 64-bit integer, decimal, boolean, NULL, date, time, timestamp or base64 binary types. The SQL stays unchanged; values are sent separately to the JDK for typed binding rather than interpolated into it. Numeric values remain text until binding, avoiding JavaScript number rounding. Temporal inputs use ISO date/time text; timestamps have no time-zone offset. NULL has no value. Up to 256 parameters are accepted, with 16 KiB per value and 64 KiB total; decimals are limited to precision and absolute scale of 1,024. SQL syntax, conversions and binding compatibility remain the driver's responsibility. The bridge checks the parameter count when the driver provides it; unsupported parameter metadata leaves validation to the driver. Turning the option off uses ordinary Statement execution. Editing values or selecting a type sends nothing. The person must review and choose **Run SQL**; the IDE does not migrate or modify schemas automatically. A submission may read or change database contents. The console shows at most 200 rows, 128 columns, 16 KiB per cell and 250,000 displayed characters, with explicit truncation indicators. Driver execution has a 30-second deadline; compiling the private bridge with the selected JDK has a separate 20-second deadline. The production desktop holds one physical JDBC connection in one native-owned JVM for the active workspace. Metadata refresh, ordinary statements and prepared statements use that connection, including for in-memory databases. Only one connection may be open at a time; connection pools and database migrations are unavailable.

**Estimate plan** explicitly requests the database's estimated execution plan for the current SQL and optional bound parameters on the existing JDBC connection. The private bridge currently advertises this operation for H2 2.x and rechecks that its live compatibility mode is `REGULAR`. Other products and compatibility modes are unavailable. The bridge uses H2's [`EXPLAIN PLAN FOR`](https://h2database.com/html/commands.html#explain), without requesting `ANALYZE`, and displays the returned bounded plan text separately from data rows. It does not infer index choices or costs in the frontend. The SQL field and parameter values remain unchanged, and editing them does not submit a plan request.

The estimated-plan operation admits one statement starting with `SELECT`, `WITH`, `TABLE`, `VALUES`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `MERGE`. A lexical boundary check handles H2's quoted strings/identifiers, whitespace-separated dollar-quoted strings and nested or line comments; one final semicolon and trailing comments are accepted. Multiple statements, an existing `EXPLAIN`/`ANALYZE` prefix and unterminated strings/comments are refused. H2 remains responsible for SQL parsing, types, binding and optimization; this check does not establish a semantic SQL model. Before the request the bridge confirms the live H2 mode, since ordinary SQL can change it after inspection. A refusal never falls back to ordinary SQL execution. Planning uses the selected driver's and server's normal preparation behavior.

Plans retain the current auto-commit setting and manual transaction. An attempted estimate counts as a statement for the existing conservative pending-work guard; it neither commits nor rolls back other work. Stop uses the same owned-worker termination path, and a failed or lost operation cannot fabricate a completed plan. **Export captured result as…** exports the already captured plan row through the existing CSV/JSON path without estimating again. A plan can contain SQL text and literals supplied by the database. Parameterized queries continue to send values separately through JDBC binding.

**Begin transaction** disables JDBC auto-commit. **Commit** and **Rollback** execute on that same connection and leave auto-commit off. **Enable auto-commit** is allowed only after a confirmed toolbar commit or rollback and before another SQL submission. The displayed statement count conservatively counts attempts, including reads and failed statements; it does not measure changed rows or interpret transaction commands embedded in SQL. The database can commit schema changes implicitly; the panel displays the driver's reported behavior. These controls cannot make a database's nontransactional schema operations reversible. **Rollback and disconnect** is the explicit action for discarding pending manual work. A successful outcome is shown only after the worker confirms it. A lost connection, timeout or failed transaction command closes the session without claiming commit or rollback success; check database state before retrying an operation whose outcome is unknown.

The Database panel stays mounted when another bottom tool window is selected, preserving its connection, SQL and bound values. Frontend guards refuse workspace switching or refresh before resetting application state while a database operation is running or manual work needs a commit/rollback decision. Native workspace activation independently checks the same condition before changing root authority. Document unload and ordinary native close are refused while an operation is running or submitted manual work remains. A failed workspace switch that advances only the UI generation can resume the original session after checking native ownership. A clean workspace transition or application exit closes the idle worker. **Stop and disconnect** is available while connecting, refreshing metadata, executing SQL or changing transaction state. It targets only the captured session or connection request. A stop that overtakes a queued startup prevents that startup from opening later. On Unix, the worker first receives a termination request and has up to two seconds for JVM/database shutdown hooks before forced termination. Windows uses process termination and remains unqualified. The IDE confirms worker termination, not a JDBC rollback or commit. Recent writes may still depend on database durability settings, particularly if forced termination is required. After stopping or losing a connection, credentials are cleared while SQL and bound parameters remain in memory for review; reconnecting and resubmitting require separate explicit actions. Statement-only cancellation that retains the connection is unavailable.

Connection metadata, results and errors are withheld immediately when their workspace is retired, including before effect-based cleanup finishes. During a workspace transition or a native ownership check after a failed switch, the same workspace's SQL, parameters and connection draft remain in memory while query actions are unavailable. Confirmed ownership restores that view; an actual workspace change resets its form and credentials. A completed database error cannot reappear in another workspace merely because no session remains to clean up.

The desktop adapter calls Rust commands that check the main window, active workspace identity, native activation generation and session identifier. Connection startup confines the selected driver JAR to the workspace and captures it in a private temporary directory beside the bridge compiled by the selected full JDK. Subsequent operations use the captured driver and connection; replacing the workspace JAR does not change an open session. The bridge receives URL and credentials once through standard input. Later session commands contain only the operation, unchanged SQL and optional typed parameters. These values are not command-line arguments or workspace files. Connection drafts, credentials, SQL and displayed results stay in memory and are cleared on explicit ordinary disconnect or workspace change; they are not saved as profiles. Stop and unexpected connection loss preserve SQL and parameter drafts for review while clearing connection details and results.

SQL and binding refusals retain a usable session when the worker confirms its state. Framing, input/output limits and request correlation refuse malformed, oversized or mismatched worker responses. The bridge encodes its JSON output explicitly as UTF-8, independently of the host console locale; a JVM file-encoding option alone does not establish the standard-output encoding. The operation deadline covers both input writing and response reading, including an early response while the input pipe is full. Unix workers use a dedicated process group; Linux also requests child termination when the native parent dies. Ordinary Linux native GUI shutdown is qualified, but arbitrary driver-spawned descendants that escape that group and other operating systems remain unqualified. The child process receives a restricted environment, bounded output and JVM memory limits. Driver code is not sandboxed and executes with the user's privileges.

The browser application does not expose this feature. The port remains in web-core and has no Tauri dependency; native commands and UI wiring belong to the desktop adapter and application. The [C4 component diagram](docs/c4/components.md) shows the controller/adapter boundary, and the [runtime interaction](docs/c4/runtime-java-database.md) shows connection, SQL, transaction and result ownership.

This slice supports JDBC drivers supplied by the user; it does not download or resolve drivers, store passwords, provide semantic SQL completion or diagnostics, estimated plans for other dialects, executed/profiling plans, migrations, schema editing or Spring/JPA integration. Real H2 bridge and native GUI verification scope is recorded in section 10.1.

**Export captured result as…** opens a native Save As dialog for a new UTF-8 CSV or JSON file. It uses the last bounded tabular response without connecting or executing SQL again. An explicit acknowledgment is required for a truncated result; the export contains only the captured rows, not a full database dump. Exports are limited to 2 MiB. JSON stores ordered column descriptors and row arrays, preserving duplicate labels, strings (including large integers represented as text), empty strings and `NULL`, plus row-count and truncation metadata. Connection details, SQL and bound values are not added as export metadata; query result cells can themselves contain sensitive data.

CSV follows the comma, CRLF and double-quote escaping rules in [RFC 4180](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4180). All non-NULL fields are quoted, including headers; SQL `NULL` is an unquoted empty field. **Prefix CSV text for spreadsheets**, enabled initially, prefixes every non-NULL header and cell with an apostrophe. This changes exported text and does not guarantee formula protection in every spreadsheet or after a file is saved again; see [OWASP CSV injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/CSV_Injection). Raw CSV is available by clearing the option. Importers can reinterpret types and empty fields, so choose JSON when exact string and NULL preservation matters.

The native host keeps one immutable captured response, correlated with its workspace activation and source request. A new query or connection retires it; closing, cancelling or retiring its JDBC session also makes it unavailable. Native workspace ownership and captured-result identity are checked before and after the dialog, without holding workspace locks while the dialog is open. The renderer supplies neither a destination nor result rows. Publication creates a new private file and refuses existing files, links and concurrent creators. Cancel writes nothing. Supporting filesystems are required; overwriting and automatic persistence are unavailable. The authority decision is recorded in [ADR 0031](ADR.md#adr-0031--native-export-of-captured-jdbc-results).

### 6.11 Java Compiler Checks

**Check Java Compiler Errors** asks RefactorKit to analyze an immutable view of the selected Java project. The view contains every open Java buffer in that project, including clean companions, and the saved contents of other Java sources. A selected JDK and a current effective project context are required. RefactorKit owns source ownership, compiler settings and semantic analysis; the IDE validates editor state and presents the result without constructing a separate semantic project model. The command does not save buffers or request project compilation. Gradle must first be explicitly evaluated when its effective model requires build code. The IDE refuses a check while an open file listed in the provider's build evidence has unsaved changes: save or discard those changes and synchronize the project first. This guard uses provider-declared build inputs, not filename-based Maven or Gradle inference; it does not establish that the provider lists every possible build input. Maven parent-input completeness and its package-specific qualification are recorded in section 10.1.

**Enable Automatic Java Compiler Checks** opts into the same read-only flow for the current desktop session. It is disabled initially and is not persisted as a workspace preference. With a Java source active and an available selected-SDK context, buffer changes schedule one check after 750 ms without further changes. A valid pending or accepted frame is reused; a completed result does not start a polling loop. A manual check consumes a scheduled check. New edits retire old results and cancel obsolete requests before the next check; late replies remain excluded by the existing editor-frame guards. **Pause automatic checks** removes scheduled work and cancels an in-flight check. Initial synchronization, build-configuration changes and unavailable or partial context still require the appropriate explicit project action. Native source-only file notifications can refresh saved-source authority automatically after a short pause while editor and workspace writes are idle. The old context is retired immediately; refresh waits for prior language-setting cleanup, rechecks workspace, settings and write readiness, and acquires a new provider snapshot without requesting build execution. Evaluated Gradle metadata is reused. Legacy notifications without a change classification keep the manual-sync fallback. Workspace/settings changes, cancellation and paused monitoring cancel queued refreshes. Automatic checks resume against the new context and the current drafts; neither context refresh nor compiler checks save source or evaluate Gradle build code. When the context explicitly reports that Java source analysis is unavailable, both manual and automatic checks explain the limit without submitting a diagnostic query or retiring the available build model. Revoking that source-analysis authority cancels pending checks and retires results even if the retained snapshot and context hashes are unchanged. Automatic checks can resume after explicit synchronization supplies source-analysis support. Problems navigation completes before another automatic check starts, so opening a new buffer cannot interrupt the requested range reveal. Controller tests cover scheduling, pause, unmount, superseded replies, changes in source-analysis availability and a deliberately delayed navigation. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:metadata-only-editor-diagnostics` profile passes one Linux release/no-bundle Maven GUI scenario with Temurin JDK 27 and the isolated Maven-input-evidence provider. The same profile also passes against the isolated SDK-27-API candidate. Both commands explain that source analysis is unavailable, a Java draft remains unchanged, build metadata remains available, no diagnostic query reaches the provider, and explicit pause/discard closes the window normally without surviving runner-owned processes. Controller tests separately verify that the frontend does not invoke the diagnostic port and that withdrawal of source-analysis authority cancels pending work. This qualifies the unavailable-analysis flow; it does not establish Java 27 semantic support or prove build execution. The focused Linux release/no-bundle Maven and Gradle profiles pass automatic repair and pause with the isolated provider on JDK 21; these GUI scenarios do not qualify deliberately delayed source opening or interactive performance on larger projects.

The diagnostic consumer preserves whether the provider used JDT, a qualified SDK compiler, or the qualified Java 25 SDK/JDT combination. It accepts only the declared provider/backend combinations and their corresponding error-code families; unknown or inconsistent provenance is refused. Java 25 SDK compiler results require an attested context schema from v2 through v7. The single Java 26 SDK backend is admitted only with an exact v7 context attestation; Java 26 SDK/JDT aggregates and older-schema claims remain refused. The IDE does not select a compiler backend or reconstruct source-set compiler settings. Adapter and native tests cover these checks. Real IDE-service and Linux native GUI qualification pass for the isolated SDK-compiler candidate with Maven and explicitly evaluated Gradle release 25; the same delivery retains JDT diagnostics under JDK 21 with release 8. Aggregate-backend provenance is consumer-tested, with mixed-backend native qualification still outstanding.

1. The desktop captures the Java buffers and their versions while checking that no editor file operation is pending. It retains their text and buffer lifetimes so an edit followed by restoration still retires the request.
2. The native command uses the retained Java project session and requires the dedicated `javaImmutableEditorOverlayDiagnostics` capability. It verifies the context schema, snapshot, selected SDK identities and complete editor-document correlation before admitting the response.
3. RefactorKit returns complete compiler errors for the analyzed source snapshot, or a typed refusal. Its analyzed-source count includes saved sources outside the editor inventory. Warnings, inspections and build execution are outside this query. Source folder lists or complete compiler options alone do not establish the provenance required by the diagnostic guard.
4. The native boundary validates each diagnostic range against the corresponding captured buffer or saved source and rechecks project authority. The frontend adapter validates the returned source text and hashes before publishing compiler-error markers and Problems entries. JDT LS warnings remain visible. Unavailable or refused checks remain distinct from a clean compiler result, including in an empty Problems panel.
5. Buffer edits, edit-and-restore, changed tab inventories, workspace changes or changed project context retire pending and accepted checks. Cancellation reaches the provider and late replies are discarded.
6. Opening a compiler problem revalidates the retained editor frame and project, then compares the opened target with the diagnostic source text before revealing its range. Opening a previously closed source retires the old check because the editor inventory changed; the explicit navigation can still finish against unchanged source. A changed disk source or an edited-and-restored companion prevents an obsolete range from being revealed. No source is saved or replaced.

The native and provider-neutral ports preserve the existing Java session, cancellation and workspace guards. The [controller tests](apps/desktop/src/features/java/useJavaEditorDiagnosticsController.test.tsx) cover editor retirement, stale-source navigation and refusal of dirty provider-declared build inputs with legacy and workspace-relative context paths. The dirty-build-input refusal also passes in both focused Linux release/no-bundle Maven GUI profiles on JDK 21 (source/target 8 and release 8): the POM draft is preserved, explicit discard restores the saved configuration, and subsequent compiler checks, diagnostic navigation and source repair succeed. The equivalent Gradle profiles also pass with the isolated provenance-corrected provider, as described in section 10.1. Other operating systems remain unqualified. Provider and native-GUI qualification, current project-layout limits and reproducible commands are recorded in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).

### 6.12 Read-only Git Review

The Agent **Changes** view can show Git hunks and open their source ranges in the existing editor. Hunks describe saved, unstaged text changes in tracked modified or added files; the interface explains that unsaved editor edits are excluded. Opening a range preserves an existing dirty buffer. Staged-only, binary and otherwise nonreviewable changes produce an unavailable explanation rather than an invented patch. Staging and other VCS mutations are outside this flow.

The native bridge and Node-hosted source ask Git for NUL-delimited status records, preserve UTF-8 filenames and map repository-relative paths into the selected workspace subdirectory. Diff requests use literal paths. Git runs without optional index locks, external diff programs, text conversion or filesystem-monitor hooks. A failed query produces an error or an unavailable review, never a fabricated clean file list.

Desktop requests include the expected workspace root. Native workers check the active workspace generation before and after reading Git results. The renderer also binds review batches to workspace identity, root and generation: it retires old batches on reopening the same workspace, stops queued requests after retirement, and ignores accessories from a different workspace. Source navigation rechecks this lifetime before opening a result. The pinned detached view does not independently acquire a main-window workspace generation.

Native Git work runs away from the UI thread. One review operation has a five-second deadline shared by its Git calls, with at most 1 MiB of stdout and 64 KiB of stderr per call. Limit or timeout failures remain visible; Unix cleanup stops the owned process group. The Node-hosted source is synchronous, with a shared five-second deadline and a 1 MiB output limit per call; it does not provide the native Unix process-group cleanup. Verification and its limits are recorded in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).

### 6.13 Local Git Source Control

The implemented interaction is shown in the [Git source-control runtime diagram](docs/c4/runtime-git-source-control.md). Components are included in the [C4 component diagram](docs/c4/components.md).

The **Git** activity and **Open Git Source Control** command expose local saved-file changes, index review, staging, unstaging, authored commits, local branch creation, renaming, reviewed deletion and switching, saved-source blame, a recent-commit summary and paginated committed history affecting the workspace. Opening the activity starts no Git command. The person explicitly trusts repository hooks and filters and requests **Refresh Git**; trust, commit-message drafts and identity choices remain in memory for that workspace activation and are reset on reopening it.

Each changed file distinguishes staged, unstaged and unsaved-editor state. **Review saved changes** presents the disk version, and **Stage reviewed saved file** is unavailable while that file has unsaved editor changes. Git actions never save buffers. **Unstage** requests an index-only restoration from HEAD, or removes the cached entry before the initial commit, without replacing an editor model. Rename pairs and recreated paths are normalized from Git's NUL-delimited status. Source paths are literal and remain within the selected workspace; directory/submodule staging and non-UTF-8 paths or link targets require the CLI.

**Review all staged changes** enables **Commit staged changes** only with a nonempty message and identity. Identity overrides apply to that commit without modifying Git configuration; a successful commit clears its message draft. Ordinary Git hooks and configured signing remain active. Trusted programs can change files or staging; the IDE neither bypasses them nor promises that a hook is read-only. Commits are refused while conflicts or a rebase/sequencer/autostash workflow remain active, or when staged files exist outside a workspace subdirectory. Opening the repository root permits reviewing those paths together. There is no automatic push, reset, discard or repository initialization. The separately reviewed local rebase workflow below is the explicit history-rewrite action.

**Saved-source blame** reads a tracked UTF-8 file from disk without saving or consuming the editor draft. The person enters a workspace-relative path and first line or chooses **Blame active saved file**. Each page shows at most 200 saved lines with commit, author, UTC date and Git's boundary/ignored-revision indicators. Uncommitted saved lines are explicitly unattributed; temporary input paths and Git's synthetic author identity are not presented as commit metadata. Opening the blamed file uses the ordinary editor lifecycle and preserves an existing draft.

The native service captures at most 512 KiB of saved source in a private temporary file and passes that captured content to [Git blame](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-blame). Git owns attribution, ordinary whole-file rename tracking and configured ignored revisions. The service verifies Git state and the captured source fingerprint before returning; subsequent pages must match that same saved fingerprint. The adapter correlates each page with its path, first line, activation and inspected revision. File changes, retired workspace/provider replies, malformed output, symlinks, binary or oversized input, missing history and bounded-process failures are refused. A failed read clears the annotation and requires **Refresh Git**. Editor drafts may remain dirty during this read and are explicitly excluded. Trusted Git filters retain their normal effects; the service does not promise a repository-wide atomic read against external writers. This is saved-line attribution; commit browsing is a separate read-only workflow below. Selecting a blame line number opens its saved source at that line. Before navigation, Git rechecks the captured page and source fingerprint against the active repository snapshot. The editor then requires the exact captured UTF-8 bytes in a clean, active buffer and rechecks its lifetime, content and workspace before revealing the location. A dirty file retains readable saved attribution but its line actions are disabled; saving or discarding remains explicit. Changed saved files, retired responses and unavailable source prevent the jump and require fresh blame. The ordinary **Open blamed file** action still preserves existing drafts.

**Commit history** browses commits reachable from the inspected HEAD in pages of 50, with explicit **Older commits** and **Newer commits** actions. The optional literal workspace-relative path filters a file or directory, including a deleted path; **History of active file** uses the current editor path without reading its draft. Git owns ancestry, path history simplification and topological ordering through [Git log](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-log). A workspace opened below the repository root sees only commits affecting that subtree. Path history does not follow renames. The recent-commit summary remains separate from the paginated view.

**Review committed changes** displays the selected commit's metadata and patch in a read-only panel through [Git show](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-show). Root commits show additions; merge commits compare against their first parent. Binary contents are not decoded, rename detection is disabled, and external diff programs and text conversion are disabled. No source buffer is opened, replaced or saved, and no index or reference mutation is requested. Each page is bound to the captured HEAD, inspected revision, activation, literal path and offset. The native service re-reads the exact page before admitting its selected commit, checks Git state before and after reading, and applies the shared five-second and 1 MiB process-output bounds. A changed repository, retired workspace/provider, malformed response, unavailable object or oversized patch retires the view and requires **Refresh Git**. Very deep or expensive history may exceed those bounds and require the CLI. All-reference graphs, search, rename-following history and comparisons between arbitrary revisions remain unavailable.

**Create local branch** creates a named local reference from the inspected HEAD while retaining the current branch, working files and index. It requires an initial commit and does not configure remote tracking. The branch selector lists at most 2,000 local branches; reference names and object identities participate in the review revision so a changed target invalidates a pending action. Git validates branch names and refuses replacing an existing branch.

**Rename local branch** requires an explicitly selected local branch and a different, unused replacement name. It uses ordinary [Git branch movement](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-branch) without force: Git moves the local reference, its configuration and reflog, and updates HEAD when renaming the current branch. No checkout or remote rename is requested, so editor drafts do not need saving and the source context remains available. The inspected revision must still match; invalid or missing names, existing destinations and branches checked out in another worktree are refused. The normal mutation transition guards remain active until the refreshed snapshot arrives. Trusted Git hooks and external writers retain their normal effects and concurrency limitations.

**Delete a local branch** requires the repository root and an explicit review of one selected local branch. The review shows its captured object identity, current HEAD, the complete number of branch commits not contained in HEAD and up to 200 of those commits. A larger range is explicitly truncated. The current branch, branches checked out in any known worktree, indirect symbolic-reference layouts and active merge/rebase/sequencer states are refused. Dirty editor buffers and saved changes can remain because deletion requests a reference change rather than a checkout.

The person types the exact reviewed branch name before choosing **Delete reviewed local branch**. Normal deletion requires every branch commit to be contained in the captured HEAD. A branch with commits outside HEAD requires the separate **Allow forced local branch deletion** choice. This IDE policy compares with HEAD, independently of a configured upstream. The native service recomputes the review and uses a [Git reference transaction](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-update-ref) to check the expected HEAD object and branch object while deleting the selected reference without following a symbolic target. Changed references, workspace retirement, reference locks and failed trusted hooks refuse the action. Known worktree ownership is checked before the transaction; concurrent external worktree creation retains Git's ordinary concurrency limitations.

Successful deletion removes the local reference and its reflog, then removes settings for that branch from the repository-local Git configuration when present. Other branches and remote references are not requested for deletion. Configuration cleanup is a separate phase: a failure, or a recreated reference detected before cleanup, reports that the reference was already deleted and requires inspection; the IDE does not claim rollback. External included configuration files are retained. There is no IDE undo. Trusted reference-transaction hooks retain their usual effects, and external Git writers can race with configuration cleanup. The rationale and authority boundary are recorded in [ADR 0034](ADR.md#adr-0034--reviewed-local-branch-deletion-with-expected-reference-identities).

**Switch local branch** requires the repository root as the workspace because checkout can affect the entire repository. It acquires the editor's external-write guard before invoking Git: unsaved buffers, pending file reads or saves, and another workspace transformation prevent the operation. Editing, saving, source creation and other Java source writes remain blocked until reconciliation finishes. Git owns saved-file conflict checks and worktree ownership; the IDE requests an existing local branch without force, automatic stash, remote guessing or recursive submodule checkout. After either success or failure, still-current clean open buffers reload from actual disk snapshots and adopt fresh save baselines. Java document changes and explorer entries refresh, and the RefactorKit project context and loaded project view are retired; semantic operations require a fresh synchronization and project-view refresh. Deleted or unreadable open files remain retained with a visible warning rather than reconstructed from Git output. Reconciliation failures are reported separately from Git's outcome. This lifecycle is defined in [ADR 0027](ADR.md#adr-0027--editor-reconciliation-around-git-branch-switches).

**Start reviewed merge** merges a selected local branch into the attached current branch at the repository root. Saved changes and untracked files must first be committed, moved or explicitly discarded by the person. The IDE requests [Git merge](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge) without automatic commit or fast-forward advancement, so even a fast-forward candidate stops for review. It disables squash, autostash and automatic rerere staging and protects ignored files from overwrite. An already integrated branch can finish without an active merge. Git's ordinary unresolved-conflict outcome is presented as **Merge in progress**, with HEAD unchanged and a typed merge-parent identity; unrelated failures remain failures.

Resolve conflicts through **Open file** and the normal editor. Save each resolution, **Refresh Git**, review its saved changes and stage it. **Review all staged changes**, an explicit message and author enable the ordinary commit action; Git creates the two-parent merge commit. A merge whose trees are identical still requires this explicit review and commit. Unresolved index stages prevent committing; the IDE does not judge conflict-marker text or replace semantic compilation. **Abort reviewed merge** requires a separate acknowledgment that saved resolutions will be discarded. It uses Git's normal abort behavior, requires saved editor buffers and rejects a changed inspected revision. Neither path silently stashes or cleans files.

Merge and abort acquire the same editor external-write guard as branch switching and reconcile open clean buffers from actual disk after either success or failure. They retire the Java semantic context and source view; explicit synchronization is required afterward. Merge-state reviews bind the merge message, parent, original HEAD and operation markers together with saved changed-file fingerprints. Merge inspection is bounded to 16 MiB of changed saved input; directory/submodule changes and larger inputs require the Git CLI. Nested workspaces, active sequencers/autostash and multi-head merge completion are unavailable in this workflow. The authority and rationale are defined in [ADR 0029](ADR.md#adr-0029--reviewed-local-merges-through-git).

**Review local rebase** reads the selected local upstream, current branch and HEAD, new base identity and ordered candidate commits without writing Git state. A clean repository root, an attached branch, one shared merge base and at most 200 linear replay candidates are required. Merge commits in the range require the Git CLI. **Start reviewed rebase** requires a separate history-rewrite acknowledgment; the native command recomputes and matches the reviewed fingerprint before Git can replace commits or saved files. Unlike the merge workflow, Git may complete the rewrite during this action. There is no automatic push, stash, squash, interactive todo editing or update of other branches.

The service uses [Git's merge rebase backend](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase), replays clean cherry-picks instead of dropping them in advance, preserves intentionally empty commits and stops if a replay becomes empty. Supported paused state shows the original branch and HEAD, new base, stopped commit and attempted step. Resolve through the editor, save, **Refresh Git**, review and stage the saved resolution, then **Review all staged changes** before **Continue reviewed rebase**. Git retains the original commit message through a noninteractive editor. **Skip reviewed rebase commit** requires an explicit decision to drop the stopped commit and discard its resolutions. **Abort reviewed rebase** separately acknowledges discarding resolutions and asks Git to restore the original branch. Retaining a newly empty replayed commit requires the Git CLI. The normal commit button remains unavailable while a rebase is active.

Each rebase source operation acquires the editor external-write guard and reconciles clean buffers from actual disk, including after failures. Java context and source view are retired and require explicit synchronization. Review revisions include bounded rebase metadata and saved changed-source hashes, so altered todo state or an externally changed saved resolution invalidates a queued action. The service refuses an added tracked path that would replace an existing ignored or untracked input. Metadata is limited to 64 regular UTF-8 files, 512 KiB each and 2 MiB total; changed saved input shares the 16 MiB inspection bound. The apply backend, executable or merge-preserving todo commands, autostash, unsupported metadata and nested workspaces require the Git CLI. The authority and rationale are recorded in [ADR 0030](ADR.md#adr-0030--reviewed-linear-local-rebase).

The native adapter rejects a different workspace root or activation before mutations and holds the workspace-activation lock until they settle. The renderer also suppresses replies from retired workspaces and checks live dirty buffers before staging. HEAD, branch, index and status bind reviews to a preflight revision; hashes of saved file contents additionally guard staging. Failures retire the review and require Refresh because a command may have completed partly. External Git processes and trusted hooks retain Git's ordinary concurrency behavior, as defined in [ADR 0026](ADR.md#adr-0026--explicit-local-git-mutations-behind-a-separate-port); these are not managed RefactorKit transactions or atomic repository-wide previews.

Normal close and workspace switching are blocked during an outstanding mutation. Git runs on native workers; subprocess calls share five-second read or thirty-second mutation deadlines, with 1 MiB stdout and 64 KiB stderr bounds per process. Timeout and output-limit failures terminate the owned Unix process group. Optional index refresh, filesystem-monitor hooks and automatic maintenance are disabled for these invocations. Status is bounded to 2,000 changed paths. Untracked UTF-8 text previews display at most 512 KiB; larger or binary files receive an explicit description. File content hashing admits at most 128 MiB per file and index inspection at most 64 MiB. A malformed or failed response is unavailable rather than a fabricated clean repository. Browser, interactive signing, commit-output consoles, all-reference history graphs and search, broader rebase/merge workflows, remote operations, package/platform qualification and additional process-termination interleavings remain future work. The Agent Changes flow in section 6.12 retains its existing read-only authority.

## Section 7: Deployment View

### 7.1 Supported Packaging Scope

The 0.1.0-alpha prerelease targets a Linux x86-64 AppImage, a macOS arm64 disk image, and a Windows x64 NSIS installer. The [release packaging workflow](.github/workflows/desktop-release-packages.yml) stages those packages from the Git Flow release branch. GitHub Releases distributes the selected packages under the annotated tag on main. The macOS alpha uses ad-hoc signing and the Windows installer uses the default WebView2 installation mode. Native workflow qualification is currently concentrated on Linux. Focused Linux/X11 acceptance verifies native window discovery and close, Java language intelligence, typing templates, core execution and source creation. It also covers selected Gradle composite workflows with a separately supplied JDK, Gradle and RefactorKit runtime. KWin Wayland acceptance covers Java editing, navigation, execution, debugging and selected Maven and Gradle refactoring workflows. Section 10.1 records the verified scope for each environment. Manual desktop registration is qualified on the controlled Linux host. Automated installation, FUSE launch, upgrades, additional compositors, Windows and macOS require separate qualification. Signed updates and an operating-system compatibility matrix are roadmap items.

The Linux bundling hook locates the WebKitGTK 4.1 runtime selected by `pkg-config` and stages its web process, network process, injected bundle and, when present, GPU process in the AppImage. This also covers builds against an installation outside the standard system directories. Packaging stops if a required helper is missing. The GUI acceptance command builds a fresh package and launches that exact file.

For manual desktop registration, place the executable AppImage at a stable absolute path. From an empty temporary directory, extract `usr/share/applications/IDE.desktop` and `usr/share/icons/hicolor/128x128/apps/ide-desktop.png` with one `--appimage-extract` invocation per path. Both files appear under `squashfs-root`. Save the desktop entry as `com.ide.desktop.desktop` in the user data directory's `applications` subdirectory, whose default is `~/.local/share/applications`. Set `Exec` to the absolute AppImage path and `Icon` to the absolute path of the copied icon. Quote a pathname containing spaces according to the [Desktop Entry Specification](https://specifications.freedesktop.org/desktop-entry/latest/exec-variables.html). The bundled entry uses `Exec=ide-desktop` inside the AppImage and needs the installed AppImage path when registered externally.

The workspace lockfile selects Tauri CLI 2.12.5. Its bundler lets GTK select the session backend. The earlier bundler forced X11, which prevented startup when a Wayland session had no XWayland server. [Tauri bundler release notes](https://v2.tauri.app/release/tauri-bundler/v2.10.0/)

Monaco is bundled locally. External tools are discovered at runtime; they are not automatically redistributed with the application. Java execution requires a compatible full JDK and the relevant project build tool or wrapper. JDK selection can be set through `IDE_JAVA_HOME` or `JAVA_HOME`; otherwise the Java runtime discovered on PATH identifies its JDK.

RefactorKit remains an external installation. The CLI searches executable launchers in absolute `PATH` entries first, then the standard `HOME/.local/share/refactorkit/bin` directory. The daemon and RefactorKit LSP retain their existing sibling lookup beside a CLI found on `PATH`, followed by the same standard user directory. Standard-directory discovery requires an absolute `HOME`; relative home and path entries do not select a workspace-local launcher. Executable installation links are resolved to their canonical files. When replacing an external RefactorKit runtime, close the IDE and reopen the project before acquiring a fresh Java context. Capabilities are probed from the discovered distribution, and unsupported operations remain explicitly unavailable. Development override controls remain opt-in. The native verification in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope) covers CLI status, daemon project context, guarded navigation and the packaged Maven and Gradle development workflows with standard-directory discovery. RefactorKit LSP, installers and other operating systems require separate verification.

The JDK selected for a Java project is independent of the Java runtime used to launch Eclipse JDT LS. Settings can persist a separate absolute JDK home for the JDT LS process; that selection takes precedence over environment discovery and is checked against the installed server's minimum runtime before a running service is stopped. Clearing the setting returns to discovery through `IDE_JDTLS_JAVA_HOME`, `IDE_JAVA_HOME`, `JAVA_HOME` and a compatible JDK on `PATH`. UI, controller, adapter and Rust tests cover preference and runtime selection. A focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI profile also verifies that a saved JDK 25 server runtime overrides a conflicting environment choice and remains independent of a JDK 21 project after restart; section 10.1 records the scope. An older project JDK therefore does not prevent a newer JDT LS runtime from serving that project. Packaged-app and other operating-system verification remain open.

JDI attachment requires the selected full JDK's debugger module and an external JVM already listening on the configured JDWP socket. It does not require a project build tool. The helper belongs to the IDE's native process lifecycle; the external target and its output belong to the launcher that started it. Current debugger availability requires Unix process ownership; runtime qualification is bounded to the Linux cases in section 10.1.

The [existing third-party notice](apps/desktop/src-tauri/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md) lists the clipboard, HTTP-client, OpenAPI-parsing and JDT bundle-reading dependencies; it is not a complete distribution license inventory. Full dependency and license review remains a release gate.

### 7.2 Development and Verification Commands

The [native desktop build workflow](.github/workflows/desktop-native-build.yml) compiles the Tauri application on GitHub-hosted Linux x64, macOS arm64, and Windows x64 runners. It builds from the JavaScript and Rust lockfiles and uploads the executable for each successful job. One GitHub Actions run verified all three compilation targets and executable uploads. The workflow skips installer creation and signing. Startup, Java tooling and native GUI acceptance require separate verification. The XCOM Foundry write transaction is compiled only on Linux because it requires Linux filesystem primitives; other desktop builds retain its existing refusal.

From the repository root:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm --filter @ide/desktop tauri dev
pnpm build:web
pnpm build:desktop
pnpm check:boundaries
pnpm typecheck:bdd
pnpm validate:docs
pnpm test:spec
pnpm test
pnpm test:story:refactor-kit-java-build-run
IDE_ALLOW_REFACTORKIT_LSP_OVERRIDE=1 \
IDE_REFACTORKIT_LSP=/path/to/refactorkit-lsp \
IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON=/path/to/refactorkit-daemon \
IDE_REFACTORKIT_ENGINE=/path/to/refactorkit \
IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_JDK=/path/to/jdk-21 \
IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_REPOSITORY=/path/to/maven-repository \
  pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:lsp
cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib
```

The RefactorKit LSP GUI profile requires a source-built LSP, daemon and engine, plus a full project JDK and populated Maven cache. It runs against a Linux release/no-bundle build and needs Tauri Driver, WebKitWebDriver, Xvfb and a D-Bus session launcher. The scenario uses Maven offline and does not qualify an installed package or another operating system.

Native recovery uses the standard library's file-lock API and requires Rust 1.89 or newer to build. The two frontend build commands compile TypeScript and Vite assets; they do not produce a native package. Build the configured AppImage with:

```bash
pnpm --filter @ide/desktop tauri build --bundles appimage --ci
```

Real Java tool acceptance is opt-in because it needs installed tools and Maven/Gradle dependency access:

```bash
cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  commands::java_execution::tests::real_ -- --ignored --test-threads=1
cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  test_discovery_tests -- --ignored --test-threads=1
cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  real_jdi_ -- --ignored --test-threads=1
pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:attach
IDE_JAVA_HOME=/absolute/path/to/jdk-25 \
IDE_JDTLS_HOME=/absolute/path/to/eclipse-jdt-ls \
  pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-language-001:appimage
```

Generated project wrappers can be qualified with empty tool caches. Set the environment variables to full JDK installations; the tests download pinned distributions and project dependencies, so network access is required:

```bash
IDE_JAVA_HOME_21=/absolute/path/to/jdk-21 \
  cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  generated_maven_wrapper_bootstraps_pinned_distribution_and_runs_starter \
  -- --ignored --test-threads=1
IDE_JAVA_HOME_21=/absolute/path/to/jdk-21 \
IDE_JAVA_HOME_25=/absolute/path/to/jdk-25 \
  cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  generated_gradle_wrappers_bootstrap_pinned_distributions_and_run_starters \
  -- --ignored --test-threads=1
```

Install and verify JDT LS using `pnpm tools:install-jdtls` and `pnpm tools:verify-jdtls`. Preparation requires Python 3.9 or later, `patch`, and a full JDK 17 or later; `IDE_JDTLS_JAVA_HOME`, then `JAVA_HOME`, then `java` on PATH selects the build runtime. The language server itself still requires JDK 25. The installer verifies the pinned archive, prepares the compiler correction from pinned source, verifies its class and unchanged resources, and atomically selects the new installation. For offline preparation, `IDE_JDTLS_ARCHIVE_CACHE` and `IDE_JDTLS_TYPE_DECLARATION_SOURCE_CACHE` may identify local files; their bytes must match the same pins. Modified source and the original signed compiler remain in the installation. The optional `test:tools:jdtls-compact-names` command requires `--derived-home`, `--jdk-home` and a new `--artifacts` directory and compares actual compiler results with JDK 25. Use a JDK supported by the installed build-tool version; a Java launcher on PATH and an unrelated debugger from another JDK are not an acceptable pairing. To qualify an explicit Java Run selection against a different default installation, export `IDE_TEST_ALTERNATE_JDK_HOME` with that other full JDK's absolute directory and run the four launch-setting checks:

```bash
cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  _launch_preserves_literal_arguments_environment_and_selected_jdk \
  -- --ignored --test-threads=1
```

With the real RefactorKit executable installed on PATH, qualify the bounded saved-source refactorings separately:

```bash
IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_ENGINE="$(command -v refactorkit)" \
  cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  installed_refactorkit_previews_and_applies_a_saved_java_method_rename \
  -- --ignored --test-threads=1
```

For saved-file formatting and import organization, use the same installed engine:

```bash
IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_ENGINE="$(command -v refactorkit)" \
  cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  installed_refactorkit_file_operations_review_apply_compile_and_rollback \
  -- --ignored --test-threads=1
```

The file-operation cases compile and execute changed Java source with `javac` and `java` from PATH and verify rollback. Set `JAVA_HOME` and prepend the selected JDK's `bin` directory to PATH when qualifying another full JDK. These native-library checks do not exercise Monaco or native window interactions.

Export `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON` with the absolute executable path of an installed API 0.2 daemon, then run the saved-source cursor qualification separately. The daemon need not be on PATH.

```bash
cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --locked --lib \
  installed_refactorkit_java_navigation_uses_utf16_and_exact_bindings \
  -- --ignored --test-threads=1
pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-cursor-navigation-native-001
```

The second command builds and launches the real Linux release/no-bundle application with an isolated fixture workspace. Its focused requirement remains partial; a passing run does not qualify broader Java project behavior or a packaged installer.

## Section 8: Cross-Cutting Concepts

### 8.1 Authority and Security

The native backend derives caller identity from the actual WebView and resolves the current registered workspace. Java execution commands are restricted to the main window. A trust checkbox acknowledges executable project code and build plugins; it is not an operating-system sandbox. Build tools may access dependency caches, the network, and other resources allowed to the user.

User/provider text is displayed as untrusted content. Semantic Markdown disables HTML. Application content-security policy and native path/session validation remain separate controls. Checksums used by software for download integrity, file revisions, or transaction binding remain necessary; redundant documentation verification tables and commit links are not maintained.

### 8.2 State, Errors, and Cancellation

Workspace generations and request identities prevent stale rendering. Capabilities are checked before offering operations. Tool failures appear in status/console surfaces; save failures also produce a visible editor alert. Java console output is bounded, and output truncation is explicitly reported.

### 8.3 Documentation and Diagrams

Keep architectural prose, status, and roadmap here. Index ADRs in section 9. Keep C4 diagrams as linked reference artifacts in the appropriate chapters rather than duplicate architecture prose. Use relative repository links or web URLs, never local filesystem document references.

### 8.4 Planned Shared Refactoring Workflow

This extends the existing exact-plan preview/apply behavior; the full workflow below is planned, not fully implemented. Its scope is IDE-mediated semantic transformations, whether requested through an editor action, quick fix, command palette, recipe or agent integration.

1. Resolve the current editor position/selection to a RefactorKit semantic target. Capture workspace generation, document revisions, project/classpath context and engine/backend compatibility. Do not guess binding identity from token text.
2. Discover the operation's actual support and mutation authority. Missing tools, refused analysis and proposal-only operations cannot acquire Apply permission through a UI checkbox or a CLI `--apply` flag.
3. Request read-only analysis against a consistent snapshot. Use an immutable editor overlay only when the corresponding engine operation and adapter are qualified; otherwise explicitly require saving. Do not persist unsaved buffers merely to manufacture a preview.
