4. Present affected files/resources, diffs, conflicts, diagnostics and external-consumer limitations. Semantic source and supported configuration/query reference changes belong to the engine plan, not ad-hoc frontend string replacement.
5. Apply only under explicit permission for the exact reviewed, still-current plan. Revalidate document/disk versions and project context; serialize conflicting transactions. Refuse stale or incomplete work rather than silently rebuilding and applying a different plan.
6. Reconcile editor contents, model URIs, selections, language-server documents and indexes for changed, moved or deleted files. Retain unrelated dirty buffers. Compiling/testing the project provides separate verification of the result, not authority to apply it first without review.
7. Record a recoverable transaction. Offer undo/rollback only when the actual provider supports it and current revisions permit it; never overwrite intervening user/agent/Git changes or add an implicit force option.

Ordinary typing and version-checked completion insertion remain editor operations. An LSP code action or generated agent patch is not, by itself, a trusted semantic refactoring plan. External filesystem writes invalidate affected snapshots even if they originated from Pi. RefactorKit owns semantic transformation algorithms; the IDE owns coordination, not a parallel AST/project-analysis engine.

## Section 10: Quality Requirements

### 10.1 Verification Scope

The packaged Java test workflows profile runs synchronized Maven and Gradle scenarios for JUnit Jupiter, TestNG, mixed JUnit engines, navigation from a test failure reported by a named class loader, and framework test debugging. Run `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaProjectTestWorkflowsAppImageNativeGui` with populated Maven and Gradle caches and selected JDK, JDT LS and RefactorKit installations. Add `--wayland` for the isolated Wayland session. With JDK 21 and local RefactorKit 0.8.0, focused replays on X11 and KWin Wayland open the exact failing line in both projects. Editing and saving the test then reruns only the failed method with the original JDK, JVM options and environment. On the same AppImage, the X11 framework debugger replays pass for Maven TestNG, Gradle Jupiter and a Jupiter method inherited from an interface in a library module. The full profile passes on X11 and KWin Wayland on the same AppImage and RefactorKit distribution. The runners verify that no session processes survive. The runner waits for the expected top-level project row before opening a source and preserves a separate window observation on a close timeout.

Once application exit is accepted, the IDE blocks new JDT LS launches and terminates a server still starting so startup cannot keep the application waiting for provider replies. A Rust regression test verifies termination of the starting child while the language-service manager is busy and refusal of subsequent startup. The full test-workflow profile passes on the Linux x86-64 AppImage with asynchronous language synchronization after disk adoption, using the RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate qualified for variable extraction from a local initializer. X11 and KWin Wayland use the same application and provider payload. Both runs cover Maven with JUnit 4 and Jupiter, where an earlier AppImage exceeded the close deadline after successful tests and source restoration. They also cover Maven TestNG, Gradle Jupiter and a Jupiter test inherited from a library interface under the debugger. Each run verifies clean native close and leaves no owned processes.

The full packaged Java test-workflows profile also passes on the AppImage with the JDT LS lifecycle correction. X11 and KWin Wayland use the same local RefactorKit 0.8.0 distribution, project JDK 21, Gradle 9.8.1 and JDT LS on JDK 25. The Gradle rerun opens the exact source line from a stack frame containing a class-loader name, saves the repair and runs only the failed method with its original settings. In the Jupiter debugger scenario, the IDE derives selection from the report, resolves an inherited method to the library source and stops on both saved breakpoints in the repaired tests. The rerun executes only the two previously failing methods and produces a fresh passing report. The scenarios preserve project inputs and verify clean exit without surviving session processes. The full profile also passes on both display backends with the subsequent Maven offline-plugin diagnosis update. The same profile also passes on both display backends with the AppImage that coordinates saved-file recovery with JDT LS, using Maven 3.9.16 and the same JDK and Gradle versions.

The packaged Maven verification profile runs a two-module reactor on Linux x86-64 on X11 and KWin Wayland with Maven 3.9.11, JDK 21, release 17 and local RefactorKit 0.8.0. Synchronization with an empty selected repository shows the Maven `offline-missing` diagnosis and offers a direct action to open Java Run. Granting workspace execution trust enables verification without invoking the wrapper or populating the repository. Explicit verification invokes the project-local wrapper with the selected repository and active and inactive profiles, builds the library JAR and passes the application's JUnit test. After removal of the fixture mirror, Java Project synchronizes, clears the recovery prompt and shows JUnit in the application's test classpath. The original sources and POMs are preserved. To repeat the test, run `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaMavenPreparationAppImageNativeGui` with `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_MAVEN` pointing to a Maven launcher and `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_REPOSITORY` pointing to a populated fixture repository.

The current AppImage and RefactorKit distribution used for the Maven verification profile also pass the packaged Gradle diagnosis and recovery scenarios, including preparation of an empty cache and a nested composite, on both display backends. The runners verify that no session processes survive.

A separate Maven reactor using source and target 17 with the compiler plugin inherited from the Maven lifecycle builds and passes its test with the same selected JDK. RefactorKit reproduced the synchronization refusal with Maven 3.9.11 and 3.9.16, which select different compiler plugin versions through their lifecycle defaults. The updated RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate returns `java.context.compilerOptionsIncomplete` with a selected SDK and retains `java.context.sdkRequired` for an omitted SDK. On X11 and KWin Wayland, the Maven verification profile shows the new guidance on this candidate, then acquires an available context after the fixture declares `maven.compiler.release`. No verification command runs and no class output is needed for that recovery. The updated AppImage also passes the existing empty-repository scenario on both backends. Native desktop-service tests with the later RefactorKit candidate that advertises the Maven runtime contract derive compiler plugin 3.13.0 from Maven 3.9.11 and plugin 3.15.0 from Maven 3.9.16. Both cases use JDK 21 and source/target 17, verify main and test compiler metadata, and pass a saved-class rename preview, Apply and exact rollback without compiling the project. Introducing a project wrapper retires the selected context and a new synchronization returns the incomplete-compiler-options refusal. A later provider candidate also qualifies a public top-level class declared on the same line as its `package` statement. The native desktop-service test verifies that the saved rename updates the class, its constructor and its filename, then restores their original state on rollback. The same AppImage and provider candidate pass the three Maven verification scenarios on X11 and KWin Wayland for each Maven distribution. Before any build, Java Project shows the default compiler plugin and complete options in both application source sets without creating module outputs. In the updated AppImage, the person then builds the synchronized application from Java Run. On both display backends, Maven reports the same compiler plugin version as the synchronized context, produces Java 17 bytecode and leaves the original project inputs unchanged. The native desktop-service test independently checks the same build and bytecode result. For the packaged scenario, set `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_MAVEN` to the standard Maven distribution’s launcher and `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_COMPILER_PLUGIN` to its expected compiler plugin version.

To qualify several native Java profiles against one AppImage, build once with the Java AppImage story runner. Pass the resulting `runtime-paths.json` to the next run with `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaMethodRefactoringAppImageNativeGui --reuse-appimage "$manifest"`. The runner checks the recorded SHA-256 before launching without a rebuild. Add `--wayland` for a supported Wayland profile and use the same explicitly selected RefactorKit runtime and toolchains across the runs.

The Linux x86-64 AppImage built with Tauri CLI 2.12.5 opens in an isolated KWin 6.8 Wayland session with XWayland disabled. A GUI check opens a Java file, changes it with keyboard input, saves it and compiles and runs the saved program with JDK 21. KWin closes the application window and the IDE exits cleanly. The navigation, debugger and Maven and Gradle development profiles described below use the same virtual display and software rendering. Hardware acceleration and other Wayland compositors require separate verification.

A separate desktop-registration check uses the same Linux x86-64 AppImage and the desktop entry and icon extracted from that file. It registers the entry in an isolated user data directory and selects it by desktop entry ID through GIO. The executable path contains spaces. `desktop-file-validate` accepts the entry, GIO launches the exact copied artifact, and its window accepts native close on both X11 and isolated KWin Wayland with XWayland disabled. Both launches exit with status zero and no processes from either isolated launch survive. The host uses the AppImage's extract-and-run mode. This check covers desktop-file discovery and launch through GIO. It leaves visual menu presentation, FUSE startup, automatic integration and upgrades unverified.

Shared button animations release their pending timers when the component closes, preventing delayed callbacks into retired UI views. Component tests cover normal animation expiration and teardown with several pending animations under React StrictMode.

The focused estimated-plan profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-database-001:plans`, passes in the Linux X11/Tauri/WebKit release/no-bundle desktop with JDK 21 and H2 2.4.240 in `REGULAR` mode. Its [native scenario](features/workspace/native-java-database.feature) creates an indexed table and pending manual work, displays the primary-key index in ordinary and bound estimated plans, and estimates a parameterized deletion without applying it. The SQL and bindings remain unchanged. A native Save As dialog exports the captured plan as JSON. The GUI refuses multiple statements and `ANALYZE`, retains the same manual transaction and successfully runs another query afterward. The pending row remains visible until explicit Rollback, after which only the original committed row remains. Explicit disconnect, normal application closure, unchanged workspace inputs and absence of surviving owned workers all pass.

A separate real-H2 test exercises the production native session and Java bridge, including plans for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE without applying those changes in the tested fixture, typed binding, quoted separators, dollar-quoted strings, nested comments, arrays, malformed/multiple-statement refusal, incorrect parameter-count recovery, a changed compatibility-mode refusal and retained manual transaction control. A separate direct production-bridge probe verifies the default auto-commit mode, a planned parameterized deletion without changing the original row, a primary-key lookup plan and confirmed normal close; this is stdin-protocol evidence rather than native GUI acceptance. Adapter, controller and panel tests cover response/session correlation, unavailable capabilities, explicit submission, exact values, refusal without ordinary-execution fallback and stale-workspace results. These results qualify the tested H2 driver and dialect, not arbitrary SQL functions, every H2 release/mode, other JDBC products, query execution/profiling, migrations, installers or other operating systems.

The integrated reference-backend profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:reference-backend`, passes on Linux X11/Tauri/WebKit in a release/no-bundle desktop with JDK 21, Maven 3.9.11 and the isolated source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 provider. Its [scenario](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) imports a Java 17 Spring Boot 4.1.2 MVC application with H2 2.4.240. RefactorKit renames an ordinary formatter helper and its bound controller/test references through managed review and Apply. Closing and reopening that applied review preserves access to the original Rollback. Java Run builds the changed project and runs real JUnit tests, including an HTTP request to a random-port server. A separately launched IDE-owned application then serves requests from the IDE HTTP Client; an explicit JDBC insert into its H2 TCP server is observed by a subsequent HTTP request to the same JVM. After stopping that application, structured JDI Debug starts a fresh JVM, stops in the controller while an IDE HTTP request is pending, exposes the integer argument `id = 1`, and completes the response after Continue. A non-Java draft created after Debug launch remains unsaved through those debugger controls and HTTP handling. Both launch actions save editors before starting, so this does not qualify launching with unsaved drafts.

The same Spring MVC/H2 scenario passes on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and in KWin Wayland with XWayland disabled, using JDK 21, cached Maven dependencies and a local RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime. Use `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:reference-backend:appimage` or its `:wayland` variant. The application and debug JVMs stop, the native window closes without owned processes remaining, and the original sources are restored. The profile qualifies the Java helper refactoring and the HTTP, JDBC and debugger paths on this backend fixture.

The same workflow explicitly resynchronizes project context between build, run, debug and cleanup when earlier actions have retired it; it does not bypass retired-context guards. The person discards the test draft through disk comparison, synchronizes, cleans Maven output through Java Run, reopens the retained review and invokes its original Rollback. Exact original fixture source/build inputs are restored, normal close succeeds and no owned application process remains. Controller tests separately cover reopening without a new preview or Apply, retry after a typed rollback refusal, unapplied-preview exclusion, and retirement on workspace activation changes, reset, provider replacement and unmount. This qualifies one combined Maven/MVC/JDBC workflow and one ordinary helper rename. It does not qualify Spring bean/configuration/endpoint semantics, JPA or query/mapping migration, other JDBC drivers, Gradle backends, transaction recovery across restart, installed-provider upgrades, installers or other operating systems. M5 remains incomplete.

Saved-source blame has real-Git production-boundary tests for committed and uncommitted lines, bounded pagination, saved-content drift with unchanged Git status, stale references, a clean filter changing the saved input during attribution, SHA-1/SHA-256 repositories, CRLF, empty files, literal Unicode/newline paths, binary/oversized/invalid UTF-8 input, symlinks and malformed porcelain output. Adapter, controller and panel tests cover response correlation, paging fingerprints, retained drafts, failure recovery and delayed workspace/provider retirement. These tests do not qualify native GUI or cross-platform behavior.

Linear local rebase has real-Git production-boundary tests for read-only history review, paused conflicts, abort and source restoration, reviewed resolution and continuation, original message retention, unchanged upstream references, several replayed commits, empty-result pause and explicit skip, stale plans/metadata/resolutions, executable-todo refusal, ignored/untracked overwrite refusal and merge-history refusal. Adapter/controller/panel tests cover typed history/status, retired responses, whole-index continuation review, separate rewrite/skip/abort acknowledgments and source reconciliation after failure. These checks do not qualify the native GUI or other operating systems by themselves.

Local merge production-boundary tests use real Git to exercise a paused conflict, abort and exact saved-source restoration, manual resolution and a two-parent commit, a fast-forward candidate that stops before committing, identical-tree merge completion, saved/untracked-change refusal, missing targets, autostash and operation-marker drift, nested-workspace refusal and saved-resolution drift with unchanged status letters. Controller tests verify editor-lease admission and reconciliation after native failure; the panel requires explicit abort acknowledgment and all-index review before committing. These checks do not establish arbitrary-hook or external-writer atomicity.

Local Git source control has production-boundary tests on private repositories for literal Unicode/newline paths, rename and deletion, recreated paths, symbolic links, unborn and detached HEAD, outside-workspace staging, index-lock failures, saved-file/index drift, ordinary hooks and commit identity. Optional metadata distinguishes absent values from command errors and timeouts. Real-Git branch tests cover literal creation without checkout, invalid and duplicate names, unborn HEAD refusal, local target drift, saved-file conflict refusal, retained untracked files, repository-root scope and active merge refusal. Branch renaming also has production-boundary coverage for the current and an inactive branch, preserved staged/unstaged bytes and HEAD object identity, moved configuration and reflog, stale selections, invalid or duplicate destinations, and a linked-worktree refusal using NUL-delimited paths containing a newline. Controller and panel tests cover explicit rename selection, retained dirty buffers, unavailable destinations and late responses from retired workspaces. Controller and panel tests cover explicit branch selection, editor-guard acquisition before Git, reconciliation after failed commands, warning propagation and retired-workspace cleanup. The read-only Monaco synchronization regression is covered by a production-component test: accepted buffer content and later model reattachment still update the visible model when editor-level edits are refused.  Controller, view, adapter and App tests cover explicit trust, review correlation, dirty-file staging refusal, aggregate staged review before commit, failed mutation recovery, workspace retirement and transition blocking.

Paginated Git history has production-boundary real-Git tests for more than two pages, root-commit patches, deleted and literal Unicode paths, SHA-256 object identities, nested-workspace confinement, first-parent merge patches, changed HEAD refusal, page membership and preservation of index, saved files and configuration. A configured external diff and text converter are not executed during the tested review. Adapter, controller and view tests cover page correlation, explicit path selection, previous/next navigation, refresh retirement and late results after activation changes. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-git-source-control-001:history` Linux release/no-bundle profile passes with Git 2.56.0 and a private 63-commit Java repository. Through the real GUI it reads older commits, reviews the initial commit and a deleted Unicode-named file, preserves an unrelated editor draft and exact index/configuration bytes, and refuses further paging after an external commit changes HEAD. Explicit disk comparison discards the test draft before normal close; no owned process remains. Merge-patch, nested-workspace and SHA-256 checks have Rust-boundary evidence, not native GUI acceptance. Large repositories, arbitrary hooks, other operating systems and installers remain unqualified.

Reviewed local branch deletion has real-Git production-boundary tests for merged and unmerged tips, exact name confirmation, forced-deletion refusal, expected HEAD and target-object checks, a switch that makes the deletion target current at the same object, stale plans, linked worktrees with newline paths, detached HEAD, SHA-256 identities, bounded commit lists and exact local configuration-section removal. A committed reference-transaction hook that floods output proves that transport failure reports an unknown outcome even when the branch was removed, with no rollback claim. A real configuration lock proves the partial outcome: the reference is removed, unrelated source/index state is preserved and the remaining settings are reported without claiming rollback. Frontend and adapter tests cover review correlation, explicit force selection, retirement after refresh or activation changes, and selecting a second branch after deleting the first. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-git-source-control-001:branch-deletion` Linux release/no-bundle profile passes with Git 2.56.0. It deletes a contained branch normally, requires an exact name and separate force choice for an unmerged branch, refuses a target advanced by an external Git command, then accepts a fresh review and confirmation. The current branch/HEAD, saved Java files, exact index and unrelated editor draft remain unchanged. Explicit disk comparison discards the fixture draft before normal close, environment restoration and zero surviving owned processes. Linked-worktree, detached-HEAD, SHA-256, transaction-race and partial-cleanup cases have Rust-boundary evidence, not dedicated native GUI acceptance. Concurrent external worktree creation, broader interruption recovery, other Git versions, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The Linux release/no-bundle [Git source-control profile](features/workspace/git-source-control.feature) passes with installed Git 2.56.0. Its basic case reviews, stages, unstages and commits only the selected saved Java version while retaining an unrelated dirty notes buffer and an untracked file. It checks real Git objects and history, a controlled pre-commit hook, unchanged Git configuration and saved inputs, and trust reset with unchanged index bytes after restart. Saved-source blame in the same native case displays the authored Java commit, pages a 450-line saved file, identifies an uncommitted saved line and refuses saved-line navigation after an external saved edit even though porcelain status remains unchanged. Blaming the active dirty notes file displays only its saved text while preserving the editor draft. Index bytes, HEAD and Git configuration remain unchanged by the blame reads. A second case holds a real pre-commit hook, rejects an X11 window-close request and a workspace switch while it is pending, then permits switching after completion. A third scenario creates a local branch without changing HEAD, renames that inactive branch, refuses an existing replacement name, renames the current branch and restores its original name while preserving an unrelated dirty notes buffer and saved Java text, then refuses a switch with that dirty notes buffer, refuses an overlapping saved-file change without stashing, and then switches after explicit source preparation. It verifies the actual Git reference, disk bytes, the public buffer/disk comparison and exact rendered Monaco text, performs a successful explicit save against the adopted revision, and returns to the original branch. A fourth native case starts with diverging Java branches. A dirty notes buffer refuses merge before source writes; after explicit discard, the merge pauses with real conflict markers, unchanged HEAD and the requested merge parent. A saved resolution is explicitly acknowledged and aborted, restoring the pre-merge disk content and clean Monaco model with a usable save baseline. Repeating the merge, editing and saving a resolution, refreshing, reviewing and staging it, and reviewing the whole index produces an explicit two-parent commit. The resolved source compiles with the selected JDK 21 `javac`; Git configuration is unchanged. The blame case also opens a clean tracked Java file from its attribution page, reveals line 201 of the 450-line saved Java fixture, and independently copies the complete buffer through the native clipboard. A changed saved source refuses a later line jump without moving that cursor or replacing the captured buffer. Line actions remain disabled for the dirty notes buffer while its saved attribution stays readable. This qualifies the tested Linux saved-line navigation path; other file layouts, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. A fifth case reviews a linear Java rebase without writing the index, requires acknowledgment, refuses a dirty notes buffer before replay, presents real conflicts and reconciles the clean open Java buffer. Explicit abort after saving a resolution restores the original branch, HEAD and source. Repeating the reviewed rebase, saving and staging a resolution, reviewing the whole index and continuing creates a new local commit with the expected upstream parent and retained original subject. The upstream reference and Git configuration remain unchanged, the reconciled buffer has a usable saved baseline, and selected-JDK `javac` compiles the result. All five cases close normally and restore their isolated environment without surviving owned processes. Native GUI empty-result skip, multi-commit replay and interruption recovery remain unqualified. This does not qualify recovery after process termination or broader merge layouts. Native GUI qualification of missing-file reconciliation, worktree/submodule layouts and interruption during checkout remains pending. Maven and Gradle context resynchronization have the separate scopes below. These are controlled local-hook fixtures, not arbitrary-hook, interactive-signing, concurrent external-index-race, interrupted-commit, large-repository, installer or cross-platform acceptance.

The focused Maven Git-context profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:git-branches`, passes on Linux X11/Tauri/WebKit with a release/no-bundle desktop, Git 2.56.0, Maven 3.9.11, JDK 21 and the isolated source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate. The [scenario](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) starts with a synchronized six-module reactor and a loaded source model. Branch switches add and remove a seventh module; the IDE retires the semantic context and source view, reloads the clean open Java buffer and requires explicit synchronization before ownership or declaration navigation is available again. The same scenario creates a private review branch, starts a merge that adds the seventh module without advancing HEAD, explicitly synchronizes and verifies provider-owned source ownership and pointer navigation. Aborting the merge retires that context and restores the six-module source/build inputs and clean buffer. Repeating the merge, synchronizing and reviewing the whole index creates an explicit two-parent commit. Three fresh executions of the app's JUnit 4 suite verify the selected JDK, JVM option and environment values. A final branch switch and synchronization restore the original inputs and module catalog while preserving the original and target branch identities. Native closure, environment restoration and process cleanup succeed. This qualifies the controlled module-addition workflow with custom build-output directories; arbitrary conflict resolution, SDK/dependency changes, deleted open files, process interruption, released-provider upgrades, packages and other operating systems remain unqualified for this combined workflow.

The separate Gradle Git-context profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-git-branches`, passes on the controlled Linux release/no-bundle desktop with Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21, Git 2.56.0 and the same source-built RefactorKit candidate. Its conventional Groovy DSL build has six Java subprojects before a branch or reviewed merge adds another. Branch switches, merge, abort and the final return retire the semantic context and source view and reconcile the clean open Java buffer. Explicit synchronization restores the actual project catalog; read-only refresh remains partial while captured Gradle metadata is stale. The new project's ownership and declaration navigation pass, as do three fresh executions of the app's JUnit 4 suite with literal JVM options and environment values. The test helper correlates each result with a new public execution-session identity, and cumulative method-output checks distinguish new execution from reused results. Provider RPC tracing records nine explicit `project.sync` requests; all seven source-changing Git operations leave that count unchanged until the person synchronizes. The acknowledged abort restores the original project inputs, and the repeated merge produces a reviewed two-parent commit before returning to the original branch and catalog. Closure and isolated-environment restoration leave no surviving owned processes. This qualifies the tested Groovy DSL fixture with custom output directories. Kotlin DSL, composite graphs, arbitrary conflicts, SDK/dependency changes, deleted open files, interrupted source changes, provider installation/upgrade, packages and other operating systems remain unqualified for this combined workflow.

The dedicated Maven and Gradle rebase-context profiles, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:git-rebase` and `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-git-rebase`, also pass on the controlled Linux release/no-bundle desktop with Git 2.56.0, JDK 21, Maven 3.9.11 or Gradle 9.8.1, and the same isolated RefactorKit candidate. Each [scenario](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) starts with six modules and a local Java change that conflicts when replayed onto a branch adding the seventh module. Rebase conflict and acknowledged abort retire the Java context and source model; explicit synchronization restores the local six-module catalog after abort. After a repeated conflict, the person saves and stages a resolution and explicitly acquires an available seven-module context before continuing. Continuation then retires that current context and loaded source view. Resynchronization restores the rewritten project's ownership and pointer declaration navigation, and a fresh app JUnit 4 execution verifies the selected JDK, literal JVM option and environment values. The rewritten commit has the expected upstream parent and original subject. A final switch and synchronization restore the original source/build inputs and six-module catalog, with the original and upstream references unchanged. Complete buffer text is checked through native keyboard copy rather than only Monaco's rendered viewport. The Gradle trace records six explicit `project.sync` requests; all six source-changing Git operations leave the count unchanged until explicit synchronization. Both scenarios close normally without surviving owned processes. Their dedicated profiles retain the 180-second native runtime deadline and bounded operation steps. This qualifies these conventional Maven/Groovy Gradle single-commit conflict fixtures, not arbitrary histories, skip, interruption recovery, SDK/dependency changes, composite or Kotlin DSL builds, installed-provider upgrades, packages or other operating systems.

Java Structure has controller and view tests for correlated provider results, exact source ranges, hierarchical filtering, expand/collapse, partial outlines, unavailable capabilities, retry, cancellation, replaced buffers, workspace activation and late navigation. View tests also verify numeric name sorting, stable overload order, filtering and guarded navigation after sorting, without another semantic query. The App test verifies its palette entry and sidebar visibility. The Linux release/no-bundle `javaLanguageIntelligenceCoreNativeGui` profile opens the activity through Commands against JDT LS 1.63, displays real type/field/method symbols for the active unsaved source, sorts sibling methods by name and restores source order, collapses and expands the hierarchy, filters a method while retaining its class, and opens the exact declaration cursor. The draft and saved inputs remain unchanged; the existing completion, hover, signature, references, call hierarchy, definition, Back/Forward and restart checks also pass, followed by normal close without surviving owned processes. This qualifies the basic Java fixture on Linux.

The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:modular-source-creation` profile also qualifies Java Structure in conventional Maven 3.9.11 and Gradle 9.6.1 root projects with a named module and project JDK 25. Gradle import through JDT LS is explicitly authorized with the selected distribution, JDK 21 build runtime and private writable cache. Each scenario opens an existing source, inserts a comment and method only into its editor draft, and checks a nested type and both `repeat` overloads. Name sorting and filtering retain the parent declaration; selecting the String overload opens the exact position in the dirty buffer, after the inserted line. Restoring the original text without saving leaves the source clean while the separate notes draft remains dirty. Original source/build inputs and the generated-source fixture remain unchanged, and normal close leaves no owned processes. This qualifies current-document symbol presentation and navigation in those project shapes. Broader Maven/Gradle layouts, cross-module bindings, native rapid-edit/workspace-switch interleavings, inherited/library members, large-file performance, AppImage/installers and other operating systems remain unqualified; the AppImage profile's authored selection is checked without executing a packaged application.

Navigation-history tests cover exact cursor restoration, same-file jumps, forward-branch replacement, the entry bound, failed opens, workspace retirement, competing navigation, preview retirement, rename/path-swap reconciliation and local keyboard handling. Dependency-preview controller tests verify selection of retained documents without rereading source and refusal after workspace retirement. Java panel tests also verify that changing JDT LS cancellation callbacks does not retire an independent RefactorKit query or leave its controls busy; changing the workspace/source scope does retire that query and admits a later request. The Linux release/no-bundle JDT LS native scenario verifies keyboard Back and header Forward around a real definition jump, exact Monaco cursor restoration, unchanged draft text and unchanged saved source. This does not qualify semantic position tracking through edits, persistence, packaged applications or other operating systems.

The Linux release/no-bundle library-navigation profile also passes its Maven and Gradle cases with both saved Java sources and immutable unsaved Java frames. Header Back returns from an actual RefactorKit dependency declaration to the exact workspace-source cursor; Forward restores the retained read-only library preview and its cursor. Unrelated drafts, Java draft text and source/dependency inputs remain unchanged, and normal close leaves no owned processes. The profile retains its exact-overload, outgoing-call-hierarchy, read-only typing and Save checks. This qualifies those dependency fixtures with the isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate; command-palette invocation, JDK source history, native rename-history interleavings, installers and other operating systems require separate native acceptance.

Manual HTTP authentication has frontend tests for Basic UTF-8 encoding, supplied Bearer tokens, environment expansion, invalid credentials, conflicting Authorization headers, limits, workspace retirement and exclusion of helper fields from saved collections. A production Rust-command test sends Basic and Bearer headers to a real loopback service and verifies their removal on redirect to another loopback port. The Linux release/no-bundle HTTP profile passes four scenarios, including actual Basic/Bearer requests accepted by a credential-checking local service, absence of credentials in the saved library, explicit saved-request reload clearing authentication, and a later unauthenticated request. The existing JSON, OpenAPI and collection transfer/restart cases remain passing in that profile. A separate native regression passes for sending the unsaved HTTP editor buffer, retiring stale file-request selection and refusing unsupported scripts. Normal close leaves no owned processes. The supplied-credential checks alone do not qualify OAuth, a credential vault, remote TLS deployment, installers or another operating system.

OAuth Client Credentials has production HTTP-transport tests against a real loopback server for the form POST, response normalization, same-origin redirect refusal and the token-response size bound. Encoder and decoder tests cover Basic versus request-body authentication, exact UTF-8 form encoding, endpoint and scope refusal, duplicate token fields, unsupported token types, expiry bounds and redacted endpoint errors. Frontend tests exercise acquisition and use as separate actions, expiry retained through the production request resolver/controller, required no-redirect transport capability, credential clearing, and delayed results after workspace, generation, port or panel retirement. The same Linux release/no-bundle HTTP profile exercises the actual token command with a credential-checking loopback service: HTTP is refused before the development exception is selected; both client-authentication forms succeed; selecting a token sends no API request; an explicit protected request succeeds; an invalid-scope response exposes no private description; expired tokens are refused at selection and again before a later API submission. Saved collections omit the helper credentials and tokens, and loading a saved request clears the helper. Normal close and process cleanup pass. This qualifies the local service-account development workflow, not a remote TLS identity-provider deployment, interactive sign-in/PKCE, automatic refresh, packages or other operating systems. A complete Rust-suite retry passes after an earlier unrelated fake-LSP fixture startup returned `ETXTBSY`; the cause of that intermittent failure remains unproven.

Browser Authorization Code/PKCE has production Rust tests for the RFC 7636 S256 vector, endpoint and registration validation, callback state/issuer/host/path checks, duplicate parameters, a real TCP callback reader with a bounded slow-header deadline, and public, Basic and request-body code-exchange forms. Frontend and adapter tests cover explicit token selection, expiry, cancellation, rejected cleanup, scope retirement and late replies. The focused Linux release/no-bundle native profile passes with the actual system URL launcher, a private Google Chrome for Testing 149.0.7827.55 profile and a controlled loopback authorization server registered as a public client. It verifies explicit browser consent, refusal of forged state and wrong issuer, provider denial, cancellation and callback replay refusal, one code exchange, explicit protected-request submission, omission of helper credentials from saved collections, and unchanged workspace files. A consent delay longer than the issued token lifetime confirms that token expiry begins at exchange rather than browser launch. Closing the IDE leaves the external browser independent; fixture teardown confirms browser exit and no owned process survivors. The existing four-scenario HTTP profile also passes after this change. Run the focused profile with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-http-client-001:oauth-browser` and `IDE_STORY_OAUTH_BROWSER_BINARY` set to the absolute path of an installed executable Chromium browser. Confidential-client exchange forms have production-builder tests, not native provider acceptance. Remote TLS providers, other operating systems, installers, full five-minute elapsed-time acceptance and broader native lifecycle interleavings remain unqualified; automatic refresh remains unavailable.

Shared-editor production tests cover exact saved-text Undo/Redo, empty and Unicode/CRLF content, successful and rejected Save, concurrent edits, queued writes, workspace retirement during metadata publication, close/reopen, explicit disk adoption, renamed/swapped buffer paths, new-file drafts, identical-text recovery and atomic content/dirty-state publication. The Linux release/no-bundle Java execution scenario also verifies keyboard Undo/Redo before Save and a new saved-text comparison after Build saves and compiles the edited source; Run, compiler-error navigation, owned-JVM Stop and native close still pass. It uses the selected JDK 21. Fresh release builds also pass the Git-review, editor-close-guards, crash-recovery and external-change native profiles. Git review verifies Undo through its actual keyboard edit groups and Redo back to the exact retained draft; close/recovery/external-change checks retain their unsaved-buffer, stale-save and explicit-discard protections. Other operating systems and packaged applications remain unqualified for these new dirty-state checks.

Read-only Git review has production-boundary tests on private Linux repositories for Unicode, whitespace, newline and literal-arrow names, pathspec syntax, nested workspace roots, index preservation, configured-program suppression and nonrepository failures. Native process tests cover output floods, nonzero exits, expired deadlines and inherited output pipes. Renderer tests cover reopening the same workspace while a review is pending, accessories from another workspace and no selected workspace.

The `pnpm test:story:req-pi-workspace-agent-001:native` Linux release/no-bundle scenario passes with real Git hunks, exact navigation of a filename combining Unicode, pathspec syntax, an arrow and trailing whitespace, and unchanged source and index bytes. A transport wrapper delays one Git diff invocation without fabricating a result; the editor switches tabs while that process is still alive, the five-second timeout becomes visible and the process exits. A later real-Git review opens a range without replacing the exact dirty draft. The person then uses the public disk-comparison and explicit-discard controls to restore the buffer. Workspace switching, session isolation and normal launcher completion leave no owned processes. Pi interaction uses a controlled test executable; successful Git calls, the native bridge, Monaco and navigation use production code. This does not qualify invalid UTF-8 filenames, detached descendants, other operating systems, packaged applications or full VCS workflows.

Maven/Gradle Rebuild has controller, command-palette, view and adapter tests for its separate capability and operation result. Production-boundary executor tests with selected JDK 21 confirm that one Rebuild removes an old output marker and recreates compiled classes while preserving source and descriptor bytes. A syntax error after the clean phase produces a failed result with no previous `Main.class`; repairing the source permits a successful Rebuild. Invalid descriptors also remain failures. A separate task-mapping test retains the selected Gradle build root and orders `:lib:clean` before `:lib:classes`. Linux release/no-bundle GUI acceptance with Maven 3.9.11 and Gradle 9.8.1 verifies the panel action on ordinary projects and the command-palette action for an included Gradle `:app` whose directory is outside its build root. The [composite GUI scenario](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) also passes with Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21 and the isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 compiler-diagnostics review candidate. That candidate returns both the included build root and the project paths for `:app` and `:library` after synchronization and reevaluation. The IDE runs the app and one discovered test, shows coverage in both modules, opens the library source and stops at an application source breakpoint. Clean and Rebuild affect the selected app and preserve the compiled library bytes and project inputs. Qualification covers this two-project composite on Linux. Provider distribution, larger or mixed-language composites and other operating systems remain open. Both profiles close normally without surviving owned processes. GUI status checks read the public execution status elements separately from console output and distinguish Build, Rebuild and prefixed test-operation names. Maven synchronized multi-module Rebuild and additional source-set mappings require separate native acceptance; plain-JDK Rebuild is unavailable. Packages and other operating systems remain unqualified.

A second Linux scenario in the [Gradle composite profile](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) uses two included builds that each declare `:app`, `pkg.Runner` and the same JUnit 4 test method. The first build includes the second with an alias different from its directory name. The nested app uses project substitution for one library in its parent build and another in a sibling build. Gradle 9.8.1 and JDK 21 run each selected app from the composite root with the corrected RefactorKit review candidate. The evaluated paths and runtime classpaths identify both substituted JARs after compilation, and repeated reevaluation succeeds. Building the nested app’s test source set invokes `:included-build:nested-app:app:testClasses`, creates its compiled test class and leaves test bodies unexecuted. With both copies of `Runner.java` open, discovery lists only the nested app’s methods and leaves their bodies unexecuted. After the person duplicates the launch configuration and switches the duplicate to Plain JDK, running the discovered method with coverage produces one passing test and opens the measured source in the second build. The active session and coverage history both show the original discovery configuration name. On the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland, **Rerun session** creates a new coverage session with the same captured configuration, executes only the same nested-build test method again, and opens the measured source in that build while both copies of the source are open. After a fresh discovery, Gradle reevaluation and selection of the first app in Java Run, debugging the discovered method still stops in the second app’s production source. Continuing completes only that test. The first application also calls a library method whose declaring class and source line have a counterpart in the second build. With both breakpoints saved, JDI stops in the library source, the IDE reports the other breakpoint as excluded, and the running JVM identifies the included library JAR as the code source. Continuing finishes the application. The IDE restores the captured project inputs and closes normally. Both scenarios also pass on the same Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and in an isolated KWin Wayland session with XWayland disabled, with Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21 and the locally packaged canonical RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime. This verifies both included-build identities and their execution paths with that candidate. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-composite:appimage` for X11 or add the `:wayland` suffix with KWin and wl-clipboard available. A separate run of the AppImage with an earlier RefactorKit 0.7.0 review candidate also passes the self-contained included-build scenario through the backward-compatible dispatch route. Other composite layouts and operating systems require separate qualification.

Two Gradle projects can publish their JARs at the same path. In an offline three-module fixture, an earlier RefactorKit 0.7.0 review candidate attributed the shared JAR to a module outside the application’s runtime dependencies. A direct replay against the corrected review candidate used Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21 and the loaded class as an independent check. A single dependency returned the correct producer, scope and file fingerprint. When both producers were dependencies, changing task order changed the loaded class. The candidate refused synchronization with `gradle.sync.runtimeArtifactOwnerAmbiguous` in both orders. Replaying the available test-source contexts through the IDE’s declaring-source lookup with the earlier candidate withheld the incorrect owner in all three configurations. With the corrected candidate the available single-dependency context identified the verified producer. The ordinary composite scenarios also pass on the Linux AppImage with that candidate. The shared-output cases were verified directly against the provider and source-ownership lookup. Adoption of the candidate remains a separate release decision.

Maven/Gradle Clean has controller, command-palette, view and adapter tests, with explicit admission for advertised runtimes and refusal for plain-JDK projects. Production-boundary executor tests with selected JDK 21 run Build, Clean and Build again on disposable Maven and Gradle projects, verify that compiled classes disappear and return while sources and descriptors stay unchanged, and confirm a deliberately broken descriptor produces a failed clean rather than success. A build-selection regression separately checks a qualified Gradle `:lib:clean` task at the captured build root. The Linux release/no-bundle build-tool GUI profile passes with Maven 3.9.11, Gradle 9.8.1 and selected JDK 21: its two application-project cases save the edited source, build, clean compiled outputs and rebuild without running the application or tests, then complete the existing execution and test workflows. The additional Failsafe scenario remains regression coverage rather than Clean acceptance. The native windows close normally with no surviving owned processes. Gradle qualification uses an explicitly writable cache; the runner's read-only default cache was separately shown to prevent native-library lock creation before project compilation. Separate Linux release/no-bundle GUI cases with the explicit-path RefactorKit runtime and selected JDK 21 also qualify Clean on the synchronized six-module Maven and Gradle reference projects. After a successful application run, the cases refresh the metadata, clean the selected application module, verify removal of its compiled class and annotation-processor source, then explicitly synchronize again and rebuild. Maven synchronization remains read-only; Gradle metadata is explicitly evaluated again. The build regenerates both outputs, the provider/module/source-set selection remains unchanged, all captured project inputs preserve their bytes, and the build output contains no application-run marker. Both windows close normally without surviving owned processes. A further Linux release/no-bundle GUI composite case with Gradle 9.8.1 and selected JDK 21 qualifies Clean and Build from the command palette for the included `:app` project whose directory is outside its build root. Clean removes the application class while preserving the included library class byte for byte; after explicit metadata reevaluation, Build recreates the application class with the same class-file target version. The provider-qualified module selection and captured project inputs remain unchanged. The same scenario completes its existing Run, selected-test, discovery, coverage and JDI debug checks and closes without surviving owned processes. Plain-JDK cleanup, packaged applications and other hosts remain unqualified or unavailable as described above.

Session-local line-breakpoint muting has decoder and interface tests plus production-boundary real-JDI qualification on selected JDK 21 and 25. The real-JVM checks cover pending source breakpoints and new logpoints while muted, preserved conditions and matching-hit counts, exhausted-count requests remaining inactive after Unmute, default activation in a fresh session, temporary Run to Cursor, and exact/superclass exception filters remaining independent. A Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario with selected JDK 21 confirms acknowledged Mute and Unmute controls, a real Run to Cursor stop while muted, removal of its temporary breakpoint, successful application completion and normal window close without surviving owned processes. This does not qualify packaged applications, other hosts or a saved mute preference.

Saved-file reconciliation retirement has production-coordinator and editor-model regression coverage: delayed Java document close and activation are tested with both successful and rejected completions after authority retirement; a delayed adapter metadata-close rejection also stops without retry or publication of moved contents. Current-workspace synchronization failures still produce a warning. These controlled asynchronous tests do not establish native workspace-switch interleavings during Apply. The Linux release/no-bundle `javaProjectModelClassRefactoringNativeGui` profile passes both project-row and command-palette scenarios on JDK 21/release 17 with CLI and daemon from the same isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 SDK candidate. The open Java tab follows move and Rollback; same-module and cross-module moves, a new destination package and dependent-module reference updates pass offline Maven verification on source copies and restore the original inputs. Java-referenced safe delete refuses and the Maven-reference case remains review-only. Normal window close and process cleanup pass. The final execution includes the v7 review correction and waits for an enabled Preview button; earlier failed configuration and palette attempts are retained as failed evidence. Default-installation discovery, broader layouts, other SDKs, packages and other operating systems are not qualified by this run.

The structured debugger's [step exclusion patterns](#63-java-execution) pass production-boundary real-JDI tests on selected JDK 21 and 25. The tests compare unfiltered Step into with exact, prefix and suffix exclusions, then verify that an explicit breakpoint still stops in an excluded class. The preexisting real-JDI frame, variable, watch and unfiltered-step regression also passes on JDK 21. Frontend and native action tests cover bounded pattern validation, legacy requests, current-stop guards, session/workspace retirement, command-palette and function-key dispatch, and preserving Continue when the filter draft is invalid. The Linux release/no-bundle `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:jdi` profile passes both completion and unresponsive-input scenarios with selected JDK 21: a real `java.*` filter skips a `Math.multiplyExact` call and returns to the application method, then the person clears the filter and continues existing debugger controls through normal close and process cleanup. The same profile also verifies that an oversized filter draft disables all three Step buttons while preserving Continue, and that F11 refuses the invalid draft without moving the suspended frame; correcting the draft allows the existing session to continue. Production-boundary real-JDI tests on JDK 21 and 25 reject an encoded command above 3,072 bytes before writing to the helper, retain the current stop, accept a command exactly at that limit and run the application to completion. Filtered command-palette dispatch remains controller-tested; filter-specific GUI behavior for valid Step shortcuts, Step over/out, Attach shapes beyond the manual fixture below, synchronized project launches, other SDKs, packages and other operating systems remains unqualified. Other profiles sharing the updated arithmetic fixture were not rerun by this check.

The Maven and Gradle scenarios in the `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:entry-points` profile have passed through the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with selected JDK 21, real Maven and Gradle six-module release-17 fixtures and the isolated qualified classic RefactorKit candidate. The combined profile also passes with the qualified literal-root provider and the [plain-JDK declaration scenario](#63-java-execution). It refuses an unsaved Java draft without changing the editor or disk, then explicitly saves, builds and synchronizes before discovery. Public controls select the provider-owned main class and preserve the partial-coverage notice. The editor context-menu action first refuses the dirty source without saving it; after Build and synchronization, it replaces a deliberately incorrect form class with the provider-owned file candidate and executes that class through Run with the selected JDK and runtime dependencies. The same scenarios synchronize again after Run retired semantic authority, request Debug from the editor, pause at JVM start, set a source-line breakpoint, inspect the real main frame and continue to successful completion. This qualifies the structured JDI route; the configured jdb route is not separately qualified by this editor-action profile. The final check uses the isolated classic candidate that also supplies the new cursor capability, and the extended scenarios also send positions from the real Monaco cursor. In each build-tool fixture, a sibling type without a declared classic main stays positively selected with no candidate and no new execution session; moving to the application type starts a distinct Run session. After another synchronization, Debug at the cursor stops on the requested source line, exposes the main frame and completes. Source files are restored, the executed binary digest matches the built artifact and native close leaves no owned processes. Both scenarios restore all source/build inputs and close without surviving owned processes. Before Build, the Maven fixture returned a typed incomplete-source-analysis refusal; this initial result remains distinct from the passing post-build path and has been reported upstream for triage. These checks qualify these saved classic-main workflows on this host. They do not qualify inherited or newer main forms, plain-JDK discovery, AppImage behavior or another operating system. Multiple candidates in one file, empty or truncated results and source-model retirement are separately covered by component tests; the native GUI fixture has one classic main per file. Consumer tests separately prove that revoking and restoring trust cannot revive an old list, and that edits during a request or before selection prevent use of its candidates.

The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:maven-jpms-v5` profile passes the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with selected JDK 21, release 21, Maven 3.9.11 and the isolated source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate. The project view requests complete JPMS facts and displays requires, exports, opens, uses and provides directives. Run and structured JDI Debug resolve the named dependency module and preserve a spaced argument and an empty argument. Debug suspends before application code and continues to successful completion. After Run creates outputs, explicit synchronization renews the project context before Debug. The source/build inputs and dependency JAR remain unchanged; normal closure leaves no owned processes. This qualifies one conventional single-module Maven project with a local modular-JAR dependency, not reactor launches, every JPMS layout, editor entry-point discovery, installers or other operating systems. Set `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON`, `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_JDK` and `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_REPOSITORY` to the selected executable, full JDK and populated offline repository.

The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:modular-source-creation` profile passes native Maven 3.9.11 and Gradle 9.6.1 cases on Linux release/no-bundle with project JDK 25 and the isolated RefactorKit candidate. Both fixtures contain a pre-existing generated Java source beneath a provider-reported output root. Opening the type wizard there displays the generated-source notice and the selected-directory destination; cancellation preserves that output and the unrelated notes draft. This qualifies presentation of provider-owned root facts, not execution of an annotation processor or code generator. Each conventional root project requests complete module-system facts, then refuses compact sources and an ordinary class without a package in the reported named source set. Refusal preserves the form, files and editor tabs. The wizard opens in the existing `example` package. An existing packaged type is refused without overwrite, and the same form then selects `other.orders`. The displayed workspace-relative destination matches the new file beneath the provider-declared source root, rather than the directory where the dialog opened. The file appears in the tree and remains empty until Save. The captured editor text compiles with the selected JDK in separate verification storage and resolves as a named module. Saving that type leaves the unrelated notes draft and original project files unchanged. Explicit notes discard and normal closure leave no owned processes. This qualifies source creation and the separate compiler/module check, not JPMS editor bindings, modular application execution, refactoring, installers or another operating system. Set the tool variables described for the compact-source profiles below. Component and projection tests cover module-fact changes before submission, preservation of refused input, named-package acceptance, unknown facts and workspace-relative source ownership. Separate selected-JDK 25 probes demonstrate that compiling a default-package class alongside a module descriptor does not establish a usable named module: module resolution rejects the unnamed package, while the packaged control launches successfully.

The separate `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:compact-source-gradle` profile passes creation, configured and editor Run, compact/inherited cursor Debug and diagnostic checks with an explicitly evaluated conventional root project, project JDK 25 and a separately configured JDK 21 build runtime on Linux release/no-bundle. Gradle 9.8.1 is qualified with creation from the source root; Gradle 9.6.1 also verifies opening the wizard inside the existing `demo` package, displaying the root destination and creating the compact file there without a duplicate in `demo`. The scenario authorizes JDT LS Gradle import explicitly. Diagnostic queries preserve the evaluated model without running Gradle again; source/build inputs, compiled bytes and modification times remain unchanged. Normal close leaves no owned processes. Real IDE-service checks independently compare compact diagnostics and repair with selected javac. The corresponding Maven GUI profile also passes creation from `demo` with the displayed root destination, followed by the full Run/Debug and diagnostic-repair workflow. Component tests separately verify the live path as name, package and source form change, and the selected-directory preview when provider ownership is unavailable. This qualifies the stated root-project fixture, not composite or custom-source-set compact launch, JPMS, installers or another operating system.

Both compact profiles require `IDE_COMPACT_SOURCE_TEST_JDK` to select a full JDK 25, `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON` to select the qualified daemon, and the JDT LS home/server-JDK settings described in section 7. The CLI defaults to the daemon sibling executable; `IDE_REFACTORKIT_ENGINE` can select it explicitly. The Gradle profile also requires `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_GRADLE`, `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_GRADLE_JDK` and a writable `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_GRADLE_USER_HOME`. The Maven profile requires `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_REPOSITORY` to identify its populated dependency cache.

The full `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:compact-source` profile passes in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with Maven, selected JDK 25, the managed corrected JDT LS distribution and the isolated RefactorKit SDK-compiler candidate. It refuses compact creation at release 21 without changing files or open drafts, changes the POM through the editor to release 25, then creates `record.java` through the compact-source wizard. The generated draft compiles with real `javac --release 25`; the scenario saves an instance main, builds a version-69 class, explicitly enters `record` in Java Run, and verifies application output from the selected JDK. With that candidate, it then selects Java 25 launcher rules, discovers the saved compact instance main, checks the provider coverage and invocation details, replaces a deliberately incorrect launch class with the provider-owned `record`, and executes it. The saved editor file action independently starts the compact main after replacing an incorrect launch class; Debug at the compact cursor performs another freshly synchronized provider selection. Real JDI stops at entry and a source breakpoint, exposes the local integer and instance receiver, and completes normally. The same mixed fixture includes a public child with an inherited public static main. Selecting the inherited profile omits the compact instance main and identifies both launch and declaring types. Run verifies that the JVM launches the child. A cursor inside its dormant inner type returns no main and starts no session, preserving the incorrect form class; moving to the child starts Debug, where a breakpoint and local value identify the parent method before successful child-launch completion. Existing sources and an unrelated editor draft are preserved, explicit draft discard restores the notes file, and normal closure leaves no owned processes. Separate production-template compiler probes qualify contextual names and preserved Unicode format characters with JDK 25, and refusal without preview at release 24. This qualifies compact-main discovery, configured and editor-file Run, compact cursor Debug, inherited-profile configured Run, and inherited cursor Debug for this Maven release-25 fixture on this host. Other file/cursor-operation combinations, other launch forms, JPMS, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The managed JDT compiler correction passes a real-compiler comparison with JDK 25 for compact contextual names, a preserved Unicode format character, explicit invalid declarations, genuine missing-variable errors and unsupported source release. Production-tool tests refuse changed compiler classes, unrelated bundle changes, modified launcher configurations and altered source, including attempts to rewrite local metadata. Installation and verification pass both with pinned local archive/source caches and with fresh downloads of the official archive, checksum and pinned source on Linux. The downloaded installation has the same compiler and runtime files as the cached preparation; only installation metadata differs. Other operating systems remain unqualified. The installed distribution passes the real native language-service initialization, error/repair, restart and graceful-stop test, and the standard language-intelligence GUI profile. The full compact-source GUI profile verifies the real missing-variable error and a fresh unused-variable warning after repair through JDT LS. Explicit SDK compiler checks then accept the valid warning-bearing draft, diagnose the missing variable and return to a clean result after restoration. Saved source, existing compiled bytes and modification times, and the execution session remain unchanged during these checks. The window closes normally with no surviving runner-owned processes. Separate real IDE-service checks compare valid compact `record.java`, `var.java` and `yield.java`, a genuine draft error and an invalid explicit declaration against selected `javac`; the production TypeScript decoder preserves SDK compiler identity. This qualifies the stated Maven and Gradle release-25, non-JPMS fixtures on Linux. Mixed-backend scopes, other SDK cells, standalone saved-source diagnostics, installers and other operating systems need separate qualification.

Application-input service checks use real selected JDK 21 and 25, Maven 3.9.11 and Gradle 9.8.1. Conventional one-module fixtures cover Run, jdb and JDI, exact Unicode and binary byte delivery across chunk boundaries, empty lines, debugger-command-looking application text, idempotent retries and EOF. Socket tests cover authentication, incomplete headers, actual backpressure, disconnect, bounded Stop and private-file cleanup. Frontend component tests cover partial UTF-8 acknowledgements, lost responses, explicit retry, EOF, queue bounds and retirement across workspace, generation, session and trust changes. Custom task, installed-package and cross-platform support remain unqualified by these checks. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:application-input` profile passes nine Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios and 72 runtime steps with selected JDK 21. Each JDK, Maven and Gradle route exercises Run, JDI and jdb in a workspace subdirectory. Public controls deliver exact Unicode text, debugger-command-looking lines and an empty line, complete the application with EOF, retain input for captured Rerun after the current form disables it, and Stop a fresh JVM waiting for input. The application writes its received bytes, and the fixture verifies the compiled class in the selected project output. The input flag, build tool, project directory and Gradle environment setting survive interface reload while trust does not. Gradle uses a private writable cache selected through the public `GRADLE_USER_HOME` environment override; its value also survives reload. Source and build inputs remain unchanged and native close leaves no owned processes. This qualifies the conventional one-module manual launch fixtures on this host, including the pinned Maven Exec plugin and built-in Gradle Application plugin. AppImage qualification is recorded below; arbitrary plugin/task overrides and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:application-input:appimage` profile builds a fresh Linux x86_64 AppImage and passes the same nine application-input scenarios and 72 runtime steps with selected JDK 21. The JDK, Maven and Gradle routes exercise Run, JDI and jdb through the packaged application, including exact bytes, EOF, captured Rerun, Stop and settings restoration. The artifact digest matches the executed AppImage, all scenario proofs pass and native close leaves no owned processes. This is qualification of these one-module input workflows on the controlled host; it does not qualify every packaged Java feature, other SDK/platform combinations, hosted CI or portability to a clean distribution. The package still uses the selected external full JDK and installed build tools. Packaging needs complete GTK/GLib data and the WebKit auxiliary processes as well as the WebKit shared libraries; this host supplies the temporary SDK through a private build namespace without changing the system installation.

The `pnpm test:story:java-compiler-source-creation:appimage` profile qualifies the core compiler and source-creation workflows through a freshly built Linux x86_64 AppImage with selected JDK 21. Real Maven and Gradle six-module projects preserve unsaved repairs while compiler locations navigate from a library source to the application, then synchronize and save a new draft before Run. Plain-JDK and conventional Maven/Gradle fixtures verify compiler failure navigation without losing editor changes; the build-tool fixtures also exercise JUnit, failed-test recovery and Maven Failsafe integration tests. Six source-creation scenarios cover new files and Java types, restricted names and forms retired on a workspace switch. The profile repeats the application-input workflows described above against the same package. Its current selection also includes the subsequently added Clean/Rebuild steps; those additional packaged steps have not been rerun and remain unqualified by the earlier package result. All scenarios in that earlier package run passed, the executed artifact digest matched the built AppImage and native close leaves no owned processes. Scenario artifact metadata must agree with the runner's selected artifact; inconsistent package claims are rejected. This qualifies these workflows on the controlled Linux/X11 host with external JDK and build tools and populated dependency caches. It does not qualify other operating systems, a clean distribution, every Java feature or the remaining roadmap.

Further application-input service checks use the provider-owned six-module Maven and Gradle reference projects with cold project outputs, cached dependencies, a separate application working directory and selected JDK 21 or 25. Run, JDI Debug and Run with JFR deliver exact bytes and EOF while retaining dependency, generated-source, source-breakpoint, SDK and launch-setting checks. The JDK opens the actual recordings. Separate one-module checks combine input and JFR through each JDK, Maven and Gradle route. The Gradle service cases deliberately omit a `gradle` command from `PATH`; the selected executable supplies the build. The working-directory profile passes two Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios with selected JDK 21, the isolated provider candidate and a custom-named Gradle executable whose directory contains no `gradle` command. Public Maven and Gradle controls send exact UTF-8 text, debugger-command-looking lines, an empty line and EOF during Run, Run with JFR, captured Rerun and JDI Debug. The application writes a byte-for-byte proof from `System.in`. Rerun retains input and the original working directory after both form settings change. JFR analysis reads the actual recording, a repeated recording has a new destination and the first recording remains unchanged. Tests ignore the enabled application-input setting and retain the module directory. Another application waits for input without EOF; Stop terminates its observed PID. Native Copy checks the complete source buffer, source and build inputs remain unchanged, and no owned process survives native close. All observed Gradle invocations confirm that `gradle` is absent from `PATH`. This qualifies application input and selected-command handling in these synchronized six-module fixtures on this host. Custom task graphs, every composite build, other SDK/platform combinations and packaged synchronized-project workflows remain outside this qualification.

On Linux, Temurin 8 passes real application input and EOF tests for plain-JDK and conventional Maven Run, jdb and JDI. Additional cold-output cases pass all three modes with synchronized Maven and Gradle projects and the isolated RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate. JDI and the Gradle build run on JDK 21 while the application runs on Java 8. The cases verify exact binary and Unicode bytes, idempotent retries and separate debugger commands. A separate plain-JDK case verifies Restart, Stop and refusal of stale input. A later native-service rerun passes synchronized Maven and Gradle Run and JDI with the locally packaged RefactorKit 0.8.0/API 0.2 runtime built from the integrated source.

The nine application-input scenarios also pass on Temurin 8 on Linux/X11 in a fresh release build without bundling and in a fresh x86-64 AppImage. Set `IDE_JAVA8_HOME` to the full project JDK and `IDE_JAVA_DEBUGGER_HOME` to the JDK 21 host. For Gradle, set `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_GRADLE` to Gradle 9.8.1 and `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_GRADLE_RUNTIME_JDK` to JDK 21. The Gradle fixture declares a Java 8 toolchain. Each scenario checks the running Java 8 home, exact input and EOF, Rerun with captured settings, Stop and process cleanup.

The repository includes specification, contract, adapter, controller/component, Cucumber, native Rust, and external-tool tests. These are complementary, not interchangeable.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:working-directory` profile passes on the Linux release/no-bundle application with application/debugger JDK 21 and JDT LS runtime JDK 25. Native form input selects a directory containing spaces, an accent and a quote; the actual application's operating-system working directory, relative resource read and output file agree with that selection, while compiler output remains in the project directory. Completed-session Rerun retains its captured directory after the form changes. Run with JFR keeps its recording under the project, Analyze recording displays actual event data, and profiled Rerun creates another destination while preserving the first recording bytes. A missing directory refuses Run without executing the previous class, while Build remains available. A named configuration survives clean WebView reload, trust remains disabled, and subsequent structured JDI Debug uses the restored application directory. The source stays unchanged and the native window closes without surviving sandbox processes. This qualifies plain-JDK GUI execution and interface reload, not whole-application restart, installers or another operating system.

Separate opt-in production-service checks pass on Linux with selected JDK 21 and 25, Maven 3.9.11 and Gradle 9.8.1: Run and JDI Debug for each of the three tool routes use the separate application directory while compilation remains in the project. Real JDK and Gradle compilation cases retarget a directory selection before application launch and observe refusal without application output. These checks qualify the conventional one-module fixtures, including Maven's pinned Exec plugin; custom plugin/task overrides remain unqualified. Synchronized-project qualification is recorded separately below.

The command palette component tests cover shortcut handling, filtering, keyboard selection, focus containment and command failures. Desktop tests also verify that package-move review is offered only for an active source associated with one package in the selected project and delegates to the existing review flow when its capability gate allows it. The desktop TypeScript check verifies its composition with current JDT LS and RefactorKit capabilities. The focused [native scenario](features/refactorkit/native-java-sdk-refactoring.feature) now passes in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI: it opens the package move from the palette, reviews and applies it, verifies an applied-source copy with offline Maven `verify`, rolls back the transaction and confirms clean application exit. This qualifies the Maven fixture on Linux; an installed package and other desktop platforms remain unqualified.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-file-creation-native-001` profile passes six scenarios/52 authored steps (64 runtime steps) in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21. It verifies generic empty-file creation and save/compile/run, plus wizard drafts for a class, interface, enum, record and annotation. Each generated type remains empty on disk until Save and then compiles.
