The generic-file scenario first verifies seven rejected type-name submissions without file or tab creation, then retires unsubmitted file, folder and Java-type forms through real workspace transitions. It opens Settings from the keyboard command palette while each creation form is still present, switches to a second workspace, verifies the form is gone and both source inventories are unchanged, and returns to the original workspace. The test waits for both the native registry and the settled selected workspace in the UI; the registry alone can change while the tree is still being remounted. Workspace confinement, clean application exit and absence of surviving owned processes pass. This is native GUI evidence for this host, not package or cross-platform qualification.

Production Rust tests verify single- and multi-module Maven/Gradle starter files, both Gradle DSL choices, project-coordinate validation, Java 27 release acceptance and refusal to replace an existing path. TypeScript component and adapter tests verify workspace-generation guards, build-system/layout/DSL selection, project-path selection and response correlation; package builds and the desktop type check cover the production contracts and wiring. The opt-in Maven tests for single- and multi-module starters pass with an installed JDK and cached artifacts using Maven offline mode. The opt-in Gradle tests cover single- and multi-module Groovy starters and single- and multi-module Kotlin DSL starters. Each runs Gradle offline and verifies compilation plus JUnit execution when the required artifacts are cached. The focused Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario also verifies Maven Java 8 and Java 27 single-module projects, Groovy multi-module and Kotlin DSL single-module projects, including wizard selection, generated files, the Java 27 compiler-release property, project-tree refresh, explicit JDK requirements, duplicate-path refusal, unchanged existing projects and clean exit. It does not compile the Java 27 project. These checks do not qualify arbitrary Gradle Kotlin DSL semantics, effective RefactorKit project context, packaged applications or other operating systems.

The opt-in Rust test `managed_jdtls_imports_gradle_with_selected_installation_and_project_properties` passes against JDT LS 1.61.0-202607102111, Gradle 9.8.0 and a selected JDK 25. Its real two-project Gradle fixture confirms that JDT LS uses the selected Gradle installation, user home and JDK, and resolves a root project's type from a library subproject when the selected project property enables that dependency. Removing the property and restarting forces Buildship to refresh the persisted projects; the dependency then becomes unresolved rather than remaining on the stale classpath. Source and build inputs remain unchanged. Run it with `IDE_JDTLS_PROJECT_JDK_25`, `IDE_JDTLS_GRADLE_EXECUTABLE`, `IDE_JDTLS_GRADLE_USER_HOME` and `IDE_JDTLS_GRADLE_VERSION` set, using `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib managed_jdtls_imports_gradle_with_selected_installation_and_project_properties -- --ignored --test-threads=1`. This is native-service integration evidence on Linux; broad multi-module layouts, GUI settings changes, installers and other operating systems still need qualification.

Read-only dependency-source consumption passes production adapter, controller, editor-command and Monaco component tests for request/context correlation, missing or obsolete editor-frame refusal, preserved unrelated drafts, delayed replies, replaced/closed buffers, changed associations, immutable tabs and blocked Save/typing. Component tests verify that the provider URI remains distinct from workspace file URIs and that library models are configured for disposal when their editor unmounts. Monaco now compares canonical parsed model URIs so encoded path separators remain matched after Monaco normalizes them; a component test reproduces this behavior. Concurrent hover and F12 declaration requests retain request-specific authority, so cancelling one request does not invalidate another; workspace, context and editor-buffer changes still revoke stale requests. A separate opt-in Rust test passes with the frozen RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 dependency-source delivery and selected JDK 21 and 25. It creates a local Maven dependency and source attachment using real `javac` and `jar`, acquires an effective release-17 context, resolves the `call(int)` JVM binding, reads its owning source file through the unchanged daemon process, and passes both responses through the production TypeScript decoder. A dirty cursor, absent attachment and changed source archive are refused or unavailable as appropriate; the changed-archive read specifically reports a stale association while the original Java source is restored. The consumer source and build descriptor remain unchanged, and the session is retired. Run `cargo test --locked --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib real_dependency_sources_use_selected_session -- --ignored --test-threads=1` with `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON` pointing to that qualified delivery and `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_JDK` to the selected full JDK. A second opt-in test, `real_dependency_declarations_resolve_exact_overload_through_selected_session`, passes with the separately frozen exact-declaration delivery and both selected JDKs. Production workspace navigation returns an empty result for the binary member; the separate declaration response identifies the integer overload's exact UTF-16 name range and passes the production TypeScript decoder. Controller/Monaco tests cover the fallback, separate preview ownership, source-range validation, attachment revalidation before opening and refusal when Java drafts have no current attested frame. Component tests verify the actual zero-to-one-based selection mapping.

The [native library navigation requirement](features/refactorkit/native-java-library-navigation.feature) is partially qualified on Linux. Source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 runs pass Maven and Gradle saved-source fixtures at Java release 17 with JDK 21 and all four Maven/Gradle saved/editor-frame combinations with JDK 25. They verify exact `sum(int)` navigation, complete named-module facts, immutable dependency-source documents, read-only typing and Save, and clean native exit; editor-frame cases preserve both Java and unrelated dirty drafts. The JDK 21 Gradle case also confirms that inferred module-path facts remain with their owning source set during aggregate analysis. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-library-navigation-native-001:module-path` Linux release/no-bundle GUI profile also passes for Maven and Gradle modular-JAR dependencies with JDK 21 and a source-built RefactorKit package. In both fixtures, the IDE displays complete module facts, F12 selects the exact overloaded dependency declaration, opens its immutable source, refuses typing and Save, preserves workspace inputs, and exits cleanly. This qualifies the tested local dependency shapes; broader JPMS layouts, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. A separate four-scenario Linux release/no-bundle GUI run with the standard user-installed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 daemon and explicit daemon path passes the Maven/Gradle saved/editor-frame matrix with JDK 21. It verifies both exact dependency overload identities, explicit source-unavailable status for binary-only targets, navigation to workspace call sites, exact F12 selection, draft preservation and clean exit. This qualifies the tested user-installed runtime only through the explicit path; automatic discovery for this implementations query, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-library-navigation-native-001` with `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON` and `IDE_JAVA_HOME`; `IDE_JDTLS_HOME` is needed for the JDT LS-specific steps. The Maven fixture keeps its local repository outside the project workspace.

The separate SDK-source GUI profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-library-navigation-native-001:platform`, qualifies Linux release/no-bundle behavior. With JDK 25 and its standard source archive, F12 selects `StringBuilder.toString`, **Open source** reopens the JDK snapshot, typing and Save do not change it, the unrelated text draft remains dirty, and the SDK archive and project inputs stay unchanged. With JDK 21 and no standard source archive, the current project context and Java editor frame are still checked, then F12 and **Open source** report unavailable without attaching a source tab or waiting on a provider query; the dirty Java editor frame and an unrelated text draft both remain unchanged. Both JDK 21 scenarios close their native windows normally with no runner-owned processes. The positive JDK 25 case requires `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON`, `IDE_JDTLS_HOME` and `IDE_JAVA_HOME` set to the qualified provider, installed language server and full JDK 25. The host used for this GUI rerun had only JDK 21, so it revalidated the unavailable-source cases without rerunning the positive JDK 25 case. SDK-source editor-frame GUI for an available archive, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

Immutable-editor dependency navigation has separately passed the real native service and production TypeScript decoder with selected JDK 21 and 25 on a Maven project with two external JARs and previous project outputs already compiled. Dirty cursor and helper buffers choose the second JAR; omitted documents, same-version changed text and a fresh version-only selection with an old association are refused. Both source inputs and dependency/build inputs remain unchanged, and all operations retain the same daemon process. Run `real_editor_dependency_sources_select_the_dirty_companion_binding_without_saving` with `--ignored --test-threads=1`, `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON` pointing to the frozen editor-source delivery and `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_JDK` to the selected full JDK. The editor-frame scenarios also pass in the real Linux release/no-bundle GUI for Maven and Gradle with each selected JDK. Physical F12 actions select the second dependency and its exact integer overload while original project outputs remain compiled; typing and Ctrl+S preserve dirty caller, helper and unrelated text buffers. Source, build, archive and compiled-output bytes remain unchanged through explicit draft discard and normal native closure. These checks qualify dependency attachments, with SDK sources, installers and other operating systems requiring separate evidence. The explicit owning-source toolbar also passes the saved/editor scenarios with both selected JDKs. Its guarded lookup/read survives an automatic Monaco definition preview and cancellation of an earlier preview; workspace, SDK and buffer changes still revoke the operation.

Selected project-JDK propagation passes production-controller and Tauri-adapter tests for explicit selection, replacement, current unsaved text, delayed semantic replies, invalid paths, serialized lifecycle operations and workspace retirement. The opt-in Rust production-path test `managed_jdtls_real_project_jdk_switch_preserves_unsaved_document` now uses managed JDT LS 1.62 with server JDK 25 and a Maven project whose source/target levels remain 21. It opens the same unsaved document under project JDKs 25, 21 and 27. Type-specific diagnostics prove that `java.lang.classfile.ClassFile` resolves with 25 and 27, is unavailable with 21, and reports the deliberately missing member for the supported SDKs. The test checks the selected SDK in service status, rejects operations from retired generations, preserves the draft and confirms that all three server processes exit. Set `IDE_JDTLS_PROJECT_JDK_21`, `IDE_JDTLS_PROJECT_JDK_25` and `IDE_JDTLS_PROJECT_JDK_27` to full JDK homes; `IDE_JDTLS_SERVER_JDK` may select the server runtime and must be Java 25 or newer for this bundle. Run with `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib commands::java_language::application::tests::managed_jdtls_real_project_jdk_switch_preserves_unsaved_document -- --ignored --exact --test-threads=1`. A focused Linux release/no-bundle project-context GUI scenario also changes a synchronized Maven project's JDK from 21 to 25, verifies that JDT LS restarts, preserves an unsaved buffer and refuses navigation against the retired context. The runtime-preference profile `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-language-001:native:runtime` passes in Linux release/no-bundle mode with an unmanifested JDT LS 1.63 distribution, project JDK 21 and a separately saved server JDK 25. With an unsaved Java buffer open, the person first saves JDK 21 as the server runtime and requests Start. The GUI presents the requirement for JDK 25 rather than a malformed-header error; no Java language-service runtime directory has been created. The person then saves JDK 25 and starts and restarts JDT LS. The panel confirms the server executable and the independent project JDK, and the editor retains the exact unsaved text while disk content remains unchanged. The setting overrides the deliberately conflicting `IDE_JDTLS_JAVA_HOME`. Native input replaces the existing JDK path through keyboard selection and paste and checks its exact value before Save. The scenario restores the original draft and fixture files, closes normally, restores its environment and leaves no runner-owned processes. This qualifies bundle-derived runtime admission and recovery for the tested distribution; the earlier JDT LS 1.62 scenario separately qualified the saved preference without the incompatible-runtime step. This qualifies the tested local setup only; packaged applications, other runtime combinations and other operating systems remain unqualified. The separate real JDT LS smoke passes with the checksum-verified pinned 1.62.0 bundle and server JDK 25; it verifies completion, hover, signature help, hierarchical document symbols, workspace symbols, semantic tokens, same-document highlights and local rename. Another real-server smoke verifies unresolved-type imports, an edit-only `instanceof` quick assist, accessor and method generation, and member sorting with bounded edits. Controller, adapter and Monaco tests cover current-document identity, UTF-16 validation and token encoding. Broader GUI SDK switching, color rendering, broad project import/dependency alignment, older runtime compatibility and other operating systems remain unqualified.


API restrictions require separate qualification from project-JDK selection. With JDT LS 1.63, server JDK 25 and Maven source/target 8, production-path probes on project JDKs 21 and 25 resolve `List.of` and report a deliberately missing `List` member from the same unsaved buffer. The new opt-in `managed_jdtls_source_target_and_release_use_distinct_sdk_apis` qualification currently fails for release 8: a fresh project on JDK 25 reports `org.eclipse.jdt.core.compiler.release=enabled` but does not report the modern `List.of` call as an API error. Queries for the open document and its project agree on Maven ownership, compiler options and selected VM. An explicit JDT LS project-JDK update succeeds but leaves the observed diagnostic unchanged. Changing a previously imported source/target project to release 8 can also leave that option disabled. The compiler option's intended API restriction is documented in [Eclipse JDT's JavaCore API](https://help.eclipse.org/latest/topic/org.eclipse.jdt.doc.isv/reference/api/org/eclipse/jdt/core/JavaCore.html#COMPILER_RELEASE). The test retains its expected restriction; this route is not declared qualified. These editor diagnostics remain a JDT LS integration issue.

The manual and automatic Java compiler-check runtime is described in [section 6.11](#611-java-compiler-checks).

The [native qualification tests](apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/refactorkit_daemon/java_editor_diagnostics_real_tests.rs) exercise the actual provider and production TypeScript decoder. Four real Maven service cases with an isolated candidate pass on JDK 21 and 25: source/target 8 accepts the selected SDK API while release 8 reports its unavailability, a dirty companion produces an error, and repairing it removes that error without saving. Independent `javac` probes agree. The JDK 25 fixture also references `java.lang.classfile.ClassFile`: JDK 21 `javac` rejects it, JDK 25 source/target 8 accepts it and emits Java 8 class files, and release 8 rejects it. The native Maven query and production TypeScript decoder agree, distinguishing the selected SDK library from the older runtime platform. The first diagnostic candidate was withheld because duplicate Java types in different files could produce a false-clean result. The native regression retains the compiler-error expectation established independently with `javac`. The corrected isolated candidate passes the IDE’s six real-service checks on JDK 21 and 25, including two compiler errors for the duplicate type in the captured and saved companion sources. The production TypeScript decoder accepts the actual responses. This qualifies those Maven service fixtures, not every project layout.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:editor-diagnostics` profile passes both Maven API profiles in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with selected JDK 21. It checks the unsaved caller and companion, an error in a saved closed source, visible compiler-error markers, navigation from Problems to the exact closed-source compiler range, repair of both companion and closed source in drafts, and retirement of the prior check after editor changes. Source/target 8 accepts the selected SDK API, while release 8 retains its API error after the other errors are repaired. All saved Java and POM bytes remain unchanged; explicit discard restores the drafts, both windows close normally and no runner-owned processes survive. The [native GUI scenarios](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature) exercise this workflow. An initial harness attempt failed its process-ownership check because the application was configured before the scenario environment lease; instantiation now follows the lease, and the ownership checks remain intact. JDK 25 has native-service qualification; this GUI result is limited to JDK 21.

An isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate now qualifies this compiler check for bounded evaluated Gradle projects. Six real IDE service cases use Gradle 9.8.1, project JDK 21 or 25 and a separate JDK 21 Gradle runtime: source/target 8 retains the selected SDK APIs, release 8 restricts them, and duplicate types in saved companions produce compiler errors. The JDK 25 probes include `java.lang.classfile.ClassFile`, distinguishing the selected SDK from the daemon's bundled JDK 21. Main and test source sets carry provider-verified provenance for their conventional and generated output roots. Diagnostic queries preserve source and build inputs and do not repeat Gradle evaluation; the existing provenance guard remains enforced. Earlier packages that omit this evidence refuse with `java.context.sourceRootProvenanceIncomplete` and receive a plain-language unavailable message rather than a clean result. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-editor-diagnostics` profile also passes both source/target-8 and release-8 scenarios in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21. It verifies unsaved build-configuration refusal, draft preservation, caller and companion errors, navigation to a saved closed source, repair and retirement on edits, unchanged saved inputs, normal close and no surviving runner-owned processes. These checks qualify the isolated candidate and reference fixtures; larger Gradle layouts, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. The default provider is unchanged.

The [real compiler-check service tests](apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/refactorkit_daemon/java_editor_diagnostics_real_tests.rs) also qualify two dependent Java modules against that isolated candidate: a Maven reactor and an explicitly evaluated Gradle multi-project build, each with JDK 21 and 25 under source/target 8 and release 8. Both open sources remain unsaved. A changed library return type produces a caller error in the application module, and repairing the caller's return type resolves it while retaining any release-8 API errors. Separate `javac` invocations verify the incompatible and repaired signatures. Provider queries preserve the original source/build bytes and retained session; Gradle evaluation is not repeated. This qualifies those two-module service fixtures, not larger dependency graphs, test-module dependencies, composites or native UI behavior. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:multi-module-editor-diagnostics` profile passes the Gradle multi-project scenario on Linux release/no-bundle with JDK 21 and source/target 8: automatic checks show the caller error after the unsaved library signature changes, then clear it after the unsaved caller repair. Original inputs are preserved, the window closes normally and no runner-owned processes survive. The earlier Gradle-provenance package omits the Maven reactor parent from `buildEvidence`, so the IDE cannot recognize that unsaved configuration as a provider-declared build input. A later isolated Maven-input-evidence candidate corrects the public evidence list. The previously failing real-service parent/child-POM check and four Maven reactor source-analysis cases pass on JDK 21 and 25. With that candidate, both Maven and Gradle scenarios also pass the Linux release/no-bundle GUI: an unsaved parent POM is refused before the check, explicit discard restores the configuration, and automatic cross-module signature error/repair checks preserve every saved input and close normally with no runner-owned processes left. The IDE continues to use provider-declared inputs without reconstructing Maven inheritance. This closes the parent-evidence gap for the tested reactor and package; external parents, imported BOMs and larger hierarchies have no independent IDE GUI qualification here. These source-analysis and reference-layout results do not establish universal build-input coverage, and the default provider remains unchanged.

The same real-service qualification also covers JUnit Jupiter 5.11.4 as a test-scoped dependency in conventional Maven and evaluated Gradle projects. Eight JDK 21/25 source/target-8 and release-8 cases resolve the annotation in an unsaved test source, capture an unsaved main-source companion and preserve the selected SDK API profile. A test-dependency type used in a main-source draft produces a compiler error; repairing that draft restores the expected result. Context classpaths and separate `javac` invocations both verify the main/test dependency boundary. These checks qualify compiler analysis, source preservation, session reuse and the production response decoder; JUnit execution is a separate workflow. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:test-source-editor-diagnostics` profile passes both Maven and Gradle scenarios in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21 and source/target 8. It verifies JUnit resolution in a test buffer, an error marker for the test-dependency type in a main buffer, automatic repair updates, saved-source Problems navigation, explicit pause and discard, unchanged source/build bytes, normal close and no surviving runner-owned processes. These checks qualify the isolated candidate and conventional reference fixtures; larger test graphs, custom source sets and other operating systems remain unqualified for this diagnostic scenario.

A separate native compiler-profile matrix with an isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate qualifies the SDK 27 API profile independently of Java 27 syntax. Real Maven and Gradle service checks pass with Temurin JDK 27 for source/target 8, 17 and 25, and for release 17. Source/target 17 can use the selected SDK API, including `java.lang.classfile.ClassFile`; release 17 rejects that newer API. Independent selected-`javac` probes agree. Each case verifies dirty-companion errors, unsaved repair, preserved saved inputs, live-session reuse and production TypeScript decoding; Gradle checks retain the evaluated model without another build-script evaluation. Matching-language source/target controls also pass on JDK 21 and 25. These tests qualify the tested compiler/API configurations, not complete language-version syntax, GUI behavior, packaged applications or the default installed provider. Java 27 source analysis remains unqualified; its metadata-only/refusal GUI flow is described in section 6.11. The same isolated candidate also passes both focused Linux release/no-bundle Maven editor-diagnostic GUI scenarios with JDK 27, source/target 8 and release 8. The provider trace verifies the selected SDK home and the distinct API profiles 27 and 8. Draft errors, automatic repair and pause, saved-source Problems navigation, dirty build-input refusal, unchanged inputs, normal close and zero owned process survivors are verified. Both corresponding Gradle GUI scenarios also pass with selected JDK 27, source/target 8 and release 8; the trace verifies API profiles 27 and 8, and the windows close normally without owned survivors. Four additional production-native Maven/Gradle cases with source/target 27 or release 27 verify the typed source-analysis refusal, unchanged inputs, retained metadata/session and unchanged evaluated Gradle model. The production TypeScript diagnostic decoder accepts these refusals without presenting a clean result. The metadata-only Maven GUI control in section 6.11 is requalified against this package. Independent provider-process checks cover legacy refusals for source/release 26 and 27 and explicit v6/v7 policies without clamping. The IDE decoder separately enforces the sealed v2–v5 API/source-language bounds. This qualifies the stated ordinary source shapes and Linux release/no-bundle GUI flows, not complete syntax coverage, Gradle metadata-only GUI behavior, installers, other operating systems or the default installed provider.

Separate external-tool checks pass with the isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 SDK-diagnostics candidate: its actual CLI accepts an explicitly selected JDK 21 or 25 for source/target 8, and reports a compiler API error for the same source under release 8. The project also contains a JavaScript test-report asset, and all source, POM and report bytes remain unchanged. This qualifies those standalone CLI cases; it does not establish correct JDT LS editor diagnostics, GUI behavior, Gradle profiles or the default installed provider.

The opt-in Rust production-path test `real_jdtls_bundle_runtime_floor_and_restarts` passes with the unmanifested JDT LS 1.63 distribution on Linux. Its JDT Core bundle declares Java 25. The test selects JDK 21 explicitly and verifies a clear compatibility refusal before server state is created, then selects JDK 25 and completes three initialize/shutdown cycles, checking each child process has exited. Set `IDE_JDTLS_HOME` to that distribution, `IDE_JDTLS_PROJECT_JDK_21` to JDK 21 and `IDE_JDTLS_JAVA_HOME` to JDK 25, then run `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib real_jdtls_bundle_runtime_floor_and_restarts -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1`. This verifies the native service boundary and real server processes. The runtime-preference GUI qualification below separately covers the refusal and recovery controls; installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

Maven profile propagation has Rust policy tests for active/inactive encoding, ambiguous profile refusal, workspace-relative project selection and canonical JDT LS project-root filtering. Tauri-adapter tests verify that the selected project path and profiles cross the native boundary and are confirmed in session status. Controller tests verify that changing profiles retires old semantics and reopens unsaved buffers under the replacement session. The opt-in Rust test `managed_jdtls_applies_active_and_inactive_maven_profiles_to_selected_project` passes against JDT LS 1.61.0-202607102111 and JDK 25. A real Maven project has an active-by-default profile that raises compiler release from 21 to 25; the test first excludes it and observes a type-specific unresolved `java.lang.classfile` diagnostic, then activates it and observes that diagnostic clear. The selected project path scopes the update, and the saved POM and Java source remain unchanged. Run it with `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib managed_jdtls_applies_active_and_inactive_maven_profiles_to_selected_project -- --ignored --test-threads=1` on a host with the managed JDT LS and a full JDK. This qualifies the production command path on Linux, not native GUI profile editing, other JDT LS versions, every Maven layout or full effective project-context alignment.

The `javaJavadocNativeGui` profile verifies keyboard selection of **Add Javadoc comment** in a Linux release/no-bundle build with project JDK 21 and JDT LS 1.63 `idecompact1` running on JDK 25. A method and a constructor each receive the two parameter tags and the declared exception tag. Only the method receives a return tag. The project JDK compiles copies of both drafts and generates documentation with doclint enabled. It reports warnings for missing descriptions and undocumented declarations. Undo restores an earlier unsaved import, Redo restores the comment, and explicit discard restores the original file. Run `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaJavadocNativeGui` to repeat the check.

The focused `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaOnTypeFormattingNativeGui` profile passes for one Eclipse Java project on Linux release/no-bundle with project JDK 21, JDT LS 1.63 `idecompact1` and server JDK 25. It first checks document and selected-line formatting, then enables the workspace typing preference and types a semicolon through the native editor. The declaration is formatted in the unsaved buffer. Disabling the preference leaves the next typed declaration unformatted; original source remains unchanged, explicit discard restores the draft and the window closes normally without forced termination. A real native-service regression separately verifies the advertised semicolon/newline/closing-brace characters and a nonempty on-type response through production normalization. It also compares two- and four-space requests on the same statement while preserving the surrounding method: the former leaves the already matching line unchanged, and the latter adjusts only its indentation. Component and controller tests cover temporary synchronization gaps, bounded waiting, workspace preference isolation, capability withdrawal, newer edits and cancellation. This qualifies the stated semicolon GUI fixture and real-server request, not every trigger/style/project combination, installers or other operating systems.

The [native Java code-action scenarios](features/workspace/native-java-code-actions.feature) define Linux release/no-bundle GUI coverage with JDT LS and JDK 25. The standard profile passes five GUI scenarios with the installed JDT LS 1.61.0-202607102111; the same acceptance has also been qualified with the project-pinned JDT LS 1.62 bundle. A separate `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-code-actions-native-001:organize-imports` profile passes with JDT LS 1.62 and JDK 25; an unsorted fixture verifies import sorting, unused-import removal, saved-source preservation, draft restoration and clean native exit. It covers an import quick fix, parameter-name inlays before and after a JDT LS restart, selected-line and document formatting, an Eclipse formatter profile whose next-line type-brace style is observed in Monaco, accessor generation, field rename, selected override/implement generation, selected delegate-method generation, inherited abstract-method implementation, `toString()`, constructor generation, `hashCode()`/`equals()` generation and member sorting. It confirms saved source stays unchanged, each operation remains in the draft, the original draft is restored through native keyboard input, and no runner-owned processes remain. A separate `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-code-actions-native-001:local-rename` profile passes with JDT LS 1.62 and JDK 25; it qualifies current-document local-binding rename for a local variable that shares its spelling with a field, verifies that only the local declaration and use change in Monaco, and confirms the field and saved file stay unchanged before cleanly restoring the draft and closing the native session. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-code-actions-native-001:parameter-rename` profile qualifies a cursor-selected String parameter rename in one overloaded method while preserving the same-named parameter in another overload, a separate method parameter and the saved source. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-code-actions-native-001:cross-file-rename` profile passes both the two-open-file and initially closed-reference scenarios with JDT LS 1.63, server JDK 25 and project JDK 21. Both rename the cursor-selected overload, retain the other overload and same-named method in another type, and update both drafts while leaving both saved files unchanged. The closed-reference scenario verifies that the companion tab is absent before rename, opens in the background, and contains the renamed reference as an unsaved draft. The active source remains selected while the rename completes. Background synchronization retains the active semantic providers, so it does not cancel that rename; active-document changes still retire the providers. Both scenarios restore their drafts, stop JDT LS and close normally without surviving owned processes. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-code-actions-native-001:semantic-type-renames` profile passes with JDT LS 1.61 and JDK 25; it verifies nested-type and record-component renames across open drafts while retaining unrelated same-spelled bindings and unchanged saved files, then restores both drafts and closes cleanly. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-code-actions-native-001:multi-document` profile passes the already-open and initially closed target fixtures with JDT LS 1.63, server JDK 25 and project JDK 21. Native Find selects the undefined method call before requesting actions. In the closed-target case, the menu leaves the target tab closed; choosing the action opens it in background, verifies the fresh proposal and updates its draft without changing either saved source. The unchanged caller remains selected while its missing-method diagnostic clears through JDT LS validation, before the target is selected. The target retains the fixture’s unrelated deliberate diagnostics, so this qualifies editor/language-service coordination rather than compilation of the fixture. Both scenarios restore their drafts and exit cleanly without surviving owned processes. File/resource renames and edits that cannot be synchronized remain unavailable. The full action catalog, other project layouts, packaged installers and another operating system remain unqualified; the requirement remains partial.

Installed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 native-library qualification passes for a signed Java method rename in a minimal Maven source layout: read-only preview with JDT binding evidence, refusal of changed rename parameters without source writes, and exact reviewed changes to declaration and call site. Formatting and import-organization cases separately preserve preview source bytes, refuse concurrent source changes before Apply, apply the actual reviewed patch, compile and execute changed source with JDK 21 and JDK 25, and restore the original file through real rollback. The same production path survives a separate daemon that exits before initialization, both before Apply and before Rollback. Unit tests verify inverse edit/create/delete/move reporting, preservation of CLI authority during daemon reset, and retirement of both providers' state at workspace shutdown.

The [Java file-operation native scenarios](features/workspace/native-java-file-operations.feature), run with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-file-operations-native-001`, pass on a fresh Linux X11 Tauri/WebKit release/no-bundle application with installed RefactorKit 0.7.0 and JDK 21. Set `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_ENGINE` to an absolute installed standalone CLI executable that works with an isolated runtime home and `IDE_JAVA_HOME` to the full JDK used to compile and execute the changed source. The native GUI verifies both operations in the Java Refactor dialog and Monaco context menu, refuses a context-menu action while buffers are dirty, then opens the saved-file review after saving. Preview preserves source bytes; Apply changes the actual file, and a separate real `javac`/`java` invocation retains its output. Public Rollback restores exact source bytes and the clean visible Monaco buffer. Build descriptors and an unrelated sentinel remain unchanged. Each application closes through the native close path without forced termination, scenario environments are restored and the runner finds no surviving sandbox processes. The requirement remains `@partial`: these conventional Maven compilation units do not qualify other source layouts, formatter styles, import-binding contexts, additional editor states, installers or operating systems.

General terminal unit tests exercise the production port adapter, transport controller and raw xterm component for provider refusal, closed requests and correlated responses, stale launches/reads, exact partial-input retries, bounded input/transcript retention, output gaps, Stop refusal and raw control-byte/resize delivery. Separate opt-in Linux Rust tests have passed through the production PTY manager with a real shell and JDK: persistent directory/environment, UTF-8 Java output, real terminal dimensions, Ctrl+C, foreground/background cleanup, natural-exit cleanup, saturated nonblocking input, output truncation and registered-root revocation. These library checks do not establish native GUI, package or cross-platform behavior. Focused Linux X11 Tauri/WebKit release/no-bundle GUI qualification has passed through the `workspaceTerminalNativeGui` profile: trust before Start; real keyboard input and Java compilation/output; retained directory/environment; hidden-panel reattachment; actual PTY resize; Ctrl+C after more than ten seconds; two independent sessions; selected-shell/background-job Stop; renderer reload revocation; and normal application-close cleanup. Observed shell and Java/job PIDs exited before scenario/runner cleanup, and the application closed without forced termination. The same profile also passes terminal Commands: showing a hidden terminal preserves its existing session, a new default-shell session starts in the verified workspace root, clearing its display leaves the shell alive, and selected Stop/Close leave the other shell and its background job running until they are explicitly stopped. Focused command tests reject captured actions after context or selected-session replacement and retain Stop after trust withdrawal. This does not qualify installers, other operating systems, deliberate OS-session escapes, abnormal application death or broader Java project/debugger behavior. Retained initial failures identified an exited shell's revoked controlling terminal, incomplete repeated-key sequences, an incorrect panel selector and terminal focus/default-shell assumptions in the WebKit test driver; these attempts were not recorded as successful qualification.

Run the terminal qualification with `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile workspaceTerminalNativeGui`. Run the real Linux manager checks with `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib terminal::linux::tests::real_pty -- --ignored --test-threads=1`.

A separate real-provider service matrix checks compiler failures in the synchronized six-module Maven and Gradle reference projects on JDK 21 and 25. After an initial successful compilation, it introduces either an unresolved symbol or a syntax error inside `main`, acquires the current project context and requests Build or Run. The context remains available, the build tool returns a nonzero compiler outcome with the exact source location, and Run does not execute the previous application classes. After restoring the source and acquiring a fresh context, the new session succeeds without retaining the old compiler locations. All original source and build-descriptor inputs are restored, and the isolated RefactorKit candidate remains unchanged. These are service-level checks of the separation between effective build metadata and source correctness.

The existing synchronized Maven and Gradle execution profiles separately pass the six-module compiler-error workflow in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21 and the isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0 candidate. A native keyboard/clipboard edit introduces a syntax error in the application; Build saves it and reports a nonzero compiler outcome. The test prepares an unsaved repair, opens the library declaration through Go to File, then follows the reported compiler location back to the application at the reported line. The repair remains dirty and the invalid saved file stays unchanged. After explicitly saving the repair and reacquiring project metadata, another unsaved source edit is made. Run saves that new edit and executes with the selected JDK and runtime dependencies. Both scenarios restore the original source/build inputs and exit without surviving owned processes. The shared fresh executable passes both profiles; packages, other operating systems and other GUI compiler-error families remain unqualified.

The reported-compiler-location collector has native parser and adapter/panel tests plus real-tool service qualification on JDK 21 and 25 with plain JDK, Maven and Gradle. Each tool compiles a two-module fixture containing a space and a Unicode character in the source path, reports the exact failing source line, retains the location after console truncation, and produces an empty location collection after repair and a successful new session. A focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario on JDK 21 separately verifies the plain-JDK source-link click, cursor reveal at the start of the reported line, preservation of a modified unsaved buffer and unchanged saved source. The Maven/Gradle Linux GUI outline with Maven 3.9.11, Gradle 9.8.1 and JDK 21 also verifies clicking a failed Run compiler location in the selected `service` project directory while the test-source tab is active, activating the correct application-source tab, revealing line 2 at column one, preserving an unsaved repair, and leaving the saved invalid source, prior application execution count and passing JUnit report unchanged. The subsequent explicit Build saves and compiles the repair without implicit Run or test execution. These GUI fixtures select one project in a workspace subdirectory; broader module graphs, packaged applications, localized compiler output and other operating systems remain unqualified for compiler-location navigation.

Java execution's deterministic Cucumber scenarios exercise the production controller, adapter, and panel over a substituted native tool boundary. Separate real-tool tests compile and execute Java, observe compilation errors, run JUnit tests through Maven and Gradle, and exercise a real jdb breakpoint, stack and locals. The launch-setting library checks have passed with JDK 25 and separately with an explicitly selected JDK 21 against that different default: plain-JDK, Maven, Gradle and jdb preserve the exact argument array, literal/empty environment values and selected runtime home without changing source or build descriptors. The expanded launch checks each execute three cases: explicit application arguments and JVM options, JVM options without application rows, and project/default launch settings with neither. System-property values, including empty values, quotes, Unicode and line breaks, reach the target JVM exactly; its input arguments and effective maximum heap prove the memory option. Gradle retains a project-defined JVM property and default application argument. Maven retains configured Exec-plugin arguments when neither IDE application arguments nor JVM options are present, and passes no application arguments when only IDE JVM options request the separate Java process. The jdb cases set a real `Main.main` breakpoint, observe the corresponding zero- or eight-element argument local and continue to the independently checked application proof. Unit tests check private launch-file permissions and deletion, incomplete configuration/JVM-option draft restoration, Run/Debug refusal before source-save preparation for incomplete or reserved launcher options, Build/Test admission when those application-only drafts are unused, size/name refusal and JDK capability correlation. Named-configuration tests exercise the production controller and panel for legacy restoration, independent duplication, selection/persistence, workspace isolation, invalid collection/name limits, visible storage failure, execution-time edit guards and rejection of stale workspace callbacks. They also retain the original failed-test session after its saved configuration is deleted. These library/unit tests do not validate the Tauri GUI or an installer; the focused expanded Maven/Gradle GUI acceptance is described below.

The manual Maven Run launch-setting test also passes on Temurin 8 and 11 and GraalVM JDK 21 with Maven 3.9.11 on Linux. The Java 8 case uses a runtime-only Maven dependency and reads an application-relative resource from a working directory containing spaces, Unicode and an apostrophe. It independently checks the selected test fixture's application JVM, heap flag, environment, empty arguments, quotes and line breaks, plus the unchanged source and POM.

Linux native-service checks on Temurin 8 qualify console jdb on a plain-JDK project and synchronized Maven and Gradle projects. The plain-JDK cases retain literal arguments, JVM properties and environment overrides, inspect a real breakpoint, stack frame and locals, and stop the suspended target. A separate test confirms that the IDE reports the debuggee's exit code 7 as a failed session. The synchronized cases build the selected module and its dependencies on a clean fixture, attach to the Java 8 application, stop at the requested source line and continue to application output. JDK 21 passes the existing console launch regression. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:debugger` profile passes on a Linux/X11 release build without bundling with both Temurin 8 and JDK 21. It verifies save before launch, breakpoint, stack and locals, method stepping, normal completion, Stop while suspended, and Stop after the debugger input queue fills. On Java 8 the test also verifies that the launcher, debugger and application have exited. The same three Temurin 8 GUI scenarios pass on a freshly built Linux x86-64 AppImage with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:debugger:appimage`. Set `IDE_JAVA_HOME` to the full selected JDK for either profile.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:java8-maven-run` scenario passes on a fresh Linux/X11 release desktop build without bundling. The same scenario passes on a freshly built Linux x86-64 AppImage with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:java8-maven-run:appimage`. Set `IDE_JAVA8_HOME` to a full Temurin 8 JDK and use Maven 3.9.11 with a populated dependency cache. Java Run restores a named configuration after reload and requires fresh workspace trust. The application confirms that its empty argument, multiline literal argument and JVM property arrived intact. It loads a runtime Maven dependency and reads a relative resource from the configured directory containing a space, Unicode and an apostrophe. The test verifies the running Java 8 home and class-file version 52. A custom JUnit 4 runner then confirms that the discovery JVM receives a literal multiline option and both methods are listed before either body is run. A fresh discovery with project-default JVM settings allows the selected method to run through Surefire on Java 8. The report contains only that method. The scenario also verifies unchanged sources and POM, native window close, and process cleanup.

Real Maven/Gradle test-JVM regressions have passed with the default JDK 25 and an explicitly selected JDK 21. They observe exact mixed-quote, backslash, Unicode, line-break and empty properties, the requested heap, environment and target runtime home. Application-only properties stay absent. Gradle retains its project JVM property; Maven's explicit options replace its overridable defaults. Repair and failed-test rerun retain those options while excluding a previously passing companion method; removing the options restores project defaults. Separate real Surefire cases with fixed `argLine` and `forkCount=0` produce passing JUnit results and tool exit zero, but the IDE reports an unconfirmed configuration. Source/build inputs remain unchanged apart from the authored test repair, and shell-looking values do not create a file. Unit tests also refuse forged or duplicate verification properties, populated suites missing confirmation, stale report reuse, oversized settings and obsolete operation responses. These are external-tool and in-process checks; their native GUI scope follows below.

The opt-in real-service Rust test `real_maven_runs_selected_failsafe_tests_and_collects_only_fresh_integration_reports` passes with installed Maven, JDK 25, Surefire and Failsafe 3.5.4, and JUnit 4.13.2. It runs a selected `class#method` through Maven `verify`, confirms the preceding Surefire phase and requested Failsafe method execute, and verifies that the structured result contains only fresh `failsafe-reports` XML and confirms the requested test JVM option. After a deliberate integration-test failure, it repairs the source and verifies that failed-test rerun retains the captured integration-test operation, selected method and test JVM option. Its coverage case additionally measures branches exercised across both Surefire and Failsafe, ignores stale unit-coverage XML, and verifies a repaired, captured Failsafe rerun produces a fresh integration report. Run it with `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib real_maven_runs_selected_failsafe_tests_and_collects_only_fresh_integration_reports -- --ignored --nocapture`. The focused `javaBuildToolsNativeGui` profile also passes on Linux X11 with a release/no-bundle desktop: its Maven Failsafe scenario verifies the separate integration-test action, selected method and fresh Failsafe report while Surefire runs earlier in the `verify` lifecycle. The same profile's coverage scenario confirms the integration-coverage action, full-lifecycle scope, measured report and Failsafe-only structured test results in the native UI. Its Failsafe fixture registers `src/integration-test/java` through Maven Build Helper and runs `MainIT` through the configured Failsafe include, while Surefire still reports the ordinary `MainTest` from `src/test/java`. A separate focused `javaFailsafeReactorNativeGui` profile passes with the release/no-bundle Linux desktop and a real two-module Maven reactor: the UI collects fresh Failsafe reports from both modules, excludes Surefire reports, and reruns the repaired failed method without rerunning the passing module. Run it with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:failsafe-reactor`; the scenario is defined in [native-java-execution.feature](features/workspace/native-java-execution.feature). These scenarios qualify one custom source root and one basic two-module reactor, not synchronized RefactorKit `INTEGRATION_TEST` context, larger or differently configured reactors, arbitrary Failsafe layouts, or other operating systems.

Save regression tests cover edits during a pending save, ordered concurrent saves, late results after invalidation, external revision conflicts, and atomic publication. The [close-race regressions](packages/web-core/src/view-models/editor-close-races.test.ts) exercise pending provider close, changed-and-changed-back edits, same-path reopen, workspace invalidation, pending saves, provider failure and unrelated tabs omitted by stale inventories. Controller tests exercise post-close generation changes, unmount, StrictMode replay, save-all refusal and retained-document reactivation failures. Comparison tests retain exact selected/companion drafts after edits or Save during deferred discard checkpointing and ignore completion after selection/workspace changes, cancellation or unmount. Adapter composition tests verify synchronous metadata/UI close without source-content writes. The [buffer-lifetime regressions](packages/web-core/src/view-models/editor-buffer-lifetime.test.ts) and [command composition tests](apps/desktop/src/features/editor/useEditorBufferLifetimeCommands.test.tsx) use the production store/view model to reopen even the identical metadata object, timestamp and text during deferred flush, checkpoint, saved notification, document close and Save completion. They preserve new clean/dirty buffers, refuse obsolete review tokens, retain companions, drop old queued writes and suppress old desktop-close notification. Normal edits during preparation and cloned saved metadata still allow a current Save/Close. These are production-code in-process tests with controlled collaborator completion, not native keyboard timing or provider rollback evidence.

Dirty-buffer guards refuse workspace switching, document unload, and native window close; listener tests also cover registration refusal, late disposal and fail-closed retired callbacks. Focused Linux tab/workspace/X11-window acceptance is described below. The held-source-Save keyboard race below has focused native Linux acceptance. Typing during asynchronous discard confirmation, earlier same-path preparation/reopen races, general unload, asynchronous third-party provider side effects and wider operating-system acceptance remain separate native qualification work. Checkpoint-based recovery and local history are implemented with the limits in section 6.5. Focused Linux GUI restart, history selection/removal, missing-source copying, journal-access failure, per-buffer capacity and truncated-journal acceptance are described below; disk-full, workspace-wide pending-draft and retained-content GUI limits, other corruption families and the wider operating-system matrix remain pending.

The [native file-opening verification](features/workspace/native-desktop-file-opening.feature) passes on a freshly built Linux release/no-bundle executable with real Tauri/WebKit drivers and Xvfb. It opens both a root file through File Explorer and a nested Java source through **Ctrl/Cmd+P**, then checks the accessible search result, selected tab, exact Monaco content, clean exit and workspace confinement. An initial run timed out waiting for File Explorer readiness; successful reruns do not explain that failure or establish a general reliability result. The [startup observer harness](tests/story/support/native-startup-observation.ts) now records bounded, redacted bootstrap/DOM snapshots on readiness and failure in private `startup-*.json` artifacts outside scenario storage leases. This prevents Cucumber's progress formatter and scenario cleanup from losing the snapshot. Inspection has a one-second limit; unavailable inspection/persistence never invents readiness or replaces the primary failure. The same fifteen-second File Explorer readiness deadline also failed in the passive external-change profile during combined regression, before any editor was opened; an unchanged fresh-build rerun passed. The cause remains unexplained, and the separate Monaco tab-layout correction does not fix or qualify general startup reliability. This focused opening/Monaco/clean-close check does not by itself qualify Java Run, dirty-close behavior, the new comparison dialog, other operating systems or an installer. Separate focused checks below cover some of these paths; M0 remains incomplete.

The [large Java package scenario](features/workspace/native-java-source-file-creation.feature) passes on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland. Scrolling File Explorer reaches the last of 121 source files, clicking it opens the expected Java editor buffer, and closing the application preserves all source files. Run `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaLargePackageAppImageNativeGui` and add `--wayland` for the Wayland session.

The `javaLanguageResponsivenessNativeGui` profile reproduces and corrects a separate interactive JDT LS wait on Linux release/no-bundle builds, using project JDK 21 and the real JDT LS 1.63 server on JDK 25. A private transport proxy forwards the real protocol frames unchanged and holds only the first formatting response for four seconds. On the preceding synchronous facade, opening another file completes only after that response is released. With the worker delegation, the GUI opens and reads the other file before release. Returning to the Java document after the delayed response confirms that its cancelled formatting edit was not applied and that saved source remains unchanged. The language service and native window close normally, the scenario restores its environment, and bounded cleanup finds no surviving processes. A separate `javaLanguageIntelligenceCoreNativeGui` regression passes real diagnostics, hover, signature help, member and type/import completion, references, callers/callees, definition navigation and restart with unsaved documents. Rust tests cover the typed asynchronous facade and existing service guards; adapter and controller tests retain their request/response and lifetime checks. The native scenarios qualify these controlled Linux interactions, not earlier intermittent startup failures, arbitrary server stalls, packaged applications or other operating systems.

The bounded startup investigation passed twenty opening and twelve passive-change attempts using the persisted DOM observer, followed by ten opening attempts and one final passive-change integration check with early bootstrap observation. A further ten-opening batch on the current worktree passed using one freshly built executable; it did not reproduce the intermittent timeout. Each diagnostic batch reuses one executable and provides bounded host observations, not independent-release reliability qualification. A separate deliberately malformed workspace-registry fixture exercised the real fifteen-second failure path: React had committed, the native bridge existed, the explorer was absent and the UI reported workspace activation failure. The snapshot survived the failure, fixture source/registry bytes were unchanged, and the clean process closed through X11. This controlled provider refusal verifies diagnostic retention, not the original cause; no timeout was increased or automatic repair introduced.

The [slow-provider startup scenario](features/workspace/native-startup-responsiveness.feature) has passed on a fresh Linux release/no-bundle application. Its private launcher delays the installed RefactorKit CLI's real `--version` invocation by four seconds and delegates all output and exit status to that executable; native IPC/provider results are not substituted. The uncorrected executable failed because the probe had completed before file/recovery readiness. Production corrections remove optional checks from initial workspace readiness and move both RefactorKit capability probes, Java status/event polling, Pi probing/command discovery and native root transitions off the UI thread. The corrected scenario observes File Explorer and recovery ready while the probe is pending, opens exact saved Java content through the explorer and Monaco, presents the actual RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 version, and closes cleanly through X11. Source bytes, private storage confinement, lease restoration and zero sandbox process survivors are independently checked. The focused requirement stays `@partial`: the controlled dependency is reproduced and corrected, while earlier intermittent timeouts, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-startup-responsiveness-native-001` with `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_CLI` set to the absolute path of an installed standalone RefactorKit launcher that works with an isolated runtime home. The scenario refuses a missing or unsuccessful CLI, has eight authored steps plus lifecycle hooks, and retains the ordinary explorer/runtime deadlines. Production-controller regressions separately delay mandatory editor restoration and all optional providers, preserve the mandatory gate, settle an optional failure independently and discard an old workspace's failure after switching or controller unmount. Initial activation also completes once during React StrictMode effect replay. These in-process checks supplement the native scenario; they do not qualify every concurrent provider/root transition.

A separate Linux AppImage startup failure occurred before React committed. The saved browser observation reported a `ReferenceError` in the IDE UI asset and an empty root, and the desktop build reported a cycle between its UI and Monaco chunks. The corrected chunk assignment keeps the editor navigation initializer with the Monaco integration. A fresh package emitted without that cycle and opened the native UI in the mixed JVM scenarios. Two other recorded failures reached React commit. One occurred during a workspace switch when WebDriver tried to retain an explorer node that the interface replaced. The GUI check now locates the node again on each poll and waits for the selected workspace. In the other failure, the Java Project panel was already visible while the test waited for File Explorer. That scenario now selects Files explicitly before waiting for the tree. These are distinct from a failure to activate the desktop workspace during startup.

Disk-comparison tests exercise the production view model, adapter, controller and dialog. Controller regressions additionally verify that retained callbacks from an old workspace, tab, editor owner or unmounted interface refuse before disk inspection or language synchronization. A superseded comparison cannot authorize discard, and duplicate confirmation starts only one checkpoint and adoption. Pending language synchronization after adoption allows the dialog to close and a fresh comparison to open. The AppImage Java editing and template scenarios verify native draft restoration on X11 and KWin Wayland. These retirement and duplicate-dispatch interleavings are verified in process, separately from native GUI workflows. They cover read-only inspection without changing the save baseline, explicit discard, refusal after buffer/lifecycle/workspace changes, pending saves, snapshot authenticity, language synchronization, keyboard interaction and retention of unrelated dirty buffers. The native IPC boundary in these adapter tests is substituted. The native recovery scenario below exercises explicit disk comparison/discard before clean close, checking inspected text, clean buffers and unchanged source bytes. The three [native disk-comparison scenarios](features/workspace/native-editor-disk-comparison.feature) passed in a controlled fresh-build Linux GUI run. They verify Escape cancellation and retained companion edits, Save while a review is open making that review obsolete, and refusal to load its old disk text after saving. Cancelled inspection does not advance the save baseline. Explicit adoption uses the inspected snapshot, not a later external revision: subsequent Save refuses over that later write. A fresh comparison/adoption permits a new edit and ordinary Save. In the X11 asynchronous-adoption case, the fixture holds the application’s recovery journal lock to keep a real checkpoint in progress. It writes a newer source revision before releasing the lock, confirms that the inspected snapshot is loaded, and verifies that Save refuses to overwrite the newer disk revision. A separate deletion scenario reports inspection/save failure without recreating the source, and acknowledges both drafts before owned application termination. These checks use real pointer/keyboard input and native IPC, with independent source-byte checks; they do not qualify in-buffer editing during modal confirmation, automatic watching, merge or other operating systems.

The [passive external-change scenario](features/workspace/native-editor-external-changes.feature) has focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI acceptance. The current scenario changes an inactive open file with a same-length external write, observes its background notice while the companion remains active, and selects the affected tab through that notice. Both exact dirty buffers and independent source bytes remain intact. Reviewing and cancelling does not advance the save baseline: Save still refuses. Explicit adoption clears only the selected buffer and its warning; a subsequent explicit edit/Save does not produce a false external-change notice over a complete polling interval. External deletion of the active file automatically reports missing without recreating it, and a later Save retains both drafts. Only a deliberate external fixture recreation and explicit discard permit the final clean X11 close; cleanup confirms no surviving processes. Production-hook tests additionally cover rotating multiple background tabs, serialized inspections, late results after close/reopen, pruning closed tabs, background inspection failures and workspace retirement; component tests cover explicit selection from the notice. Those tests do not establish native behavior for larger tab inventories. No private Monaco access, injected IPC result or substituted filesystem tool drives the GUI acceptance. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-editor-external-changes-001:native`. The requirement remains `@partial`, outside the validated aggregate: recursive watching, background deletion in the GUI, transient changes, wider lifecycle/error cases, merge, other operating systems and installers remain unqualified.

Recovery tests exercise native private storage, source-byte preservation, workspace/session separation, corrupt journals, interrupted temporary writes, symlink refusal, retention limits and survival after an owned checkpoint worker is forcibly terminated. Native storage boundary tests additionally admit exactly 1 MiB UTF-8 and refuse one more byte without modifying the prior journal, preserve all owners at the 64-pending-draft limit, and reject content beyond 16 MiB without evicting drafts while trimming older history first. Malformed/truncated JSON, wrong schema/workspace binding, duplicate or invalid identities, traversal, excessive sequence and unknown fields refuse list/read/remove/checkpoint operations while retaining the invalid bytes and unchanged project sources. Restoring the exact valid bytes makes the issued checkpoint readable again. These are direct production-store tests, not GUI qualification of every boundary or physical disk exhaustion.

Frontend tests cover throttled/latest checkpoints, immediate pre-save capture, stale restore refusal, dirty-buffer restoration, language synchronization and explicit removal. Additional regressions keep initial inventory loading distinct from ready, retain a failed-draft warning after a successful inventory refresh, reject false success during pending writes, and revalidate a repaired journal on an explicit retry with no new drafts. The worker test uses production storage and real processes; it does not itself qualify the full Tauri application or hardware power loss.

A separate [native recovery scenario](features/workspace/native-editor-recovery.feature) has passed in two controlled runs, each using a freshly built Linux release/no-bundle executable and real Tauri/WebKit drivers. It edits a UTF-8 buffer through the keyboard, waits for both the UI acknowledgment and the persisted checkpoint, sends SIGKILL only to the observed owned executable, and launches a second GUI process with the same isolated workspace and storage. It verifies no automatic buffer restoration, cancel without source changes, explicit dirty-buffer restoration, retention of an unrelated dirty buffer and the original checkpoint, refusal of Save after an external disk write, and clean exit after explicit disk-version discard. Disk bytes are checked independently; the external fixture write is the only permitted source change. The first attempt failed because the test clicked Monaco's overlaid input proxy; the corrected test clicks its visible text surface and verifies focus, without weakening assertions or extending the runner deadline.

Run this focused acceptance with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-editor-recovery-001:native`. It has 19 authored steps; Cucumber also reports lifecycle hooks. The restart profile selects `@native-recovery-restart`, keeping its original one-scenario scope separate from the additional history/error profiles below. The recovery/history requirement retains `@partial` and remains outside the validated aggregate pending storage failures beyond the qualified bounded ENOSPC cases, broader GUI retention/corruption and lifecycle paths, and OS acceptance. A passing focused restart scenario is not power-loss, installer, OS-matrix or startup-reliability qualification and does not promote the existing Java/Kotlin declarations.

Additional [recovery scenarios](features/workspace/native-editor-recovery.feature) have passed in two controlled fresh-build Linux runs. The history scenario creates real acknowledged versions through editing and checkpoint commands, reviews both exact texts without replacing newer edits, restores the selected version while retaining its original entry and companion draft, refuses removal of the current draft, cancels removal without changing journal bytes, and deletes only the separately confirmed entry. DOM rows expose the provider-issued checkpoint identity so selection remains unambiguous even when filename, timestamp and byte length match.

The same history profile also qualifies the workspace-wide count limit in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI. It creates three acknowledged companion versions and 103 acknowledged source versions through native keyboard editing and explicit checkpoints. Once the limit is exceeded, the durable journal and visible active-file inventory retain exactly the newest 100 histories; earlier companion histories are removed before newer source histories, while both current drafts remain. The oldest and newest retained source histories can be reviewed and cancelled without replacing either draft. Explicitly restoring the newest retained version preserves the companion draft and saved source bytes. Both scenarios close normally without owned process survivors. This qualifies count-based history rotation for the tested two-file workspace, not the 64-pending-draft or 16 MiB workspace limits, other operating systems, or packaged applications.

The missing-source scenario terminates the owned IDE after acknowledgment, deletes the source externally, then restarts with the same storage. Review keeps the text available but disables replacement; real pointer/keyboard selection and copying are checked against the native X11 clipboard. It closes without recreating the source. This copying check additionally requires Python GTK 3 introspection on the Linux test host. The storage-access scenario temporarily renames the valid journal and obstructs its pathname with a directory, retaining the original private bytes. A newer checkpoint visibly fails while ordinary source Save still succeeds. Repairing the pathname and explicitly retrying restores ready status and leaves the earlier checkpoint selectable. This is a real filesystem access failure, not simulated IPC; it is not disk-full, retention-capacity, corruption or power-loss qualification.
