The [storage-full scenarios](features/workspace/native-editor-recovery.feature), run with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-editor-recovery-001:storage-full:native`, pass separately for source storage and recovery storage in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI. Each native driver and application runs with a private 1 MiB tmpfs mounted only at the selected scenario directory. A filesystem probe fills it until the kernel returns `ENOSPC`; it does not replace IDE commands, writes or results. With source storage full, explicit Save visibly fails, exact saved bytes and the dirty buffer survive, the acknowledged checkpoint remains readable and failed temporary saves are removed. Releasing space and retrying Save succeeds. With recovery storage full, a newer draft fails checkpointing without changing the previously acknowledged journal bytes or losing its buffer. Explicit source Save succeeds on the separate writable filesystem. After space is released, explicit checkpoint retry retains earlier history and clears the obsolete pending draft. Both cases restore their original source through the editor, close normally, restore their environment and leave no owned process survivors. The host disk is not filled. This qualifies these controlled Linux tmpfs cases, not quotas, inode exhaustion, network filesystems, power loss, post-publication durability errors, installers or other operating systems.

Cucumber separately reports lifecycle hooks. These checks use real release/no-bundle Tauri/WebKit GUI processes, not installers or substituted providers. Both controlled runs restore each scenario's environment/storage lease and leave zero sandbox process survivors after bounded cleanup. Comparison and recovery remain `@partial`; existing Java/Kotlin statuses are unchanged. The earlier unexplained File Explorer startup timeout remains an independent reliability investigation.

Two further [recovery scenarios](features/workspace/native-editor-recovery.feature), selected by `@native-recovery-capacity-corruption`, have passed in two controlled fresh-build Linux release/no-bundle runs. The capacity case starts with a 1 MiB UTF-8 source, creates real small checkpoints, then uses bounded keyboard Undo and typing to produce a buffer of 1,048,577 bytes but only 524,289 UTF-16 code units. The production adapter rejects it before checkpoint IPC; the visible failure retains the exact buffer, companion draft, issued original entry and prior journal bytes. Refresh cannot hide the failure. Explicit ordinary **Save** still succeeds; checkpointing the remaining valid companion returns recovery to ready and retains the earlier small source version as history. The capacity limit applies to recovery drafts, not to all source saves.

The corruption case terminates only the owned IDE after acknowledgment, then deliberately truncates its real issued journal while retaining the exact valid bytes, and restarts using the same storage. Startup reports unreadable recovery without overwriting the journal or restoring buffers. An explicit external fixture repair followed by **Checkpoint now**, with no dirty buffers, revalidates storage and presents the original issued draft without writing sources or the journal. A second truncation preserves dirty source/companion buffers through checkpoint failure and ordinary source Save; repair and retry acknowledge the companion while retaining the previous-session draft. Its exact review is cancelled without replacing the saved buffer. Corrupt-byte copies are retained for independent checks until isolated scenario cleanup; the product performs no automatic repair, quarantine or reset.

Large-buffer equality is checked through real Ctrl+A/C and the native GTK/X11 clipboard, not private Monaco getters or concatenated virtual viewport lines. Initial driver assertions mistook visual line segmentation for buffer newlines and assumed all word-grouped typing was one Undo operation; bounded real Undo groups and full clipboard comparison corrected those observations without relaxing byte equality or extending the native runner deadline. Python GTK 3 introspection is required. This qualification is specifically one-byte-over per-buffer admission and syntactically truncated journals: physical disk-full, all corruption families, workspace-wide pending-draft and retained-content GUI limits, power loss, other operating systems and installers remain separate. Recovery stays `@partial`, with existing validated aggregates and Java/Kotlin declarations unchanged.

The [native close-guard scenario](features/workspace/native-editor-close-guards.feature) has passed in two controlled runs on a freshly built Linux release/no-bundle executable. It edits two buffers using real keyboard input, introduces an external disk revision, and verifies that closing the conflicting tab, selecting another registered workspace and requesting the owned window close retain edits and show the expected refusal. The native close request is a genuine X11 `WM_DELETE_WINDOW` message to the unique IDE window belonging to the identity-checked application, not a signal, JavaScript event or WebDriver session deletion. A tab with a current save revision is saved before closing; explicitly adopting the conflicting disk version permits workspace switching and normal native close. Independent byte and registry checks preserve the external write, saved companion and destination sentinel.

A second close-guard scenario holds a genuine Linux write lease on the original source inode without modifying it. The already-acknowledged dirty tab then requests ordinary Close/Save; a real lease-break notification observes blocked source access. The person types newer text through the visible Monaco surface before explicitly releasing the lease. Independent disk/buffer checks establish that Save wrote only its earlier captured text while the newer exact buffer stayed dirty and open with a visible refusal; the unrelated dirty companion and its original disk bytes remain unchanged. Only a later explicit Save persists the newer text. Explicit companion discard permits genuine clean X11 close.

This test exposed native synchronous source I/O blocking the window thread: the initial real run timed out in the close-request step while the source lease was held. Moving native editor reads/writes to a four-slot blocking-worker pool corrected this path without changing the fifteen-second explorer or ninety-second native runtime deadlines. Rust tests separately exercise worker admission, release, error/panic handling and off-caller execution. The [lease observer](tests/story/support/native-source-file-lease.ts) uses Python's Linux `fcntl` support and refuses unsafe fixtures; its twelve-second fixture bound is below the host's kernel lease-break timeout. Admission requires filesystem/kernel lease support. This is held ordinary source-I/O/keyboard acceptance, not physical disk exhaustion, power loss, general worker cancellation, every close/confirmation race, an installer or another operating system. Original failure and later passing artifacts remain separate evidence.

The focused [native Java execution scenario](features/workspace/native-java-execution.feature) passes on a fresh Linux release/no-bundle build with JDK 21. It opens **Java Run** through the visible **Commands** palette entry, then verifies initially disabled untrusted actions, explicit trust, keyboard-edited source saved before Build, a real compiled class, successful Run with both console output and an application-written file, a visible compiler failure without executing the old class, opening its reported source line while preserving an unsaved repair, and Stop reaping the observed owned JVM. It checks executable/environment/start-time identity before observing cancellation, then closes the clean IDE through X11. Evidence records the compiled class-file version and effective runtime executable. This is plain-JDK Linux GUI evidence, not Maven/Gradle, JUnit, dependency-project, debugger or installer GUI qualification.

The focused **jdb debugger** profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:debugger`, has passed three Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios with selected OpenJDK 21. Each uses the actual Java Run controls to refuse untrusted Debug, save a keyboard edit, start with application code suspended, set and clear a source-line breakpoint, continue, inspect stack/locals/threads, evaluate an expression and step into/over/out of a method. Independent application-written files verify the exact application arguments, JVM property, environment and runtime JDK. A second caller step completes the returned-value assignment before the following source statement; newly appended console output distinguishes this from an earlier breakpoint or callee-local observation.

The completion case independently reads the expected result; the suspended Stop case leaves it absent. The third case sends SIGSTOP only to the identity-checked owned jdb process and fills its real input through repeated public Evaluate clicks. The visible queue-full refusal retains a responsive Stop action. All cases observe both debugger and debuggee PIDs gone before window close or runner cleanup, preserve the exact saved source, close normally through X11, release scenario leases and leave zero sandbox process survivors. The profile has 45 authored steps plus lifecycle hooks and retains the existing runtime deadline. These are jdb console controls, not structured JDI/DAP state or variable trees. Conditional JDI qualification is described separately below. Maven/Gradle debugger classpaths, remote attach, hot swap, other operating systems and installers remain separate qualification or implementation work; the native requirement stays `@partial`.

Production-controller tests separately reject captured debugger callbacks after workspace change, unmount or Stop and suppress a delayed old-session error after a new session starts. Opt-in Rust tests pass real jdb breakpoint/stack/locals/Stop and launch-setting checks with default GraalVM JDK 25; the latter also selects a different OpenJDK 21 installation explicitly. The **structured JDI debugger** profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:jdi`, has passed two fresh Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios with selected OpenJDK 21. Public controls refuse untrusted Debug, save a keyboard edit, launch suspended, set and verify a real source-line breakpoint, select the main and Reference Handler threads, inspect caller/callee frames, read local/object fields, paginate a 44-element array and add field/index watches. The bounded read-only evaluator handles numeric and boolean expressions, string and character values and literals, and concatenation of strings with primitive values. **Evaluate once** displays the typed result for the selected stop and frame while leaving the persistent watch set unchanged. A native watch and one-time evaluation both return `"ready:!7"` from string and character fields without invoking application conversion methods. One-time evaluation also locally evaluates holder.text.length() from a captured JDI String value; the native GUI case evaluates "" + holder.text.length() + holder.marker to "5!", `0x1_0 + 0b10` to `18`, `holder.values[base + 26]` to `33`, and `(byte) holder.number` to `7` with its `byte` result type. Numeric, computed-index and cast evaluations leave the persistent watch set unchanged. The expanded flow sets the breakpoint through a real Monaco glyph-margin click before Debug. Both cases restore the saved choice after a clean WebView reload. The completion case additionally closes the first native window normally and starts a new application process using the same scenario storage; the breakpoint and launch settings return while trust remains disabled. After a keyboard source edit, explicit review and **Rebind active file** update the choice without saving the source. Debug saves that text and loads the pending point before application code starts. The cases observe the verified glyph and selected-frame line at the breakpoint and during stepping, remove source markers on a later keyboard edit, and clear both the runtime breakpoint and saved choice through the margin. F9 against that changed text does not alter the breakpoint or disk file; **Retry source binding** retains the visible refusal. Restoring and explicitly saving the captured text restores the source association. A deliberately throwing application `toString` is never invoked; a requested method-call watch receives a visible refusal. Before selecting the caller frame, the scenarios enter `base = 99` without submitting it. The caller has an empty assignment field and disabled **Set local**; returning to the callee retains an empty field and the actual value `base = 7`. At the selected callee's return line, **Set local** changes `value` from 42 to 43; stepping out clears that submitted assignment, the caller shows 43 and the completed application writes and prints 43. Stepping reaches the expected callee, return, call site and completed assignment before the next source statement. Independent files verify the captured arguments, JVM property, environment, JDK and result.

The completion case exits normally. The other continues to the running application, pauses it through JDI, then sends SIGSTOP only to the identity-checked owned helper. Repeated public watch submissions fill the real input pipe; queue-full refusal leaves Stop responsive. Both cases observe helper and debuggee PIDs gone before window close or runner cleanup, preserve the saved source, close normally, release scenario leases and leave zero sandbox process survivors. The profile has two scenarios and 40 runtime steps including lifecycle hooks. The current verification uses a JDK 21 application/debugger and an explicitly selected JDK 25 JDT LS runtime on Linux. The runner allows 180 seconds overall for application restarts, inspections and the nonreading-helper case; individual step deadlines remain bounded. An earlier attempt reported a malformed LSP header during source-save preparation, before JDI started. A production-path characterization reproduces that symptom when the unmanifested JDT LS 1.63 distribution starts on JDK 21: its plain-text startup failure reaches protocol stdout. Bundle-derived runtime admission now refuses that incompatible selection before launch. This explains the reproduced configuration failure; other malformed-header causes still require their own diagnosis. These focused cases qualify initial JDI inspection, selected-local mutation, one-time bounded evaluation and Pause/Stop, not the full M4 debugger scope, build-tool debugger classpaths, installers or other operating systems.

The same structured JDI scenarios pass from a freshly built Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and in a private KWin 6.8 Wayland session with XWayland disabled. The application and debugger use JDK 21, and JDT LS runs on JDK 25. The normal case restores its source breakpoint after WebView reload and a full application restart, verifies frames, variables, stepping and the local mutation, and completes. The other case pauses the application, observes the debugger's full input queue and stops both JVMs from the IDE. Both cases preserve the explicitly saved source, close through the compositor and leave no surviving runner-owned processes. An earlier AppImage run refused Debug after WebView reload when a Java document was already synchronized. The native service now accepts an identical workspace, session, document version and content. A separate real JDT LS test verifies that conflicting versions and content are rejected.

The structured debugger AppImage also qualifies primitive local assignment on X11 and KWin Wayland. The person assigns an `Integer` to a `long` local, then attempts to assign that `long` to an `int` local and observes a refusal with the previous value preserved. The rest of the debugger session completes and the owned processes exit. Real JDI tests on JDK 21 and 25 cover additional primitive conversions, floating-point rounding, boolean unboxing, null refusal and exact writes to byte and short locals.

The **conditional JDI debugger** profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-execution-native-001:conditions`, has passed on a fresh Linux release/no-bundle application with selected JDK 21. An empty nonwritable cache whose process output does not explain the access failure remains an unknown cause. A complete writable cache yields an available effective context. The IDE preserves the primary refusal code and exact bounded provider message, with no effective context on failure and no raw path, URL or controlled secret from the build output in the message. Source inputs remain unchanged. The previous candidate without stack-trace collection fails the same initialized-lock check by returning an unknown cause. These are real-provider/native-service checks. Native GUI qualification is recorded separately below; standard installation and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-diagnostics` profile passes both Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios with the isolated diagnostic candidate, project JDK 21 and Gradle 9.8.1. Each starts with actual denied native-library cache locks or an empty offline cache. Evaluate Gradle displays the exact bounded provider refusal, including its reported cause, and publishes no effective or partial context. The message exposes no raw process path, URL or controlled secret printed by the build script. The person changes the cache through the form and explicitly evaluates again; a complete writable cache produces an available model and displays the resolved JUnit test dependency. No project class output is created, source/build inputs stay unchanged, both windows close normally and no sandbox processes survive. This qualifies the selected refusal-and-recovery panel workflows, not a standard installation, arbitrary Gradle failures, other cause categories or other operating systems.

The same Gradle refusal and recovery scenarios pass on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland with `LC_ALL=it_IT.UTF-8` in the IDE process, Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21 and the local RefactorKit 0.8.0/API 0.2 candidate containing the Gradle locale correction. The cache paths contain spaces and an accented character. The IDE receives `gradle.sync.cause.cachePermissionDenied` for the denied lock and `gradle.sync.cause.offlineDependencyUnavailable` for the empty offline cache. It displays the bounded provider messages, exposes no effective context on either refusal, and recovers after the person selects a writable populated cache. Both profiles preserve project inputs, produce no project classes and close without process survivors. On both display backends, the current AppImage also verifies **Edit Gradle user home** against a real cache permission refusal. The action reopens closed Gradle settings and focuses the path input. After the person changes it and explicitly evaluates again, Java Project clears the recovery action and obtains the dependency without compiling project sources. Controller and panel tests separately cover the provider’s cache read-only result and distinguish it from filesystem errors without a known location. The IDE daemon transport sets `LANG` and `LC_ALL` to `C.UTF-8`, so these package checks qualify the application running in an Italian locale. RefactorKit separately qualifies a daemon launched directly under an Italian locale.

Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-diagnostics:appimage` or `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-diagnostics:appimage:wayland` with the selected Gradle, JDK, populated dependency cache and candidate runtime. For the preparation scenario, set `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_REPOSITORY` to a local Maven repository containing JUnit 4.13.2 and Hamcrest 1.3. The fixture serves those artifacts on loopback and gives Gradle a separate empty cache. The Wayland profile uses the private compositor and clipboard tools described above.

The packaged replays also verify that the offline-dependency refusal shows recovery instructions, the cache-permission refusal omits dependency instructions, and successful reevaluation clears the instructions. The plugin-diagnostics candidate extends the same AppImage profile on X11 and KWin Wayland to a build declaring Spring Boot 4.1.2 with `apply false`. With Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21 and an empty cache, Java Project shows the distinct offline plugin resolution refusal and guidance without exposing plugin coordinates or repository URLs from the process output. Reevaluation with a populated cache publishes the project context and clears the guidance without compiling sources.

The Spring Boot plugin scenario also verifies **Open Gradle project terminal** for a nested project directory containing a space. The terminal form shows the selected directory and starts no shell before trust and **New terminal**. The test checks the resulting shell's working directory and closes the session before reevaluating the project.

The same diagnostics profile exercises **Prepare Gradle dependencies** on one Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland, with Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21 and a local RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate. A Java project in a nested directory initially refuses offline synchronization with an empty Gradle user home. After trust and explicit preparation in Java Run, the selected cache contains the JUnit and Hamcrest artifacts downloaded from a loopback Maven repository. With that repository stopped, another explicit evaluation publishes the effective context and shows the test dependency. Preparation and evaluation create no Java classes and preserve the project inputs. A subsequent real offline Gradle test succeeds, and each native session closes without surviving processes.

On the AppImage with the recovery actions in both activities, those scenarios verify that **Open Java Run for Gradle preparation** appears for the dependency and plugin refusal cases. The cold-cache scenario opens Java Run through the action and observes no download before trust or after trust alone. It returns through **Open Java Project** after preparation and explicitly evaluates the preserved project settings. The diagnostics profile and both six-module reference workflows pass on that AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland with the same RefactorKit runtime.

The composite preparation scenario starts with an empty cache and a Java project in a nested included build. After Java Run prepares the root composite, the test stops the loopback repository and evaluates the composite offline. Java Project shows the nested build identity and JUnit classpath before compilation. The subsequent qualified Gradle test task runs offline and produces a passing JUnit report. The diagnostics profile passes on the AppImage with Gradle 9.8.1 on X11 and KWin Wayland. The nested-build scenario also passes with Gradle 8.14.6 on X11. Separate real Gradle runs on both versions verify preparation of a composite with circular include references.

The focused TestNG preparation scenario passes on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland with Gradle 9.8.1, JDK 21 and the local RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate. It starts from an empty selected Gradle cache and verifies the dependency refusal and explicit trust. The loopback Maven repository temporarily returns HTTP 503. Java Run reports a failed preparation and withholds the synchronization shortcut. After repository recovery, a second explicit request starts a new preparation session on the same cache and fetches TestNG 7.10.2 and its runtime dependencies. After stopping the repository, Java Project shows TestNG on the effective test classpath and the fixture has no compiled source output. A subsequent explicit offline Gradle test produces a passing TestNG report. The project inputs remain byte-for-byte unchanged, and the native application exits without owned processes remaining. For this scenario, the local Maven repository must contain TestNG 7.10.2, SLF4J API 1.7.36, JCommander 1.82, jQuery WebJar 3.7.1 and the associated parent POMs.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:working-directory` profile passes both Maven and Gradle scenarios in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI, using the isolated RefactorKit r005 candidate, project/application/debugger JDK 21, configured JDT LS runtime JDK 25, Maven 3.9.11 and Gradle 9.8.1. Each six-module fixture begins without compiled project outputs and uses prepopulated dependency caches. The person edits and saves the Java source, synchronizes the project, selects `app/main` and enters a workspace-relative application directory containing spaces, an accent and a quote. Run and JFR read a relative resource and write independent Java/property/operating-system directory and JDK proofs. A fresh explicit synchronization precedes the new JFR launch because execution retired the prior context. JFR remains under the app module; Analyze recording displays actual event data. After the visible directory changes, completed-session Rerun retains its captured directory, creates another recording and preserves the first recording bytes. After fresh synchronizations, all three selected-module JUnit cases keep the module directory and JDI Debug starts suspended before continuing from the application directory. Source and build inputs are restored exactly through native editing and Save; both windows close and leave no sandbox processes. Gradle's populated user home must be writable by the native application. This qualifies these panel workflows on Linux, not arbitrary project layouts, active-process profiling Restart, installers or other operating systems.

Both six-module Maven and Gradle working-directory scenarios pass on X11 and in private KWin Wayland with XWayland disabled, using the same Linux x86-64 AppImage and local RefactorKit 0.8.0/API 0.2 distribution as the packaged project coverage tests, with JDK 21. The application reads exact multiline Unicode input, receives EOF and reports the selected working directory independently of the build tool. JFR saves its recording under the application module's `.ide/flight-recordings` directory, and Java Run opens the real event summary. A captured rerun retains the original directory and input setting despite form changes, creates a distinct recording and preserves the first recording bytes. Tests retain the module directory, and JDI Debug receives application input while Stop reaps a second JVM waiting for input. The IDE windows close normally and the process scan finds no remaining scenario processes. On X11, run `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaProjectWorkingDirectoryAppImageNativeGui`. For Wayland, run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:working-directory:appimage:wayland` with the Wayland clipboard tools and populated dependency caches.

The separate manual-path JFR regressions pass on JDK 21 and 25 for plain JDK, Maven and Gradle with a different application directory. Two real-JVM project-path cases retain a comma, accent and either a single or double quote in the recording destination. Native tests refuse JFR filename substitutions and unrepresentable quote combinations before launch. These tests cover the recording-path correction; they do not qualify arbitrary JFR settings or filesystem races.

Discovery and captured selection also pass through this native service on Maven and Gradle with selected JDK 21 and 25, starting without project compilation outputs. Discovery reports all three compiled JUnit methods without executing their bodies; selecting one executes only that method with the original JDK, JVM property and environment despite a different current configuration draft. Failed-test rerun passes after an explicit source repair, executes only the previously failed method and refuses withdrawn trust. Coverage verifies fresh passing tests and actual covered instructions and application-source lines. Maven additionally passes discovery and repeated execution with inherited custom output directories; alternate-profile coverage has selected JDK 25 verification. The missing-method Maven case reports failed task state with unavailable results even though the build tool exits zero. These checks qualify the production native service and real tools, not the corresponding module-context GUI workflows.

The focused synchronized-module GUI profiles, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:execution` for Maven and `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-execution` for Gradle, have passed on Linux with selected JDK 21 and 25, the real daemon and their six-module reference projects. Each case begins without application class output. A native unsaved keyboard edit survives metadata synchronization; Gradle evaluation is explicitly authorized and requests no compilation. Java Run then saves the edit before acquiring fresh metadata and compiling. The person selects app/main without assembling a dependency classpath; application output confirms the selected JDK, generated source and runtime-only dependency. The original source is restored and explicitly saved through the editor, and the native window closes with all original project inputs preserved and zero owned process survivors. The ordinary native runner deadline remains unchanged; earlier failed Gradle snapshot and decoder attempts are not counted as acceptance.

The focused synchronized-module wrapper profile, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:wrappers`, has passed two Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios with the real project-context daemon and selected JDK 21. The focused `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaProjectMavenCommandsNativeGui` and `javaProjectGradleCommandsNativeGui` profiles pass in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with selected JDK 21 and the isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate. The separate `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:custom-output` profile has passed on Linux with selected JDK 21 for both six-module Maven and Gradle projects. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-custom-source-set` profile has passed on Linux with a release/no-bundle GUI, JDK 21, Gradle 9.8.0 and a RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon advertising `project.context`. After Build, Run and discovery compile outputs, the GUI synchronizes project context before the next operation; Run also proves that a class from `integrationTest` is on the selected runtime classpath. A separate coverage profile also passes and exercises this duplicate-task fixture; it verifies the selected task, production JaCoCo report, measured `Runner.java`, and Monaco covered-line decoration. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-kotlin-dsl` profile has passed on Linux in the release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21, Gradle 9.8.0 and a RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon advertising `project.context`. Its Kotlin DSL fixture contains `:app` and `:library`, with `:app` depending on the library. After an explicitly saved source edit and authorized Gradle evaluation, the synchronized module selector includes `library / main`; Java Run selects `app / test` and runs `:app:test`. The fresh JUnit report contains one passing test, which verifies a Kotlin DSL configured JVM property and calls `Greeter` from the library. The GUI checks the task output and both modules’ compiled classes. All project inputs are preserved, the native window exits cleanly and no runner-owned processes remain. A separate offline Gradle run also passes this fixture. The dedicated `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-multimodule-coverage` profile also passes in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21 and Gradle 9.8.1: `:app:test` measures covered production lines in both `Runner.java` and `:library`'s `Greeter.java`, opens the uniquely mapped dependency source, and shows covered-line decorations in Monaco. Navigation requires an available synchronized context, a report module root that matches one provider-declared non-generated main source root, and the source buffer to be open and unchanged through the run. Generated roots are excluded even when the provider also lists them among ordinary roots. When those conditions cannot establish one source file, coverage remains visible but source navigation and decorations stay unavailable. This qualifies a conventional two-module Java dependency in one Gradle build. A separate one-included-build GUI scenario now proves provider-qualified project identity, Run, test discovery, one selected JUnit test and source-level Debug: the selector resolves `gradle/included-build :app`, Gradle 9.8 compiles `:app` and `:library`, and Run reports its marker under JDK 21. Discovery reports three compiled JUnit methods without running them; the GUI selects one method and verifies its captured JDK/test properties and environment. After a sync/evaluation following the test, the IDE reacquires the provider-qualified context, stops at a JDI source breakpoint in `Runner.java`, completes Debug and verifies the JVM exits. This qualifies the one-fixture included-build workflow for Run, selected-test discovery/execution, app-and-library coverage with source navigation, and Debug; broader included-build workflows remain unqualified. Other arbitrary Kotlin DSL semantics, larger module graphs, plugin combinations, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The mixed JVM profiles `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-mixed-jvm` and `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:maven-mixed-jvm` qualify the Linux release application before packaging with JDK 21, Kotlin 2.0.21 and the isolated RefactorKit review candidate. Gradle 8.10.2 uses `IDE_JAVA_MIXED_GRADLE_REPOSITORY` for a local Maven-format repository containing the Kotlin JVM plugin marker, compiler and transitive dependencies as regular files. Maven 3.9.11 uses a reactor with one application module. Set `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_REPOSITORY` to a local repository populated with its Kotlin Maven and Java compiler plugins, the Kotlin standard library and their transitive dependencies. The Maven proof uses offline execution and an Eclipse JDT LS installation selected through `IDE_JDTLS_HOME`. It uses JDK 25 for the language-server process and JDK 21 for the project.

The GUI synchronizes each project before it has compiled output. Java Run starts the selected Java main class with the effective runtime classpath. Java calls a Kotlin method that calls back into Java. The scenarios check the output and both compiler products. A second launch under JDI stops at a saved breakpoint in the Java callback, shows the Kotlin caller in the stack, highlights the Java execution line and completes after Continue. Both scenarios restore source and build inputs and close normally. Kotlin frame display establishes the location reported by the JVM. Kotlin editor breakpoints and other operating systems remain unqualified for these fixtures.

Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:mixed-jvm:appimage` to build one fresh Linux x86-64 AppImage and exercise both scenarios from that package. The controlled X11 run uses the AppImage extraction-and-run mode and the same external Gradle, Maven, JDK, JDT LS and RefactorKit installations. It covers the Gradle definition and rename checks and the Maven context resynchronization described below. Installer and update behavior require separate verification.

On the compiled Gradle fixture, an older provider returned an empty successful definition result for the Kotlin type and its static method. A RefactorKit 0.8.0 review candidate returns `java.definitionKotlinSourceUnqualified` for both queries and still resolves the Java control declaration. The Linux Gradle GUI profile verifies that F12 displays the same reason on the Kotlin method call, preserves the current source, and reveals the exact declaration of a Java method from another call in the same file. Opening the Kotlin declaration from Java requires a qualified source mapping from RefactorKit. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-kotlin-definition` profile verifies that mapping with the isolated capability-advertising RefactorKit 0.8.0 review candidate, Gradle 8.10.2, Kotlin compiler 2.0.21 and JDK 21. Configure the compiler paths from section 6.6 and use the same external tools and offline repository as the mixed JVM Gradle profile. After Run has compiled both languages, F12 opens the real `Greeter.kt` buffer at the saved type and method declarations. The GUI scenario then saves a Kotlin method change that shifts its declaration while leaving the compiled class file untouched. F12 reports `java.definitionKotlinBinaryDrift` and keeps the Java source open. Run recompiles both languages, the application prints the changed result, and F12 opens the method at its new line after synchronization. The native Linux release application and Linux x86-64 AppImage both restore source inputs and close without surviving owned processes. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-kotlin-definition:appimage` for the same scenario from a fresh package on Linux X11. The workflow uses the isolated provider and explicitly configured compiler files. The package does not supply those tools. A direct saved-source RefactorKit rename preview also reported low risk and edited only the Java declaration when the Kotlin source called it. Applying the diff to a disposable copy caused `compileKotlin` to fail on the original method name. The original source stayed intact. A separate RefactorKit 0.8.0 review candidate refuses the same saved-source member rename on compiled Gradle and Maven fixtures with `java.renameMember.kotlinConsumerClosureUnavailable`. Direct daemon calls confirm that the refusal returns no plan and leaves both Java and Kotlin sources unchanged. The Gradle native GUI profile also opens Review Java Member Rename from the cursor. The editor draft-preview route displays the reason supplied by RefactorKit, keeps Apply disabled, and preserves the project files and clean editor buffer. It then synchronizes again and completes Debug. On Maven, a fresh daemon can complete cursor selection and refuse the draft preview for the same reason. In the native post-Run workflow, the provider can report a changed snapshot at context verification or cursor selection before preview, even though project file contents stay unchanged while opening the review. The last successful context recorded the test output directory as missing, and a copy captured during the refusal contained that empty directory. An instrumented run observed the JDT LS process create it during Maven project import. The native Maven scenario starts JDT LS, synchronizes against a fixture with no test output directory, and creates the empty directory before requesting Preview. The IDE reports the changed project inputs and keeps Apply disabled. After explicit synchronization, the editor preview reaches RefactorKit and shows the Kotlin-consumer refusal. Both attempts preserve the source files and buffer, and the scenario completes Debug and closes normally. Release adoption, cross-language navigation and complete rename coverage remain in the [mixed Java and Kotlin backlog](#145-missing-capabilities-by-language).

The focused Maven and Gradle project-debugger scenarios in `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:debugger` have passed in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with selected JDK 21, a capable `project.context` daemon and the six-module reference projects. Both begin without application class output. Maven keeps an unsaved editor draft through metadata synchronization and saves it when Debug begins. Gradle explicitly saves its draft before the separately authorized metadata evaluation, so the evaluated project snapshot includes the source that Debug will compile; evaluation requests metadata only. In both cases JDI suspends at entry, then stops at the saved `pkg.Runner` breakpoint before the application dependency-output statement. Continuing confirms generated and runtime-only dependencies and the selected JDK. Each debuggee exits with code zero, its owned process disappears, the temporary PID file is removed, and original project inputs remain intact after normal IDE close. During the suspended source breakpoint, both GUIs show the synchronized module's provider-suggested `pkg.Runner.class` output, select that suggestion and successfully HotSwap the running class; the Gradle native story now requires a real project-output suggestion instead of accepting manual entry. These scenarios qualify the selected modules and runtime classpaths in their reference projects; other Gradle settings, installers and operating systems remain unqualified.

The focused module-test GUI commands are `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:discovery`, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:coverage`, `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-multimodule-coverage` and `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:rerun`, selecting separate scenarios from the [native project-context requirement](features/refactorkit/native-java-project-context.feature). Discovery, coverage and failed-test rerun pass with Maven and Gradle reference projects in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI. The tests use visible controls to synchronize app/main, save source edits before the build operation when required, and run the selected module without seeded compilation outputs. Discovery reports compiled test methods without executing their bodies; selecting a method runs only that method with the captured JDK, test JVM property and environment despite later form changes. Coverage reports measured application instructions and source lines. Its Maven scenario opens a measured `Runner.java` line, verifies cursor navigation and observes a Monaco coverage decoration. The Gradle scenario opens measured `Runner.java`, follows a covered line and verifies a Monaco decoration when the available project context yields a unique source mapping; source-mapping tests verify that partial context refuses navigation. A further Gradle scenario selects `app / integrationTest`, runs the mapped `:app:integrationTest` task and confirms that JaCoCo reports covered lines from production `Runner.java` without presenting `IntegrationRunnerTest.java` as production code; the GUI also opens that source and checks its covered-line decoration. It passes with JDK 21, Gradle 9.8.1 and the available `project.context` provider. The dedicated Gradle Kotlin DSL scenario also passes: a selected `:app:test` run reports covered production lines for the app and its local Java `:library` dependency. This limited two-module case does not qualify larger module graphs. A separate included-build GUI scenario maps coverage for both the selected app and its library, opens `Greeter.java`, and verifies covered-line decoration; partial or ambiguous source contexts still suppress source links and decorations. The failed-test rerun starts with a real failure, opens the reported `RunnerTest` at its failing line, repairs it in Monaco and saves it. For Gradle, ordinary synchronization refreshes the saved-source context using the retained evaluation receipt; build-file changes still require explicit evaluation. Maven reuses its synchronized context. Visible test-setting changes do not alter the JDK or environment captured by the failed run; only the failed method runs again, and the reported test location opens in the editor. Native clipboard reads verify the edited source. Each case restores its fixture inputs and exits with no runner-owned process survivors. This qualifies selected JUnit 4 module-test workflows on Linux release/no-bundle builds; the separate JUnit Jupiter module-test GUI qualification below covers one passing test for each build tool. Broader frameworks, larger multi-module graphs, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

All six synchronized project coverage scenarios pass on X11 and in private KWin Wayland with XWayland disabled, using the same Linux x86-64 AppImage and RefactorKit 0.8.0/API 0.2 distribution as the Maven recovery profile, with JDK 21. In both Maven and Gradle reference modules, selecting a measured JaCoCo line opens the exact line in `Runner.java` and Monaco displays coverage decoration. Both build tools also pass the workspace-root scenarios described in section 6.3. The custom Gradle `integrationTest` scenario measures and opens production source when two tasks share the compiled test output and only one uses the selected source set's runtime classpath. The Gradle Kotlin DSL scenario separately measures application and local library code and waits for the coverage decoration on the selected library editor. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:testng` profile passes two Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios with selected JDK 21 and the capable `project.context` daemon, one using Maven and one Gradle. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:mixed-engines` profile passes two Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenarios with selected JDK 21 and the capable `project.context` daemon, one using Maven 3.9.16 and one Gradle 9.8.1. Other engine combinations, broader module layouts, coverage, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The project-context consumer has separate production-path verification. Adapter and React controller tests cover ordered classpaths, partial/unavailable responses, snapshot and SDK correlation, source ownership, cancellation, changed settings and stale workspace results. Native guard tests cover capability admission, path/SDK/profile validation and honest partial/refused outcomes. The opt-in Rust test `real_refactorkit_project_context_reads_maven_modules_sources_scopes_and_refuses_stale_evidence` has passed with the newly built RefactorKit daemon providing `project.context`, real offline Maven, the six-module reference project and selected JDK 21. It also passes the actual native/provider response through the TypeScript decoder, resolves secondary main and same-path test types, refuses a changed POM with obsolete evidence and preserves original inputs. Set `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON` to that capable launcher and run it with `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml --lib real_refactorkit_project_context -- --ignored --test-threads=1`; the test defaults to JDK 21 and accepts `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_JDK` for another full JDK. This is native-library/provider verification, not GUI or installer acceptance.

Java project-input tracking distinguishes source edits from build inputs, including Gradle applied scripts, catalogs and lockfiles plus Maven wrapper/configuration metadata; generated outputs, caches and unrelated files are excluded. Source edits retire the semantic context but retain the evaluated Gradle receipt; build-input edits invalidate both. Rust tests cover classification, invalidation, debounce ordering, and a real host filesystem watcher that observes source and POM changes while ignoring a README edit. Tauri-adapter tests validate event workspace, generation, project path, watcher identity and optional change classification. Controller tests cover source-only read refresh, build-change and legacy manual fallbacks, workspace/cancellation/write guards, paused monitoring and language-setting cleanup. A full context synchronization first retires its previous watcher; queued events are accepted only when their watcher identity and captured project snapshot still match the active context. Rust tests cover this supersession boundary. Together with the focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI stories above, this verifies the bounded native workflow; packaged application behavior and watcher behavior on Windows and macOS remain unqualified. Initial synchronization and build-script evaluation remain explicit user actions; classified source-only changes can refresh saved-source context through the guarded read-only path in section 6.11. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:external-source-editor-diagnostics` profile passes Maven and Gradle reference scenarios in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21 and the isolated Maven-input-evidence provider. Changing a closed saved Java source updates automatic compiler errors under a new snapshot while two open Java drafts remain unchanged. The provider trace contains no additional Gradle synchronization, and a real counter in the Gradle build script confirms that source refresh does not re-evaluate it. Explicit cleanup restores the fixture inputs, the windows close normally and no runner-owned processes survive. Larger projects, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified for this refresh flow.

Saved formatting, import organization and class rename pass Apply, independent builds of source copies and rollback in the six-module Maven Linux GUI with selected JDK 21. The IDE disables JDT output-folder cleaning through a private [Eclipse plug-in customization file](https://help.eclipse.org/latest/topic/org.eclipse.platform.doc.isv/reference/misc/runtime-options.html) loaded before project import. The preference `org.eclipse.jdt.core.builder.cleanOutputFolder=ignore` preserves build-tool output even when m2e requests an explicit clean build; autobuild remains disabled. Private configuration bytes are checked before launch, and altered configuration is refused. The GUI regression compares existing compiled classes and copied resources across language-service configuration and synchronization before admitting the refactoring workflow. Both ordinary and instrumented runs preserve all original output contents. Runtime instrumentation also observes the JDT clean path executing without deleting those output files. This qualifies the conventional six-module Maven fixture with JDT LS 1.63 on Linux, not arbitrary project preference overrides, Gradle output layouts, persisted-state migrations, packaged applications or other operating systems. Snapshot admission remains unchanged and still refuses genuine project changes.

Applying verified Gradle preview options now checks the selected JDT compiler independently of the JVM that runs JDT LS. A private, bounded Java helper calls the public [JavaCore.latestSupportedJavaVersion API](https://help.eclipse.org/latest/topic/org.eclipse.jdt.doc.isv/reference/api/org/eclipse/jdt/core/JavaCore.html#latestSupportedJavaVersion()); its result is retained for the active language-service session. The requested preview release must match that compiler release, because [Eclipse supports preview features only for its latest supported Java release](https://help.eclipse.org/latest/topic/org.eclipse.jdt.doc.user/tasks/task-using_batch_compiler.htm). An incompatible compiler or failed capability probe refuses the setting change with an explanation. The server JVM still has to satisfy the bundle runtime requirements, but matching its version to the project preview release is no longer used as evidence of compiler compatibility. Real native-library probes on the same JDK 25 runtime report compiler release 26 for the selected JDT LS 1.61 distribution and 27 for the derived JDT LS 1.63 distribution; unit tests cover exact-release admission and malformed or ambiguous probe output.

The focused `javaGradlePreviewNativeGui` profile passes on Linux in the release/no-bundle application with `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_GRADLE_PREVIEW_RELEASE=27`, Gradle 9.6.1 running on JDK 21, an explicitly selected JDK 27 Java toolchain, derived JDT LS 1.63 running on JDK 25, and the isolated RefactorKit candidate. The project declares its Java toolchain and disables automatic JDK discovery and downloads. Before explicit context evaluation, JDT LS reports the preview-feature mismatch; the real Gradle build compiles the preview source. The IDE then applies the provider-verified preview option and clears that diagnostic. An unrelated missing-type error must appear in an unsaved editor draft after application, and the original draft is restored without saving. Project source and build inputs stay unchanged, the native window closes normally and no owned process survives. Gradle 9.6.1 itself fails to configure a minimal project when run on this JDK 27 with an unsupported class-file-version error; the qualified workflow uses the separate runtime and toolchain described above. Earlier Java 21 and Java 25 GUI runs established setting application and disappearance of the preview diagnostic without the unrelated-error control; they do not establish working diagnostics with the currently selected compiler. The separate per-document availability check covers imported compiler options when Java documents are validated; the Gradle application guard still protects changes to verified settings.

Controller regressions separately reject language-setting callbacks after cancellation, context retirement, reacquisition with the same hashes, workspace changes and unmount; they also reject late results and schema/project/hash mismatches. The App and adapter tests preserve the current-context integration. These interleavings are verified in process, not forced cancellation during native application. Packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The focused `javaProjectScaffoldNativeGui` profile has passed on Linux X11 with a release/no-bundle desktop. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:scaffold` with `IDE_JAVA_27_HOME` set to JDK 27 and the Maven and Gradle offline cache variables set to populated local directories. Its native scenario creates Maven Java 8 and Java 27 starters and Gradle Groovy DSL and Kotlin DSL starters through the Java Project wizard, refuses duplicate Maven and Groovy project folders without changing their contents, refreshes the project tree, and verifies that project creation itself produces no build output and that synchronization requires an explicitly selected JDK. The latest harness run uses offline Maven 3.9.16 with JDK 25 and Gradle 9.8.1 with JDK 25 to build, test and launch the GUI-created Java 8 Maven single-module project, Java 21 Gradle Groovy two-module project and Java 21 Gradle Kotlin DSL single-module project. It also builds and runs the Java 27 Maven starter and both Java 27 Gradle DSL starters with JDK 27. All seven generated JUnit test cases pass and each application prints its expected greeting. The Gradle starters pin JUnit Platform Launcher 1.10.2 to match JUnit Jupiter 5.10.2. The harness verifies that the GUI-created Java 27 Maven starter and both Java 27 Gradle DSL starters compile offline with JDK 27, pass their JUnit test, emit class-file major version 71 and print their greetings. These are real build-tool checks of the wizard output; they do not exercise effective project synchronization through RefactorKit. A separate opt-in real-tool qualification calls the production scaffold generator for Java 27 and builds, tests and runs all six single- and multi-module Maven, Gradle Groovy and Gradle Kotlin DSL starter shapes; every project emits Java 27 class files and its JUnit tests pass. The updated GUI scenario now also passes with checks for generated Maven and Gradle wrapper files, checksum pins and launcher variants; the application closes cleanly and runner-owned process cleanup reports no survivors. Separate opt-in Rust tests run the generated wrappers with empty, isolated tool caches. For Gradle, JDK 21 selects 8.14.6 for a Groovy starter and JDK 25 selects 9.8.0 for a Kotlin DSL starter; both wrappers download the pinned distributions, verify their configured checksums, build the project, pass its JUnit test and run the application. For Maven, JDK 21 runs the generated `mvnw` against an isolated distribution home and artifact repository; it downloads Maven 3.10.0, verifies the pinned distribution checksum, passes the JUnit test and launches the compiled application. An opt-in production-boundary test passes Maven Java 27 preview import through the pinned JDT LS 1.63 build with server and project JDK 27: JDT LS applies source/compliance 27 and preview enabled, reports zero Java errors for the pattern-switch fixture, preserves source and exits cleanly. The matching Gradle 9.8.1/JDK 27 test confirms Gradle compiles the same preview source while JDT LS initially imports preview disabled and reports one diagnostic. The Linux native Gradle preview scenario clears this mismatch after RefactorKit supplies complete preview compiler facts for its Java 21 fixture. An initial native attempt did stop at that refusal because it requested generic `project.context` before Gradle evaluation. After explicit Gradle evaluation, the candidate provides an attested metadata-only `project.context.v7`, and the focused native GUI story in section 11 verifies that Java 27 Gradle `--enable-preview` reaches JDT LS and clears its initial diagnostic. Java 27 source analysis remains unqualified. The separate wrapper tests qualify first-use wrapper execution through the production scaffold generator on Linux. The native wizard scenario qualifies actual Java 27 Maven build, test and application execution through the installed Maven tool; it does not qualify Java Project synchronization through RefactorKit. A separate Maven smoke check also verifies checksum validation and distribution extraction using a local archive behind a test downloader. Existing checks qualify generated project builds and launches on Linux; they do not qualify project synchronization, packaged applications or other operating systems, and broader Java project import workflows remain incomplete.

On the Linux x86-64 AppImage, the Spring Boot Maven starter passes an IDE-driven creation, test and run workflow on X11 and KWin Wayland with JDK 21 and a local RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime. The Spring Boot Gradle Groovy and Kotlin DSL starters also pass on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland with JDK 21 and a local RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime. The [native Java language-intelligence scenario](features/workspace/java-language-service.feature) passes on one Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland. The managed JDT LS 1.63 `idecompact1` installer passes in an empty Linux user data directory with the pinned upstream downloads. Verification checks the derived compiler and launcher configuration. The Java project-model controller and panel are implemented: the controller gates scan/symbols on the provider's advertised capability and authorized workspace, builds a bounded outline from RefactorKit's returned symbols, preserves honest unavailable/error states, and routes selected source locations through guarded Java navigation. Production controller, panel and adapter tests cover this path, and the focused project-model story harness drives the production controller and Tauri adapter through a deterministic in-process provider boundary. A Linux release/no-bundle Maven GUI profile with RefactorKit 0.7.0 refreshes live engine scan/symbols output, verifies the reported `pkg.Runner` source location in the panel, and uses those rows for class move, rollback and referenced-delete refusal; the updated Maven scenario also verifies that a POM-referenced type remains unchanged with Apply disabled. It also opens a class from the outline and verifies that its tab follows the moved source path and returns to the original path on rollback; the project-context GUI profile separately verifies navigation to an engine-reported location. On the larger Maven reference reactor, the Linux release/no-bundle native GUI with the source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon now moves `pkg.MigrateToLibrary` from the app module into the existing `fixtures.library` package in its dependency module, updates the app reference, passes offline `mvn -o verify` on an applied-source copy (three tests, no failures), then rolls back the exact inputs and open tab. The GUI exits cleanly. This qualifies the existing-package cross-module class move for this Maven fixture and daemon build; new target packages, other project layouts, released packages and other operating systems remain open. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:gradle-project-model` scenario separately evaluates a real Gradle project, refreshes the same panel from the engine symbols command, and verifies the Gradle `pkg.Runner` location while preserving an unsaved Maven draft and project inputs; the Linux native window closes normally without process survivors. A separate Gradle `moveClass` story now verifies v3 context attestation, Apply, an offline test on an applied-source copy, rollback and clean GUI exit. Broader project layouts, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified, so [the Java project-model requirement](features/refactorkit/java-project-model.feature) remains `@partial`.

Selected Maven repository propagation to JDT LS has component-level verification. Rust tests check that the native service supplies the Maven user-settings path, preserves the default user's mirrors, proxy/server settings and credentials while changing only `localRepository`, rejects malformed settings and paths, restricts the generated file on Unix, and removes it on session cleanup. Adapter and React tests confirm the selected repository in session status and restart the service when project settings change. These checks do not run the selected-repository flow through the native GUI or establish equality of the providers' resolved dependency graphs; package and cross-platform behavior remain unqualified.

The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001` command selects the real GUI project-context scenario. Set `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_DAEMON`, `IDE_JAVA_HOME`, `IDE_JDTLS_HOME`, `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_GRADLE_JDK`, `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TEST_GRADLE`, `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_MAVEN_REPOSITORY` and `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_GRADLE_USER_HOME` to the capable daemon, installed language server, selected SDKs, Gradle executable and populated offline dependency caches. The native runner adds the configured Gradle executable directory to the isolated application `PATH`. For JDT LS 1.63.0, set `IDE_JDTLS_JAVA_HOME` to a full JDK 25 or newer; this server runtime is independent of the selected project JDK. The IDE builds the Maven reference outputs before launch; RefactorKit does not manufacture them. The Linux X11/Tauri/WebKit release/no-bundle scenario with Maven 3.9.16 verifies six Maven modules, generated roots, distinct classpath scopes, project-model navigation to the reported line, unsaved-draft preservation, and separate main/test source ownership. It compiles a new test source after context acquisition, verifies that changed compiled output makes old ownership evidence stale, explicitly synchronizes the project again, and resolves ownership under the refreshed context. A changed POM is refused. Gradle first remains partial without executing a build; a separate explicit evaluation then enables effective module and ownership queries. A complete native run with selected Maven JDK 27 and Gradle JDK 25 switches JDT LS between those SDKs, confirms the restart and retained draft, refuses navigation with the former context, and opens the exact inherited declaration from an unsaved caller through F12. The v2-schema navigation path is also verified in the release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21 selected for both project contexts; after switching from Gradle back to Maven, F12 opens the same inherited declaration while retaining the unsaved caller. A separate complete Linux release/no-bundle run with JDT LS 1.61 and JDK 21 passed all 34 steps, including Maven module and classpath checks, main/test source ownership, stale-context retirement and reacquisition, explicit Gradle evaluation, and inherited F12 navigation. Monaco reports the reveal as complete only after the target model and buffer are current and the caret remains stable; later mouse or keyboard movement ends automatic restoration. Source and build inputs remain preserved and the window exits normally. This run used a daemon built from the current dirty RefactorKit checkout and does not qualify the pinned JDT LS 1.62/JDK 25 pairing, a clean RefactorKit build or release, an installer, or another operating system; the wider requirement remains `@partial`.

Configured-context navigation has passed the production native service and TypeScript/controller tests separately. Real Maven reference projects built with selected JDK 21 and 25 resolve the inherited integer method to its library-module declaration; the native project-context story also passes with Maven JDK 27 and Gradle JDK 25. The production service refuses another SDK, changed Maven profiles and a stale POM with the previous context. With JDK 25 and the source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon, the Linux release/no-bundle library-navigation GUI profile passed twice consecutively across Maven and Gradle projects and saved and dirty editor frames. Each case resolved the exact overload and source, kept dependency tabs read-only, preserved the dirty editor draft where applicable, and closed the native application without forced termination; sandbox cleanup found no surviving processes. This qualifies the exercised layouts and provider build on Linux only. Broader dependency/project configurations, a released RefactorKit build, refactoring mutation authority and another operating system remain unqualified.

SDK-bound immutable Java navigation has passed the real native application service with selected JDK 21 and 25 on the six-module Maven reference project. An unsaved caller selects the String overload instead of the saved integer call, an independently modified declaration supplies its dirty source/range, and references include captured caller text. The separate native Java language-intelligence scenario described in section 10.1 qualifies JDT LS diagnostics, completion with same-document import edits, hover, signature help, and references with guarded call-site navigation for one basic Java project; it preserves saved source and discards its temporary drafts. Gradle saved-source formatting preview, Apply and rollback session sharing has separate native-library qualification in section 10.1.

The [native cursor-navigation profile](features/refactorkit/native-java-cursor-navigation.feature) passes on Linux against a two-module Maven reactor (`app` depends on `core`). The focused native GUI profiles `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:drafts` and `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:draft-imports-rename` now also pass against the source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 daemon and a real Maven fixture. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:project-model` for the native Java Project class-operation scenario. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:gradle-cross-module-class-move:appimage` profile qualifies a separate Gradle move using the same AppImage and RefactorKit candidate. Explicit Gradle synchronization and shared-session consumption have real native-library verification with selected JDKs 21 and 25. The opt-in test `real_refactorkit_gradle_context_shares_evaluation_with_source_queries_and_editor_preview` builds a two-module Gradle fixture with release 17, then checks that ordinary context acquisition performs no evaluation. The explicit action yields an effective context; source inspection, dirty String-overload definition and cursor method-rename preview reuse it without another build evaluation. Actual context, navigation and preview responses pass the production TypeScript decoders and document-content verification. Changed project properties, changed build inputs and retired sessions refuse old authority; session loss returns partial metadata without executing Gradle automatically. A saved-source change can refresh the current snapshot without another evaluation or modification of the original provider synchronization result. The test also submits a read-only definition request against a source snapshot invalidated by a saved edit: the query is refused, semantic authority is retired, and the same daemon and evaluated model remain available for ordinary synchronization. A changed build descriptor is tested through a read-only request as well; retaining the daemon must not make the obsolete build model available. The build-script evaluation marker stays unchanged until the explicit recovery action. These source-refusal recovery cases have separate Gradle 9.8.1 verification with JDKs 21 and 25 against the isolated r005 candidate. The test also covers saved-source formatting and cross-module class-rename preview, Apply and rollback in the retained session. The renamed library type and application caller compile with the selected JDK using `javac --release 17`; rollback restores the original source bytes. Session identity remains unchanged and the build-script evaluation marker does not advance during either mutation. The shared source-inspection and refactoring cases have passed with real Gradle 9.8 and selected JDKs 21 and 25 using the capable RefactorKit daemon. The editor-owned transaction bridge has passed direct native qualification with the capable packaged RefactorKit provider and selected JDK 21 and 25. Changed captured versions, saved-source drift, unreviewed plans and repeated file application are refused. The Maven class-rename case stops and reopens the daemon, discovers the persisted transaction, refuses unknown editor content without edits and restores the original draft through recovery. Gradle retains its explicit evaluation without automatic repeat execution; restart recovery with renewed Gradle evaluation remains unqualified. Production editor-store, view-model, orchestration and adapter tests separately verify atomic buffer/tab changes, save-revision transfer, no Save calls, bounded overlays and unknown confirmation handling. These direct native/provider and in-process buffer checks do not qualify the application dialog, native GUI mutation, process interruption during partial multi-file moves, installers or another operating system.

Java batch cleanup is implemented as one reviewed saved-source plan. **Review Java Cleanup** in Commands, or `batch-cleanup` in Java Refactor, lets the person select 2–16 distinct workspace-relative Java files and choose formatting or import organization for each file. The file selector reuses the bounded workspace file search and offers distinct Java paths within the selected project directory. Search errors, incomplete directory traversal and result limits are visible. Late responses after a new query, workspace or project change, or the start of review cannot change the selection. Paths can also be entered directly. File discovery does not establish semantic ownership: every file must belong to the selected synchronized project; the first selected file anchors the review. RefactorKit owns the transformations and diagnostics. The IDE rejects drafts, missing project authority, file aliases, unsupported actions and plans whose edits or reported affected files differ from the selection. Apply retains the exact ordered actions, SDK and saved snapshot; it never falls back to editor overlays or the legacy CLI. Nested intent is copied independently from UI state and adapter requests. Rollback uses the existing guarded transaction route. RefactorKit refuses the whole batch for overlapping, unsupported, high-risk or no-op constituents.

The r005 consumer has contract, UI-selection, controller and adapter tests, plus native production-service acceptance with real RefactorKit, JDK 21 and offline Maven. The service cases review and apply import organization to two selected files, compile the reactor, roll back exactly, and refuse changed selections, SDK/profile identities and later edits. The UI accepts mixed per-file action choices and freezes the reviewed selection. Component tests also cover project-directory filtering, duplicate results, partial and truncated search results, failed searches, keyboard cancellation, stale responses and workspace/project/review changes. Both the Maven and Gradle native GUI scenarios select their second file through the production workspace search before reviewing the mixed batch. The focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI profile passes with selected JDK 21 and the isolated r005 package: the Commands action opens the selection, duplicate paths are refused without changing source, and explicit synchronization precedes the valid mixed import/format review. Apply edits exactly the two selected files, an applied-source copy passes offline Maven verification, and Rollback restores every original input and the clean open buffer. The window closes normally, scenario settings are restored, no owned processes remain, and the package stays unchanged. An earlier attempt refused a changed snapshot before preview; the strict comparison remains in place and synchronization is explicit. The r005 capability catalog leaves batch formatter profile support undisclosed. The IDE refuses batches containing formatting while a workspace profile is selected on that runtime and directs the person to individual formatting. Import-only batches remain available. The existing batch-cleanup backlog tracks provider discovery. Run the focused Maven Linux release/no-bundle profile with `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:batch-cleanup`. The paired `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:gradle-batch-cleanup` profile also passes with r005, Gradle 9.8.1 and selected JDK 21. It explicitly builds the synchronized Gradle app, verifies the materialized annotation-processor source and class-file major version 61 for the project target 17, and reacquires the context before preview. The valid mixed batch uses an attested v3 context, applies exactly the selected source edits, passes offline Gradle tests on a copy, and rolls back the original inputs and clean editor buffer. The native window closes normally with restored scenario settings, no owned processes and an unchanged provider package. The isolated provider candidates for a selected batch formatter profile have upstream packaged-daemon tests. Independent live probes of both the initial candidate and its successor confirm that their Java refactoring advertisement remains identical to r005. The successor also passes independent production-service acceptance through the IDE with selected JDK 21 and 25 for the existing import-only batch path: Apply, offline Maven verification, exact Rollback and refusal of stale selection, SDK/profile identity and later edits. The package files remain unchanged. These service tests do not qualify the successor in the native GUI or admit its formatter-profile extension. The IDE consumer admits the selected profile for a saved batch containing formatting only when one live `batchCleanup` capability row advertises `features.formatterProfile=true`. Preview must attest the exact XML path, profile name and hash, and Apply checks the reviewed hash against the current saved XML. The local 0.8.0 reference package lacks this feature flag and retains the batch-profile refusal. Import-only cleanup continues to omit the formatter profile. The native qualification profile, `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaBatchFormatterProfileAppImageNativeGui`, passes on Linux x86-64 X11 and KWin Wayland with the same AppImage and a RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate that advertises the feature. It selects Team Java in Settings, finds the second file through workspace search, verifies the provider attestation and matching Apply approval, and confirms the selected style in the saved source. Offline Maven and Gradle builds pass on applied-source copies. Rollback preserves an external edit on refusal and restores the original inputs exactly after explicit retry. Both sessions close without leaving owned processes. Add `--wayland` to replay the profile on Wayland. Default installed-provider behavior, complete cleanup/style coverage, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The focused `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaConstructorReferencesNativeGui` profile separately passes Add Parameter with a constructor reference in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI, using selected JDK 21/release 17 and the isolated corrected RefactorKit candidate.
