The adaptation option starts unchecked and is explicitly selected. The reviewed plan adds the argument to the constructor and direct call, replaces the reference with a lambda that retains the functional-interface arity, and preserves the boolean overload and its call. A distinct fresh applied-source copy passes offline Maven `verify`; exact Rollback restores all original inputs and the clean editor buffer. The window closes normally with no surviving processes, and the runtime payload and archive remain unchanged. Other functional interfaces, constructor references in other signature operations, broader overloads and platform coverage remain unqualified. Constructor delegation has separate qualification below.

The focused `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaConstructorDelegationNativeGui` and `javaConstructorDelegationVariantsNativeGui` profiles pass constructor parameter rename, addition, reordering, removal of an unused parameter and type change with the same isolated corrected RefactorKit candidate, selected JDK 21/release 17 and Linux release/no-bundle GUI. Each Maven fixture selects a package-private constructor in a public class and includes one `this(...)` call, one `super(...)` call from a same-file subclass, and an unrelated private boolean overload. The reviewed provider plan preserves both delegation bindings and the unrelated overload, and the changed delegation arguments are checked after Apply. A distinct fresh applied-source copy for every operation passes offline Maven `verify`, including tests for both delegation paths and the boolean overload. Exact Rollback restores all workspace inputs and the clean editor buffer. Both profiles close normally without surviving processes; the candidate runtime and archive remain unchanged. This qualifies these same-file delegation shapes only; cross-file and longer chains, public or protected constructor API changes, constructor call-site selection, varargs, other build layouts, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified. The combined `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaConstructorRefactoringAppImageNativeGui` profile passes on Linux x86-64 X11 with the local RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime, Maven 3.9.11 and JDK 21. It joins the direct-call and delegation cases for all five signature changes with the constructor-reference adaptation case. The native session checks offline Maven verification of each changed-source copy, exact rollback and clean exit.

The [Introduce Parameter Object scenario](features/refactorkit/native-java-sdk-refactoring.feature) passes on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland with the local RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime, Maven 3.9.11 and JDK 21. The person selects a saved private static method with two adjacent integer parameters and chooses a type name and both parameters in declaration order. The daemon creates a nested private static final class and updates the direct same-class call. Offline Maven verification on the applied-source copy runs a JUnit check that distinguishes the original and reversed argument orders. Rollback restores the original inputs and the clean editor buffer, and the application exits cleanly. Run `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaParameterObjectAppImageNativeGui` and add `--wayland` for Wayland. RefactorKit separately qualifies Java 8 and typed refusals for reversed or noncontiguous parameters. Other method and call-site shapes and Gradle require separate IDE verification.

The [Extract Delegate profile](features/refactorkit/native-java-sdk-refactoring.feature) passes on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland with JDK 21, Maven 3.9.16, Gradle 9.8.1 and a RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate. From a saved private method, the IDE first requests a group that omits a constant used by a selected helper. The provider identifies the missing dependency, Apply remains unavailable, and saved inputs are preserved. The corrected Gradle request reuses the evaluated context. The reviewed plan moves the helpers and constant into a private static nested type, and the original public method calls the delegate. An offline JUnit test from the applied-source copy verifies the original result in each build tool. Rollback restores the exact saved inputs and the open source buffer. The IDE closes without surviving processes. Run `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaExtractDelegateAppImageNativeGui` or add `--wayland` for KWin.

The focused `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaFunctionalReferencesNativeGui` profile passes in the Linux release/no-bundle application with selected JDK 21, project release 17 and the sealed RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate. It explicitly enables Add Parameter adaptation for one package-private static two-parameter method referenced by an `IntBinaryOperator`. The provider replaces the method reference with a two-argument lambda containing the new default argument and updates the ordinary direct call. The applied-source copy passes offline Maven `verify` with the same result, then exact Rollback restores the original method reference, method declaration and call. Source/build inputs are preserved, the window closes normally and no process survives cleanup. This qualifies that static-reference shape; other functional-interface/type shapes, receiver forms, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The [packaged reference migration profile](features/refactorkit/native-java-sdk-refactoring.feature) passes on the Linux x86-64 AppImage on X11 and KWin Wayland with JDK 21, Maven 3.9.16 and the RefactorKit candidate that advertises `thisMethodReferenceMigration`. The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:parameter-removal` profile passes one Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario with JDK 21 and the locally rebuilt RefactorKit 0.7.0 package. Other parameter-use and call-site shapes, released packages and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaGradleModuleRenameGroovyNativeGui` and `javaGradleModuleRenameKotlinNativeGui` profiles pass independently against an isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 upgrade in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with selected JDK 21 and Gradle 9.8.1. The fixtures retain one Groovy `include` with six literal project names and one Kotlin `include` with two literal project names. Explicit Gradle evaluation produces available, provider-qualified modules. Application-module rename first refuses Apply while a Java draft is unsaved; the saved settings and draft remain intact. After explicit discard and a fresh preview, managed Apply changes the logical project identity and adds its physical-directory mapping, preserves the source directory, and an independent copy passes offline Gradle tests under the renamed project. Managed Rollback restores the original settings bytes and other saved project inputs. Both profiles separately pass the referenced library's `java.renameGradleModule.inboundProjectDependencyUnsupported` refusal with Apply disabled, the unsaved draft preserved and saved inputs unchanged. Every scenario closes normally and runner cleanup finds no survivors. Earlier positive attempts against the preceding isolated candidate failed before Apply with `java.renameGradleModule.settingsIncludeUnsupported`; the successful runs use the same regression fixtures rather than narrowing their settings. Focused contract, module-picker, dialog, controller, App and native-boundary tests cover complete-capability admission, canonical paths and ambiguous settings/module identities. The upgrade changes only the Java JAR relative to the constructor candidate; the embedded runtime and C payload remain identical, and no default installation is replaced. The four Gradle cases also pass on the Linux x86-64 AppImage under X11 and KWin Wayland with RefactorKit 0.8.0 and JDK 21. Run `pnpm test:story:java-module-rename:appimage` or its `:wayland` variant to exercise Maven and both Gradle settings DSLs. The Maven case also passes on both backends with the corrected provider described under [Java Project Context](#68-java-project-context). For Gradle module rename, acceptance covers the tested literal settings and physical paths. SDK 26/27, conditional settings, arbitrary mappings, included builds and other operating systems remain open.

The focused Gradle inbound profile passes on the same Linux x86-64 AppImage and RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate under X11 and KWin Wayland, with Gradle 9.8.1 and JDK 21. It exercises a two-module Java build with a literal project dependency in Groovy and Kotlin DSL, plus refusal of a computed Groovy dependency. The managed cases require an advertised capability, a diff of the consumer build script, exact replacement of the project path, offline compilation, execution of compiled Java code and byte-exact rollback. The Maven module rename with pre-existing output directories also passes on both backends with this same application and provider. Run `pnpm test:story:java-gradle-module-rename-inbound:appimage` or its `:wayland` variant. The application profile passes on X11 and KWin Wayland with the extended RefactorKit 0.8.0 candidate, Gradle 9.8.1 and JDK 21. It covers the original Groovy and Kotlin fixtures with the application plugin, JUnit and additional build statements and dependencies. The reviewed change updates the selected project reference, preserves the physical paths and all other dependency declarations, and passes offline `:app:test` and `:app:run` on a copy. The original scripts and saved sources are restored byte for byte. The two application fixtures also pass with the later AppImage that coordinates saved-file recovery with JDT LS. Run `pnpm test:story:java-gradle-application-module-rename:appimage` or its `:wayland` variant.

The focused `node scripts/run-native-desktop-story.mjs --profile javaFieldTypeNativeGui` profile passes in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with selected JDK 21/release 17 and the isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate. The positive Maven case invokes Change Field Type from Commands on a private mutable `int` field. RefactorKit returns an attested field selection and a managed preview; Apply changes only that declaration to `long`, retaining a same-named local and another field. A distinct fresh applied-source copy passes offline Maven `verify`, including its JUnit result assertion, and exact Rollback restores all original inputs and the clean editor buffer. The negative editor-menu case selects the otherwise equivalent public field: the provider returns `java.typeRepair.fieldNotPrivate`, the IDE explains the refusal, withholds Apply and preserves saved inputs and the clean buffer. Both windows close normally without process survivors; the runtime payload and archive remain unchanged. Focused contract, cursor-action, dialog, adapter, controller and native-boundary tests cover the new intent and field identity requirements. This qualifies these fixtures only; broader provider, build-layout, field-type, recovery and platform coverage remains open. The companion `node scripts/run-native-appimage-java-story.mjs --profile javaFieldTypeAppImageNativeGui --wayland` profile passes both cases on the Linux x86-64 AppImage with the local RefactorKit 0.8.0 runtime, Maven 3.9.11 and JDK 21. Both native windows close without surviving owned processes.

The focused `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-sdk-refactoring-native-001:make-public` profile passes three scenarios in the Linux release/no-bundle GUI with JDK 21 and a source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 package. The IDE selects a final private method and a private non-final method in a final class through the provider's mutation-selection query, reviews and applies each `changeVisibility` preview, passes offline Maven `verify` on separate applied-source copies, and rolls back each operation. A third scenario selects a private non-final method in an extensible class; RefactorKit explains the unproven external override risk, Apply remains disabled, and the source and project file manifest remain unchanged. All three scenarios exit cleanly. RefactorKit daemon regression tests also verify stable/compiler/managed-stable capability reporting, exact preview/apply/rollback with method binding restored, and the same fail-closed refusal without source or transaction mutation. This qualifies these two supported method shapes and the refusal boundary on the tested Linux/JDK 21 source-built provider route; inherited or overridden methods, other method shapes, released packages, installers, and other operating systems remain unqualified.

The manual HTTP client has production-boundary verification: Rust tests validate requests and limits and exercise real loopback request/response plus response truncation; adapter and feature tests cover response correlation, explicit submission, stale-generation rejection, visible transport failures, no-workspace gating and draft clearing on workspace change. Focused parser tests cover bounded OpenAPI JSON/YAML parsing, server variables, local path/request-body/example reference chains, URI-fragment and JSON Pointer escapes, cycles, inherited-key rejection and reference/output limits. A shared JSON body is imported across two hundred operations without repeated serialization; oversized individual expansions and aggregate distinct YAML-expanded examples refuse. Controller tests reject captured imports and sends after workspace activation changes or unmount before any network call. These tests qualify their parser/controller scope, not native GUI or remote-reference compatibility. Its Linux release/no-bundle GUI stories send a manual JSON POST and load an OpenAPI JSON operation against an isolated local service. They confirm that opening the client, loading the document and selecting the operation do not send a request, that the displayed `201` response follows **Send**, that the workspace snapshot stays unchanged, and that the IDE and service close cleanly without surviving sandbox processes. The current OpenAPI 3.1 GUI case first refuses a missing local path reference without sending or filling the request, then imports a real user-selected local JSON file and resolves its path item, request body and JSON example from components in that document. Only explicit Send delivers the expected method, URL, content type and exact JSON body to the local service. The current Linux release/no-bundle profile passes after local file loading and its composition-start guard were added. WebDriver selects actual filesystem files through the native WebView file input: oversized and invalid UTF-8 files leave the existing specification unchanged, and a valid file populates it exactly without sending a request. The operating-system file-picker dialog is not driven by this check. Real FileReader component tests cover YAML/BOM input and cancellation during ordinary edits and composition start; controlled file-reader tests additionally reject late events after a new selection, workspace activation change or teardown. Native IME behavior, cancellation of a stalled host filesystem read, other reference shapes and output-limit refusals, packages and other operating systems remain outside this file-import GUI scope. A further Linux GUI scenario explicitly saves a templated request and named environment, closes the IDE process, opens a new IDE process against the same private configuration, restores both definitions and sends one resolved request. The local service observes the expanded URL, header and body only after **Send**; saving, restarting and selecting definitions send nothing. Stored request templates remain unexpanded, and receiving the response leaves the collection file unchanged. Source-tree snapshots are unchanged by the HTTP actions except for the explicitly selected new collection export file. Across restart, the fixture permits only the workspace registration marker’s lifecycle timestamp to refresh while checking its other fields and the rest of the workspace. Opening collections in the compact bottom panel also exercises scrolling, adding headers and editing the body without overlapping controls. The same native collection scenario exports JSON equal to the saved library, loads an actual UTF-8 JSON file through the native WebView file input without changing storage or sending traffic, keeps matching saved entries while adding a request and environment, and verifies the additions after process restart. Actual oversized and invalid UTF-8 files are refused while retaining the import text. The OS file-picker dialog is not driven. Real FileReader feature tests cover BOM input, repeated selection and cancellation during manual edits, composition start, explicit cancellation and workspace changes; the shared bounded reader also retains the OpenAPI read-limit, stale-callback, disable and teardown checks. Native IME behavior, stalled filesystem-read cancellation, installers and other operating systems remain outside the file-import qualification; export limitations are described in section 6.9. Parser and feature tests separately cover keep/replace collision policies, literal template round trips, invalid versions and duplicate names, input and merged-library bounds, stale review revisions, workspace retirement and native save refusal without a success claim. Replacing collisions is feature-tested; the native scenario qualifies the default keep policy. The native scenario also exports the saved library to a new workspace JSON file, compares its contents with private collection storage, checks owner-only Unix permissions, refuses an existing destination without changing it, and verifies that every other workspace file is retained. Rust tests cover stale collection revisions, invalid and escaping paths, missing parents, create-only publication and temporary-file cleanup. Adapter and feature tests cover response correlation, explicit export, provider failure and workspace retirement. A controller regression also refuses callbacks retained from a replaced adapter and ignores its delayed export failure; that provider-replacement interleaving is verified in process, separately from the GUI. Storage tests cover physical persistence, separate workspaces, stale data and activation revisions, lock contention, explicit release while a forked child retains the descriptor, malformed and oversized files, private permissions, and Unix symlink/hard-link refusal. Controller tests discard delayed reads and saves after workspace/generation changes; variable tests cover literal single-pass expansion, missing values, JSON braces and bounded amplification. A separate Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario qualifies HTTP-file submission against a real loopback server: a POST with explicit HTTP/1.1 uses an unsaved file-variable edit, selection is retired after editing, script execution is refused, the response retains file attribution, and the saved source and workspace remain unchanged after explicit buffer discard and normal closure. Parser and feature tests additionally cover CRLF body preservation, duplicate headers, XML bodies, file-variable dependencies and environment precedence, expansion limits, malformed requests, unavailable protocol support and live-editor checks before submission. Native `.rest` selection, environment overrides in request files, remote TLS, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. This qualifies the tested local HTTP, basic route-selection and local collection-restart flows on Linux; remote HTTPS/TLS, authentication lifecycle, native transfer between different workspaces, outside-workspace export and third-party interchange, encrypted credential storage, broad OpenAPI compatibility, browser support, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.

Native-selected HTTP collection export has production filesystem, adapter and controller coverage for external UTF-8 destinations, create-only publication, existing files and links, stale library revisions, duplicate export attempts, cancellation and retired workspace/port replies. A renderer-supplied destination is rejected by the native command request decoder. The Linux X11/Tauri/WebKit release/no-bundle HTTP profile also passes the actual GTK save-dialog flow: native keyboard input cancels the first chooser, creates a new JSON file with spaces and an accented filename outside the workspace, then selects the existing destination and observes the backend refuse replacement. The exported bytes match the saved library, permissions are owner-only, the request draft and saved library remain unchanged, and no HTTP request is sent by export. The surrounding collection workflow still restores templates after restart and sends only after explicit submission. Windows, macOS, installers, filesystem publication failures and forced workspace changes while the native chooser is open remain unqualified; retired renderer lifetimes have controller coverage, and native workspace checks are implemented before and after destination selection.

Declared OpenAPI parameters have production-helper verification against the published scalar, array and flat-object serialization examples, plus local-reference/override behavior, query separator protection, content-based values, scalar cookies, null example preservation, nesting/size limits and alias-expanded defaults. Component tests cover draft retention on refusal, preparation before Send, preparation after edits, authentication entered for the selected operation and retirement on specification or workspace changes. The Linux release/no-bundle HTTP GUI profile passes with a locally referenced Path Item containing the required path parameter, referenced operation-level query/header definitions, an override of a path-level query definition, repeated form query values and a text/plain custom header. The local service receives the exact encoded Unicode/slash path and reserved query characters, the literal header and JSON body only after explicit Send. Missing required values and later parameter edits keep Send unavailable until preparation succeeds. Existing collection transfer, native Save As and manual authentication scenarios remain passing, with clean native closure and no owned process survivors. This qualifies the tested flow with simple path serialization, form query serialization and text/plain header content on Linux; the other serializer styles have in-process coverage. General schema validation, implicit schema example generation, server-specific delimiter escape conventions, remote references, security schemes, broad cookie behavior, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.



The Java database port, Tauri adapter, controller and panel have focused tests for workspace/request correlation, explicit trust and SQL submission, schema refresh, results and credential clearing on workspace change. Parameter tests cover exact ordered values, explicit execution, NULL editing and disconnect cleanup. A production Rust-to-JDK bridge regression passes with H2 2.4.240 on JDK 21 and 25 for all nine parameter types, including the maximum signed 64-bit integer, a 38-digit decimal, fractional temporal values, binary data and NULL. A value containing a quote and SQL-like text remains literal data. Quoted and commented question marks are interpreted by the driver. Missing/excess parameters and invalid decimal/date values refuse execution without inserting rows, and later ordinary queries still succeed. Controlled worker regressions cover a full stdin pipe and output overflow. The private bridge compiles and runs against H2 2.4.240 on the available JDK: a file-backed database accepted table creation and insertion, returned a selected row, and exposed table/column metadata. The focused native Linux release/no-bundle scenario exercises the same production Rust command and desktop UI. It confirms that no H2 database file exists before **Connect**, then verifies an empty schema, explicit table creation and insertion, schema refresh, the selected `Ada` row, unchanged workspace contents, clean window close and zero surviving sandbox processes. A separate native scenario uses bound parameters to insert and select SQL-like text, return the exact 64-bit integer, refuse a mismatched parameter count, preserve the inputs and recover with a valid query. The table remains available with the expected row count. The SQL text retains its placeholders. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-database-001:native` with `IDE_STORY_JAVA_DATABASE_DRIVER_PATH` set to an absolute H2 driver JAR path. Persistent-session bridge tests pass with H2 2.4.240 on JDK 21 and 25: an in-memory database survives multiple calls on the same connection, rollback removes pending rows, commit survives reconnection, explicit close rolls back later pending work, and modifying the original workspace JAR does not alter the captured driver. A controlled worker that returns a response before reading a full input pipe still reaches its deadline and is terminated. Request deserialization and frontend tests cover transaction ownership, unavailable sessions, confirmed outcomes, cleanup without implicit rollback, same-workspace generation recovery, and refusing workspace transitions before editor/reset or native activation calls. A Linux native GUI scenario confirms manual mode, visibility of pending data on the same connection, session and SQL retention across Terminal/Database changes, refusal of native window close, rollback, commit, explicit rollback/disconnect, and only committed data after reconnect. The same GUI scenario refuses a workspace switch while manual work is pending, verifies that the original session still answers queries, and accepts a clean switch after reconnecting in auto-commit mode; the connection and credentials are cleared in the destination. A separate real bridge test on JDK 21 and 25 stops an executing H2 Java alias after the alias writes its worker PID, confirms the process has exited, and reopens the database to observe the committed row without the pending row. It also stops a controlled compiler during connection startup, refuses a startup whose stop request arrived first, and rejects stop requests for another workspace or session. This tests the production session owner directly; native GUI startup cancellation is not inferred from the controlled compiler test. The native query-stop scenario verifies the driver has entered its blocking operation before clicking Stop, confirms worker exit and the unknown-outcome message, retains the exact SQL/parameter draft, and reconnects explicitly. Ordinary shutdown behavior and the configured H2 DML results are qualified; durability under forced process termination remains database-dependent. This qualifies the described H2 DML transaction flow on Linux, not implicit DDL rollback, other JDBC drivers or database servers, packaged applications or other operating systems.

Captured-result export has production encoder, create-only publication, adapter and component tests for exact strings and NULL, duplicate labels, CSV quoting and optional prefixes, partial-result acknowledgment, output limits, cancellation, mismatched replies, and delayed replies after result/workspace/port retirement. Filesystem tests refuse existing files, symbolic and hard links and concurrent creators. On Linux X11 with the release/no-bundle desktop, H2 2.4.240 and selected JDK 21, the database native profile passes its connection, prepared-query, transaction, cancellation and schema-suggestion scenarios. It also verifies native Save As cancellation, a new Unicode CSV filename, exact prefixed CSV bytes, refusal of an existing destination and JSON arrays retaining duplicate labels, Unicode, an integer beyond JavaScript's exact numeric range, NULL and empty strings. The query/result identity remains unchanged during export; workspace contents are preserved, ordinary close succeeds and no owned processes survive. Production bridge tests on JDK 21 verify Unicode values through ordinary prepared execution and a persistent session with an explicit UTF-8 output writer. Truncation acknowledgment, captured-result retirement and delayed renderer replies have controlled-test coverage. Native dialog interleavings during a new query or workspace activation, other drivers, browser export, installed packages and other operating systems remain unqualified. The HTTP native profile also passes its existing collection Save As workflow with the shared X11 chooser helper.

Driver-quoted schema insertion has focused production-helper, panel and adapter tests for delimiter escaping, catalog filtering, metadata limits, exact UTF-16 selection replacement, UTF-8 submission bounds, stale-view refusal, keyboard acceptance and insertion without execution. The native bridge reads quoting and current catalog from JDBC, and a real H2/JDK 21 session test verifies those fields while retaining its driver-pinning and transaction checks. The Linux release/no-bundle H2 GUI profile passes five scenarios: the connection/query, typed-parameter, manual-transaction/workspace-switch and Stop cases remain passing, and the new schema-selection case composes a query using a table name with spaces and embedded quotes plus a reserved-word column. Button and Ctrl+Space entry, keyboard selection, driver-quoted insertion, unchanged query-result identity before explicit Run, the returned row and Cancel preserving SQL all pass. The destination workspace immediately hides the prior connection's schema and results; production controller tests also inspect intermediate render frames and preserve same-workspace drafts while native generation recovery is pending. Every scenario closes normally, preserves workspace files and leaves no owned processes after cleanup. This qualifies H2 2.4.240 with selected JDK 21 on the controlled Linux host. Backtick/bracket formatting has unit coverage only; other databases, semantic SQL assistance, large-schema performance, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified.


The focused `java26ScaffoldNativeGui` profile passes one Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario. Run `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:scaffold-java26`; it creates Maven and Gradle Groovy DSL starters targeting release 26, verifies their pinned wrapper distributions, generated source/test files and project-tree refresh, and confirms that no Maven `target` or Gradle `build`/`.gradle` output is created. This scenario does not synchronize or compile the projects. The separate `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:unsupported-release-context` profile uses a release/no-bundle Linux GUI and the installed RefactorKit daemon to attempt Maven synchronization for Java 26 and 27 reactors. For both releases, the provider reports that they are outside its supported Java 8–25 range; the IDE presents no available context, preserves all Maven inputs and creates no build output. The separate `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:scaffold-java26-build` profile passes a Linux release/no-bundle native GUI scenario on the controlled host. It confirms that the new projects have no outputs immediately after creation, then explicitly runs offline Maven 3.10.0 and Gradle 9.6.1 with Temurin JDK 26.0.2.1; each generated JUnit test passes, both applications print their greeting, and both class files have Java 26 major version 70. The native window closes and the runner reports no surviving sandbox processes. This qualifies these generated starter shapes with installed tools and populated local caches, not generated-wrapper first use, RefactorKit synchronization or another host. Current Java 26 project-context admission requires v6 or v7. The `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:java26-maven-context` and `pnpm test:story:req-ide-java-project-context-native-001:java26-gradle-context` profiles both pass on Linux release/no-bundle with the isolated SDK-27-API candidate, Temurin JDK 26.0.2.1, release 26 and qualified v7 analysis; Gradle 9.8.1 runs separately on JDK 21. They verify rename refusal before processor output exists, context retirement and explicit reacquisition, Build with annotation-processor output and Java 26 bytecode, cursor Apply/Undo, and saved-source Apply with independent build/test and Rollback. Original inputs are restored, native closure is normal and no owned processes survive. This qualifies the ordinary six-module reference shapes, not full Java 26 syntax, packaging or another operating system. An earlier candidate refused Maven source/target 26 in v7 with `java.platform.compilerApiUnqualified` and could return unqualified v6 metadata. The isolated RefactorKit 0.8.0 review candidate now returns qualified v7 context and JDK 26 compiler diagnostics in direct daemon checks for both Maven release 26 and source/target 26. The managed rename workflows use release 26. Standalone scaffold/build qualification above remains independent of provider context.

The negative check against isolated RefactorKit r004 is verified on both six-module fixtures: `refactor.editor.preview` refuses a rename while `generated.GeneratedGreeting` is absent, leaving Apply disabled and sources unchanged. A preserved Maven fixture and an independent provider probe establish five compiler errors, all caused by the missing generated type or its imports in the main and test source. V2 and v7 return the same errors; changing context schema does not repair missing compiler inputs. The panel labels the legacy analysis counter as diagnostics, because the provider's `warningCount` field can include compiler errors and does not provide their severity distribution. The refusal is therefore legitimate, rather than evidence that SDK 26 itself is unsupported. Build tools own processor execution; project discovery and read-only synchronization do not generate a replacement source. If the provider cannot produce an editor preview, the IDE asks the person to check compilation diagnostics and the selected project context; it does not infer that unopened source files caused the failure. A correlated native refusal that explicitly reports a retired session also retires the displayed context and asks for synchronization. Adapter tests reject retirement metadata for another workspace, request or document, and controller tests preserve a newer selected context when an older preview fails. The focused Maven Java 26 Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario also passes the recovery notice check: the old effective/partial context is no longer displayed before explicit resynchronization, after which Build, cursor Apply/Undo and saved-source Apply/build-copy/Rollback complete. This qualifies the tested Maven route; the Gradle positive workflow still requires the corrected provider candidate. The provider's separately passing packaged-daemon gate covers bounded saved-source v7 binding/navigation, diagnostics and managed rename for Maven and Gradle. The tested candidates remain separate from the installed provider; broader regressions and distribution qualification remain open. Gradle's explicit Build now succeeds and produces the real generated source, but its subsequent editor preview is refused by the IDE's strict context check. The IDE forwards the acquired context schema through editor preview and transaction requests; a real native-service regression with a qualified Gradle v7 context still receives v2 in the successful preview. RefactorKit has confirmed that its editor response hardcodes v2 instead of projecting the requested context schema. The consumer retains exact schema comparison. The isolated r005 package corrects the projection and passes six packaged-daemon cases across Maven/Gradle v2, v3 and v7. The real native Gradle service regression also passes with selected JDK 26 and project release 17: it verifies v7 definition and editor preview through the production TypeScript decoder, durable editor transformations with Apply/Undo, saved-source formatting and rename with Apply/Rollback, and refusal of stale build inputs and lost sessions without implicit build-script evaluation. Its negative cases acquire current context and use the actual document images and versions returned by Undo, so obsolete test inputs cannot substitute for the intended refusal. The focused Gradle Java 26 profile also passes on Linux release/no-bundle with r005, Gradle 9.8.1 running on JDK 21, and project JDK 26: it verifies the pre-build semantic refusal, displayed-context retirement and explicit recovery, real annotation-processor output and class-file major version 70, cursor rename Apply/Undo, saved rename Apply, offline Gradle tests on a source copy and exact Rollback. The successful editor previews attest v3; the service test separately qualifies v7. Original inputs are restored, the window closes normally, no owned processes remain, and the package files stay unchanged. The same r005 package also passes the focused Maven Java 26 GUI workflow with v2 editor previews, including context recovery, both rename modes, offline Maven verification and exact source restoration. ### 10.2 Repeatable M0 Regression and Required Production Gates

`pnpm verify:m0` runs documentation, boundaries, BDD types, lint, unit/spec/scaffolding tests, locked Rust library tests and the web build sequentially. `pnpm verify:m0:native` separately runs 20 fresh release/no-bundle Linux GUI profiles for opening, slow-provider startup, restart recovery, close guards, plain-JDK execution, Java 26 preview-language editing, Maven/Gradle/JUnit and multi-module Failsafe execution, jdb controls, structured JDI inspection and unresponsive-debugger Stop, conditional/logpoint breakpoints, independent test JVM configuration, compiled JUnit and TestNG discovery/selection, comparison, history, recovery failures, per-buffer capacity/truncated journals, real bounded-filesystem ENOSPC and passive external changes. `pnpm verify:m0:all` combines them. Inspect the fixed plan without running checks using `node scripts/run-m0-regression.mjs --suite all --plan`.

The core gate passes on the controlled Linux source checkout, including the current local Git workflows described in [section 6.13](#613-local-git-source-control). The Rust library run leaves explicitly ignored tests unexecuted. Native GUI qualification remains scoped per workflow in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope); opt-in real-tool tests retain their separate admission and are not enabled by the core gate.

The scaffolding checks discover unchanged repository profiles together through [Cucumber’s programmatic dry-run API](https://github.com/cucumber/cucumber-js/blob/main/docs/javascript_api.md) in one isolated worker per test process. Each profile retains its own configured source, tag and authored-step selection. Profiles with the same explicitly configured support paths can share the loaded definitions when their feature selections differ. Implicit support paths are tied to the selected feature directories. Profiles whose support differs from the loaded definitions use a fresh CLI discovery. The frozen selections serve repeated scenario-count, tag and binding assertions within the existing five-minute scaffolding deadline. A real-Cucumber regression compares batched results with fresh CLI results for tags, scenario outlines and changed source coordinates, verifies that hooks and step bodies do not run, and refuses missing bindings. Actual native runner invocations continue to use fresh CLI discovery. The base Java project-context profile excludes the dedicated Git branch and rebase scenarios; those remain selected by their focused Maven and Gradle profiles.

For a separate bounded startup investigation, run `pnpm probe:startup:native --attempts 10`, optionally adding `--profile editorExternalChangesNativeGui`. The [diagnostic runner](scripts/probe-native-startup.mjs) admits only these two real GUI profiles and one to twenty-four sequential attempts, builds once per invocation, stops on the first failed attempt and records remaining attempts as unrun. Private `test-results/native-startup-probe/run-*/result.json` reports identify executable reuse and individual native artifact directories. The ordinary fifteen-second explorer and ninety-second runtime deadlines, native ownership and cleanup remain unchanged. This opt-in diagnostic is outside the fixed M0 regression plan and does not establish hosted CI or qualify reliability. Its latest Linux release/no-bundle run completed all configured desktop-file-open attempts against one fresh executable; every selected scenario passed, and all startup snapshots showed the Tauri origin, committed React root and native bridge. This bounded sample does not explain the earlier timeouts. Inspection of retained observations distinguishes two later failures from an initial bootstrap timeout: one had Java Project selected with File Explorer absent; another raised a WebDriver stale-element error during a workspace transition despite a committed React root, native bridge and visible tree. The native helper now queries a fresh tree node on every readiness poll and treats a stale lookup or display check as not ready within the original fifteen-second deadline. Focused helper tests cover replacement, hidden nodes and error propagation, and the Java source-file creation profile passes its workspace transitions, generated-type compilation and normal close with this helper. This corrects the observed acceptance-helper race; it does not change application startup behavior or explain every earlier failure.

The runner captures actual child exit codes, signals, deadlines and cancellation, stops on the first failure, and records unrun checks rather than declaring them successful. The native desktop and Java AppImage entry points route interrupt and termination signals through the same cancellation path. A Linux AppImage replay interrupted with SIGTERM verifies that cancellation stops the owned process group and that the sandbox scan reports no survivors. Private run directories under `test-results/m0-regression/` hold per-check logs and `result.json`. Commands have individual deadlines and the whole run has a 90-minute cancellation deadline; native profiles retain their own bounded process ownership and cleanup. Native driver fixtures create isolated Unix process groups and stop their descendants even if the parent has already exited, so inherited output pipes cannot keep the acceptance command alive. A real-process regression verifies this cleanup while leaving a separate process group running. Lint currently allows its existing warnings; coverage thresholds and opt-in real-provider tests are not silently added by this command. Ignored Rust tests remain ignored. Logs can contain source paths or fixture output and must be treated as private test artifacts, not public telemetry.

The storage-full profile requires Linux Bubblewrap with permission to create private mount namespaces. It is included in the native M0 plan, whose full twenty-profile sequence passes on the controlled Linux host.

A clean host needs the repository's Node/pnpm dependencies, Rust and native Tauri build prerequisites. The Linux GUI suite additionally needs real Tauri/WebKit drivers, Xvfb, D-Bus, Python GTK 3 introspection for clipboard acceptance, Python's standard XML parser for JUnit evidence, Python `fcntl` for debugger pipe inspection and a filesystem/kernel supporting Linux source file leases for the close race, a full JDK 21 including its JDI module for Java fixtures, a full JDK 26 for the Java 26 scaffold build, preview-language and project-context profiles, and a full JDK 27 plus Gradle 9.8.1, a separate JDK 21 Gradle runtime, populated Maven/Gradle caches and the isolated source-built RefactorKit candidate for the Java 27 project-context profile. Set the relevant profile environment variables to select those tool installations and populated caches; Java project-context GUI profiles require `IDE_JAVA_CONTEXT_TRACE=1` for the synchronization evidence checks. The Java 26 preview-language profile also needs `IDE_JAVA_26_HOME` and `IDE_JDTLS_HOME` set for Eclipse JDT LS 1.62; the Java 27 preview-language profile needs `IDE_JAVA_27_HOME` and `IDE_JDTLS_HOME`; compatible installed Maven/Gradle with dependency access or populated caches are needed for the build-tool cases. Set `IDE_JAVA_HOME` and `JAVA_HOME` to the selected runtime when necessary. The startup responsiveness profile also requires an installed RefactorKit CLI and `IDE_REAL_REFACTORKIT_CLI` as described in section 10.1. Each native profile builds a fresh executable; this is not installer qualification. The current `pnpm verify:m0` core gate and the complete twenty-profile `pnpm verify:m0:native` sequence pass on the controlled Linux host. The native phase covers 38 expanded scenarios and 622 runtime steps including lifecycle hooks, with a fresh release/no-bundle build for each profile. It uses the selected JDK 21, JDK 26 for the preview-language fixture, Maven 3.9.11, Gradle 9.8.1, JDT LS 1.63 and an explicitly selected isolated RefactorKit 0.7.0/API 0.2 candidate. Build and runtime metadata agree, source/configuration inputs remain unchanged throughout the sequence, and every profile's bounded cleanup reports no surviving owned processes. The candidate archive and payload remain unchanged, and the default RefactorKit installation is not replaced. The scope is the listed baseline fixtures; newer focused Java GUI qualifications remain separately scoped in section 10.1. These two commands were run separately; this does not claim an execution of `pnpm verify:m0:all`, hosted CI, an installer, another operating system or resolution of earlier intermittent startup failures. On the same host, the Tauri release binary and AppDir were built and appimagetool produced the configured x86_64 AppImage after the official Type 2 runtime was supplied locally. Its runtime-version query passed. The AppImage packaging GUI scenario passes 1 scenario and 16 steps, including native X11 window discovery, WM_DELETE close and a clean process scan. The packaged Java profile passes 2 scenarios and 41 steps with JDK 25 and Eclipse JDT LS 1.62. The intelligence scenario verifies diagnostics, hover, signature help, member and type completion with import edits, references, call hierarchy, definition navigation, preservation of unsaved drafts across a JDT LS restart, saved-source preservation, draft restoration and clean native close. The template scenario verifies standard-output, main-method and five additional Java templates, counted-loop tab stops, unchanged saved sources and clean native close. Other Java 27 project layouts and preview-language cases, installed-provider upgrade behavior, hosted CI, other Linux environments, Wayland and another operating system remain outside this scope. The other native regression results qualify this host's release/no-bundle profiles, not broader behavior than each requirement's separately documented scope.

The [GitHub Actions M0 workflow](.github/workflows/m0-core.yml) runs `pnpm verify:m0` on pushes, pull requests and manual dispatches using Ubuntu 24.04, Node.js 22, pnpm 11.9 and stable Rust. It installs the Linux Tauri build prerequisites and grants the job read-only repository access. This exercises the core documentation, boundary, type, lint, unit/spec/scaffolding, Rust-library and web-build checks; it does not run the 20 native GUI profiles, qualify other operating systems, or build an installer. The workflow source is configured, but hosted execution and repository branch protection have not been verified. Repository owners must confirm successful hosted runs and make the check required where appropriate. Native GUI CI, cross-platform coverage and packaging remain separate work. Per-check M0 logs can contain source paths or fixture output; the workflow does not upload them, so hosted artifact access and retention are not configured.

Before general release, require automated build/test/boundary checks, a native-GUI and OS matrix, dependency/license review, packaging/update validation, accessibility checks, and large-project performance budgets. Existing coverage reporting has no mandatory thresholds. A passing narrow test suite is not a production-readiness verdict.

## Section 11: Risks and Technical Debt

- A Ready JDT LS session and working hover do not establish diagnostics for an unsupported older preview level. The Java 26 preview incompatibility and required explicit backend selection are scoped in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope); the per-document compiler check marks incompatible diagnostics as unavailable rather than treating an empty result as success. Checks of unopened projects and broader import combinations remain unqualified.


General PTY execution and process ownership currently require Linux. Terminal transcripts are bounded and may omit old output; interface reload closes previous general shell sessions. Deliberately detached OS sessions, abnormal application death and other operating systems need separate implementation or qualification. Java debugger attachment and measured coverage have separate execution lifecycles. Automatic compile/reload coordination and effective multi-module Java integration remain incomplete. The installed RefactorKit daemon passes the tested ordinary two-module project-context/query paths, while the non-fatal error-recovery path is qualified only with the source-built daemon. Cancellation latency and packaged error-recovery behavior remain unqualified (see section 6.6).

- General native workspace activation reliability remains unqualified. Section 10.1 distinguishes the controlled slow-provider startup dependency, the AppImage UI chunk failure and post-activation test failures. Earlier failures without bootstrap evidence remain unexplained. Some other native provider operations still perform synchronous work, and CLI descendant pipe/process cleanup needs broader qualification; background probing alone does not bound every stalled task.
- Rich Maven/Gradle import, SDK selection, generated roots, dependency views, and multi-module synchronization remain incomplete. Gradle supports selected-source-set Build/Run/Debug and maps custom Test execution, discovery and coverage by compiled class directories; when tasks share outputs, the candidate must use the selected source set's configured runtime classpath, whose resolved paths are checked before execution. Other ambiguous mappings are refused. GUI qualification covers Build, Run, discovery, test execution, coverage and a JDI breakpoint for one custom `integrationTest` source set with a same-output decoy task, while other task mappings, layouts and broader discovery configurations remain unqualified. The IDE consumes typed Maven `custom` and `integration-test` source sets; for the latter, it requests context v4–v7 according to advertised provider support and maps only one complete, unambiguous Failsafe execution to `verify`, collecting fresh reports from its declared directory. Local unit tests cover v4 and v7 consumer behavior; native GUI evidence for synchronized Maven Failsafe is described in section 10.1. Other operations and arbitrary Maven `custom` source sets remain refused; additional project layouts and broad compiler/dependency accuracy remain unqualified.
- RefactorKit-backed type and direct-call hierarchy are available with the workspace-source and partial call-graph limits described in section 5.2. Framework intelligence, broader inspections and code generation, broader test discovery, coverage-source association outside complete synchronized contexts with one open, unchanged, provider-declared main source, and advanced debugger workflows remain below IntelliJ-class expectations. Multi-open-document quick fixes, edit-only quick assists, and standard refactor code actions that return text edits for synchronized documents are implemented and unit-tested. Focused Linux native GUI profiles qualify a real JDT LS method-creation quick fix across two open drafts and the import, formatting, inlay-hint and generator actions listed in section 10.1; a release/no-bundle profile also verifies the try/catch quick assist with JDT LS 1.62 and JDK 25. Broader action catalogs, project layouts, installers and other operating systems remain unqualified. Import organization, whole-document formatting and selected-line formatting still apply to the active synchronized Java document. The desktop can apply an existing workspace-contained Eclipse formatter XML profile through a filtered native file picker; the Linux GUI scenario verifies selection, JDT LS restart, unsaved-draft preservation and the configured next-line type-brace style. The formatter-profile GUI scenario also opens the XML through Settings, edits and saves the brace setting, restarts JDT LS, verifies the changed style on the unsaved Java buffer and restores the fixture XML before clean exit. This qualifies Linux release/no-bundle behavior with JDK 25 and JDT LS 1.62; packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified.
- Java debugging requires Unix process ownership. Manual configuration needs explicit runtime libraries; synchronized project launch obtains its runtime classpath from RefactorKit. Named-module Run/Debug is implemented for the synchronized main source set when RefactorKit returns provider-qualified v5 JPMS facts: the IDE checks that one module descriptor is current and contained by the selected module, then builds the module path from provider entries and the unique compiled module output and launches with `--module-path` and `-m`. Partial, stale, or ambiguous JPMS metadata is refused. Focused Rust tests cover the metadata gate, and production-boundary tests run a modular fixture and debug a named module through structured JDI with a full local JDK; the Run fixture is also verified with Oracle GraalVM JDK 25. A focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI story against source-built RefactorKit 0.7.0 now qualifies Gradle v5 named-module Run and structured JDI Debug on Oracle GraalVM JDK 25: it verifies the dependency module and literal arguments including a spaced and empty value, suspends before application code, continues to exit 0, and re-synchronizes JPMS context after Gradle creates outputs. The bounded Maven JDK 21 GUI qualification is described in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope). Broader Maven and Gradle shapes, packaged applications and other operating systems remain unqualified. Plain-JDK jdb controls and structured JDI inspection, source-margin breakpoints, selected-frame lines, conditional/matching-hit controls, bounded logpoints, caught/uncaught exception breakpoints, one-time bounded read-only expression evaluation and Pause/Stop have focused Linux GUI acceptance, including nonreading debugger input. Saved source choices and guarded startup loading are implemented; their qualification is described in section 10.1. Focused synchronized main-source JDI has native-library verification, and one Maven and one Gradle project GUI scenario verify saved source breakpoints and effective runtime dependencies. Both project-debugger GUI scenarios select the provider-suggested output for `pkg.Runner`, confirm HotSwap while suspended, and verify that the selected class file lies beneath a materialized workspace directory on the captured runtime classpath. Project context and runtime-output directories are revalidated before and after the sidecar build and before reload. This qualifies those checks for two reference project fixtures, not proof of the exact bytes loaded by the JVM or general source/output provenance. Arbitrary source provenance and broader project layouts remain unqualified. Socket attachment is implemented separately from launch. A focused Linux GUI scenario maps an external frame's runtime source path to one captured Java file under the configured manual project path and verifies a source-line breakpoint after the current editor and disk text pass the captured fingerprint check. This associates JDI source metadata with a local file; it does not verify that the external VM loaded bytecode built from that file. Missing or ambiguous mappings are refused, and remote hosts and other operating systems remain unqualified. Explicit compiled-class HotSwap, a build task beside an active JDI session and bounded discovery of prepared class names from the connected JVM are implemented. The class list can suggest a binary name and report class-loader ambiguity, but it does not prove which workspace file produced loaded bytecode or identify its compiled output. Build-time comparison can propose changed files for listed JVM classes as described in section 6.3; exhaustive discovery, automatic redefinition and binding loaded classes to verified local class-file artifacts remain incomplete. Full Java expression evaluation remains unavailable. The bounded evaluator supports decimal, octal, hexadecimal and binary integer literals, decimal and hexadecimal floating-point literals, and legal numeric underscore separators; numeric and boolean operators, lazy conditional `?:` expressions, explicit casts among primitive numeric types plus boolean identity casts, Java bitwise and shift operators, runtime `instanceof` checks for loaded reference types, reads from locals, object fields, initialized loaded-class static fields and array elements selected by literal or computed `int` indexes, string and character values/literals, string concatenation with primitive and unboxed wrapper values, Java unboxing conversion for captured bootstrap `Boolean`, `Character` and numeric wrappers in primitive contexts, [as specified by the JLS](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-5.html#jls-5.1.8), and selected java.lang.String operations (length, isEmpty, charAt, substring, indexOf, lastIndexOf, equality, and search/prefix/suffix checks). It reads the wrappers' primitive fields from captured JDI objects without invoking application code and preserves reference identity when comparing two wrappers; arbitrary method calls and application-object conversion remain unavailable. Real-JDI library tests cover selected String operations, bitwise/shift watch values, literal-index object/static-array paths, computed local `int` indexes into object-field and static arrays, primitive-cast result typing, and `instanceof` plus static-field reads in watches and conditional breakpoints; a separate Java oracle checks numeric-literal, computed-index and primitive-cast semantics. Native GUI acceptance covers String.length(), the bounded one-time results for numeric literals, a computed object-array index and a primitive byte cast, conditional and exception breakpoints, and String/character interpolation plus locally computed `String.indexOf` and `lastIndexOf` results in logpoints without invoking debuggee methods. Expanded wrapper-unboxing expression checks pass in production-boundary real-JDI tests with OpenJDK 21 and 25. The Linux release/no-bundle conditional-debugger GUI verifies unboxing of all eight standard wrapper classes in a matching-hit condition and logpoint on OpenJDK 21. The saved-logpoint reactivation scope is described in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope). Packaged and other-operating-system GUI behavior remains unqualified. Run with JFR, its selected-JDK event-type summary, bounded per-type timeline, selected event payload fields and sampled stack frames now have real-tool verification on JDK 21 and focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI acceptance; stack traces are limited to 32 frames, and installer and other operating-system qualification remain outstanding.
- Some RefactorKit paths decode bounded CLI output; typed, versioned result formats would reduce provider-version coupling. Live-engine refactoring qualification, including dependency-classpath cases, remains incomplete.
- Recovery/history is checkpoint-based, bounded and unencrypted. Configurable exclusions/retention, exhaustive source history, storage failures beyond the qualified bounded Linux source/recovery ENOSPC cases, workspace-wide pending-draft and retained-content GUI limits, additional corruption families, concurrent lifecycle paths, power loss and the OS matrix remain incomplete beyond the focused Linux restart/history/missing-source/storage-access/per-buffer-capacity/truncated-journal checks and the external-write-during-adoption GUI scenario. Native close/exit protection has focused Linux dirty-tab/workspace/X11-window and held-source-Save keyboard-edit acceptance; confirmation/preparation/reopen races, general unload/error paths and the wider OS matrix remain unqualified.
- Maven v7 Failsafe and annotation-processor qualification is scoped in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope). Other reactor modules can still have partial processor facts, so generated-root coverage is incomplete. The earlier command-level timeout remains unexplained despite a complete passing rerun with the unchanged deadline. For v7 Maven contexts, the IDE refuses test JVM options when execution is in-process, incomplete, ambiguous or redacted, or when a configured `argLine` would need replacement. Older context versions rely on fresh report-property confirmation after execution; broader composition preserving arbitrary project instrumentation remains M4 work.
- The native six-module Gradle test fixture passes on Gradle 9.8.1. On Gradle 9.6.1, the default JUnit task also reports the package-private `Unrelated` helper class as an invalid test; a disposable reproduction confirms that `--tests pkg.RunnerTest` passes on 9.6.1 and an unfiltered run passes on 9.8.1. This observed version-specific test-discovery difference remains delegated to Gradle and has not been worked around by changing the IDE's default task semantics.
- Maven Failsafe execution, selection, report collection, failed-test rerun and JaCoCo integration coverage have real-tool coverage. RefactorKit provider acceptance now covers v4 execution, selector and report metadata plus partial, ambiguous and inactive cases; a focused app/library reactor Story checks module-specific Build Helper roots, Failsafe selectors and report paths, and prevents one module's integration roots from entering the other module's classpath. The IDE requests v4 or v5, refuses incomplete or ambiguous facts, and uses the declared report directory in synchronized project execution; focused Rust/UI tests cover this path. Native Linux GUI qualification selects and executes distinct app and library Failsafe source sets, checks their individual roots and report directories, and confirms passing results with a v4-capable daemon. Nonstandard execution/report configurations, larger reactors, packaged applications, and other operating systems remain unqualified.
- Java Run has focused plain-JDK and one-module Maven/Gradle/JUnit 4 Linux GUI acceptance, plus one JUnit Jupiter and one TestNG module test through each synchronized build tool, one synchronized JUnit 4/Vintage and Jupiter module suite through each build tool, standalone TestNG execution from saved configurations, JUnit 4/Jupiter and TestNG discovery/selection GUI and real-tool checks, and plain-JDK jdb/JDI acceptance including one-shot Run to Cursor. A focused Linux release/no-bundle GUI scenario using JDK 25 and TestNG 7.10.2 verifies workspace-trust gating, a plain-JDK suite with one pass and one failure, fresh JUnit XML, rerun of the repaired failed method, discovery without test-body execution, captured method execution after current settings change, confined dependencies and reports, and clean native close; installers, other operating systems and broader framework configurations remain unqualified. Synchronized Maven and Gradle module Run and focused Maven and Gradle module-debugger GUI scenarios have the scope described in section 10.1. Other mixed-engine combinations and broader framework-specific configurations remain pending. Starter wrapper generation and first-use downloads are qualified with pinned Maven and Gradle distributions on Linux (see section 10.1). Packaged applications, other operating systems, advanced debugging, hosted-run verification, required branch protection and signed updates remain open.
- The desktop HTTP/OpenAPI and JDBC tools remain bounded first slices. Manual requests, basic paste-based route selection and explicit JDBC queries have focused Linux native GUI acceptance; other products’ collection formats, encrypted credential storage, full OpenAPI support, broader OAuth provider interoperability and refresh flows, persistent credential/session management, semantic SQL assistance, migrations, Spring/JPA integration, browser support, packaging and other operating systems remain open.
- Local saved-file staging, unstaging, index review, authored commits and paginated HEAD history with commit review are implemented through the separate Git activity described in [section 6.13](#613-local-git-source-control). Local branch creation, renaming, reviewed deletion and switching are implemented; switching includes editor reconciliation. Saved-source blame is implemented with bounded pages and saved-version checks. Reviewed local merges, manual saved-source conflict resolution, explicit merge commits and acknowledged abort are implemented. Reviewed linear local rebase, continuation, skip and abort are implemented. All-reference history graphs and search, broader rebase/merge workflows and remote workflows remain roadmap work. Agent review retains its read-only behavior in [section 6.12](#612-read-only-git-review). Verification scope and platform limits are maintained in [section 10.1](#101-verification-scope).
- Broader enterprise tooling, a plugin runtime, full Git workflows, and remote/container tooling are roadmap work.

## Section 12: Glossary and References

- **Port:** provider-neutral interface used by application logic.
- **Adapter:** platform/tool implementation of a port.
- **Workspace generation:** version used to reject work from an older workspace context.
- **Language server / LSP:** process and Language Server Protocol used for editor document intelligence.
- **Semantic target:** declaration or reference resolved against language bindings, not merely matching text.
- **Snapshot / editor overlay:** a consistent source/project state, optionally including unsaved buffers without changing working-tree files.
- **Mutation authority:** the admitted provider operation's permission to produce applicable changes; preview-only output and user consent alone do not supply it.
- **CI / PTY:** continuous integration / pseudoterminal for an interactive process.
- **OAuth 2.0:** authorization framework for obtaining limited API access from an authorization server.
- **PKCE / S256:** Proof Key for Code Exchange and its SHA-256 challenge transformation, used to bind an authorization code to a native verifier.
- **JDBC:** Java Database Connectivity, the standard Java API for database connections, metadata and SQL execution.
- **JPA:** Jakarta Persistence API for object/relational persistence mapping.
- **PID / pidfd:** operating-system process identifier / [Linux process file descriptor](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pidfd_open.2.html) that pins a process for [signalling](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pidfd_send_signal.2.html).
- **JaCoCo:** Java Code Coverage; agent and build-tool reporting used to measure executed Java bytecode, branches and source lines.
- **JFR:** Java Flight Recorder, the JDK's low-overhead JVM event recording facility.
- **JVM / JDWP / JDI / jdb:** Java Virtual Machine, its debugging wire protocol, debugger API, and JDK command-line debugger.
- **DAP:** Debug Adapter Protocol connecting debugger tools to editor clients.
- **C4:** system-context, container, component, and code views of software architecture.
